domains/java/completablefuture.spoken:
CompletableFuture represents a computation that may not be done yet. You can start it, attach callbacks that run when it completes, chain multiple async operations together, and combine results from multiple concurrent operations — all without blocking threads.

SupplyAsync starts an asynchronous computation that returns a value. By default it uses the ForkJoin common pool, but you should pass a custom Executor for I/O-bound work to avoid blocking ForkJoin threads. ThenApply transforms the result like a map. ThenCompose is for when your transformation itself is asynchronous — like calling a service that returns a CompletableFuture.

The real power is combining multiple concurrent operations. AllOf lets you wait for multiple independent operations to complete — for example, fetching user data, orders, and preferences in parallel and combining all three once all are done. This is much faster than sequential calls.
domains/java/completablefuture.question: What is CompletableFuture and how do you use it for asynchronous programming in Java?
domains/java/completablefuture.title: CompletableFuture Basics

domains/java/modern-java-features.spoken:
Records are a concise way to declare immutable data classes. In a single line you declare the type and its fields, and Java generates the canonical constructor, accessor methods, equals, hashCode, and toString automatically. This eliminates the boilerplate that previously required either Lombok or many manual lines of code.

The best use cases are DTOs, API request and response models, value objects, and any data that you just want to hold and pass around without modification. A record with user ID, name, and email is a perfect fit — you create it once with all its data and pass it around.

The key limitation is immutability — you can't have mutable fields in a record, which is intentional. You also can't use a record as a JPA entity because JPA requires a no-argument constructor and mutable fields. Records also can't extend classes, though they can implement interfaces.
domains/java/modern-java-features.question: What are Java Records, when should you use them, and what are their limitations?
domains/java/modern-java-features.title: Java Records (Java 16+)

domains/java/streams-lambdas.spoken:
A lambda expression is an anonymous function that can be passed around as a value. Before Java 8, if you wanted to pass behavior to a method, you had to create an anonymous class, which was verbose. Lambdas are a shorter way to implement functional interfaces — interfaces with exactly one abstract method.

The four core functional interfaces from java.util.function cover most needs. Function takes an input and produces an output. Predicate takes an input and returns a boolean. Consumer takes an input and returns nothing — used for side effects. Supplier takes nothing and produces a value — used for lazy evaluation.

Method references are a cleaner syntax when your lambda just calls an existing method. Instead of x -> System.out.println(x), you write System.out::println. Instead of x -> x.toLowerCase(), you write String::toLowerCase. These are equivalent but more readable when the lambda body is a single method call.
domains/java/streams-lambdas.question: What are lambda expressions and functional interfaces in Java, and how do they work?
domains/java/streams-lambdas.title: Lambda Expressions and Functional Interfaces

domains/java/aws-core.spoken:
A Region is a geographic location — like Mumbai (ap-south-1) or Virginia (us-east-1) — that contains multiple Availability Zones. An Availability Zone is essentially one or more physically separate data centers within the region, with independent power, cooling, and networking. The physical separation means a failure in one AZ — a power outage, flood, or hardware failure — doesn't affect the others.

For backend architecture, AZs are the foundation of high availability. You deploy your application in at least two AZs behind a load balancer. If one AZ has a problem, the load balancer routes all traffic to instances in the healthy AZ. Your database runs in Multi-AZ mode, where the standby is in a different AZ and automatic failover happens in minutes.

Region choice matters for latency and compliance. If your users are in India, running in ap-south-1 Mumbai gives 10-20ms latency versus 200ms from us-east-1. If you're handling EU user data, GDPR may require you to run in eu-west or eu-central regions.
domains/java/aws-core.deep:
## AWS Global Structure

```
AWS Cloud
├── Region: us-east-1 (N. Virginia)
│   ├── AZ: us-east-1a (Data Center Cluster A)
│   ├── AZ: us-east-1b (Data Center Cluster B)
│   └── AZ: us-east-1c (Data Center Cluster C)
├── Region: ap-south-1 (Mumbai)
│   ├── AZ: ap-south-1a
│   ├── AZ: ap-south-1b
│   └── AZ: ap-south-1c
└── Region: eu-west-1 (Ireland)
    ├── AZ: eu-west-1a
    └── ...
```

## Multi-AZ Architecture (Java Backend)

```
                    Internet
                       │
               [Route 53 DNS]
                       │
            [Application Load Balancer]
                 /            \
    AZ-1a                         AZ-1b
    [EC2/ECS App Server]    [EC2/ECS App Server]
           │                        │
    [RDS Primary]  ←──────→  [RDS Standby]
    (AZ-1a)        sync repl   (AZ-1b)
```

## Key Regional vs Global Services

| Service | Scope |
|---------|-------|
| EC2, ECS, RDS | Regional (choose AZ) |
| S3 | Regional (globally accessible) |
| IAM | Global |
| Route 53 | Global |
| CloudFront | Global (edge locations) |
| VPC | Regional |

## Spring Boot: Configuring AWS SDK Region

```java
@Configuration
public class AwsConfig {
    @Value("${aws.region:ap-south-1}")
    private String region;

    @Bean
    public S3Client s3Client() {
        return S3Client.builder()
            .region(Region.of(region))
            .credentialsProvider(DefaultCredentialsProvider.create())
            .build();
    }
}
```

domains/java/aws-core.title: AWS Regions, Availability Zones and Global Infrastructure

domains/java/ecs-deployment.spoken:
ECS is Amazon's container orchestration service. You package your Spring Boot application as a Docker container, push it to ECR, and define a Task Definition specifying which image to run, how much CPU and memory to allocate, which ports to expose, and environment variables to inject.

An ECS Service ensures a specified number of task instances are always running. If a task crashes, the service automatically starts a replacement. When deploying a new version, the service does a rolling update — starting new tasks before draining old ones — so deployments are zero-downtime.

Fargate is the mode I recommend for most teams. You never manage EC2 instances — you specify CPU and memory for your containers and AWS handles all host infrastructure. You pay per second of container runtime. EC2 launch type makes sense when you need specific instance types, GPU support, or want to optimize costs for predictable high-volume workloads.
domains/java/ecs-deployment.deep:
## Task Definition (Fargate)

```json
{
  "family": "spring-backend",
  "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"],
  "networkMode": "awsvpc",
  "cpu": "1024",
  "memory": "2048",
  "taskRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456:role/app-task-role",
  "executionRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456:role/ecs-execution-role",
  "containerDefinitions": [{
    "name": "spring-api",
    "image": "123456.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/spring-api:abc1234",
    "portMappings": [{"containerPort": 8080}],
    "environment": [
      {"name": "SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE", "value": "prod"}
    ],
    "secrets": [
      {"name": "DB_PASSWORD",
       "valueFrom": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:...:secret:/prod/db-credentials:password::"}
    ],
    "healthCheck": {
      "command": ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -f http://localhost:8080/actuator/health || exit 1"],
      "interval": 30, "timeout": 5, "retries": 3, "startPeriod": 60
    },
    "logConfiguration": {
      "logDriver": "awslogs",
      "options": {
        "awslogs-group": "/ecs/spring-backend",
        "awslogs-region": "ap-south-1",
        "awslogs-stream-prefix": "ecs"
      }
    }
  }]
}
```

## Deploy Rolling Update

```bash
# Register new task definition, update service
aws ecs update-service \
  --cluster prod-cluster \
  --service spring-api \
  --task-definition spring-backend:6 \
  --deployment-configuration 'minimumHealthyPercent=100,maximumPercent=200'
# minimumHealthyPercent=100: never reduce count below desired during deploy
# maximumPercent=200: allow 2x tasks during rollout (old + new running simultaneously)
```

domains/java/ecs-deployment.title: ECS Fundamentals — Clusters, Services and Tasks

domains/java/iam-security.spoken:
IAM controls access to AWS resources. The key concepts are users for human identities, roles for service identities, and policies that define what actions are allowed or denied on which resources.

For a Java application, never use IAM users with access keys. Create an IAM role and attach it to your EC2 instance, ECS task, or Lambda. The AWS SDK automatically retrieves temporary credentials from the instance metadata service. These credentials rotate automatically every few hours — far more secure than static keys.

Least privilege means granting the minimum permissions necessary. If your application only reads from DynamoDB, don't give it dynamodb:* — give it specifically dynamodb:GetItem and dynamodb:Query on the exact table ARNs it needs. This limits the blast radius if the application is ever compromised.
domains/java/iam-security.question: How does AWS IAM work and how do you implement least privilege for a Java application?
domains/java/iam-security.title: IAM Roles, Policies and Least Privilege

domains/java/rds-spring.spoken:
RDS is Amazon's managed relational database service. You provision a PostgreSQL instance and AWS handles the operational overhead — patching the database engine, taking automated backups, monitoring disk space, and managing Multi-AZ failover. Your application just connects to it like any other PostgreSQL database, using the endpoint DNS name.

The important distinction is always using the endpoint DNS name, never the IP address. During a Multi-AZ failover event, the standby gets promoted to primary and the DNS name switches to point to the new primary. If you hardcoded an IP, your application would fail permanently. With the DNS name, your connection pool reconnects automatically after a brief disruption.

For security, always put RDS in private subnets. Only your application security group should be able to reach the RDS security group on port 5432. Store credentials in Secrets Manager and read them at startup — never hardcode database passwords in your configuration files.
domains/java/rds-spring.deep:
## Spring Boot Configuration

```yaml
# application.yml (production)
spring:
  config:
    import: "aws-secretsmanager:/prod/myapp/db-credentials"
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://${rds_host}:5432/${rds_dbname}
    username: ${rds_username}
    password: ${rds_password}
    driver-class-name: org.postgresql.Driver
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 10
      minimum-idle: 3
      connection-timeout: 30000
      idle-timeout: 600000
      max-lifetime: 1800000
  jpa:
    database-platform: org.hibernate.dialect.PostgreSQLDialect
    show-sql: false
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate
  flyway:
    enabled: true
    locations: classpath:db/migration

# RDS endpoint format:
# mydb.xxxxxxxxxx.ap-south-1.rds.amazonaws.com
```

## Handling Multi-AZ Failover

```yaml
# HikariCP reconnects automatically when DNS changes (failover ~60s)
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      # Reconnect quickly after failover
      connection-timeout: 5000        # fail fast if connection attempt hangs
      validation-timeout: 3000        # validate connection quickly
      keepalive-time: 30000           # prevent idle connection drops
      connection-test-query: SELECT 1  # validate before lending
```

## Read Replica Endpoint

```yaml
# RDS provides separate endpoints for read replicas
# Primary (read/write): mydb.xxxxx.rds.amazonaws.com
# Read replica: mydb-replica.xxxxx.rds.amazonaws.com

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://mydb.xxxxx.rds.amazonaws.com:5432/appdb  # writes

# Add read-only datasource for read replicas
# Use AbstractRoutingDataSource to route @Transactional(readOnly=true) to replica
```

## RDS Parameter Group for Spring Boot

```sql
-- Custom parameter group settings for a Java app:
-- max_connections = 200 (but use PgBouncer to keep actual connections < this)
-- shared_buffers = {DBInstanceClassMemory/4} (25% RAM via formula)
-- log_min_duration_statement = 1000 (log slow queries)
-- timezone = 'UTC'
-- random_page_cost = 1.1 (for SSD storage — default 4.0 is for HDD)
```

domains/java/rds-spring.title: Setting Up RDS PostgreSQL with Spring Boot

domains/java/s3-storage.spoken:
S3 is object storage — you store files as objects identified by a key within a bucket. Unlike a file system, there are no real directories. Keys just look like paths using slashes, but they're actually flat. The bucket name must be globally unique across all AWS accounts and regions.

For a Spring Boot application, the main use cases are storing user uploads like profile pictures and documents, storing application-generated files like PDF reports, and serving static assets. Files uploaded to S3 can be made publicly accessible via their URL, or kept private and accessed via presigned URLs that give temporary access without requiring AWS credentials.

S3 durability is 11 nines — AWS replicates every object across at least three AZs within the region. You almost never need to think about data loss with S3. What you do need to think about is access control, versioning for important files, and lifecycle policies to move old files to cheaper storage classes automatically.
domains/java/s3-storage.question: How does AWS S3 work and how do you integrate it with a Spring Boot application for file storage?
domains/java/s3-storage.title: S3 Fundamentals — Buckets, Objects and URLs

domains/java/exceptions-best-practices.spoken:
Checked exceptions are part of a method's contract — the compiler forces callers to either handle them or declare them. They're appropriate when the caller can and should do something meaningful about the failure — like `FileNotFoundException` where the caller might prompt for a different file path.

Unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and subclasses) don't require declaration or handling. They represent programming errors — like `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException` — or conditions the caller typically can't recover from.

Modern Java practice, especially in Spring, heavily favors unchecked exceptions for domain and business exceptions. Checked exceptions pollute call chains — every method in the call stack must declare the exception even if it can't handle it. Spring's entire `DataAccessException` hierarchy is unchecked, allowing repository exceptions to propagate naturally to error handlers without being declared at every layer.
domains/java/exceptions-best-practices.question: When should you use checked versus unchecked exceptions?
domains/java/exceptions-best-practices.title: Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions

domains/java/functional-programming.spoken:
Java Streams provide a declarative, functional-style pipeline for data processing. The key principle is lazy evaluation: intermediate operations like `filter`, `map`, and `flatMap` are not executed when you call them — they build a pipeline description. Only when you call a terminal operation like `collect`, `forEach`, or `reduce` does the pipeline execute, and even then it processes elements one at a time, short-circuiting when possible.

The most commonly used operations: `filter` for selection, `map` for transformation, `flatMap` for flattening nested structures, `collect` with `groupingBy`/`toMap`/`joining` for aggregation, and `reduce` for folding. `Optional` is deeply integrated — `findFirst()` and `findAny()` return `Optional` to force you to handle the empty case.

Parallel streams — `stream.parallel()` — process in the ForkJoinPool but add overhead and have ordering/side-effect constraints. Use only for computationally expensive operations on large datasets.
domains/java/functional-programming.question: How do Java Streams work and what are the most useful stream operations?
domains/java/functional-programming.title: Java Streams API

domains/java/generics-wildcards.spoken:
Generics provide compile-time type safety — instead of casting from `Object` and risking `ClassCastException` at runtime, the compiler verifies types at compile time. `List<String>` guarantees you only add and get `String` objects without explicit casting.

Type erasure is how Java implements generics: at compile time, the compiler checks generic types, then removes (erases) them from the bytecode. `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` both become just `List` at runtime — you can't use `instanceof List<String>` or create `new T[]` because the type parameter is gone.

This is why `List<String>` is not a subtype of `List<Object>` even though `String` is a subtype of `Object` — this would break type safety since you could add an `Integer` to a `List<Object>` reference that points to a `List<String>`.
domains/java/generics-wildcards.question: How do Java generics work and what is type erasure?
domains/java/generics-wildcards.title: Generics — Type Safety and Type Erasure

domains/java/multithreading-concurrency.spoken:
Thread safety can be achieved through several mechanisms, each with different trade-offs. The safest approach is immutability — if an object can't change state, multiple threads can read it simultaneously without synchronization. Java records and `final` fields support this.

When you need shared mutable state, the options are: `synchronized` (simple but coarse-grained — only one thread at a time), `ReentrantLock` (same behavior, more control — tryLock with timeout, fairness), or atomic classes like `AtomicInteger` and `AtomicLong` which use Compare-And-Swap (CAS) for lock-free thread-safe operations.

For collections, use the `java.util.concurrent` package: `ConcurrentHashMap` for maps (no global lock — segments are locked independently), `CopyOnWriteArrayList` for lists that are read frequently but rarely modified, `BlockingQueue` for producer-consumer patterns.
domains/java/multithreading-concurrency.question: What are the main approaches to thread safety in Java?
domains/java/multithreading-concurrency.title: Thread Safety Approaches

domains/java/oop-principles.spoken:
SOLID is a set of five principles that guide object-oriented design toward code that's maintainable and extensible.

Single Responsibility means each class has one reason to change — if `OrderService` also sends emails, it has two reasons to change (order logic changes AND email template changes). Extract emailing into a separate class.

Open/Closed means classes should be open for extension but closed for modification. When adding a new payment method, you shouldn't modify the `PaymentProcessor` — instead, add a new class implementing the `PaymentProvider` interface. The processor never needs to change.

Liskov Substitution says a subclass must be substitutable for its parent without breaking behavior. A `Rectangle` extending `Square` violates this if setting width also sets height — callers expecting rectangle behavior get surprised.

Interface Segregation means keep interfaces focused — don't force a class to implement methods it doesn't need. Split a fat `UserService` interface into `UserReader` and `UserWriter` if some consumers only read.

Dependency Inversion means high-level modules depend on abstractions, not implementations. `OrderService` should depend on `PaymentGateway` (interface), not `StripePaymentGateway` (concrete class).
domains/java/oop-principles.question: Explain the SOLID principles with Java examples.
domains/java/oop-principles.title: SOLID Principles

domains/java/reflection-annotations.spoken:
Reflection allows Java code to inspect and manipulate classes, methods, constructors, and fields at runtime — things that are normally determined at compile time. You can discover class structure, invoke methods by name, access private fields, and instantiate objects from class names stored as strings.

It's the foundation of most Java frameworks: Spring uses reflection to discover beans and inject dependencies, Jackson uses it to serialize/deserialize objects to JSON, Hibernate maps entity fields to database columns, and JUnit discovers and runs test methods — all without you writing explicit wiring code.

The main limitation is performance: reflection calls are significantly slower than direct method calls because the JVM can't optimize them as aggressively (no JIT inlining). They also bypass compile-time checks and encapsulation. Use reflection only in framework infrastructure code — never in hot business logic paths.
domains/java/reflection-annotations.question: What is Java Reflection and what are its use cases and limitations?
domains/java/reflection-annotations.title: Java Reflection API

domains/java/connection-pooling.spoken:
Connection pooling pre-establishes a set of database connections that application threads reuse. Without a pool, every query would require a TCP handshake, authentication, and session setup — typically 20-50ms of overhead per query. With a pool, a thread acquires an existing connection in microseconds.

HikariCP is Spring Boot's default pool and is widely considered the fastest JVM connection pool. The most important setting is `maximumPoolSize`. A common mistake is setting it very large — say 200 — thinking more connections means more throughput. The opposite is often true: too many connections cause the database to spend CPU on context switching between sessions rather than executing queries. A commonly cited formula is (CPU cores × 2) + number of disk spindles, which for a 4-core server with SSDs gives about 9 connections.

`connectionTimeout` controls how long a thread waits if the pool is exhausted. If this is too short and your pool is undersized, you'll get `SQLTransientConnectionException` under load.
domains/java/connection-pooling.question: How does connection pooling work and how do you configure HikariCP in Spring Boot?
domains/java/connection-pooling.title: HikariCP and Connection Pool Tuning

domains/java/indexing.spoken:
An index is a separate data structure (B-tree by default in most RDBMS) that allows the database to locate rows without scanning the entire table. Without an index, every query does a full table scan — O(n). With a B-tree index, lookup is O(log n). The trade-off: indexes consume disk space and must be updated on every write.

You should index columns that appear frequently in WHERE clauses, JOIN conditions, or ORDER BY clauses on large tables. For composite indexes (multiple columns), the order matters — the database can use the index for queries on the leftmost columns, but not if you skip the first column.

The covering index technique is powerful for read-heavy queries: if you include all the columns a query needs directly in the index, the database never touches the main table — it answers the query entirely from the index.
domains/java/indexing.deep:
## B-Tree Index Structure

```
Table: orders (10 million rows)
Columns: id, user_id, status, total, created_at

WITHOUT index on user_id:
  SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42
  → Full table scan: read all 10M rows → slow (seconds)

WITH B-tree index on user_id:
  → B-tree lookup: O(log 10M) ≈ 23 comparisons → fast (milliseconds)

B-Tree structure:
         [500]
        /     \
    [250]      [750]
   /     \    /     \
[100] [375] [600] [900]

Each node stores key values and pointers to child nodes or data rows.
Leaf nodes are linked → range scans are efficient.
```

## When to Index

```sql
-- INDEX THIS: High-cardinality columns in WHERE/JOIN
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
-- Cardinality: 1M unique users → index very selective → big win

-- DON'T INDEX THIS: Low-cardinality columns
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(status);
-- Cardinality: only 5 statuses (PENDING, CONFIRMED, etc.)
-- Index returns 20% of rows → full scan might be faster
-- Exception: combine with other high-cardinality columns in composite index

-- INDEX ORDER BY columns on large result sets:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_at ON orders(created_at);
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
-- Without index: sort 10M rows → with index: read 20 from sorted structure

-- INDEX JOIN columns:
CREATE INDEX idx_order_items_order_id ON order_items(order_id);
SELECT o.id, i.product_id FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON o.id = i.order_id;
-- order_id is FK — always index FK columns!
```

## Composite Index — Column Order Matters

```sql
-- Composite index: (user_id, status, created_at)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_status_created ON orders(user_id, status, created_at);

-- Leftmost prefix rule:
-- ✓ Can use index:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;                          -- Prefix: user_id
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 AND status = 'PENDING';  -- Prefix: user_id, status
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 AND status = 'PENDING'   -- All three
    AND created_at > '2024-01-01';

-- ✗ Cannot use index (skips user_id):
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'PENDING';         -- No user_id → can't use
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01'; -- No user_id → can't use

-- Optimize column order: most selective first + matches common query patterns
-- If you always filter by user_id → put it first
-- If most queries filter by user_id + status → (user_id, status) together
```

## Covering Index

```sql
-- Query: get order id and total for a user
SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;

-- Regular index on user_id:
-- 1. Look up user_id = 42 in index → get row pointers
-- 2. Fetch actual rows from table → read 'id' and 'total'
-- (Two I/O operations: index + table)

-- Covering index includes all needed columns:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_covering ON orders(user_id, id, total);
-- 1. Look up user_id = 42 in index → directly read id and total from index
-- (One I/O operation: index only — no table access)

-- PostgreSQL: EXPLAIN shows "Index Only Scan" for covering indexes
-- MySQL: EXPLAIN shows "Using index" in Extra column

-- EXPLAIN ANALYZE example:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
-- Shows: Index Only Scan using idx_orders_user_covering
--        Rows: 15, actual time: 0.05ms (vs 450ms without index)
```

## Index Impact on Writes

```
Table with 5 indexes:
  idx_user_id
  idx_status
  idx_created_at
  idx_user_status_created (composite)
  idx_user_covering

INSERT into orders:
  → Write row to table
  → Update ALL 5 indexes
  → 6× write operations (1 table + 5 indexes)

UPDATE orders SET status = 'CONFIRMED' WHERE id = 1:
  → Update table row
  → Update idx_status (value changed)
  → Update idx_user_status_created (status changed)
  → 3× write operations

Conclusion:
  - High-write tables: minimize indexes
  - Read-heavy tables: more indexes acceptable
  - Remove unused indexes: query pg_stat_user_indexes / sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats
```

## Production Reality

Always add indexes on foreign key columns (MySQL doesn't do this automatically). Use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to verify index usage — sometimes the query planner skips the index if it estimates a full scan is faster (usually correct for small tables or low-cardinality filters). Periodically audit unused indexes using your database's index usage statistics. In PostgreSQL, `pg_stat_user_indexes` shows scan counts — drop indexes with zero scans (in production, over a representative period).
domains/java/indexing.question: How do database indexes work and how do you decide which columns to index?
domains/java/indexing.title: How Database Indexes Work

domains/java/nosql-integration.spoken:
Redis is the most popular caching layer for Java backends. Spring Boot's cache abstraction lets you add caching to service methods with simple annotations: `@Cacheable` caches the result on the first call and returns the cached value on subsequent calls with the same arguments. `@CacheEvict` removes entries when data changes. This abstraction works with Redis, Caffeine, or any other cache provider without changing business code.

The most important operational concern is TTL. Always set a time-to-live on cached values — without it, stale data can live in the cache indefinitely, causing subtle bugs that are hard to reproduce. The TTL should balance freshness requirements against DB load reduction.

Redis is also used for more than caching: distributed session storage, rate limiting counters, distributed locks with Redisson, and pub/sub messaging. Understanding these secondary use cases shows depth.
domains/java/nosql-integration.question: How do you integrate Redis caching in a Spring Boot application?
domains/java/nosql-integration.title: Redis Caching in Spring Boot

domains/java/partitioning-sharding.spoken:
Partitioning splits a large table into smaller segments within the same database server. Range partitioning by date is the most common example — January data in one partition, February in another. The database can then skip irrelevant partitions when you query by date, dramatically speeding up time-range queries and making it easy to archive old data by dropping an entire partition.

Sharding takes this further by distributing data across completely separate database servers. Each server (shard) holds a subset of the data determined by the shard key — for example, user IDs 1-1M on shard 1, 1M-2M on shard 2. This provides horizontal scaling beyond what any single server can handle.

Sharding comes with serious complexity: you lose cross-shard JOINs, distributed transactions become much harder, and re-sharding as you grow is operationally painful. Most applications should exhaust vertical scaling, read replicas, caching, and partitioning before considering sharding.
domains/java/partitioning-sharding.question: What is the difference between database partitioning and sharding?
domains/java/partitioning-sharding.title: Database Partitioning vs Sharding

domains/java/query-optimization.spoken:
Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes because the database maintains the index structure on every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE. The decision of which columns to index should be driven by actual query patterns, not guesswork.

The primary candidates for indexing are: columns in WHERE clauses that filter large tables, foreign key columns used in JOINs, and columns in ORDER BY clauses when you need sorted results without full scans. The order of columns in a composite index matters — put the most selective column first, and think about which queries can use the index prefix.

For a JPA-heavy application, run your queries with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` in PostgreSQL or `EXPLAIN` in MySQL and look for sequential scans on large tables. Those are your index candidates. Add the index via Flyway migration and verify with another EXPLAIN.

domains/java/docker-compose.spoken:
Docker Compose lets you define an entire multi-container application in a single YAML file. Running docker compose up starts all defined services in the right order, creates networks so they can communicate by service name, and manages volumes for persistent data. It's the standard tool for local development and testing of multi-service applications.

The key services for a typical Java backend stack are the application itself, a PostgreSQL database, Redis for caching, and optionally Kafka for messaging. Each gets its own service definition with its image, environment variables, ports, and volume mounts. Services on the same Compose network can reach each other by their service name — the Spring Boot app connects to postgres:5432 and redis:6379 without any IP configuration.

The most important caveat with depends_on is that it only controls start order, not readiness. PostgreSQL may be accepting connections before it's finished initializing, and your Spring Boot app might connect too early and fail. The fix is to use depends_on with a health check condition, which waits until the dependency reports healthy before starting dependent services.
domains/java/docker-compose.deep:
## Complete Java Backend Compose File

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
name: my-java-app

services:
  # ===== Spring Boot Application =====
  app:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: dev
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/appdb
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: appuser
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
      SPRING_DATA_REDIS_HOST: redis
      SPRING_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS: kafka:9092
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy  # wait for health check
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - app-network
    restart: unless-stopped

  # ===== PostgreSQL =====
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: appdb
      POSTGRES_USER: appuser
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"  # exposed to host for local DB tools
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      - ./scripts/init.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U appuser -d appdb"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 20s
    networks:
      - app-network

  # ===== Redis =====
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: redis-server --requirepass ${REDIS_PASSWORD}
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "-a", "${REDIS_PASSWORD}", "ping"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
    networks:
      - app-network

  # ===== Kafka (KRaft mode — no Zookeeper) =====
  kafka:
    image: confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.6.0
    ports:
      - "9092:9092"
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@kafka:9093
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://0.0.0.0:9092,CONTROLLER://0.0.0.0:9093
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://kafka:9092
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER
      KAFKA_LOG_DIRS: /var/lib/kafka/data
      CLUSTER_ID: MkU3OEVBNTcwNTJENDM2Qk
    volumes:
      - kafka-data:/var/lib/kafka/data
    networks:
      - app-network

volumes:
  postgres-data:
  redis-data:
  kafka-data:

networks:
  app-network:
    driver: bridge
```

## .env File

```bash
# .env — committed with safe defaults; override in CI/prod
DB_PASSWORD=devpassword
REDIS_PASSWORD=devredis
```

## Common Commands

```bash
docker compose up -d             # start all services in background
docker compose up -d app         # start only one service
docker compose logs -f app       # stream app logs
docker compose exec app /bin/sh  # shell into running container
docker compose down              # stop and remove containers
docker compose down -v           # also remove volumes (wipe data!)
docker compose ps                # show running services and health
docker compose restart app       # restart one service
```

domains/java/docker-fundamentals.spoken:
Docker containers are process isolation mechanisms — they use Linux kernel features like namespaces and control groups to make a process think it has its own filesystem, network, and process space, while actually sharing the host kernel. Virtual machines emulate entire hardware and run a completely separate kernel. This makes containers dramatically more lightweight: a container starts in milliseconds and uses megabytes, while a VM takes minutes to boot and uses gigabytes.

The tradeoff is isolation strength. Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel vulnerability could theoretically affect all containers on that host. VMs have a hypervisor boundary that provides much stronger isolation. For most web application workloads, container isolation is sufficient. For multi-tenant environments where you're running code from different customers, VMs or stronger container isolation techniques are used.

A Docker image is a stack of read-only filesystem layers built from a Dockerfile. Each instruction creates a new layer. When you run an image as a container, Docker adds a thin writable layer on top. Multiple containers can run from the same image without duplicating the read-only data — they all share the image layers.
domains/java/docker-fundamentals.deep:
## Container vs VM Architecture

```
Virtual Machines:
┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
│  App + Libs  │  │  App + Libs  │
│  Guest OS    │  │  Guest OS    │  (each has full OS — 2-20GB each)
└──────┬───────┘  └──────┬───────┘
       └────────┬─────────┘
          Hypervisor
          Host OS
          Hardware

Docker Containers:
┌────────┐  ┌────────┐  ┌────────┐
│App+Libs│  │App+Libs│  │App+Libs│  (just app + deps — 50-500MB each)
└────┬───┘  └────┬───┘  └────┬───┘
     └───────────┼────────────┘
             Docker Engine
             Host OS Kernel (shared)
             Hardware
```

## Image Layers

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre        # Layer 1: base JRE (~200MB, pulled once)
WORKDIR /app                        # Layer 2: create directory
COPY target/app.jar .               # Layer 3: your JAR (~50MB)
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

# Layer 1 is cached and reused across all your Spring Boot images
# Only layer 3 changes on each build → fast rebuilds
```

## Essential Docker Commands

```bash
# Build image
docker build -t my-app:1.0 .
docker build -t my-app:1.0 --no-cache .  # rebuild from scratch

# Run container
docker run -d --name my-app \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \
  -e DB_HOST=postgres \
  --network my-network \
  my-app:1.0

# Inspect and debug
docker logs my-app -f          # stream logs
docker exec -it my-app /bin/sh  # interactive shell
docker stats my-app             # CPU/memory usage

# Cleanup
docker stop my-app && docker rm my-app
docker image prune -f           # remove unused images
```

domains/java/git-internals.spoken:
Git is fundamentally a content-addressable key-value store. Every piece of data — file content, directory structure, commit metadata — is stored as an object in .git/objects/, named by the SHA-1 hash of its content. Identical content always has the same hash, so Git never stores the same file content twice even across different commits.

The four object types form a directed acyclic graph. A blob stores raw file content. A tree is like a directory — it lists names and SHAs for blobs and other trees. A commit points to a root tree that represents the entire project snapshot, and to its parent commit. Following parent pointers from any commit traces the full history.

Branches are astonishingly simple — just a text file in .git/refs/heads/ containing the SHA of the latest commit. Creating a branch is just creating a new file with a SHA. Merging updates that file. This is why branching in Git is instantaneous — there's no copying, no heavy operation, just writing 40 characters to a file.
domains/java/git-internals.deep:
## Object Structure

```
Commit Object: abc123
├── tree: def456            ← root directory snapshot
├── parent: a1b2c3d         ← previous commit
├── author: Alice <alice@example.com> 2024-01-15 10:00:00
└── message: feat: add payment service

Tree Object: def456
├── blob ghi789  src/PaymentService.java
├── blob jkl012  src/PaymentController.java  
└── tree mno345  src/                        ← subdirectory = subtree

Blob Object: ghi789
└── (raw content of PaymentService.java)
```

## Inspecting Git Objects

```bash
# Get the commit SHA
git log --oneline -1
# abc1234 feat: add payment service

# Inspect the commit object
git cat-file -p abc1234
# tree def456789abcdef...
# parent a1b2c3d4...
# author Alice ...
# feat: add payment service

# Inspect the tree
git cat-file -p def456789
# 100644 blob ghi789... PaymentService.java
# 100644 blob jkl012... PaymentController.java

# Inspect a blob
git cat-file -p ghi789
# (content of PaymentService.java)

# Branch is just a pointer
cat .git/refs/heads/main
# abc123456789abcdef...  (SHA of latest commit)

# HEAD points to current branch
cat .git/HEAD
# ref: refs/heads/main
```

## Content Deduplication

```
Commit 1: UserService.java → blob SHA: aaa111
Commit 2: UserService.java (unchanged) → blob SHA: aaa111  (SAME!)
          PaymentService.java (new) → blob SHA: bbb222

Git stores blob aaa111 only ONCE even though it appears in 1000 commits.
Changing one byte of UserService.java creates a new blob ccc333.
→ Git is extremely space-efficient for files that change infrequently.
```

domains/java/git-workflows.spoken:
For modern Java backend teams doing continuous deployment, GitHub Flow is the most practical approach. Developers create short-lived feature branches from main, implement the change, open a pull request for code review, and merge to main after CI passes and the review is approved. Main is always deployable. This keeps the workflow simple and reduces the merge conflict overhead that comes with longer-lived branches.

Trunk-Based Development takes this further — branches are even shorter-lived, often merged within a day or two. This requires feature flags to hide incomplete work in production. Teams doing TBD tend to ship faster and have fewer merge conflicts, but it requires a mature CI/CD pipeline and good feature flag management.

Gitflow is worth knowing because many companies use it, but it adds complexity — a long-lived develop branch that diverges from main, separate release branches, and hotfix branches. It makes sense for software with formal versioned releases, like a library or enterprise application, but it's overkill for a continuously deployed microservice.
domains/java/git-workflows.deep:
## GitHub Flow

```bash
# 1. Create feature branch from main
git checkout main && git pull
git checkout -b feature/add-payment-service

# 2. Implement and commit regularly
git add -p  # stage changes interactively
git commit -m "feat(payments): add Stripe payment gateway integration"
git commit -m "test(payments): add integration tests for payment flow"

# 3. Push and open PR
git push -u origin feature/add-payment-service
# → Open PR on GitHub/GitLab

# 4. After review + CI passes → squash merge to main
git checkout main && git merge --squash feature/add-payment-service
git commit -m "feat(payments): add Stripe payment gateway integration (#123)"
git push

# 5. Deploy main automatically via CI/CD
# 6. Delete feature branch
git branch -d feature/add-payment-service
git push origin --delete feature/add-payment-service
```

## Gitflow (for versioned releases)

```
main     ──────────────────────────────── v1.0 ──────── v1.1
               ↑ merge                     ↑ merge
develop  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
               ↑ merge     ↑ merge
feature/A ─────────────────
feature/B          ─────────────────
           ↑ branch from develop

Hotfix: branch from main → merge to main AND develop
Release: branch from develop → merge to main AND develop
```

## Branch Protection Rules (GitHub)

```yaml
# GitHub branch protection for 'main':
require_pull_request_reviews:
  required_approving_review_count: 1
require_status_checks:
  strict: true  # must be up to date with main before merging
  contexts:
    - "CI / build-and-test"
    - "CI / integration-tests"
dismiss_stale_reviews: true
require_conversation_resolution: true
restrict_pushes: true  # no direct push to main
```

## Conventional Commits

```bash
# Structured commit messages enable automated changelogs and semantic versioning
git commit -m "feat(auth): add OAuth2 Google login"
git commit -m "fix(orders): prevent duplicate order creation on retry"
git commit -m "perf(cache): add Redis caching for product list"
git commit -m "refactor(db): extract database migrations to separate module"
git commit -m "docs(api): update OpenAPI spec for payments endpoint"
git commit -m "test(inventory): add unit tests for stock reservation"

# Breaking change (triggers major version bump)
git commit -m "feat(api)!: change order response format to include nested items

BREAKING CHANGE: order.products[] renamed to order.items[]"
```

domains/java/garbage-collection.spoken:
Java has several GC algorithms with different trade-offs between throughput, pause time, and memory overhead.

G1GC is the default since Java 9 and a good general-purpose choice. It divides the heap into regions and collects the highest-garbage regions first, aiming to meet a pause time target. It works well for heaps from 4GB to 32GB.

ZGC and Shenandoah are designed for latency-sensitive workloads where even short pauses are unacceptable — they achieve sub-10ms pause times regardless of heap size by doing most GC work concurrently with the application. The trade-off is slightly lower throughput.

ParallelGC prioritizes throughput over pauses — it uses multiple threads for GC but still pauses the application. Good for batch processing where throughput matters more than individual request latency.

In practice, start with G1GC, enable GC logging, measure pause times, and only switch algorithms if measurements show pauses are actually a problem.
domains/java/garbage-collection.deep:
## GC Algorithm Comparison

```
Algorithm   | Default For  | Pause Time     | Throughput | Memory Overhead | Best For
------------|--------------|----------------|------------|-----------------|---------------------------
SerialGC    | Single-core  | High (seconds) | Low        | Low             | Embedded, micro services
ParallelGC  | Java 8       | Medium (100ms+)| High       | Low             | Batch processing, analytics
G1GC        | Java 9-21    | Low (< 200ms)  | Medium     | Medium          | General purpose, web apps
ZGC         | Java 15+     | Ultra-low(1ms) | Medium     | High            | Latency-critical (trading)
Shenandoah  | OpenJDK      | Ultra-low(1ms) | Medium     | High            | Same as ZGC
```

## Configuring GC

```bash
# G1GC (recommended for most Spring Boot apps)
java -Xms4g -Xmx4g \
  -XX:+UseG1GC \
  -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 \\     # Target pause: G1 TRIES to stay under this
  -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=16m \\     # Region size (auto-tuned if not set)
  -XX:G1NewSizePercent=20 \\      # Min Young Gen as % of heap
  -XX:G1MaxNewSizePercent=40 \\   # Max Young Gen as % of heap
  -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/gc.log:time:filecount=5,filesize=10m \
  -jar myapp.jar

# ZGC (Java 15+, for < 10ms pause requirement)
java -Xms8g -Xmx8g \
  -XX:+UseZGC \
  -XX:ZCollectionInterval=1 \\   # Force GC at least every 1 second
  -jar myapp.jar
# ZGC is generational in Java 21+ (-XX:+ZGenerational)

# Parallel GC (batch jobs)
java -Xms4g -Xmx4g \
  -XX:+UseParallelGC \
  -XX:ParallelGCThreads=8 \\    # Use 8 threads for GC
  -jar batch-processor.jar
```

## GC Log Analysis

```
G1GC log output (with -Xlog:gc):

[0.245s] GC(0) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause)
          Eden: 256M->0M, Survivors: 0->32M, Old: 0->12M
          Heap: 256M->44M
          3.123ms         ← Pause time

[5.234s] GC(14) Pause Young (Normal) 128M->45M(2048M) 4.5ms

[30.456s] GC(89) Pause Full (Allocation Failure)
           Heap: 1900M->800M(2048M) 1456ms  ← PROBLEM! 1.4 second pause

DIAGNOSIS:
  'Pause Full (Allocation Failure)' → Old Gen full → emergency Full GC
  Causes:
    1. Memory leak: objects accumulating in Old Gen
    2. Heap too small for workload
    3. Too many long-lived objects (caches, static state)

  Solutions:
    1. Take heap dump, analyze with Eclipse MAT or VisualVM
    2. Increase -Xmx (if leak isn't the cause)
    3. Review caching strategy (Caffeine with size limit instead of HashMap)
```

## Understanding GC Phases (G1GC)

```
G1GC PHASES:

1. Minor GC / Young GC (Concurrent):
   - Triggered when Eden fills
   - Stop-the-world: typically 5-50ms
   - Evacuates live objects from Eden → Survivors or Old Gen
   - Frequency: every few seconds under normal load

2. Concurrent Marking (runs WHILE app is running):
   - G1 tracks which objects are live
   - No pause — runs concurrently
   - Starts when heap occupancy > InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent (default 45%)

3. Mixed GC:
   - After marking, G1 knows which Old Gen regions have most garbage
   - Collects Young Gen + high-garbage Old Gen regions
   - Multiple rounds, each with a short pause
   - This is G1's secret: targeted, incremental Old Gen collection

4. Full GC (emergency, last resort):
   - Single-threaded by default until Java 10 (then parallel)
   - Long pause (seconds)
   - Triggered when G1 can't keep up with allocation
   - Target: never happen in production
```

## Production Reality

The most impactful GC tuning for Spring Boot services: set `-Xms` = `-Xmx` (prevents dynamic heap resizing), tune `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` for G1GC based on your SLA (200ms is reasonable for APIs), and always enable GC logging. Don't tune blindly — GC log analysis with a tool (GCEasy.io, GCViewer) will show you what's actually happening. The most common GC problem in Spring Boot apps is unbounded caches filling Old Gen — switch from HashMap caches to Caffeine with a size limit.

domains/java/jvm-architecture.spoken:
The JVM has several memory regions. The heap is where all object instances live and is what GC manages. It's divided into Young Generation (newly created objects — Eden and two Survivor spaces) and Old Generation (long-lived objects that survived multiple GC cycles).

Metaspace (introduced in Java 8, replacing PermGen) stores class definitions: method bytecode, class structure, constant pool. It's backed by native memory and grows automatically by default, which is why you should set `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` in production.

Each thread has its own stack, which stores stack frames — one per method call. A frame holds local variables, the operand stack for computation, and a reference back to the constant pool. Stack is fixed per thread (default 512KB-1MB) — deep recursion causes StackOverflowError.

Code Cache is where JIT-compiled native code is stored — the C2 compiler's output for hot methods.
domains/java/jvm-architecture.deep:
## JVM Memory Structure

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        JVM PROCESS MEMORY                       │
│                                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────────┐ │
│  │              HEAP               │  │      METASPACE        │ │
│  │  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌──────┐ │  │  Class definitions    │ │
│  │  │  YOUNG GEN      │  │ OLD  │ │  │  Method bytecode      │ │
│  │  │  ┌──────┬─┬─┐   │  │ GEN  │ │  │  Annotations          │ │
│  │  │  │Eden  │S│S│   │  │      │ │  │  Constant pool        │ │
│  │  │  │      │0│1│   │  │      │ │  │  (unbounded by        │ │
│  │  │  └──────┴─┴─┘   │  │      │ │  │   default!)           │ │
│  │  └─────────────────┘  └──────┘ │  └───────────────────────┘ │
│  │  Minor GC here ────────────────│                            │ │
│  │  Major/Full GC ─────────────────────────────────────────── │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────┘                           │ │
│                                                                  │
│  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐  │
│  │ THREAD STACKS    │  │  CODE CACHE    │  │ DIRECT MEMORY  │  │
│  │ (per thread)     │  │  JIT output    │  │ ByteBuffer     │  │
│  │ Stack frames     │  │  Native code   │  │ .allocateDirect│  │
│  │ Local variables  │  │  (profiling)   │  │ (NIO, Netty)   │  │
│  └──────────────────┘  └────────────────┘  └────────────────┘  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Heap — Object Lifecycle

```
OBJECT ALLOCATION FLOW:

1. new Order() → allocated in Eden (Young Gen)
   Eden fills up → Minor GC triggered

2. Minor GC (stop-the-world, but very fast: 5-50ms):
   - Live objects in Eden copied to Survivor 0 (S0)
   - Dead objects in Eden collected
   - Objects in S0 that survived previous GC copied to S1, age incremented
   - Objects with age > MaxTenuringThreshold (default 15) → promoted to Old Gen
   - S0 and S1 roles swapped

3. Old Gen fills up → Major/Full GC triggered:
   - Much slower (100ms - several seconds)
   - Collects entire heap
   - Should be infrequent — minimize promotions to Old Gen

MONITOR:
  Minor GC frequency: > 1/sec suggests high allocation rate → increase Eden size
  Major GC frequency: > 1/10min suggests memory leak or undersized Old Gen
  Promotion rate: if objects promote before dying, they fill Old Gen prematurely
```

## Stack — Per Thread

```java
// Stack frame created for each method call:
public String processOrder(Long orderId) {      // Frame 1 created
    Order order = findOrder(orderId);           // Frame 2 created for findOrder()
    // Frame 2 destroyed when findOrder() returns
    return format(order);                       // Frame 3 created
}                                              // Frame 1 destroyed

// Each frame contains:
// - Local variables (orderId, order)
// - Operand stack (for intermediate computations)
// - Reference to constant pool (for string literals, etc.)

// Default stack size:
// -Xss512k  (512KB per thread)
// 200 threads × 512KB = 100MB just for stacks!
// Increase if you get StackOverflowError from deep call chains

// StackOverflowError:
public int infiniteRecursion(int n) {
    return infiniteRecursion(n + 1);  // Each call adds a frame
    // Eventually: Thread stack filled → StackOverflowError
}
```

## Metaspace — Class Metadata

```java
// Metaspace grows when:
// 1. New classes are loaded:
Class.forName("com.example.SomeClass");  // Loads class into Metaspace

// 2. Dynamic class generation:
// Spring proxies, CGLIB, Hibernate entity enhancements, reflection proxies
// Each proxy = new class = Metaspace usage

// 3. Class loaders not being GC'd (memory leak):
// Application creates ClassLoader, loads classes, ClassLoader goes out of scope
// BUT: if any loaded class is still referenced → ClassLoader can't be GC'd
// → Metaspace grows indefinitely

// CONFIGURE IN PRODUCTION:
// -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m
//   Without limit: Metaspace grows until native OOM
//   With limit: OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace (at least it's predictable)

// DIAGNOSE:
jcmd <pid> VM.metaspace  // Show Metaspace usage breakdown
```

## OutOfMemoryError Types

```
OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
  → Heap is full (Old Gen exhausted or heap too small)
  → Solutions: -Xmx increase, find memory leak with heap dump

OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded
  → GC spending > 98% of time but reclaiming < 2% of heap
  → Effective OOM — app barely running under GC pressure
  → Solutions: heap dump analysis, fix leak or increase heap

OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace
  → Too many classes loaded (dynamic proxies, class loader leak)
  → Solutions: set -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize, find class loader leak

OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory
  → Off-heap direct memory exhausted (ByteBuffer.allocateDirect)
  → Common with Netty, NIO frameworks
  → Solutions: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, check for direct buffer leaks

StackOverflowError
  → Thread stack exhausted (deep recursion)
  → Solutions: increase -Xss, fix infinite recursion, use iteration
```

## Production Reality

Always set both `-Xms` (initial heap) and `-Xmx` (max heap) to the same value in production — prevents heap resizing which causes pauses and memory fragmentation. Set `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` — an unbound Metaspace can silently consume all native memory, causing OS-level OOM kills. Enable GC logging: `-Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/app/gc.log:time,uptime:filecount=5,filesize=10m` — it's essential for diagnosing GC pauses in production.
domains/java/jvm-architecture.question: What are the different memory areas in the JVM and what does each store?

domains/java/memory-analysis.spoken:
A memory leak in Java is when objects can't be garbage collected because some live reference (intentionally or accidentally) still points to them. The symptoms are characteristic: heap usage grows steadily over time, GC frequency increases, Old Gen fills up progressively, and eventually you get an OutOfMemoryError after hours or days of running.

To diagnose, I first confirm it's a leak by looking at heap usage trend over time in monitoring (Grafana/Prometheus). If heap grows without bound after GC cycles, it's a leak. Then I take a heap dump — either via `jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump` or via Spring Boot Actuator's `/actuator/heapdump` endpoint. I analyze it in Eclipse Memory Analyzer (MAT) which can automatically identify the 'leak suspects' — objects taking the most retained heap.

Common causes: static collections that grow without bound (a cache without size limit), event listeners added but never removed, ThreadLocal values not cleaned up, and inner class references holding onto outer class instances.
domains/java/memory-analysis.question: How do you identify and fix memory leaks in a Java application?
domains/java/memory-analysis.title: Diagnosing Memory Leaks in Java

domains/java/profiling-debugging.spoken:
Performance profiling is about measuring before optimizing. The first step is identifying whether the bottleneck is CPU (high CPU, slow computation), I/O (threads waiting on DB or network), or garbage collection (frequent GC pauses). Monitoring metrics give you this picture — Micrometer exposes CPU, GC, thread, and memory metrics.

For CPU profiling, async-profiler is the tool of choice — it's low-overhead and safe to run in production. It produces flame graphs where the width of each block represents the proportion of CPU time that method took. Wide blocks at the top of the flame are your bottlenecks.

For I/O and thread issues, thread dumps are invaluable — `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` gives a snapshot of every thread's current stack trace. If you see 50 threads all blocked on `SocketInputStream.read()`, you have I/O bottleneck, not CPU. If you see circular waits, you have a deadlock.

Java Flight Recorder (JFR) is the continuous recording option — minimal overhead, always on, captures events over time.
domains/java/profiling-debugging.deep:
## Profiling Workflow

```bash
# STEP 1: Identify the problem type from metrics
# CPU > 80%: CPU-bound → use CPU profiler (async-profiler)
# CPU < 20%, threads BLOCKED/WAITING: I/O-bound → thread dump + DB analysis
# Frequent Full GC, growing heap: Memory → heap dump analysis
# High response time variability: GC pauses → GC log analysis

# STEP 2a: CPU Profiling with async-profiler
# Download: https://github.com/async-profiler/async-profiler

# Profile for 60 seconds, output flame graph:
./asprof -d 60 -f /tmp/flamegraph.html <pid>

# Or attach to running JVM:
./asprof start <pid>
sleep 60
./asprof stop -f /tmp/flamegraph.html <pid>

# Profile allocation (find what's allocating most):
./asprof -e alloc -d 60 -f /tmp/alloc.html <pid>

# STEP 2b: Thread dump for I/O / deadlock analysis:
jcmd <pid> Thread.print > /tmp/threads.txt
# OR:
jstack <pid> > /tmp/threads.txt

# STEP 2c: Java Flight Recorder (JFR):
# Enable on startup:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=/tmp/recording.jfr,\
     duration=60s,settings=profile -jar myapp.jar

# Trigger recording on running app:
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/recording.jfr
# Open in JDK Mission Control (JMC) for analysis
```

## Reading Flame Graphs

```
FLAME GRAPH READING GUIDE:

  Width of block = % of CPU time spent in that method (and its callees)
  Height = call depth (bottom = main, top = leaf methods)

  HOT SPOT EXAMPLE:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                   CPU TIME (100%)                    │
  ├───────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┤
  │  Jackson.serialize()  │  Other stuff (45%)           │
  │  (55% of CPU time!)   │                              │
  ├────────────────────┬──┤                              │
  │ObjectMapper.write()│  │                              │
  ├────────────────────┤  │                              │
  │JsonGenerator      │  │                              │
  └───────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

  → Jackson serialization taking 55% of CPU
  → FIX: Use Jackson streaming API, pre-configure ObjectMapper,
          or reduce serialization frequency

  ANOTHER PATTERN — I/O waits (not CPU):
  If flame graph shows mostly WAITING state in threads
  → threads blocked waiting for I/O, not consuming CPU
  → CPU profiler won't help — use thread dump + DB EXPLAIN ANALYZE
```

## Thread Dump Analysis

```
THREAD DUMP SECTIONS:

Normal state (RUNNABLE executing code):
"http-nio-8080-exec-1" #25 daemon prio=5
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
   at com.example.OrderService.calculateTotal(OrderService.java:45)
   at com.example.OrderController.createOrder(OrderController.java:78)

Blocked on DB (normal for DB calls):
"http-nio-8080-exec-2" #26 daemon prio=5
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
   at java.net.SocketInputStream.read(Native Method)  ← Waiting for DB response
   at org.postgresql.core.QueryExecutor.execute(...)

Blocked on lock (potential deadlock):
"http-nio-8080-exec-3"
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
   waiting to lock <0x7f45b1c23400> (a com.example.OrderService)
   at com.example.OrderService.reserve(...)
   - owned by: "http-nio-8080-exec-7"  ← exec-7 owns the lock exec-3 needs

"http-nio-8080-exec-7"
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED
   waiting to lock <0x7f45b1c23401> (a com.example.InventoryService)
   at com.example.InventoryService.update(...)
   - owned by: "http-nio-8080-exec-3"  ← DEADLOCK! 3 waits on 7, 7 waits on 3

DEADLOCK FOUND:
  exec-3 owns lock A, waiting for lock B
  exec-7 owns lock B, waiting for lock A → DEADLOCK
  FIX: Always acquire locks in the same order, or use tryLock() with timeout
```

## Instrumentation with Micrometer

```java
// Add timing to your hot paths:
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final MeterRegistry meterRegistry;
    private final Timer orderCreationTimer;
    private final Counter orderErrorCounter;

    public OrderService(MeterRegistry meterRegistry) {
        this.meterRegistry = meterRegistry;
        this.orderCreationTimer = Timer.builder("order.creation")
            .description("Time to create an order")
            .tag("service", "order")
            .publishPercentiles(0.5, 0.95, 0.99)  // Percentiles
            .register(meterRegistry);
        this.orderErrorCounter = Counter.builder("order.errors")
            .tag("type", "creation")
            .register(meterRegistry);
    }

    public Order createOrder(CreateOrderRequest request) {
        return orderCreationTimer.recordCallable(() -> {
            // All the work happens here — timed automatically
            Order order = buildOrder(request);
            validateInventory(order);
            processPayment(order);
            return orderRepository.save(order);
        });
    }
}
// Prometheus metrics exposed at /actuator/prometheus:
// order_creation_seconds_count, order_creation_seconds_sum
// order_creation_seconds{quantile="0.95"} 0.245  ← p95 latency: 245ms
```

## Production Reality

async-profiler is the go-to tool for production CPU profiling — it uses perf_events or AsyncGetCallTrace to sample with < 2% overhead and doesn't suffer the safepoint bias of earlier JVM profilers (which only sample at safepoints, missing some hot paths). For continuous observability, enable JFR with a low-overhead settings profile (`settings=jdk.jfr.consumer.defaults`) — it captures GC events, thread events, exceptions, and lock waits continuously with < 1% overhead. Enable it by default in production.

domains/java/profiling-debugging.title: Profiling Java Applications

domains/java/kafka-architecture.spoken:
Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. Unlike a traditional message queue where messages are deleted after consumption, Kafka retains records for a configurable period — usually 7 days — and consumers track their position in the log using offsets. This means you can replay events, have multiple independent consumer groups each reading the same topic, and even replay historical events from the beginning.

Topics are divided into partitions, and partitions are the unit of both ordering and parallelism. Within a partition, records are strictly ordered. Across partitions, there's no ordering guarantee. When you produce a record, you choose a partition — either randomly, by round-robin, or by a key that deterministically maps to a partition. Records with the same key always go to the same partition, which is how you guarantee ordering for related events.

Consumer groups enable parallel consumption. Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer within a group. With three partitions and three consumers in a group, each consumer handles one partition. Adding a fourth consumer leaves one idle — you can't have more active consumers than partitions.
domains/java/kafka-architecture.deep:
## Kafka Architecture

```
Kafka Cluster (3 brokers)
├── Topic: orders (3 partitions)
│   ├── Partition 0: [msg0, msg1, msg4, msg7]
│   ├── Partition 1: [msg2, msg5, msg8]
│   └── Partition 2: [msg3, msg6, msg9]
│
├── Producer: sends messages → partitioner decides which partition
└── Consumer Group "inventory-service"
    ├── Consumer 1 → reads Partition 0
    ├── Consumer 2 → reads Partition 1
    └── Consumer 3 → reads Partition 2
    (3 partitions, 3 consumers: perfect balance)
```

## Key Concepts

| Concept | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| Topic | Named stream (like a log file) |
| Partition | Ordered, immutable sequence within topic |
| Offset | Record's position within partition |
| Producer | Writes records to partitions |
| Consumer | Reads records, tracks offset |
| Consumer Group | Shares partitions for parallel consumption |
| Broker | Kafka server node |
| Replication | Partitions replicated across brokers for fault tolerance |

## Offset Management

```
Partition 0: [msg0] [msg1] [msg2] [msg3] [msg4]
              off=0   off=1   off=2   off=3   off=4

Consumer committed offset: 3
→ Consumer has processed up to msg2 (offset 2)
→ Next read will start at offset 3 (msg3)

If consumer restarts → reads from offset 3 (no messages lost, no duplicates
if exactly-once enabled)
```

## Replication for Fault Tolerance

```
Partition 0, replication-factor=3:
  Leader:   Broker 1 (reads and writes go here)
  Follower: Broker 2 (replicates from leader)
  Follower: Broker 3 (replicates from leader)

If Broker 1 fails:
  Zookeeper/KRaft elects Broker 2 or 3 as new leader
  Producers/consumers reconnect to new leader automatically
```
domains/java/kafka-architecture.question: What is Apache Kafka and what are its core architectural concepts?
domains/java/kafka-architecture.title: Kafka Core Concepts

domains/java/kafka-patterns.spoken:
A consumer group lets multiple consumers divide the work of processing a topic. Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer in the group. If you have 6 partitions and 3 consumers, each consumer handles 2 partitions concurrently. This is how Kafka achieves horizontal scalability — you increase partitions and consumers together to increase throughput.

The partition count is the ceiling on parallelism. If you have 6 partitions and 8 consumers in the same group, 2 consumers sit idle because there are no partitions to assign them. Conversely, if you need more throughput from an existing topic, you can increase the partition count — but partitions can only be added, never removed, so plan capacity in advance.

Multiple consumer groups are a powerful pattern. A topic can be consumed by many completely independent groups, each maintaining its own offset. Your order-service can consume the payments topic to update order status, while analytics-service consumes the same topic to update dashboards, and audit-service consumes it for compliance logging. Each group progresses at its own pace without affecting the others.
domains/java/kafka-patterns.question: How do Kafka consumer groups work and how do partitions enable parallel processing?
domains/java/kafka-patterns.title: Kafka Consumer Groups and Partitions

domains/java/spring-kafka.spoken:
Spring Kafka provides a KafkaTemplate abstraction similar to JdbcTemplate. It handles serialization and producer lifecycle, exposing a clean API for sending messages. The send method returns a CompletableFuture for async success/failure handling without blocking.

On the consumer side, @KafkaListener works like @RabbitListener — annotate a method with the topic and consumer group, and Spring handles polling, deserialization, and offset management. Spring Boot auto-configures everything from your application.yml.

You write custom bean configuration mainly when you need multiple producer configurations — different serializers for different topics, or different error handling per listener.

domains/java/spring-kafka.title: Spring Kafka Setup and KafkaTemplate

domains/java/gradle.spoken:
Maven and Gradle both handle dependency management, compilation, testing, and packaging, but they take fundamentally different approaches. Maven uses XML and a fixed lifecycle — you configure plugins to hook into predefined phases. This makes Maven predictable and easy to understand, but rigid when you need to do something unconventional.

Gradle uses a Groovy or Kotlin DSL and is far more flexible — build logic is actual code, not configuration. This makes complex builds easier to express, and makes it straightforward to add custom tasks. The other major advantage is performance: Gradle tracks which inputs and outputs have changed and only rebuilds what's necessary. Its build cache can even reuse outputs from other machines, which makes a huge difference in CI for large projects.

For a new Spring Boot microservice, either works well. I'd choose Gradle if the project is complex with many custom build steps, if it's part of a large multi-project build where incremental compilation matters, or if the team already knows Gradle. I'd choose Maven if the team is primarily Java-focused with strong Maven familiarity and you want maximum ecosystem compatibility and tooling support.
domains/java/gradle.question: What are the key differences between Gradle and Maven, and when should you choose each?
domains/java/gradle.title: Gradle vs Maven

domains/java/maven.spoken:
Maven is a build tool that manages the entire lifecycle of a Java project — from downloading dependencies to compiling, testing, packaging, and deploying. Everything is driven by pom.xml, the Project Object Model, which declares the project's identity through groupId, artifactId and version, its dependencies, and how to build it.

Spring Boot projects inherit from spring-boot-starter-parent, which is a carefully curated POM that sets up sensible defaults — Java version, encoding, plugin configuration, and most importantly, a dependency management section with compatible versions for hundreds of libraries. When you add spring-boot-starter-web without a version, Maven resolves the correct compatible version from the parent.

The dependency scope determines when a dependency is on the classpath. Compile is the default — available everywhere. Test is only for test compilation and execution, not packaged into the final JAR. Runtime is needed at runtime but not to compile the application — like a database driver. Provided means the container or runtime provides it, so don't include it in the JAR — like servlet-api when deploying to a server.
domains/java/maven.deep:
## Standard Spring Boot pom.xml

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <!-- Inherit Spring Boot defaults: dependency management, plugin config -->
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>3.2.5</version>
        <relativePath/>
    </parent>

    <!-- Project identity (GAV) -->
    <groupId>com.mycompany</groupId>
    <artifactId>order-service</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <packaging>jar</packaging>

    <properties>
        <java.version>21</java.version>
        <!-- Override any dependency version from parent BOM -->
        <postgresql.version>42.7.3</postgresql.version>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <!-- Compile scope (default) -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
            <!-- No version needed — resolved from parent BOM -->
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
        </dependency>

        <!-- Runtime scope — driver not needed to compile, just to run -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
            <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
            <scope>runtime</scope>
        </dependency>

        <!-- Test scope — only in test classpath -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <!-- Spring Boot plugin: repackage into executable fat JAR -->
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <configuration>
                    <excludes>
                        <exclude>
                            <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
                            <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
                        </exclude>
                    </excludes>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
```

## Key Maven Commands

```bash
./mvnw clean package          # clean + compile + test + package JAR
./mvnw clean package -DskipTests  # skip tests (not recommended for CI)
./mvnw test                   # run tests only
./mvnw spring-boot:run        # run Spring Boot app directly
./mvnw dependency:tree        # show full dependency tree
./mvnw dependency:analyze     # find unused/undeclared dependencies
./mvnw help:effective-pom     # show final resolved POM
./mvnw versions:display-dependency-updates  # check for newer dependency versions
```

## Dependency Scopes

| Scope | Compile | Test | Runtime | Packaged |
|-------|---------|------|---------|----------|
| compile | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| test | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| runtime | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| provided | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
