domains/java/maven.title: Maven POM and Project Structure

domains/java/api-gateway.spoken:
An API Gateway is the single entry point for all client requests. Instead of clients knowing about 10 different microservice URLs, they talk to the gateway, which routes requests to the appropriate service. This solves multiple problems: clients don't need to track service URLs, you can do auth/rate-limiting once at the gateway instead of in every service, and you can do protocol translation (HTTP/2 externally, HTTP/1.1 internally).

Spring Cloud Gateway is the Spring ecosystem's gateway built on Reactor — it's non-blocking and handles routing via predicates (path matching, header matching) and filters (add/remove headers, rate limiting, circuit breaking).

The main risk is that the gateway becomes a bottleneck or single point of failure. Keep it stateless, deploy it as multiple instances, and keep business logic out of it — it should only route and apply cross-cutting concerns.
domains/java/api-gateway.question: What is an API Gateway and what problems does it solve in a microservices architecture?
domains/java/api-gateway.title: API Gateway Pattern

domains/java/circuit-breaker.spoken:
A Circuit Breaker protects your service from cascading failures when a downstream dependency is struggling. It works like a real circuit breaker: in CLOSED state it passes requests through normally; when failures exceed a threshold, it trips to OPEN and fails fast without calling the downstream service; after a wait period, it moves to HALF_OPEN and lets a few test requests through to see if the service has recovered.

With Resilience4j in Spring Boot, you annotate the method with `@CircuitBreaker` and specify a `fallbackMethod`. The fallback receives the exception and returns a default or cached response, keeping the user experience degraded-but-functional instead of completely broken.

The key metric to configure is `failureRateThreshold` — at what percentage of failures should the circuit open? Combined with `slidingWindowSize` (how many recent calls to evaluate), you tune sensitivity to failure.
domains/java/circuit-breaker.question: What is the Circuit Breaker pattern and how do you implement it with Resilience4j in Spring Boot?
domains/java/circuit-breaker.title: Circuit Breaker Pattern

domains/java/distributed-tracing.spoken:
Distributed tracing answers the question: "For this user request that touched 5 services, where did it spend its time and where did it fail?" Each request gets a unique trace ID that propagates through all services via HTTP headers. Each service creates spans — one span per service involvement — and reports them to a centralized backend like Zipkin or Jaeger, which stitches them into a waterfall timeline.

In Spring Boot 3, this is done with Micrometer Tracing (which replaced Spring Cloud Sleuth). You add the dependency, configure a sampling rate and exporter, and trace propagation happens automatically — RestTemplate, WebClient, and Feign clients all propagate the trace context without any code changes.

The critical operational insight: always include the trace ID in your log output via MDC. When a user reports an issue with a request ID, you can search logs across all services using that single trace ID and reconstruct exactly what happened.
domains/java/distributed-tracing.question: How do you implement distributed tracing in Spring Boot microservices?
domains/java/distributed-tracing.title: Distributed Tracing with Micrometer and Zipkin

domains/java/fundamentals.spoken:
Microservices decompose an application into independently deployable services, each owning its own data store and business capability. The key trade-off is that you gain independent scaling, deployment, and team autonomy at the cost of distributed systems complexity: network failures, eventual consistency, cross-service tracing, and operational overhead.

For a small team or early-stage product, a well-structured monolith is almost always the right choice — it's easier to refactor, test, deploy, and reason about. Microservices make sense when you have multiple teams stepping on each other's deployments, when different parts of the system have dramatically different scaling needs, or when you need to use different technology stacks for different capabilities.

The classic guidance: start with a monolith, identify seams where services naturally want to form, and extract when the pain of staying monolithic outweighs the cost of distribution.
domains/java/fundamentals.deep:
## Monolith vs Microservices — Honest Comparison

```
Dimension           | Monolith              | Microservices
--------------------|-----------------------|---------------------------
Deployment          | One artifact          | 10s or 100s of services
Development speed   | Fast initially        | Slower start, scales well
Testing             | Simpler (in-process)  | Complex (inter-service)
Debugging           | Stack trace           | Distributed tracing
Data consistency    | ACID transactions     | Eventual consistency
Scaling             | Scale entire app      | Scale hot services only
Team structure      | One team feasible     | Team per service (Conway)
Infrastructure      | Simple                | Service mesh, registries
Local development   | One process           | Docker Compose / minikube
Operational cost    | Low                   | High (Kubernetes, mesh)
```

## When Microservices Make Sense

```
GOOD INDICATORS:
  ✓ Multiple teams (5+ developers per domain)
  ✓ Different scaling requirements:
    - Search service: CPU-heavy, needs 20 instances
    - Auth service: low traffic, 2 instances fine
    - Upload service: I/O heavy, needs more disk
  ✓ Different release cadences:
    - Core order service: monthly release (stable)
    - Recommendation service: weekly releases
  ✓ Technology diversity justified:
    - ML model service in Python
    - High-performance matching engine in Go
    - Core business logic in Java
  ✓ Compliance isolation:
    - Payment processing needs PCI scope isolation
    - GDPR-sensitive user data separate from analytics

WARNING SIGNS:
  ✗ Team of 3 people with 10 microservices
  ✗ All services deployed together anyway
  ✗ Distributed monolith (services tightly coupled via sync calls)
  ✗ Shared database across services
  ✗ No observability (logging, tracing, metrics) in place
```

## Service Boundary Design — Domain-Driven

```java
// WRONG: Technical layers as services
service: UserDataService     // All user data access
service: EmailService        // All email sending
service: DatabaseService     // Shared DB access

// RIGHT: Business capabilities as services
service: OrderService        // Order placement, order management
service: InventoryService    // Stock levels, reservations
service: PaymentService      // Payment processing, refunds
service: NotificationService // Email, SMS, push notifications
service: UserService         // User profiles, preferences

// Each service:
//   - Has its OWN database (no shared DB!)
//   - Owns its domain entities end-to-end
//   - Exposes an API (REST or events)
//   - Can be deployed independently
```

## Data Ownership Rule

```
CRITICAL RULE: Each service owns its data.
No direct DB queries from Service A into Service B's DB.

WRONG:
OrderService → SELECT * FROM users WHERE user_id = ?  (UserService's DB!)

RIGHT:
OrderService → GET /api/users/42 (UserService's API)
             OR
OrderService caches the user info it needs at order creation time
             OR
OrderService subscribes to UserUpdatedEvent to keep local copy

Reason: if two services share a DB, they're not independent —
schema change in shared DB breaks both, defeats the purpose.
```

## Production Reality

For an interview, a good answer acknowledges both sides. You've worked in a monolith, you know the benefits (simplicity, easy refactoring). You understand microservices trade-offs and would only advocate for them when team size and operational maturity justify the complexity. Mentioning Conway's Law — that your architecture will reflect your team communication structure — shows architectural maturity.
domains/java/fundamentals.question: What are microservices and when should you choose them over a monolith?
domains/java/fundamentals.title: Microservices vs Monolith

domains/java/saga-pattern.spoken:
In microservices, you can't use a single ACID transaction that spans multiple services, because each service has its own database. The Saga pattern breaks a distributed transaction into a sequence of local transactions in each service, connected by events or commands. If a step fails, previously completed steps are undone using compensating transactions.

There are two approaches: choreography, where each service publishes events and other services react, and orchestration, where a central saga orchestrator sends commands to each service in sequence. Choreography is simpler to implement but harder to visualize and debug. Orchestration gives you a clear control flow and is easier to reason about, at the cost of a central coordinator that becomes a critical component.

The key limitation to acknowledge: sagas provide eventual consistency, not ACID. Between step 2 completing and step 3 starting, the data is in a temporarily inconsistent state. Your business rules must tolerate this.
domains/java/saga-pattern.question: How do you handle distributed transactions in microservices using the Saga pattern?
domains/java/saga-pattern.title: Saga Pattern for Distributed Transactions

domains/java/service-discovery.spoken:
Service discovery solves the problem of dynamic service addresses. In a containerized environment, services spin up and down with different IPs and ports. Rather than hardcoding addresses, each service registers itself with a central registry (Eureka Server) including its host, port, and health status.

When Service A needs to call Service B, instead of using a hardcoded URL, it asks the registry for instances of 'ORDER-SERVICE', gets back a list, and picks one (client-side load balancing). Spring Cloud makes this transparent: you just annotate your RestTemplate or WebClient with `@LoadBalanced` and use the service name as the hostname.

In Kubernetes, you'd typically use Kubernetes native service discovery (DNS-based, via Services and kube-dns) rather than Eureka, since K8s already provides this functionality built-in.
domains/java/service-discovery.question: How does service discovery work in Spring Cloud using Eureka?
domains/java/service-discovery.title: Service Discovery with Eureka

domains/java/advanced-features.spoken:
For JSONB indexing, the choice of GIN operator class matters. The default GIN index supports both @> containment queries and ? key-existence queries but stores more data. Using jsonb_path_ops gives a smaller, faster index but only supports @> containment — no key-existence checks.

For frequently queried specific keys, an expression index on the extracted text value is faster than a full GIN index because it's a smaller, more targeted B-tree index. Something like an index on (metadata ->> 'brand') enables fast equality and range queries on that single key.

jsonpath is the modern way to write complex JSON traversal. It's a path language similar to XPath for XML that can filter arrays, navigate nested objects, and apply predicates in a single readable expression rather than chaining multiple operators.
domains/java/advanced-features.deep:
## GIN Index Options

```sql
-- Default GIN: supports @>, ?, ?|, ?&
CREATE INDEX idx_meta_gin ON products USING GIN (metadata);

-- jsonb_path_ops: smaller, faster for @> only
CREATE INDEX idx_meta_path ON products USING GIN (metadata jsonb_path_ops);
-- Use when you only need containment queries

-- Expression index: for equality on a known key
CREATE INDEX idx_meta_brand ON products ((metadata ->> 'brand'));
-- Supports: WHERE metadata ->> 'brand' = 'TechCo' with B-tree efficiency
```

## Advanced Queries

```sql
-- Containment: products with both tags
WHERE metadata @> '{"tags": ["laptop", "pro"]}'::jsonb;

-- Key exists
WHERE metadata ? 'discount_code';

-- jsonpath: products with ram > 8
WHERE metadata @@ '$.specs.ram > 8';

-- jsonpath exists: has any item with price < 100 in array
WHERE jsonb_path_exists(metadata, '$.items[*] ? (@.price < 100)');

-- jsonpath query: extract matching items
SELECT jsonb_path_query_array(metadata, '$.items[*] ? (@.category == "electronics")')
FROM orders;
```

## Expand JSONB for Aggregation

```sql
-- Expand array of order items to rows
SELECT order_id,
       item ->> 'product_id' AS product_id,
       (item ->> 'quantity')::INT AS qty,
       (item ->> 'price')::NUMERIC AS price
FROM orders,
     jsonb_array_elements(metadata -> 'items') AS item;

-- Expand object keys to rows
SELECT product_id, key, value
FROM products,
     jsonb_each_text(metadata) AS kv(key, value)
WHERE key LIKE 'spec_%';
```

## Partial JSONB Updates in Spring

```java
@Modifying
@Query(value = """
    UPDATE products
    SET metadata = jsonb_set(metadata, '{stock}', :stock::jsonb)
    WHERE id = :id
    """, nativeQuery = true)
void updateStock(@Param("id") Long id, @Param("stock") String stock);

// Call: repo.updateStock(1L, "42");
```

domains/java/postgresql-basics.spoken:
PostgreSQL is an object-relational database that strictly follows the SQL standard and has a much richer feature set. For a Java backend, it's generally the better choice because of its support for complex data types like JSONB for flexible schema columns, arrays, range types, and powerful features like window functions, recursive CTEs, and full-text search — all built in without plugins.

MySQL historically had faster simple read performance and is simpler to set up, which made it popular for web applications in the early 2000s. But for the kind of analytical and complex transactional queries a Java backend typically runs, PostgreSQL's query planner and execution engine are generally superior.

PostgreSQL's MVCC implementation means readers never block writers and writers never block readers. A long-running report query won't hold up inserts. This is crucial for a backend that needs to handle concurrent reads and writes without one type of operation starving the other.
domains/java/postgresql-basics.deep:
## Feature Comparison

| Feature | PostgreSQL | MySQL |
|---------|-----------|-------|
| SQL compliance | Excellent | Partial |
| JSONB support | Native, indexed | JSON type, limited |
| Window functions | Full support | Basic support |
| Full-text search | Built-in | Via MyISAM or plugin |
| Array types | Native | Not supported |
| Range types | Native | Not supported |
| Partitioning | Declarative (PG10+) | Available |
| Materialized views | Supported | Not natively |
| Custom types/functions | Extensive | Limited |

## Spring Boot Configuration

```yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/appdb
    driver-class-name: org.postgresql.Driver
  jpa:
    database-platform: org.hibernate.dialect.PostgreSQLDialect
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate  # use Flyway/Liquibase for migrations
```

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
    <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>
```

domains/java/caching-patterns.spoken:
Cache-aside, also called lazy loading, is the most common caching pattern. When the application needs data, it first checks the cache. If the data is there — a cache hit — it returns immediately without touching the database. If not — a cache miss — it fetches from the database, stores the result in the cache for future requests, and returns the data. This pattern is lazy: data only enters the cache when it's actually requested.

Spring Cache makes this almost invisible. The @Cacheable annotation on a service method automatically implements the check-and-load logic. Spring checks if a result is cached for the given key; if so, returns it without executing the method; if not, executes the method and caches the result before returning. You write normal service code and the caching just works.

The critical counterpart is @CacheEvict for maintaining consistency. When you update or delete a user, the cached version is stale. Annotating the update method with @CacheEvict removes that entry from Redis, forcing the next read to fetch fresh data from the database. A common mistake is forgetting to evict on updates, which leads to users seeing outdated data until the TTL expires.

domains/java/caching-patterns.title: Cache-Aside Pattern with Spring

domains/java/redis-data-structures.spoken:
Redis is an in-memory data structure store that operates at sub-millisecond latency — typically under a millisecond for simple operations. This makes it orders of magnitude faster than a relational database for the kinds of operations where raw speed matters: caching frequently queried data, storing user sessions, implementing distributed locks, and building real-time leaderboards.

The key architectural decision is that Redis is single-threaded for command execution. This means each command executes atomically without concurrent modification — no race conditions on individual operations. When two clients write the same key simultaneously, Redis serializes those writes in the order they arrive.

For a Java Spring Boot backend, the most common uses are as an L2 cache to reduce database load, as a session store for distributed sessions across multiple application instances, and as a shared distributed lock to coordinate actions that should only happen on one instance at a time — like a scheduled job or inventory reservation.
domains/java/redis-data-structures.question: What is Redis and what are its main use cases in a Java backend application?
domains/java/redis-data-structures.title: Redis Overview and Use Cases

domains/java/spring-data-redis.spoken:
Spring Boot auto-configures Lettuce as the Redis client by default. Lettuce is asynchronous and non-blocking — it uses a single connection shared across threads rather than a connection pool, which is more efficient for high-concurrency scenarios. For Spring's synchronous RedisTemplate, this still works fine because Lettuce handles multiplexing internally.

The most important configuration decision is serialization. By default, RedisTemplate uses Java serialization, which produces binary data that isn't human-readable and creates versioning issues if your classes change. Always configure explicit serializers — StringRedisSerializer for keys so they're readable in Redis CLI, and GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer for values so objects are stored as readable JSON.

For production, you'll also want connection pooling configured. Even though Lettuce uses one connection for pipelining, having a small pool allows multiple concurrent pipeline operations and provides reconnection resilience.
domains/java/spring-data-redis.question: How do you configure Spring Data Redis with Lettuce and what are the key configuration choices?
domains/java/spring-data-redis.title: Spring Data Redis Setup and Configuration

domains/java/api-design.spoken:
Good REST API design centers on resources and HTTP semantics. URLs identify resources using nouns, not verbs — `/api/orders/42` identifies an order, not an action on it. The HTTP method conveys the action: GET to read, POST to create, PUT to replace, PATCH to partially update, DELETE to remove. This lets clients and infrastructure (caches, load balancers) behave predictably.

Idempotency is critical for reliability: GET, PUT, and DELETE can be safely retried on network failures — they produce the same result. POST is not idempotent by default — sending twice creates two orders. Handle this with idempotency keys for non-idempotent operations.

Versioning strategy should be decided upfront. URL versioning (`/v1/`, `/v2/`) is the most visible and easiest for clients to adopt. Header versioning (`Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=2`) is cleaner architecturally but harder to test in a browser. Choose one and be consistent.
domains/java/api-design.question: What are the principles of good REST API design?
domains/java/api-design.title: REST API Design Best Practices

domains/java/exception-handling.spoken:
Consistent error responses are a fundamental API quality requirement. Every error, regardless of cause, should follow the same JSON structure so clients can parse errors uniformly. RFC 7807 defines a standard format — Problem Details for HTTP APIs — that includes `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, and optionally custom fields.

For validation errors, include field-level errors so clients can highlight the specific invalid fields. For business errors, include an `errorCode` that the frontend can map to user-friendly messages without relying on message text (which might change).

Never include internal details in error responses: stack traces, SQL queries, file paths, or exception class names. Log them on the server; return sanitized messages to clients. Always include a `requestId` or `correlationId` — when a user reports an error, you need to find the corresponding log entry.
domains/java/exception-handling.question: How do you design and implement consistent error responses in a REST API?
domains/java/exception-handling.title: Structured Error Responses

domains/java/rest-fundamentals.spoken:
REST — Representational State Transfer — is an architectural style with six constraints defined by Roy Fielding. The most impactful for web APIs are statelessness and uniform interface.

Statelessness means every request from client to server must contain all information needed to understand the request — no session state stored on the server. This enables horizontal scaling: any server instance can handle any request because no session affinity is needed.

Uniform interface means using standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH) with their established semantics, identifying resources by URIs, and representing them with standard formats (JSON, XML). Cacheability requires responses to declare whether they can be cached, enabling proxies and browsers to cache appropriately.

True REST is often called 'RESTful' in common usage, but most APIs don't implement all constraints (especially HATEOAS — Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State). What we commonly call REST APIs are actually HTTP APIs following most REST conventions.
domains/java/rest-fundamentals.deep:
## The Six REST Constraints

```
1. Client-Server
   - Separation of UI from data storage
   - Client manages UI; server manages data
   - Enables independent evolution of each

2. Stateless
   - Server maintains NO client state between requests
   - Each request self-contained: auth, context, parameters
   - Sessions in database (JWT carries auth state in token itself)
   - Enables: load balancing, scaling, failure recovery

3. Cacheable
   - Responses explicitly marked cacheable or not
   - Cache-Control: max-age=3600, public
   - GET responses typically cacheable; POST/PUT/DELETE not
   - Reduces server load, improves performance

4. Uniform Interface (most distinctive REST constraint)
   - Resource identification in requests (URI)
   - Resource manipulation through representations
   - Self-descriptive messages (Content-Type header)
   - HATEOAS (rarely fully implemented)

5. Layered System
   - Client can't tell if talking to origin server or proxy
   - Enables: CDN, API gateways, load balancers
   - No assumption about intermediaries

6. Code on Demand (optional)
   - Server can send executable code to client
   - E.g., JavaScript returned in API response
   - Rarely used
```

## HTTP Methods and Their Semantics

```
GET    — Read resource, no side effects, cacheable, idempotent
POST   — Create resource or trigger action, not idempotent
PUT    — Replace entire resource, idempotent (same result if called multiple times)
PATCH  — Partial update, not necessarily idempotent
DELETE — Remove resource, idempotent

Idempotent: calling N times has same result as calling once
  Idempotent: GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS
  Not idempotent: POST (creates new resource each time), PATCH (depends)

// Example:
POST /api/orders           → Creates new order each call (not idempotent)
PUT  /api/orders/42        → Replaces order 42 (idempotent)
DELETE /api/orders/42      → Deletes 42 (idempotent — deleting deleted is still deleted)
PATCH /api/orders/42       → Updates specific fields (may not be idempotent)
```

## HTTP Status Codes (Must Know)

```
2xx Success:
  200 OK           — GET, PUT, PATCH success with body
  201 Created      — POST success, include Location header
  204 No Content   — DELETE success, or PUT with no response body
  202 Accepted     — Async processing started (not completed yet)

3xx Redirection:
  301 Moved Permanently   — Resource URL changed permanently
  304 Not Modified        — Cached version is current (ETag matched)
  307 Temporary Redirect  — Redirect, keep HTTP method

4xx Client Error:
  400 Bad Request         — Malformed request, validation failure
  401 Unauthorized        — Not authenticated
  403 Forbidden           — Authenticated but insufficient permission
  404 Not Found           — Resource doesn't exist
  405 Method Not Allowed  — GET on POST-only endpoint
  409 Conflict            — Business conflict (duplicate, state conflict)
  422 Unprocessable Entity— Validation failure (alternative to 400)
  429 Too Many Requests   — Rate limited

5xx Server Error:
  500 Internal Server Error  — Unexpected server failure
  502 Bad Gateway            — Upstream service returned invalid response
  503 Service Unavailable    — Server overloaded or down for maintenance
  504 Gateway Timeout        — Upstream service timed out
```

## Statelessness in Practice

```java
// STATEFUL: server stores user's cart in session — bad for scaling
@PostMapping("/cart/add")
public Cart addToCart(
        @RequestBody Product product,
        HttpSession session) {  // Server-side state!
    Cart cart = (Cart) session.getAttribute("cart");
    if (cart == null) cart = new Cart();
    cart.add(product);
    session.setAttribute("cart", cart);
    return cart;
    // Problem: specific server must handle all requests for this user
}

// STATELESS: client sends all context; server is stateless
@PostMapping("/cart/add")
public Cart addToCart(
        @RequestBody AddToCartRequest request,
        @AuthenticationPrincipal UserDetails user) {
    // Cart stored in DB — any server can handle
    Cart cart = cartService.getOrCreateCart(user.getUsername());
    cart.add(request.getProductId(), request.getQuantity());
    return cartRepo.save(cart);
    // Any server instance can handle this — scales horizontally
}
```

## Production Reality

In interviews, knowing the HTTP method semantics is critical — especially idempotency. A retry of a `PUT` request should be safe; a retry of a `POST` might create duplicates. Design `POST` endpoints to be idempotent using client-generated idempotency keys when duplicate creation is a concern (payment systems, order creation).

domains/java/rest-fundamentals.title: REST Architectural Constraints

domains/java/spring-mvc-controllers.spoken:
`@RestController` combines `@Controller` and `@ResponseBody` — every method return value is serialized to the response body (typically JSON). You put the base URI on the class with `@RequestMapping` and use `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`, `@DeleteMapping`, `@PatchMapping` on methods.

For extracting data from the request: `@PathVariable` for URI template variables, `@RequestParam` for query parameters, `@RequestBody` for the request body (deserialized via Jackson), `@RequestHeader` for specific headers, and `@AuthenticationPrincipal` for the current user from Spring Security.

The most important design principle: controllers should be thin. They extract HTTP request data, delegate to a service method, and map the result to an HTTP response. No business logic, no data access, no complex conditionals. This makes controllers trivial to test with `@WebMvcTest` which doesn't need the full application context.
domains/java/spring-mvc-controllers.question: How do Spring MVC's request mapping annotations work and what are best practices for controller design?
domains/java/spring-mvc-controllers.title: Request Mapping and Handler Methods

domains/java/versioning.spoken:
API versioning allows you to evolve your API while maintaining backward compatibility for existing clients. There are three main strategies: URI versioning, header versioning, and query parameter versioning.

URI versioning — `/api/v1/orders`, `/api/v2/orders` — is the most widely adopted. It's explicit, easily readable in browser URL bars, and works perfectly with caching. The downside: purists argue it violates REST since the same resource has different URIs for different representations.

Header versioning — `Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json` — is technically more RESTful: the resource URI is stable, the version is part of content negotiation. But it's harder for clients to test, Swagger tooling is less straightforward, and it can interfere with caching.

In practice, URI versioning wins on simplicity and developer experience. Most major APIs (Stripe, Twilio, GitHub) use it.
domains/java/versioning.question: What are the different API versioning strategies and what are their trade-offs?
domains/java/versioning.title: API Versioning Strategies

domains/java/actuator.spoken:
Spring Boot Actuator adds production-ready operational endpoints to your application with zero configuration. Once you add the `spring-boot-starter-actuator` dependency, you immediately get HTTP endpoints for health checks, metrics, environment inspection, thread dumps, heap dumps, and much more.

In a production environment, Actuator is what your monitoring system talks to. Kubernetes uses `/actuator/health` for liveness and readiness probes. Prometheus scrapes `/actuator/prometheus` for metrics. Your ops team uses `/actuator/env` to verify configuration without SSH-ing into servers.

Security-wise, only `/actuator/health` and `/actuator/info` are exposed over HTTP by default. You explicitly enable others via `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`. This default-closed approach is intentional — endpoints like `/actuator/env` and `/actuator/heapdump` expose sensitive data and must be deliberately opened and secured.
domains/java/actuator.deep:
## Key Endpoints

| Endpoint | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `/actuator/health` | App and dependency health status |
| `/actuator/metrics` | Counter, gauge, timer metrics |
| `/actuator/info` | App version, git info, custom data |
| `/actuator/env` | All environment properties |
| `/actuator/loggers` | View/change log levels at runtime |
| `/actuator/mappings` | All registered request mappings |
| `/actuator/threaddump` | JVM thread dump |
| `/actuator/prometheus` | Prometheus-format metrics |

## Enabling Endpoints

```properties
# Expose all endpoints over HTTP
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*

# Expose specific endpoints
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,loggers

# Change base path (default is /actuator)
management.endpoints.web.base-path=/management

# Run actuator on a different port (recommended for internal-only access)
management.server.port=8081
```

## Production Reality

Run Actuator on a separate management port (`management.server.port=8081`) and restrict that port to your internal network via firewall rules. This is simpler and more reliable than trying to secure individual endpoints with Spring Security rules.
domains/java/actuator.question: What is Spring Boot Actuator and why is it useful?
domains/java/actuator.title: Spring Boot Actuator

domains/java/application-properties.spoken:
The simplest way to configure the server port is with `server.port=8081` in `application.properties` or `application.yml`. But Spring Boot's property binding supports multiple override mechanisms with a strict precedence order.

Command-line arguments have the highest priority: `java -jar app.jar --server.port=8082`. Environment variables come next: `SERVER_PORT=8082`. Then profile-specific property files, then `application.properties`, and finally the default of 8080.

Setting `server.port=0` is a useful trick for integration tests — Spring Boot assigns any available free port at startup, and you can inject the actual port via `@LocalServerPort`. This avoids port conflicts when running tests in parallel.
domains/java/application-properties.deep:
## Configuration Methods

```properties
# application.properties
server.port=8081
```

```yaml
# application.yml
server:
  port: 8081
```

```bash
# Command-line (highest priority)
java -jar app.jar --server.port=8082

# Environment variable
export SERVER_PORT=8082
```

## Property Source Precedence (highest to lowest)

1. Command-line arguments
2. System properties (`-Dserver.port=8082`)
3. Environment variables
4. Profile-specific files (`application-prod.properties`)
5. `application.properties`
6. Default (`@Value` defaults)

## Random Port for Tests

```java
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
class ApiTest {
    @LocalServerPort
    private int port;

    @Test
    void testEndpoint() {
        // Use 'port' variable — no hardcoded port
        RestTemplate rt = new RestTemplate();
        rt.getForObject("http://localhost:" + port + "/api/health", String.class);
    }
}
```

## Production Reality

Never hardcode ports in `application.properties` for production deployments. Use environment variables instead — it keeps the same artifact deployable across environments and avoids merge conflicts when different teams change the port.
domains/java/application-properties.question: How do you configure the server port in Spring Boot?
domains/java/application-properties.title: Configuring Server Port

domains/java/auto-configuration.spoken:
Spring Boot auto-configuration automatically configures your application based on the jars on the classpath. When you add spring-boot-starter-web, Spring Boot detects Spring MVC and Tomcat are present and configures a DispatcherServlet, an embedded Tomcat server, and Jackson — all without you writing a single line of config.

The mechanism works through `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, which is included in `@SpringBootApplication`. It loads a list of configuration classes from `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` in Spring Boot 3, or `spring.factories` in Boot 2. Each of those classes uses conditional annotations — mainly `@ConditionalOnClass` to check if a library is present, and `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` to back off if you've already defined your own bean.

The key design principle is: sensible defaults you can always override. If you define your own `DataSource` bean, Spring Boot detects it and skips creating one. Run your app with `debug=true` to see the full conditions report — it shows exactly what was configured and what was skipped and why.
domains/java/auto-configuration.question: What is Spring Boot auto-configuration and how does it work?
domains/java/auto-configuration.title: Spring Boot Auto-Configuration

domains/java/devtools-profiles.spoken:
Profiles in Spring allow you to group configuration and bean definitions that should be active in a particular environment. When a profile is active, Spring loads a corresponding `application-{profile}.properties` file that overrides or extends the base `application.properties`.

Beyond property files, you can annotate beans with `@Profile("prod")` so they're only registered in the Spring context when the `prod` profile is active. This is useful for things like using a real email service in production and a stub in development.

You activate a profile in multiple ways: `spring.profiles.active=prod` in properties, `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod` as an environment variable, or `--spring.profiles.active=prod` as a command-line argument. You can activate multiple profiles simultaneously — they're additive, not exclusive.
domains/java/devtools-profiles.question: What are Spring profiles and how do you use them?
domains/java/devtools-profiles.title: Spring Profiles

domains/java/embedded-servers.spoken:
Embedded Tomcat is a fully functional Servlet container packaged inside your Spring Boot application JAR. When you include `spring-boot-starter-web`, Spring Boot auto-configures and starts Tomcat as part of the application startup — no external Tomcat installation required.

This fundamentally changed Java deployment. Before Spring Boot, you'd package a WAR file and deploy it to an already-running Tomcat instance. With embedded Tomcat, your application is `java -jar app.jar` — portable, consistent, and deployable anywhere a JVM runs. The same artifact runs on a developer's laptop and in production without environment-specific configuration of an external server.

Spring Boot starts Tomcat programmatically using `TomcatServletWebServerFactory`, registers the Spring DispatcherServlet into Tomcat's servlet context, and Tomcat begins accepting HTTP connections. From the outside, it's indistinguishable from a traditional Tomcat deployment.
domains/java/embedded-servers.question: What is embedded Tomcat and how does it work in Spring Boot?
domains/java/embedded-servers.title: Embedded Tomcat

domains/java/testing.spoken:
`@SpringBootTest` loads the complete Spring application context — all your beans, auto-configurations, and the embedded server if you choose. It's the annotation for integration tests where you need to verify that components work together correctly.

The `webEnvironment` attribute controls the server setup. `MOCK` — the default — creates a mock servlet environment without starting a real HTTP server, used with `MockMvc`. `RANDOM_PORT` starts a real embedded server on a random port — use `@LocalServerPort` to inject the actual port. `NONE` loads the context without any web environment.

The key judgment call is when to use `@SpringBootTest`. It's slower than focused slice tests because it loads everything. Use it when you're testing cross-cutting concerns, database interactions end-to-end, or HTTP layer integration. For testing just the web layer, use `@WebMvcTest`. For just the data layer, use `@DataJpaTest`. Don't use `@SpringBootTest` by default for every test.
domains/java/testing.question: What is @SpringBootTest and when should you use it?
domains/java/testing.title: @SpringBootTest

domains/java/aop.spoken:
Spring AOP has five core concepts. An **aspect** is a class annotated with `@Aspect` that encapsulates cross-cutting logic — logging, security checks, transaction management. A **join point** is a point in program execution where advice can be applied — in Spring AOP, this is always a method invocation. A **pointcut** is an expression that selects which join points to intercept. **Advice** is the code that runs at a join point, with types: `@Before` (before the method), `@After` (always after), `@Around` (wraps the method), `@AfterReturning` (on success), `@AfterThrowing` (on exception).

Spring AOP is proxy-based — it creates a CGLIB or JDK dynamic proxy around your bean. This means it can only intercept method calls made through the Spring proxy. Calling a method within the same class — `this.method()` — bypasses the proxy and AOP doesn't fire.
domains/java/aop.question: What are the core concepts of Spring AOP?
domains/java/aop.title: AOP Core Concepts

domains/java/bean-lifecycle.spoken:
The Spring bean lifecycle has several distinct phases. First, the bean is instantiated via constructor. Then Spring performs dependency injection — setting `@Autowired` fields, calling setter methods. Then `BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization()` runs — this is where AOP proxies are created. Then the initialization callback runs — `@PostConstruct` method or `afterPropertiesSet()`. Then `BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization()` runs — the bean is wrapped in its final proxy form. The bean is now ready to serve requests.

At shutdown, Spring calls the destroy callback — `@PreDestroy` method or `destroy()`. This is where you release resources: close connections, flush buffers, cancel scheduled tasks.

The `BeanPostProcessor` hooks are the most powerful and least understood. Spring's AOP, transaction management, caching, and Spring Security all work by registering `BeanPostProcessor` implementations that wrap your beans in proxies during this lifecycle phase.
domains/java/bean-lifecycle.question: What are the phases of a Spring bean's lifecycle?
domains/java/bean-lifecycle.title: Spring Bean Lifecycle

domains/java/custom-components.spoken:
Custom validation has two parts. First, define an annotation with `@Constraint(validatedBy = YourValidator.class)` — this links the annotation to its implementation. The annotation must have three mandatory attributes: `message`, `groups`, and `payload`. Second, implement `ConstraintValidator<YourAnnotation, ValueType>`, which has two methods: `initialize()` for setup from annotation attributes, and `isValid()` containing the actual validation logic.

Spring integrates with JSR-303 bean validation. When your controller receives a request body annotated with `@Valid`, it triggers validation on all fields. Your custom constraint works the same as built-in ones like `@NotNull` or `@Email`.

For cross-field validation — like confirming password matches confirmation field — you create a class-level annotation and a `ConstraintValidator<YourAnnotation, YourClass>` that receives the entire object to compare fields.
domains/java/custom-components.question: How do you create a custom bean validation constraint?
domains/java/custom-components.title: Custom Bean Validation

domains/java/dependency-injection.spoken:
Spring supports three types of dependency injection: constructor, setter, and field injection.

Constructor injection is the recommended approach. Dependencies are passed as constructor parameters, making them mandatory and immutable once set. The class is honest about what it needs — you can see all dependencies at a glance. And crucially, you can instantiate the class in a plain unit test without Spring, just `new MyService(mockDep1, mockDep2)`.

Setter injection is for optional dependencies. You inject via a `@Autowired` setter method, which means the object can be created without the dependency and configured later. Useful for optional plugins or when you need to change a dependency after construction.

Field injection uses `@Autowired` directly on a field. It looks concise but it's the worst option — you can't inject dependencies without reflection, making unit testing painful. You either use Spring context in tests or use field injection workarounds. Avoid it for anything other than test classes.
domains/java/dependency-injection.question: What are the different types of dependency injection in Spring?
domains/java/dependency-injection.title: Types of Dependency Injection

domains/java/spring-internals.spoken:
`BeanFactory` is Spring's basic IoC container interface — it creates beans, manages dependencies, and provides bean retrieval. `ApplicationContext` extends `BeanFactory` and adds enterprise-level features.

The additions in `ApplicationContext` include event publishing via `ApplicationEventPublisher`, resource loading via `ResourceLoader`, internationalization support, automatic `BeanPostProcessor` registration, and automatic `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` registration. Most importantly, `ApplicationContext` eagerly creates all singleton beans at startup, which catches configuration errors immediately.

`BeanFactory` creates beans lazily — only when first requested. In practice, nobody uses `BeanFactory` directly in application code. Spring Boot's `SpringApplication` always creates an `ApplicationContext`. `BeanFactory` awareness is useful for understanding Spring internals.
domains/java/spring-internals.question: What is the difference between ApplicationContext and BeanFactory?
domains/java/spring-internals.title: ApplicationContext vs BeanFactory

domains/java/entity-relationships.spoken:
A `@OneToMany` relationship maps one entity to a collection of another. The critical parameter is `mappedBy` — it tells JPA that the foreign key lives on the many side, not in a join table. Without `mappedBy`, JPA creates an unnecessary join table.

`FetchType.LAZY` is the default for `@OneToMany` and you should keep it that way. If you change it to EAGER, every query for the parent entity will join and load all children — even when you only need the parent's fields. This causes significant performance problems at scale.

For bidirectional relationships, you must keep both sides in sync. When adding an item to an order, you set `item.setOrder(order)` and also `order.getItems().add(item)`. A helper method on the parent entity — `addItem(Item item)` — keeps this in sync and prevents inconsistent state.
domains/java/entity-relationships.question: How do you map a @OneToMany relationship and what are the key considerations?
domains/java/entity-relationships.title: @OneToMany Relationship

domains/java/hibernate-internals.spoken:
`SessionFactory` is a heavyweight, thread-safe factory created once per application — it holds class metadata, the second-level cache, and connection pool references. Creating it is expensive, so it's a singleton.

`Session` is a lightweight, per-request object that wraps a JDBC connection. It's not thread-safe — you should never share a Session between threads. It represents a unit of work: it maintains the first-level cache and tracks dirty entities within a transaction.

In Spring, you typically don't work with `SessionFactory` and `Session` directly. Spring wraps them with `EntityManagerFactory` and `EntityManager` from the JPA spec. When you annotate a method with `@Transactional`, Spring opens an `EntityManager` (backed by a Hibernate Session), binds it to the thread, and closes it when the method completes.
domains/java/hibernate-internals.question: What is the difference between SessionFactory and Session in Hibernate, and how does Spring manage them?
domains/java/hibernate-internals.title: SessionFactory and Session

domains/java/jpa-fundamentals.spoken:
A JPA entity is a Java class mapped to a database table. The minimum requirement is `@Entity` on the class and `@Id` on the primary key field. By default, the class name becomes the table name and each field becomes a column — you override with `@Table(name = "custom_name")` and `@Column(name = "custom_column")`.

`@GeneratedValue` configures how the primary key is generated. `IDENTITY` relies on the database's auto-increment column — PostgreSQL serial, MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT. `SEQUENCE` uses a database sequence object — more efficient in bulk inserts because IDs can be pre-allocated. `AUTO` lets the provider decide.

Entities must have a no-argument constructor — Hibernate uses it to instantiate objects during query results loading. It can be `protected`, not necessarily `public`.
domains/java/jpa-fundamentals.question: What is a JPA entity and what annotations define one?
domains/java/jpa-fundamentals.title: JPA Entity Basics

domains/java/n-plus-one-problem.spoken:
The N+1 problem occurs when you load N entities and then trigger N additional queries — one for each entity — to load their associated data. You get 1 query to fetch the list, then N queries for the lazy association, totalling N+1 queries.

It happens because lazy loading is deferred: Hibernate loads a proxy instead of the actual data. When your code — or the JSON serializer — accesses the proxy, Hibernate issues another database query. If you're iterating a list of 100 orders and each access to `order.getUser()` triggers a query, you've just executed 101 queries when 1 would have sufficed.

N+1 is insidious because it's invisible in development with small datasets. With 5 orders in dev, 6 queries is fine. In production with 10,000 orders, 10,001 queries per request is catastrophic.
domains/java/n-plus-one-problem.question: What is the N+1 query problem and how does it occur in Hibernate?
domains/java/n-plus-one-problem.title: N+1 Problem Explained

domains/java/transactions.spoken:
Transaction propagation controls how a transactional method behaves when called from another transactional context.

`REQUIRED` — the default — joins an existing transaction if one is active. If not, it starts a new one. This is the right choice for most business logic: operations belong to the same unit of work.

`REQUIRES_NEW` always starts a brand new transaction, suspending any outer transaction. Use this when you need to commit independently of the calling transaction — the classic example is audit logging. If the main business transaction rolls back, you still want the audit log committed.

`NOT_SUPPORTED` runs the method without a transaction, suspending any outer transaction. Useful for long reads that shouldn't hold a transaction open. `MANDATORY` requires an active transaction and throws if none exists — use to enforce that a method must always be called within a transaction.
domains/java/transactions.question: What are the different transaction propagation behaviors in Spring?
domains/java/transactions.title: Transaction Propagation

domains/java/authentication.spoken:
Spring Security works as a chain of servlet filters that intercepts every HTTP request before it reaches your controllers. The `DelegatingFilterProxy` is registered with the servlet container and delegates to Spring's `FilterChainProxy`, which applies a `SecurityFilterChain` bean containing ordered security filters.

Each request passes through filters in order. Authentication filters check for credentials — like `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter` for form login or a custom `JwtAuthenticationFilter` for token-based auth. If authentication succeeds, the `Authentication` object is stored in `SecurityContextHolder`, which is thread-local. Downstream filters and controllers can then access the current user from it.

If an authentication or authorization failure occurs, `ExceptionTranslationFilter` intercepts the exception and either sends a 401 response or redirects to a login page.
domains/java/authentication.question: How does Spring Security's filter chain work?
domains/java/authentication.title: Spring Security Filter Chain

domains/java/authorization.spoken:
Spring Security models roles as `GrantedAuthority` objects attached to the `Authentication` token. When you call `hasRole('ADMIN')` in SpEL, Spring checks whether the authenticated user has a `GrantedAuthority` with the value `ROLE_ADMIN` — the `ROLE_` prefix is added automatically. If you use `hasAuthority()` instead, you must provide the full string including the prefix.

You configure URL-level access rules in `SecurityFilterChain` using `.authorizeHttpRequests()`, and method-level access using `@PreAuthorize`. Both approaches are complementary — URL rules protect endpoints broadly, while method security enforces finer-grained rules like resource ownership.

Roles are typically stored in a `roles` or `user_roles` table in the database and loaded when `UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername()` is called.
domains/java/authorization.question: How do you implement role-based access control in Spring Security?
domains/java/authorization.title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

domains/java/cors-csrf.spoken:
CORS — Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — is a browser security mechanism that blocks requests from one origin (like `https://myapp.com`) to a different origin (like `https://api.myapp.com`) unless the server explicitly allows it.

When a browser makes a cross-origin request, it first sends a preflight `OPTIONS` request asking the server what's allowed. The server responds with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` headers. If the response permits the actual request, the browser proceeds.

In Spring Security, CORS configuration must happen before any authentication filter runs — because the preflight `OPTIONS` request carries no credentials. You configure a global `CorsConfigurationSource` bean, and Spring Security applies it to all endpoints. Important: don't use `allowedOrigins("*")` with `allowCredentials(true)` — the browser rejects this combination.
domains/java/cors-csrf.question: What is CORS and how do you configure it in Spring Security?
domains/java/cors-csrf.title: CORS Configuration in Spring Security

domains/java/jwt.spoken:
A JWT has three parts separated by dots: header, payload, and signature — all Base64URL encoded. The header declares the algorithm (like `HS256` or `RS256`). The payload contains claims — standard ones like `sub` (subject/user ID), `exp` (expiration), `iat` (issued at), and custom ones you define. The signature is computed from the encoded header and payload using a secret key.

The key insight: JWT payloads are NOT encrypted. Anyone can decode a JWT and read its claims — Base64 is just encoding, not encryption. The security is in the signature: modifying any part of the token invalidates the signature, and the server detects this. So the server can trust the claims without a database lookup, but you should never put sensitive information like passwords in the payload.

With HMAC (symmetric), the same secret signs and verifies — don't share it. With RSA (asymmetric), a private key signs and anyone with the public key can verify — useful for microservices where verification doesn't require the secret.
domains/java/jwt.question: How is a JWT structured and how does signing work?
domains/java/jwt.title: JWT Structure and Signing

domains/java/oauth2.spoken:
OAuth2 defines several grant types for different scenarios. Authorization Code is the standard flow for web and mobile apps: the user is redirected to the identity provider's login page, authenticates there, and the provider sends a code back to your application. Your server exchanges this code for an access token. The user's password never reaches your application.

PKCE — Proof Key for Code Exchange — extends Authorization Code for public clients like SPAs and mobile apps that can't keep secrets. Before the redirect, the client generates a code verifier and sends its hash. When exchanging the code for a token, it sends the original verifier — the server verifies the hash matches, preventing code interception attacks.

Client Credentials is for machine-to-machine: a service authenticates with its client ID and secret to get a token for calling another service. There's no user involved. This is the standard flow for microservice-to-microservice calls.
domains/java/oauth2.deep:
## Authorization Code Flow

```
1. User clicks "Login with Google"
2. App redirects to Google:
   https://accounts.google.com/oauth2/auth?
     response_type=code
     &client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID
     &redirect_uri=https://yourapp.com/callback
     &scope=openid email profile
     &state=random-anti-csrf-state

3. User authenticates at Google
4. Google redirects back:
   https://yourapp.com/callback?code=AUTH_CODE&state=random-anti-csrf-state

5. Your server exchanges code for tokens:
   POST https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token
   {
     grant_type: authorization_code,
     code: AUTH_CODE,
     redirect_uri: https://yourapp.com/callback,
     client_id: YOUR_CLIENT_ID,
     client_secret: YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET  ← Server-side only!
   }

6. Response:
   { access_token: "...", id_token: "...", refresh_token: "..." }
```

## PKCE Flow (SPA/Mobile — No Client Secret)

```
1. Client generates:
   code_verifier = random 43-128 char string
   code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier))

2. Authorization request includes:
   &code_challenge=<hash>
   &code_challenge_method=S256

3. Token exchange includes:
   code_verifier=<original>
   (No client_secret! Public client)

4. Auth server: SHA256(code_verifier) == code_challenge? → issue token
   Attacker who intercepts code: doesn't have code_verifier → can't exchange
```

## Client Credentials Flow

```java
// Service-to-service authentication
// Service A calls Service B:

// Step 1: Get access token from auth server
POST /oauth2/token
Authorization: Basic BASE64(client_id:client_secret)
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
grant_type=client_credentials&scope=read:orders write:orders

Response: { "access_token": "...", "token_type": "Bearer", "expires_in": 3600 }

// Step 2: Call Service B with the token
GET /api/internal/orders
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

// Spring OAuth2 Client auto-handles token acquisition and refresh:
@FeignClient(name = "order-service")
@RequestMapping("/api")
public interface OrderServiceClient {
    @GetMapping("/orders")
    List<Order> getOrders();
}
// Configure with spring.security.oauth2.client.registration...
```

## Grant Type Selection Guide

```
Scenario → Grant Type
-----------------------------------------
Web app (server-rendered) → Authorization Code
SPA (React/Angular) → Authorization Code + PKCE
Mobile app → Authorization Code + PKCE
Service-to-service (no user) → Client Credentials
Legacy app (unavoidable) → ROPC (avoid if possible)
Device with limited UI (TV) → Device Authorization Grant

DEPRECATED — DO NOT USE:
  Implicit Flow → replaced by Auth Code + PKCE
  ROPC (Resource Owner Password Credentials) → security risk
```

## Production Reality

For login with Google/GitHub/social providers: Authorization Code + PKCE is always correct. For internal microservice auth: Client Credentials with short-lived tokens (1 hour). Store client secrets in a secrets manager, not config files. Consider using an identity provider like Keycloak, Auth0, or Okta instead of implementing OAuth2 yourself — the spec has many edge cases and security pitfalls.
domains/java/oauth2.question: What are the main OAuth2 grant types and when do you use each?
domains/java/oauth2.title: OAuth2 Grant Types

domains/java/indexes-performance.spoken:
A B-tree index is a balanced tree of sorted values where each leaf node holds the indexed column value and a pointer to the actual row in the table. The tree is kept balanced so that every lookup takes the same number of steps, giving O(log n) performance. For a table with a million rows, that's roughly 20 comparisons versus a million for a sequential scan.

Leaf nodes in a B-tree are linked to each other in order. This is what makes range queries efficient — once the index finds the first matching value, it can walk the leaf nodes sequentially to collect the rest of the range without going back to the root.

The cost of having an index is write performance. Every INSERT must add an entry to every index on that table. Every DELETE must remove from every index. UPDATE is effectively a delete plus insert in each index. A heavily indexed table can be two to five times slower for writes. This is why you index only what your actual query patterns require.
domains/java/indexes-performance.deep:
## B-tree Structure (Conceptual)

```
                    [50]
                   /    \
              [25]        [75]
             /    \      /    \
         [10,20] [30,40] [60,70] [80,90]
          ↓  ↓    ↓  ↓    ↓  ↓    ↓  ↓
        Row Row  Row Row  Row Row  Row Row
        Ptrs     Ptrs     Ptrs     Ptrs
```

Leaf nodes are linked: [10,20] → [30,40] → [60,70] → allows range scan without going to root

## Index Scan vs Sequential Scan

```sql
-- Small result set → index scan (log n lookups)
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE id = 12345;  -- single row, index wins

-- Large result set → seq scan might be cheaper
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > 1;  -- 99% of rows, skip index overhead
-- Optimizer picks seq scan here — reading all pages is faster than jumping around
```

## Index Bloat and Maintenance

```sql
-- Check index size vs table size
SELECT indexname,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) AS index_size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE relname = 'orders'
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(indexrelid) DESC;

-- Rebuild bloated index without locking (PostgreSQL)
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer_id;

-- Check bloat from dead tuples
SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, n_live_tup
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE n_dead_tup > 1000;
```

## Hash Index — Equality Only

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_email_hash ON users USING HASH (email);
-- Faster equality lookup: WHERE email = 'foo@bar.com'
-- Cannot do range: WHERE email LIKE 'foo%' → fails
-- Cannot sort: ORDER BY email → cannot use this index
```
domains/java/indexes-performance.question: How does a B-tree index work internally and how does the database use it to answer queries faster?
domains/java/indexes-performance.title: How Database Indexes Work Internally

domains/java/joins-subqueries.spoken:
A CTE, or Common Table Expression, is a named temporary result set you define at the top of a query using the WITH keyword. It lives only for the duration of that single statement. The main benefit is readability — instead of deeply nested subqueries you break a complex query into clearly named steps that read like paragraphs of a story.

CTEs can also be referenced multiple times within the same query, whereas a subquery gets re-executed each time it's referenced. This matters for both performance and avoiding code duplication.

Recursive CTEs are a uniquely powerful tool for traversing hierarchical data. You define an anchor query that gives you the starting rows, then a recursive part that keeps joining back to the CTE itself to walk down the hierarchy. This is how you find all subordinates of a manager in an org chart, or all descendants of a category in a product tree.
domains/java/joins-subqueries.deep:
## Basic CTE vs Nested Subquery

```sql
-- Hard to read nested subquery
SELECT name FROM (
    SELECT name, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS avg_sal, salary
    FROM employees
) t WHERE salary > avg_sal;

-- Same logic as a readable CTE
WITH dept_averages AS (
    SELECT name, department, salary,
           AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS dept_avg
    FROM employees
)
SELECT name, department, salary
FROM dept_averages
WHERE salary > dept_avg;
```

## Chaining CTEs

```sql
WITH
recent_orders AS (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
    FROM orders
    WHERE created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
high_value AS (
    SELECT customer_id, total
    FROM recent_orders
    WHERE total > 1000
)
SELECT c.name, hv.total
FROM high_value hv
JOIN customers c ON hv.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY hv.total DESC;
```

## Recursive CTE — Org Chart

```sql
-- Walk all reports under manager id=1
WITH RECURSIVE org_tree AS (
    -- Anchor: start with the manager
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS depth
    FROM employees
    WHERE id = 1

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive: join to children, increment depth
    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, ot.depth + 1
    FROM employees e
    JOIN org_tree ot ON e.manager_id = ot.id
)
SELECT id, name, depth FROM org_tree ORDER BY depth, name;
```

## Performance Note

In PostgreSQL 12+, CTEs are inlined by default (same as subqueries). To force materialization:
```sql
WITH cte AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT ... FROM big_table)
SELECT * FROM cte JOIN cte c2 ON ...;
-- Computes once, reuses twice
```
domains/java/joins-subqueries.question: What is a CTE in SQL and when should you prefer it over a subquery?
domains/java/joins-subqueries.title: CTEs (Common Table Expressions) Explained

domains/java/sql-fundamentals.spoken:
SQL executes clauses in a specific logical order that's different from how you write the query. The engine starts with FROM and JOIN to assemble the full dataset, then WHERE to filter individual rows before any grouping happens, then GROUP BY to aggregate, then HAVING to filter those aggregated results. Only after all that does SELECT run to pick which columns you want, followed by ORDER BY and finally LIMIT.

This matters practically because it explains common errors. You cannot use a SELECT alias in your WHERE clause because WHERE runs before SELECT evaluates that alias. You cannot put aggregate functions like COUNT or AVG directly in a WHERE clause because grouping hasn't happened yet — use HAVING for that.

Understanding this order makes you a much faster debugger. When you see an error about aggregate functions in WHERE, you immediately know the fix is to move the condition to HAVING. When an alias doesn't resolve, you know to repeat the expression or use a subquery.
domains/java/sql-fundamentals.deep:
## Logical Execution Order

```sql
SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal   -- 6: evaluate columns
FROM employees                               -- 1: start here
JOIN departments USING (dept_id)             -- 2: apply joins
WHERE hire_date > '2020-01-01'              -- 3: filter rows (before grouping)
GROUP BY department                         -- 4: aggregate into groups
HAVING AVG(salary) > 80000                  -- 5: filter groups
ORDER BY avg_sal DESC                       -- 7: sort
LIMIT 10;                                   -- 8: cut
```

## Common Mistakes This Prevents

```sql
-- WRONG: aggregate in WHERE
SELECT department, COUNT(*) FROM employees
WHERE COUNT(*) > 5 GROUP BY department; -- Error!

-- RIGHT: use HAVING
SELECT department, COUNT(*) FROM employees
GROUP BY department HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

-- WRONG: alias in WHERE
SELECT salary * 1.1 AS new_salary FROM employees
WHERE new_salary > 100000; -- Error!

-- RIGHT: repeat the expression
SELECT salary * 1.1 AS new_salary FROM employees
WHERE salary * 1.1 > 100000;
```

## Performance Insight
Filter early with WHERE — fewer rows to group means less work in GROUP BY. Use HAVING only for conditions that genuinely require the aggregate result.
domains/java/sql-fundamentals.question: In what order does SQL actually execute the clauses in a SELECT statement?
domains/java/sql-fundamentals.title: SQL Query Execution Order

domains/java/transactions-acid.spoken:
Pessimistic locking locks the data as soon as you read it and holds that lock until your transaction is done. No other transaction can modify that data in the meantime. This guarantees consistency but hurts throughput — transactions queue up waiting for locks, and long-held locks can cause timeouts or deadlocks.

Optimistic locking doesn't take a lock at read time at all. Instead, you track a version number on each row. When you write, you check that the version hasn't changed since you read it. If another transaction modified the row in the meantime, the version won't match and your write fails with a conflict error. You then decide to retry or inform the user.

The right choice depends on contention. If many transactions are competing to modify the same data, optimistic locking becomes inefficient because retries mount up. High-contention scenarios like inventory reservation or account transfers benefit from pessimistic locking to ensure correctness without retries. For typical web application use cases where conflicts are rare — most users edit their own data — optimistic locking gives better throughput and doesn't waste locks on reads that might never conflict.
domains/java/transactions-acid.question: What is the difference between optimistic and pessimistic locking and when do you use each?
domains/java/transactions-acid.title: Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking

domains/java/caching-strategy.spoken:
Caching strategy depends on read/write ratio and consistency requirements. Cache-aside (lazy loading) is the most common: the application checks the cache, loads from DB on a miss, and stores the result in cache. It's flexible but means the first request after a cache miss is slow, and you must manually handle cache invalidation.

Write-through caches update the cache synchronously on every write. This keeps the cache consistent with the database but doubles write latency. It makes sense for data that's read frequently right after being written.

Write-behind is the aggressive option: write to cache immediately, flush to DB asynchronously. Reads are fast, writes are fast, but you risk losing recent writes if the cache goes down before flushing. Only appropriate when some data loss is acceptable.

Beyond strategy, cache hierarchy matters: serve from the browser cache first (free), then CDN for static content, then an in-process cache like Caffeine for hot data, then Redis for distributed state.
domains/java/caching-strategy.question: What are the different caching strategies and how do you choose the right one?
domains/java/caching-strategy.title: Caching Strategies for System Design

domains/java/database-design.spoken:
I start with the entities: what are the main nouns in the system? For an e-commerce system: users, products, categories, orders, order_items, payments, addresses. Then I define relationships: a user has many orders; an order has many order_items; each order_item references a product.

For OLTP (transactional) systems, I normalize to at least 3NF — eliminate redundant data. An order_item stores quantity and price_at_time_of_order (since the product price might change), not the product's current price. This is a common interview gotcha: storing the price at order time, not a foreign key to the current price.

Then I add indexes: foreign keys, columns used in WHERE and ORDER BY, and composite indexes for common query patterns. Finally, I consider what common reporting queries need — if they're too slow with normalized data, I might add a denormalized summary table or views.
domains/java/database-design.deep:
## E-Commerce Schema Design

```sql
-- USERS table
CREATE TABLE users (
    id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    email           VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    password_hash   VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    full_name       VARCHAR(100),
    role            VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'CUSTOMER',
    email_verified  BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
    -- Audit fields (every table should have these):
    created_at      TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at      TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),
    deleted_at      TIMESTAMP  -- NULL = active, set = soft-deleted
);

-- ADDRESSES (separate table: one user can have multiple)
CREATE TABLE addresses (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
    type        VARCHAR(20),  -- 'SHIPPING', 'BILLING'
    line1       VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    line2       VARCHAR(255),
    city        VARCHAR(100),
    state       VARCHAR(50),
    country     CHAR(2),   -- ISO 3166: 'US', 'GB'
    postal_code VARCHAR(20),
    is_default  BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
    created_at  TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_addresses_user_id ON addresses(user_id);

-- PRODUCTS table
CREATE TABLE products (
    id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    sku             VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    name            VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    description     TEXT,
    category_id     BIGINT REFERENCES categories(id),
    base_price      DECIMAL(12, 2) NOT NULL,  -- Price may change over time
    stock_quantity  INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    is_active       BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
    created_at      TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at      TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_products_category ON products(category_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_products_sku ON products(sku);

-- ORDERS table
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id                  BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id             BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
    status              VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING',
    -- Store shipping address AT ORDER TIME (user may change address later)
    shipping_address_id BIGINT REFERENCES addresses(id),
    -- Snapshot the address fields directly (for immutable order record):
    shipping_line1      VARCHAR(255),
    shipping_city       VARCHAR(100),
    shipping_country    CHAR(2),
    shipping_postal     VARCHAR(20),
    subtotal            DECIMAL(12, 2),
    tax_amount          DECIMAL(12, 2),
    shipping_amount     DECIMAL(12, 2),
    total               DECIMAL(12, 2),
    notes               TEXT,
    created_at          TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at          TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(status);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_at ON orders(created_at DESC);
-- Composite: user's orders by status
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_status ON orders(user_id, status);

-- ORDER_ITEMS table
CREATE TABLE order_items (
    id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id        BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
    product_id      BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
    product_name    VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,  -- Snapshot name (product might change)
    quantity        INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
    price_at_time   DECIMAL(12, 2) NOT NULL,  -- KEY: price when ordered, not current price!
    line_total      DECIMAL(12, 2) GENERATED ALWAYS AS (quantity * price_at_time) STORED
);
CREATE INDEX idx_order_items_order_id ON order_items(order_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_order_items_product_id ON order_items(product_id);

-- PAYMENTS table
CREATE TABLE payments (
    id                  BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id            BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
    amount              DECIMAL(12, 2) NOT NULL,
    currency            CHAR(3) DEFAULT 'USD',
    status              VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,   -- PENDING, COMPLETED, FAILED, REFUNDED
    payment_method      VARCHAR(30),             -- CREDIT_CARD, PAYPAL, etc.
    gateway_reference   VARCHAR(255),            -- Transaction ID from payment gateway
    processed_at        TIMESTAMP,
    created_at          TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_order_id ON payments(order_id);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_payments_gateway_ref ON payments(gateway_reference)
    WHERE gateway_reference IS NOT NULL;  -- Prevent duplicate payment records
```

## Design Decisions Explained

```
WHY price_at_time in order_items:
  Products prices change. If you store just product_id and look up the current
  price, the order total will be wrong after a price change.
  ALWAYS store the price at the time of the transaction.

WHY copy address fields in orders:
  User might change their address later. You need the original shipping address
  for legal and shipping purposes. Store a snapshot.

WHY separate payments table (not just a status column in orders):
  An order can have multiple payment attempts (first fails, second succeeds).
  Also enables partial payments and refunds as separate rows.

WHY soft delete (deleted_at) instead of DELETE:
  Regulatory: you often can't delete customer/order data for compliance reasons.
  Referential integrity: deleting a user breaks FK references in orders.
  Audit: you want to know when and why something was deleted.
  Pattern: WHERE deleted_at IS NULL (use partial index for performance)

CREATE INDEX idx_active_products ON products(id)
    WHERE is_active = TRUE AND deleted_at IS NULL;
```

## Entity-Relationship Summary

```
users ──< addresses          (1 user, many addresses)
users ──< orders             (1 user, many orders)
orders ──< order_items       (1 order, many items)
products ──< order_items     (1 product, in many orders)
orders ──< payments          (1 order, 1+ payment attempts)
categories ──< products      (1 category, many products)
categories ──< categories    (self-referential: subcategories)
```

## Production Reality

The most common design mistake is forgetting to snapshot prices and addresses at order time. This causes incorrect order history and is very painful to fix in production. Also: always put `created_at` and `updated_at` on every table — they're free to add, and you'll regret not having them for debugging and analytics. Add a database-level trigger or use JPA `@CreatedDate`/`@LastModifiedDate` to set them automatically.
