mistakes: Not knowing that narrowing truncates (doesn't round) — (int) 3.9 gives 3, not 4
interview/java/type-casting.direct: **Widening** is implicit — smaller type to larger type (`int → long → double`), done automatically with no data loss. **Narrowing** is explicit — larger type to smaller type (`double → int`), requires a cast, and may lose data through truncation or overflow.
interview/java/type-casting.spoken:
The way I think about it is **direction plus safety**. When you go from a smaller type to a larger one — `int` to `long`, or `long` to `double` — that's **widening**, and Java does it for you automatically with no cast, because the bigger type can hold every value the smaller one could. Nothing is at risk, so Java stays out of your way.

Going the other direction — `double` to `int`, or `int` to `byte` — is **narrowing**, and Java refuses to do it silently. You have to write the cast yourself, putting `(int)` in front of the value. That cast is basically your signature saying you accept that data might be lost. And it really can be lost two ways. Casting `9.99` to an `int` gives you `9`, not `10`, because it **truncates toward zero** rather than rounding — that's the one freshers get wrong most often. And casting `300` to a `byte` gives you `44`, because `byte` only goes to `127` and the value wraps with no exception at all.

The order worth memorizing is `byte`, `short`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double` — every step rightward is free, every step back needs a cast. The key insight I'd leave them with: **the cast silences the compiler, it doesn't protect your value**. So I only narrow when I've already checked the number actually fits.

mistakes: Not explaining why default methods were added — missing the Collections API evolution story.
interview/java/default-and-static-method.direct: Default methods are methods in an interface that have a concrete implementation using the default keyword. They allow interfaces to add new methods without breaking existing implementations. Classes can override default methods or use them as-is.
interview/java/default-and-static-method.spoken: Default methods let you add new methods to an interface with a concrete implementation. They were added in Java 8 to solve a huge problem — how do you add new methods to existing interfaces without breaking millions of lines of code? The answer was the default keyword. When Java wanted to add stream support to collections, they couldn't just add a stream method to the Collection interface because every class implementing it would break. So they made it a default method with an implementation, and suddenly every ArrayList and HashSet got streaming for free. You can think of it like this — abstract methods are mandatory, you must implement them. Default methods are optional upgrades that come with the interface. If you don't override them, you get the default behavior. If you need something custom, you can override. I've used this when extending our payment processing interface — we added a default generateInvoice method that worked for most payment types, but our subscription processor overrode it with custom logic. The key thing interviewers want to hear is that you understand why they exist — it's about evolving APIs without breaking backward compatibility.

mistakes: Thinking @FunctionalInterface creates the constraint — the annotation only validates it
interview/java/functional-interfaces.direct: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). It can have multiple default and static methods. The @FunctionalInterface annotation verifies this at compile time. Functional interfaces are the target type for lambda expressions.
interview/java/functional-interfaces.spoken: A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method. That's the key rule. The single abstract method is what allows you to use a lambda expression as an implementation of that interface. So when you write something like orders.filter with a lambda that takes an order and returns a boolean, that lambda is implementing a functional interface — in this case, Predicate. Now, the interface can also have default methods and static methods, as many as you want. Those don't count toward the rule because they already have implementations. The at-FunctionalInterface annotation is optional, but it's a good practice. It tells the compiler to check that you really do have exactly one abstract method. If you accidentally add a second one later, you'll get a compile error instead of breaking all your lambdas. Java provides four main built-in functional interfaces: Predicate for testing, Function for transforming, Consumer for side effects, and Supplier for producing values. But you can create your own when those don't fit. One mistake freshers make is thinking the annotation is required. It's not. Any interface with one abstract method works. Runnable is a functional interface and it doesn't have the annotation. The annotation just helps catch mistakes early.

mistakes: Describing lambda syntax without explaining functional interfaces — the type a lambda actually targets
interview/java/lambda-expressions.direct: A lambda expression is a short, unnamed function you can pass around as a value. Introduced in Java 8, it replaces verbose anonymous classes and powers the Streams API. Lambdas only work with functional interfaces — interfaces with exactly one abstract method.
interview/java/lambda-expressions.spoken:
A lambda expression is a short, unnamed function that you can pass around as a value.

Before Java 8, passing behaviour meant writing an anonymous class — 5-6 lines for what is conceptually one line of logic. A custom sort comparator needed a full Comparator class definition.

With lambdas, you write just the logic — like (a, b) arrow a.compareTo(b). Same result, one line.

Why was it introduced? Java 8 added the Streams API for processing collections. Streams need you to pass functions — filter items where length is greater than five, transform each item to uppercase. Without lambdas, every step would need an anonymous class, making streams unreadable. Lambdas make it clean.

One rule to remember: lambdas only work with functional interfaces — interfaces with exactly one abstract method. The lambda provides the implementation of that one method.

mistakes: Thinking method references are a completely different feature from lambdas rather than just a more concise syntax for the same thing.
interview/java/method-references.direct: A method reference is shorthand syntax for a lambda expression that only calls an existing method. Instead of writing (x) -> obj.method(x), you write obj::method. It makes code cleaner when the lambda does nothing but delegate to a single method call.
interview/java/method-references.spoken: A method reference is a shorter way to write a lambda when the lambda just calls one existing method. Instead of writing something like x goes to x dot length, you'd write String colon colon length. They use the double colon operator to reference the method. The reason you'd use them is purely readability. When you're working with streams or functional interfaces, your code gets cleaner because you're not repeating the obvious parameter passing. For example, in a stream pipeline, names dot stream dot map with String colon colon toUpperCase is easier to read than names dot stream dot map with a lambda that takes s and returns s dot toUpperCase. It's the same thing under the hood though. The compiler converts both to the exact same bytecode, so there's no performance difference at all. One thing to watch out for is that the method signature has to match what the functional interface expects. If you're using forEach which takes a Consumer with one parameter, you can't reference a method that needs two parameters. That won't compile. The best advice is to use method references when they make your intent clearer to someone reading the code, not just because they're shorter. Sometimes a lambda with an explicit parameter name actually explains what's happening better, especially if the transformation isn't obvious.

mistakes: Treating Optional like a null wrapper and calling get() without checking, which defeats its purpose and can throw NoSuchElementException.
interview/java/optional-class.direct: Optional<T> is a container object that may or may not hold a non-null value. It was introduced in Java 8 to explicitly represent the absence of a value in method return types, replacing null returns and forcing developers to consciously handle the empty case, thereby reducing NullPointerException occurrences.
interview/java/optional-class.spoken: Optional is a container class introduced in Java 8 that either holds a value or is empty. Before Optional, we'd return null when a method couldn't produce a result, which led to tons of NullPointerExceptions. The problem was that null doesn't tell you whether absence is expected or a bug. Optional makes it explicit in the return type. If I see a method returning Optional of User, I immediately know it might not find a user, so I need to handle that. You can chain operations like map and filter on it, or use orElse to provide a default. For example, in a repository method that searches for a user by email, returning Optional of User forces the caller to think about the not-found case. The key mistake freshers make is calling get without checking if the value's present—that just throws NoSuchElementException, which defeats the whole point. You should use orElse, orElseGet, or ifPresent instead. Optional was designed specifically as a return type to communicate absence, not as a field or parameter type. It's really about making your API clearer and safer.

mistakes: Thinking a Stream is like a List that stores data — missing that it's a computational abstraction
interview/java/stream-basics.direct: A Stream is a pipeline for processing data — it doesn't store data, it processes it. A Collection stores data. Streams support lazy evaluation (operations happen only when a terminal operation is called) and can be consumed only once, unlike Collections which can be iterated multiple times.
interview/java/stream-basics.spoken: So a Stream is basically a pipeline for processing data, while a Collection is a container that stores data. The big difference is that a Collection like an ArrayList holds all your elements in memory and you can loop through it as many times as you want. But a Stream doesn't store anything — it's just a sequence of operations you're going to apply to data. For example, if I have a list of orders and I call list-dot-stream-dot-filter-dot-map-dot-collect, that's building a processing pipeline. The cool part is lazy evaluation — those filter and map operations don't actually run until I call collect at the end. This lets Java optimize things, like stopping early if I use findFirst. Another key thing is that streams are single-use. Once you run a terminal operation like collect or forEach, the stream is consumed and you can't use it again. If you try, you'll get an IllegalStateException. Collections don't have this limitation — you can iterate over an ArrayList ten times if you want. In production, I'd use a Collection when I need to store data and access it multiple times, like a cache. I'd use a Stream when I'm doing a one-time transformation, like filtering a list of users by role and converting them to DTOs for an API response. The stream approach is cleaner because it's declarative — I'm saying what I want, not writing explicit loops with temporary variables.

mistakes: Confusing filter (selection based on condition) with map (transformation of values), or thinking they modify the original collection.
interview/java/stream-operations.direct: filter() keeps only elements that match a given condition using a Predicate, while map() transforms each element into a new value using a Function. Both are intermediate operations that return a new Stream and are lazily evaluated until a terminal operation is called.
interview/java/stream-operations.spoken: I'd say filter and map are two fundamental stream operations that do very different things. Filter is about selection—you give it a condition through a Predicate, and it keeps only the elements that pass that test. Map is about transformation—you give it a Function, and it converts each element into something new. The key difference is filter might give you fewer elements but they're unchanged, while map gives you the same number of elements but transformed. Let me give you a concrete example. Say you've got a list of orders and you want email addresses of customers with unpaid orders. You'd use filter to keep only the unpaid orders, then map to extract the email field from each order object. Both are intermediate operations, which means they're lazy—nothing actually happens until you call a terminal operation like collect. One pitfall freshers hit is trying to use map to remove elements by returning null. That doesn't work—you'll just get nulls in your stream. Always use filter for removal decisions and map for transforming what remains. That separation of concerns makes stream pipelines much cleaner and easier to read.

mistakes: Opening a new connection per request, hurting performance and overloading the DB.
interview/java/connection-pooling.direct: **Connection pooling** keeps a set of database connections **open and reusable** so the app borrows and returns them instead of creating one per request. It's critical because opening a connection (TCP + auth) is **expensive**; pooling removes that per-request cost, caps total connections, and is essential for throughput under load.
interview/java/connection-pooling.spoken: Connection pooling means keeping a set of database connections open and ready, so the application borrows one when it needs to run a query and returns it afterward, instead of creating a brand-new connection for every request. It's critical because opening a database connection is genuinely expensive: it involves a TCP handshake and an authentication round-trip, often tens of milliseconds. In a web application handling thousands of requests, if every request opened and closed its own connection, you'd waste an enormous amount of time on that overhead, and you'd also risk overwhelming the database, which has a limit on how many connections it can handle. A connection pool solves both problems. It keeps a bounded set of connections already open. The application borrows one from the pool, runs its query, and then returns it, and importantly when you call close on a pooled connection it goes back to the pool to be reused rather than being destroyed. So the expensive handshake happens rarely instead of per request, and the maximum pool size caps the total number of connections to protect the database. This is why essentially every production application uses a connection pool, and in Spring Boot the default is HikariCP, which is fast and lightweight, configured automatically from your datasource properties.
interview/java/connection-pooling.deep:
Pool size isn't 'as big as possible' — oversized pools overload the DB and add contention.

A common heuristic is `connections ≈ (core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count`; in practice you start small (e.g. 10), **measure** under load, and tune.

Pool size should roughly match the DB's capacity for concurrent work, not the app's thread count.

Opening a new connection per request, hurting performance and overloading the DB.

mistakes: Using the wrong port or subprotocol, or forgetting required params (MySQL 8 needs serverTimezone) so the connection silently fails at startup.
interview/java/jdbc-connection.direct: A **JDBC URL** has the form `jdbc:<subprotocol>://<host>:<port>/<database>?<params>`. The `jdbc:` prefix is fixed; the **subprotocol** (e.g. `mysql`, `postgresql`) tells `DriverManager` which driver to use; then come the **host**, **port**, **database name**, and optional query params like `useSSL=false&serverTimezone=UTC`.
interview/java/jdbc-connection.spoken: A JDBC URL is the string that tells the driver which database to connect to and how. Its general form is jdbc colon, then a subprotocol, then colon slash slash, then host colon port slash database, optionally followed by a question mark and parameters. The jdbc colon prefix is fixed; every JDBC URL starts with it, and it's how DriverManager recognises the string. The subprotocol is the important part for routing, things like mysql, postgresql, or oracle colon thin, because DriverManager walks its list of registered drivers and asks each one whether it can handle this URL, and the subprotocol is the match key. After that comes the host and port, for example localhost colon three three zero six for MySQL or five four three two for PostgreSQL, then the database or schema name. Finally, you can append query parameters after a question mark, separated by ampersands, for options like useSSL equals false, serverTimezone equals UTC, or a character set. A concrete MySQL example is jdbc colon mysql colon slash slash localhost colon three three zero six slash shop question mark serverTimezone equals UTC. Common mistakes to avoid are using the wrong port for the database, forgetting a required parameter like the server timezone for MySQL, which can actually throw an error, and typos in the subprotocol, which show up as a no suitable driver found message rather than a connection failure. I also keep the username and password out of the URL and out of source control, supplying them separately.

mistakes: Using Statement instead of PreparedStatement for parameterized queries, leading to SQL injection, or forgetting to close Connection, Statement, and ResultSet.
interview/java/jdbc-overview.direct: JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) is the standard Java API for connecting to relational databases, executing SQL statements, and processing result sets. It exists because without a standard API, every database vendor would expose a different protocol, forcing developers to write database-specific code that could not be ported. By defining a small set of interfaces (Driver, Connection, Statement, ResultSet) and letting vendors provide implementations, JDBC lets the same Java code talk to PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, or any other JDBC-compliant database with only a driver swap and a URL change.
interview/java/jdbc-overview.spoken: JDBC is the standard Java API for talking to relational databases. The core idea is that JDBC defines a set of interfaces -- Driver, Connection, Statement, ResultSet -- and each database vendor provides the concrete implementation. So the same Java code can talk to PostgreSQL, MySQL, or Oracle with just a driver swap and a URL change. The typical flow is: get a Connection from DriverManager, create a PreparedStatement with parameterized SQL using question-mark placeholders, bind the parameters, execute the query, and iterate over the ResultSet. PreparedStatement is critical because it prevents SQL injection and lets the database cache the compiled query plan. I always use try-with-resources to close the Connection, Statement, and ResultSet because leaking database connections is a classic production problem. In practice, most teams layer JPA or Spring Data on top of JDBC, but understanding JDBC is essential for debugging and performance tuning.

mistakes: Thinking JPA replaces JDBC entirely — in reality, JPA uses JDBC under the hood as the database driver layer
interview/java/jdbc-vs-jpa.direct: **JDBC** is a low-level API where you write raw SQL, manually manage connections, and map `ResultSet`s to objects yourself. **JPA** is a high-level **ORM** specification that treats database rows as Java objects, generates SQL automatically, and handles persistence — **Hibernate** is its most popular implementation, and it runs on top of JDBC.
interview/java/jdbc-vs-jpa.spoken: JDBC is the low-level API where you write SQL as strings and manually convert database rows into Java objects. JPA is a higher-level specification that lets you work with entities — you save an Order object and JPA generates the SQL for you. The key thing is that JPA doesn't replace JDBC. It actually uses JDBC underneath. Think of it like this: JDBC is the engine, JPA is the automatic transmission built on top of it. When you use Hibernate, which is the most common JPA implementation, it's generating SQL statements and then using a JDBC driver like PostgreSQL's driver to execute them. You'd choose JDBC when you need precise control — maybe you're writing a complex report with five table joins and window functions. That's hard to express with JPA's entity model. You'd choose JPA when you're doing standard business logic with clear domain objects. If you're building a customer management system where you create customers, update their addresses, and delete old accounts, JPA handles all that with minimal code. One thing freshers miss is that you don't have to pick just one. In a real Spring Boot app, you'll use JPA repositories for most CRUD operations and then drop down to JdbcTemplate when you hit a query that's awkward in JPA. That's totally normal and expected.

mistakes: Treating it as security-only, or still concatenating values.
interview/java/prepared-statement.direct: A **PreparedStatement** is a precompiled, parameterized SQL statement that uses `?` placeholders bound with setter methods. It's preferred over `Statement` for two reasons: it **prevents SQL injection** (values are bound as data) and it's **faster for repeated execution** (parsed/planned once).
interview/java/prepared-statement.spoken: A PreparedStatement is a parameterized, precompiled SQL statement. You write the SQL with question-mark placeholders, and then bind the actual values using setter methods like setInt and setString. It's preferred over a plain Statement for two main reasons. The first is security: because the parameter values are sent to the database separately from the SQL text, the input is always treated as data rather than executable code, which completely prevents SQL injection. The second is performance: the database parses and builds the execution plan for a PreparedStatement once, and then every subsequent execution just rebinds the new values and reuses that plan, which makes it noticeably faster in loops and batches. There's a third, quieter benefit too: PreparedStatement handles type conversion and escaping for you. You don't have to worry about quoting strings, formatting dates, or escaping special characters, because the driver does it correctly based on the parameter type, including handling NULLs. So in practice I use PreparedStatement for essentially every query that has parameters or runs more than once, which is almost everything, and I only fall back to a plain Statement for static, parameterless one-off SQL like a CREATE TABLE.

mistakes: Reading a column before calling next(), or assuming it's a loaded list.
interview/java/result-set.direct: A **ResultSet** is a **cursor** over the rows returned by a query. It starts positioned **before the first row**; you call **`next()`** to advance (it returns `false` when rows run out) and `getXxx("col")` to read columns. It's forward-only by default and must be closed.
interview/java/result-set.spoken: A ResultSet is a cursor over the rows that a query returns. It's important to understand it's a cursor, not a fully loaded list in memory; it points at one row at a time. The cursor starts positioned before the first row, which is the key detail people forget. So to read data, you first call next, which moves the cursor to the next row and returns true if there's a row there, or false when you've run off the end. That's why the standard pattern is a while loop on rs dot next. Inside the loop, you read each column with the typed getters, like getInt and getString, and you can read either by column name, which is more readable, or by a one-based column index. By default a ResultSet is forward-only, meaning you iterate through it once from start to finish, and it's tied to the Statement and Connection that produced it, so once those are closed the ResultSet is invalid. That's why you close it when you're done, ideally with try-with-resources. The mistakes to avoid are trying to read a column before calling next, since the cursor starts before the first row, treating the ResultSet like a reusable list, and using zero-based column indices when they're actually one-based.
interview/java/result-set.deep:
A **ResultSet** is a **cursor** over the rows returned by a query.

It starts positioned **before the first row**; you call **`next()`** to advance (it returns `false` when rows run out) and `getXxx("col")` to read columns.

It's forward-only by default and must be closed.

mistakes: Building queries by concatenating user input with + .
interview/java/sql-injection-jdbc.direct: **SQL injection** is when attacker-controlled input is **concatenated into a SQL string**, so the input becomes executable SQL instead of data. Classic example: typing `' OR '1'='1` into a login bypasses the password check. It works because the query and the data are mixed into one string the DB then parses.
interview/java/sql-injection-jdbc.spoken: SQL injection is an attack that happens when user-supplied input is concatenated directly into a SQL statement, which lets an attacker change what the query actually does. The root cause is that you're mixing two different things, the SQL code and the user's data, into a single string, and then handing that whole string to the database to parse. So if the input contains SQL syntax, the database can't tell it's supposed to be data and executes it as code. The textbook example is a login form. Suppose the query is select star from users where name equals quote, plus the username, plus quote. If the attacker types apostrophe OR apostrophe one equals apostrophe one, the where clause becomes a condition that is always true, so it returns all users and bypasses authentication entirely. And it gets worse: attackers can read data from other tables, dump sensitive information, or even destroy data with something like semicolon DROP TABLE users. The damage isn't limited to logins; any query built by concatenation, like a search box or a sort parameter, is vulnerable. The fix is to use parameterized queries, which in JDBC means a PreparedStatement with question-mark placeholders and setString. With that, the driver sends the SQL and the data to the database separately, so the input is always treated as a literal value and can never become executable SQL.
interview/java/sql-injection-jdbc.deep:
**Second-order (stored) SQL injection** is when a malicious payload is safely **stored** first, then later **read back and concatenated** into a query that runs it.

Unlike first-order (input used immediately), the attack triggers on a *later* request — so even validated-on-input data is dangerous if you trust it and concatenate it later.

**SQL injection** is when attacker-controlled input is **concatenated into a SQL string**, so the input becomes executable SQL instead of data. Classic example: typing `' OR '1'='1` into a login bypasses the password check. It works because the query and the data are mixed into one string the DB then parses.

Building queries by concatenating user input with + .

mistakes: Defaulting to Statement and building SQL with string concatenation.
interview/java/statement-types.direct: JDBC has three statement types: **Statement** (static SQL, no parameters), **PreparedStatement** (parameterized + precompiled, prevents SQL injection — the default choice), and **CallableStatement** (calls stored procedures). All three send SQL; they differ in parameterization and safety.
interview/java/statement-types.spoken: JDBC gives you three types of statements for sending SQL, and they differ mainly in parameterization and safety. The first is Statement, which executes static SQL with no parameters. The problem is that if you build a Statement by concatenating user input into the SQL string, you open yourself up to SQL injection, so plain Statement is rarely the right choice when input is involved. The second is PreparedStatement, which uses question-mark placeholders for parameters, is precompiled by the database, and is safe against SQL injection because the values are sent separately from the SQL. This is the default I reach for in almost every case. The third is CallableStatement, which is used to call stored procedures, with a syntax like curly-brace call proc with question marks, and it supports both input and output parameters. It's also worth knowing they form an inheritance chain: PreparedStatement extends Statement, and CallableStatement extends PreparedStatement, so each adds capability on top of the previous. So the short version is: Statement for static SQL with no input, PreparedStatement for any parameterized query, which is the safe and fast default, and CallableStatement specifically for stored procedures.

mistakes: Interleaving setup, calls, and assertions, or having multiple Act steps so the test checks several behaviors
interview/java/assertions.direct: **Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA)** is a three-phase structure for a test: **Arrange** the inputs and the object under test, **Act** by calling the one method being tested, then **Assert** the observable result. Keeping each phase distinct makes a test read top-to-bottom and ensures it exercises exactly one behavior.
interview/java/assertions.spoken:
Arrange-Act-Assert is the standard way I structure a unit test, and it has three phases. In the Arrange phase I set up everything the test needs — the inputs, the object I'm testing, and any collaborators. In the Act phase I make a single call to the method I'm actually testing and capture its result. And in the Assert phase I check the observable outcome against what I expected.

Keeping those three phases distinct, usually with a blank line or a short comment between them, makes the test read top-to-bottom so anyone can immediately see the setup, the action, and the expectation. For example, in a shopping cart test, I'd arrange by creating a cart and adding two items, act by calling total, and assert that the total is the sum.

The most useful discipline that falls out of this is the single Act. If I notice I have two actions in one test, that's a strong signal I'm testing two different behaviors and I should split it into two tests. That keeps each test failing for exactly one reason, which makes debugging much faster.

AAA is essentially the same idea as Given-When-Then from behavior-driven development — Given is Arrange, When is Act, Then is Assert. The mistakes I'd avoid are interleaving the phases, having multiple Act steps, and letting the Arrange phase balloon, because a giant setup usually means the class under test has too many dependencies. To stand out, I'd connect AAA to Given-When-Then and stress that a single Act keeps a test focused.

mistakes: Mixing JUnit 4 imports (org.junit.Test) with JUnit 5, or marking the test method public/returning a value out of habit
interview/java/junit5-basics.direct: **JUnit 5** is the standard testing framework for Java, made of three modules: **JUnit Platform** (the launcher that runs tests), **JUnit Jupiter** (the modern API with `@Test` and `Assertions`), and **JUnit Vintage** (runs old JUnit 4 tests). A basic test is a method annotated with `@Test` that arranges inputs, calls the code, and verifies the result with a static assertion like `assertEquals`.
interview/java/junit5-basics.spoken:
JUnit 5 is the standard unit-testing framework for Java, and it's what Spring Boot uses by default. The thing that's different from JUnit 4 is that it's modular — it's actually three pieces. The first is the JUnit Platform, which is the foundation that discovers and launches tests; that's what your IDE and Maven hook into. The second is JUnit Jupiter, which is the API I actually write against — the Test annotation, the lifecycle annotations, and the Assertions class. The third is JUnit Vintage, which is a bridge that lets old JUnit 4 tests run on the new platform, so a team can migrate gradually.

Writing a basic test is simple. I create a class, and inside it a method annotated with Test. In JUnit 5 I don't need to make the class or the method public — package-private is fine. Inside the method I follow Arrange, Act, Assert: I build my inputs and the object under test, I call the method I'm testing, and then I verify the result with a static assertion like assertEquals, passing the expected value first, then the actual.

The one gotcha I'd call out is the import. The Test annotation has to come from org dot junit dot jupiter dot api. If you accidentally import the JUnit 4 Test annotation from org dot junit, the test just won't be picked up. To stand out, I'd name the three modules and explain that Jupiter is the API I write while the Platform is what runs it.

mistakes: Putting all logic in one ATM class instead of separating hardware components, state management, and business rules into distinct objects
interview/java/atm-design-basics.direct: An ATM system has core classes: ATM (Singleton controller), Card, Account, BankServer (external verification), CashDispenser (manages denominations), CardReader, and ATMState hierarchy (State pattern). The ATM flows through states: Idle → CardInserted → Authenticated → SelectAction → Processing → DispensingCash, with each state handling only valid transitions.
interview/java/atm-design-basics.spoken:
I'd open by saying an ATM is essentially a state machine, because that framing drives the whole design. The machine moves through phases — idle, card inserted, authenticated, selecting an action, and dispensing cash — and the main source of bugs is letting the wrong action happen in the wrong phase, like withdrawing before you've authenticated.

For the classes, I find the nouns: the ATM itself as the controller, Card and Account for the customer, a BankServer for external verification, a CashDispenser that manages bill inventory, and a CardReader. Then I model the phases with the State pattern. I define an ATMState interface with the operations — insertCard, enterPin, withdraw — and a concrete state class for each phase. The ATM holds a currentState reference and delegates every action to it. Each state only implements the transitions that are valid for it; anything invalid throws an IllegalStateException. So IdleState accepts a card and moves to CardInsertedState, but if you call withdraw on it, it refuses.

I'd make the ATM a Singleton since there's one controller per machine, and I'd keep responsibilities separate — the BankServer verifies the PIN and account, the CashDispenser handles the cash, the ATM just coordinates. On security I'd stress that you never store the PIN; you verify it through the bank and discard it. The big mistake to avoid is a single God class with phase flags and if-else chains everywhere — that's exactly what the State pattern cleans up.
interview/java/atm-design-basics.deep:
Key patterns: (1) State pattern for clean state machine (Idle, CardInserted, Authenticated, DispensingCash states), (2) Singleton for ATM controller (one instance per machine), (3) Strategy pattern for account types (Savings vs Checking have different withdrawal limits), (4) Command pattern for each ATM action (enables undo and audit logging), (5) Facade pattern where ATM class hides CashDispenser, CardReader, BankServer complexity from user interaction layer.

The ATM flows through states: Idle → CardInserted → Authenticated → SelectAction → Processing → DispensingCash, with each state handling only valid transitions.

mistakes: Treating every noun as a class without filtering, or missing behavioral entities like managers and controllers that coordinate system operations.
interview/java/identify-classes.direct: Identify nouns in the problem statement — these become candidate classes. Filter to entities that have both data (attributes) and behavior (methods). Actors like managers and controllers often become classes or interfaces. Validate each class by ensuring it has clear responsibilities.
interview/java/identify-classes.spoken:
My go-to technique is noun-verb analysis. I read the problem statement and underline the nouns, because nouns are usually the candidate classes — things like Member, Book, Order, ParkingSpot. The verbs become candidate methods, so borrow, pay, park. And adjectives or descriptive words usually become attributes, like a book's title or a spot's size.

But I don't blindly turn every noun into a class. I filter. A real class should have both data and behaviour and a single clear responsibility. So something like price is just a value — it's an attribute on a product, not its own class. A word like late is a condition, not an entity. I also watch for synonyms; if the prompt says customer in one place and user in another, that's probably one class, not two.

The one thing freshers often miss is actor classes. Words like manager, librarian, or administrator describe people who act on the system, and they frequently deserve a class or at least a service, especially when they have permissions or behaviour that differs from a regular user. Once I have my filtered list of classes, I treat that as step one and move on to the relationships — which classes contain which, which inherit from which. Identifying the classes is the foundation, but the design only takes shape once you connect them.
interview/java/identify-classes.deep:
Abstract class provides partial implementation with fields and concrete methods for IS-A relationships with shared code (Vehicle with common fields).

Interface is a pure contract with no state for CAN-DO relationships (Payable, Parkable).

Identify nouns in the problem statement — these become candidate classes. Filter to entities that have both data (attributes) and behavior (methods). Actors like managers and controllers often become classes or interfaces. Validate each class by ensuring it has clear responsibilities.

mistakes: Freshers often collapse Book and BookItem into one class, missing that one book title can have multiple physical copies with independent states
interview/java/library-management-design.direct: A library management system needs entities for catalog (Book), physical inventory (BookItem), users (Member, Librarian), and transactions (BookLending, Reservation, Fine). The key distinction is Book represents the catalog entry while BookItem represents each physical copy with its own barcode and availability status.
interview/java/library-management-design.spoken:
I'd lead with the single most important modelling decision, because it's where most people slip: separating Book from BookItem. A Book is the catalog entry — title, author, ISBN — and there's exactly one per title. A BookItem is a single physical copy with its own barcode and an availability status. So the library has one Book record for Clean Code but maybe five BookItems on the shelf. A member borrows a BookItem, never the abstract Book, because you can only physically check out a copy.

From there the other classes follow naturally. Member and Librarian are the users, with Librarian having extra permissions. BookLending represents an active checkout, capturing the item, the member, the issue date, and the due date. Reservation is a hold on a title, and Fine is an overdue charge. The relationships are a Book having many BookItems by composition, and a Member having many active loans.

I'd put borrowing rules on the Member — a canBorrow method that checks they have no outstanding fines and haven't hit the loan limit. For behaviour, I'd mention I'd use Strategy for search and fine calculation so those can vary, and Observer so that when a copy is returned, the next member in the reservation queue gets notified. The big mistake to avoid is collapsing Book and BookItem into one class, because then you simply can't represent multiple copies or know which one is checked out.
interview/java/library-management-design.deep:
Calculate fine during book return by comparing return date to due date.

If overdue, fine equals overdue days multiplied by daily rate.

Use a FineCalculator strategy to encapsulate rate logic (standard, premium members might have different rates). Member entity tracks outstanding fine balance that must be cleared before new borrowing is allowed.

mistakes: Jumping into code without identifying entities and relationships, or violating the Open/Closed Principle by hard-coding implementations instead of coding to interfaces.
interview/java/lld-approach.direct: Low-Level Design (LLD) is the process of defining the internal structure of a software system at the class and method level -- specifying classes, their fields, method signatures, relationships (inheritance, composition, dependency), and the design patterns that govern them. It exists because high-level design (HLD) says what the system should do but not how the code should be organized, and without LLD, developers would each interpret the architecture differently, producing inconsistent, hard-to-maintain code. An LLD interview tests whether you can translate a vague problem statement into a clean, extensible class design grounded in SOLID principles and standard patterns.
interview/java/lld-approach.spoken: Low-Level Design, or LLD, is the process of defining the internal structure of a software system at the class and method level. Where high-level design tells you what components the system has and how they communicate, LLD tells you what classes to write, what fields and methods each class has, and how they relate to each other. It exists because without it, every developer would interpret the architecture differently and you would end up with inconsistent, hard-to-maintain code. In an LLD interview, the interviewer gives you a problem statement like designing a parking lot or a vending machine, and you need to identify the entities, assign responsibilities using SOLID principles, choose the right relationships, and apply design patterns where they add value. I always prefer composition over inheritance, code to interfaces so the design is extensible, and use dependency injection so the classes are easy to test in isolation.

mistakes: Freshers spend 30 minutes writing perfect code for one class instead of showing the overall design first, leaving no time to discuss trade-offs.
interview/java/lld-interview-strategy.direct: A 45-minute LLD interview should follow this rough allocation: 5 minutes to clarify requirements and scope, 5 minutes to identify core entities and relationships, 10 minutes to sketch a class diagram on the whiteboard, 15 minutes to write key Java class skeletons with method signatures, and 10 minutes to discuss design patterns, trade-offs, and extensibility.
interview/java/lld-interview-strategy.spoken:
I treat the forty-five minutes as a budget and keep a rough clock in my head. I spend the first five minutes clarifying — scope, constraints, what's explicitly in and out. The next five identifying the core entities and their relationships using noun-verb analysis. Then about ten minutes sketching the class diagram, with boxes, the key fields and methods, and the relationship arrows. The biggest chunk, around fifteen minutes, goes to writing key Java skeletons — turning the diagram boxes into actual classes with real method signatures. And I save the last ten minutes for discussing design patterns, trade-offs, extensibility, and answering follow-ups.

The single most common way people mismanage this is overspending on the diagram. It's tempting to make it perfect, but if you burn twenty minutes drawing boxes you've got nothing left to show you can actually translate that into code, and that's exactly what interviewers want to see. So I cap the diagram deliberately and move to skeletons. Under time pressure, signatures and relationships matter more than complete method bodies — I'll stub a method with a comment rather than implement every line.

The other thing I do throughout is narrate. I think out loud so the interviewer can follow my reasoning, because in a design interview the process is the product. And I never skip clarification to save time, because designing the wrong thing faster doesn't help anyone.

probes.text: Verbally announce your time allocation at the start: 'I'll spend 5 minutes clarifying, then 10 on the class structure' — shows metacognitive awareness and planning ability.
Evaluating whether the candidate can manage time effectively under pressure and prioritize design activities in a structured manner.

mistakes: Computing average rating on-the-fly from all reviews on every product page load (terrible performance at scale), forgetting verifiedPurchase flag leading to fake reviews, or updating Product's averageRating synchronously in the same transaction causing lock contention
interview/java/online-shopping-design.direct: The Review entity has fields: reviewId, productId, userId, rating (integer 1 to 5), reviewText (optional comment), verifiedPurchase (boolean indicating if user actually bought the product), createdAt, and updatedAt. Product entity has denormalized fields averageRating and reviewCount for fast display. When a user submits a review, ReviewService validates they purchased the product, saves the Review, then publishes a ReviewCreatedEvent. A background listener recalculates Product's averageRating and reviewCount asynchronously, avoiding locking Product rows on every review submission. This eventual consistency trade-off improves write throughput.
interview/java/online-shopping-design.spoken:
The Review entity is straightforward at first glance — a review id, the product id, the user id, an integer rating from one to five, an optional text comment, a verified-purchase flag, and created and updated timestamps. I'd validate the rating bounds right at construction, which a Java record makes clean with a compact constructor that throws if the rating is outside one to five.

What lifts this above plain CRUD are two design decisions. The first is the verified-purchase check. Before I accept a review, the ReviewService asks the order repository whether this user actually bought this product, and sets the verifiedPurchase flag accordingly. That single flag is what lets the UI show a 'verified purchase' badge and is a basic defence against fake reviews.

The second is denormalization. The product listing page needs to show an average rating and a review count, and you do not want to recompute an average over thousands of reviews every time someone loads the page. So I store averageRating and reviewCount directly on the Product, and update them whenever a new review comes in. I'd be explicit about the trade-off here, because that's what an interviewer is listening for: denormalizing makes reads fast but introduces a write-time cost and a consistency concern. For ratings, eventual consistency is perfectly acceptable — if the average is a second stale, nobody cares — so it's a good trade.
interview/java/online-shopping-design.deep:
Inventory management requires a separate Inventory entity tracking availableStock and reservedStock for each product.

When a user adds items to cart and proceeds to checkout, the system calls reserveStock atomically (using database row-level locking or optimistic locking with a version field) to decrement available and increment reserved.

This prevents overselling when multiple users buy simultaneously. On successful payment, convert reserved to sold (decrement reserved). On order cancellation or timeout, return reserved stock to available. For multi-warehouse setups, Inventory has a warehouseId field, and allocation algorithms pick the optimal warehouse based on customer location.

mistakes: Creating a single God class that does everything or missing key entities like ParkingTicket, leading to difficulty tracking vehicle entry/exit times.
interview/java/parking-lot-design.direct: A parking lot system needs ParkingLot (manages floors), ParkingFloor (manages spots), ParkingSpot (tracks occupancy), Vehicle hierarchy (Car, Motorcycle, Truck), ParkingTicket (entry/exit tracking), and FeeCalculator (pricing logic). Use Singleton for ParkingLot, Strategy for fee calculation, and Factory for vehicle creation.
interview/java/parking-lot-design.spoken:
I'd start by clarifying scope — multiple floors, what vehicle types, and whether pricing is hourly. Then I find the nouns in the problem, because nouns usually become classes. Here that's ParkingLot, ParkingFloor, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, ParkingTicket, and a FeeCalculator. The verbs — park, unpark, calculate fee — become the methods.

The most important modelling decision is the relationships. A ParkingLot has a list of floors, and each floor has a list of spots — that's composition, because a spot can't exist without its floor. Vehicles are different: Car, Motorcycle, and Truck all inherit from an abstract Vehicle class, because each one is-a vehicle. I'd give Vehicle an abstract method like requiredSize so each subclass declares what spot it needs, instead of writing if-else chains on the type.

For the flow: on entry, the lot searches floors for a free spot that fits, marks it occupied, and issues a ParkingTicket that records the vehicle, the spot, and the entry time. On exit, the customer hands back the ticket, the FeeCalculator works out the charge from the duration, payment is taken, and the spot is freed.

Then I'd layer in patterns where they earn their place: Strategy for the FeeCalculator so pricing rules can change without touching the lot, Factory for creating vehicles, and Singleton for the lot since there's only one. I'd also mention that spot assignment must be thread-safe, since multiple gates operate at once — a synchronized claim on the spot stops two cars taking the same place. That shows I'm thinking about behaviour, not just structure.

mistakes: Confusing relationship arrows (especially inheritance vs interface implementation) or forgetting that class diagrams show structure, not runtime flow.
interview/java/uml-class-diagram-basics.direct: A UML class diagram represents classes as boxes divided into three sections: name at the top, attributes in the middle, methods at the bottom. Relationships between classes are shown using different line styles: solid arrows for inheritance, dashed arrows for interface implementation, diamonds for composition/aggregation, and plain lines for association. Visibility markers like + (public) and - (private) prefix members.
interview/java/uml-class-diagram-basics.spoken:
A UML class diagram captures the static structure of a design. Each class is drawn as a box split into three sections: the class name at the top, its attributes in the middle, and its methods at the bottom. In front of each attribute or method you put a visibility marker — a plus for public, a minus for private, and a hash for protected — so the diagram communicates access control at a glance.

But the boxes are only half the story; the lines between them carry just as much meaning, and that's where people slip. A solid line with a hollow triangle pointing at the parent means inheritance, an is-a relationship via extends. A dashed line with a hollow triangle means a class implements an interface. A filled diamond means composition — strong ownership, where the part can't live without the whole, like a parking floor inside a lot. A hollow diamond means aggregation, a weaker ownership where the part can exist independently, like players in a team. And a plain line is a general association, meaning one class just uses or knows about another.

The last detail I'd mention is multiplicity — the little numbers at each end of a line, like one and star, that say a lot has one-to-many floors. So when I read or draw a class diagram, I'm reading the boxes for structure and the line styles and arrowheads for how the classes relate, because getting the arrowheads right is what proves you actually understand composition versus inheritance.
interview/java/uml-class-diagram-basics.deep:
Draw the interface as a box with <<interface>> above the class name and only method signatures inside (no attributes).

Each implementing class uses a dashed line with a hollow arrow pointing to the interface.

If you have an abstract class, write the name in italics and use a solid line with hollow arrow for subclasses. You can mix both: an interface with multiple implementations, one of which is abstract with its own subclasses.

A common mistake is confusing relationship arrows (especially inheritance vs interface implementation) or forgetting that class diagrams show structure, not runtime flow.

mistakes: Not knowing about automatic activation mechanisms — thinking manual -P flags are the only way to trigger profiles
interview/java/build-profiles.direct: You activate Maven profiles using the -P flag like mvn package -Pprod, by setting activeByDefault to true in the profile definition, or automatically through activation conditions like environment variables, JDK versions, OS detection, or file presence checks. Once activated, the profile's configuration overrides or extends the base build.
interview/java/build-profiles.spoken: There are a few ways to activate Maven profiles depending on your needs. The most direct is using the -P flag, like mvn clean package -Pprod. That explicitly activates the prod profile for that build. But in real projects, you don't want to rely on developers remembering flags. So you can set activeByDefault to true in the profile definition, which means that profile runs automatically unless you activate a different one. For example, our dev profile might be activeByDefault so when someone clones the repo and runs mvn package, it just works with local settings. Then there's automatic activation based on conditions. You can activate a profile when an environment variable is set, like BUILD_ENV equals production. This is huge for CI/CD because your Jenkins or GitLab pipeline just exports BUILD_ENV equals production, and Maven activates the right profile automatically. The build logs show exactly what happened without relying on someone passing the right flag. You can also activate based on JDK version, which is useful if you're supporting multiple Java versions with different compiler settings. Or based on file presence — like only run integration tests if integration-test.properties exists. One thing to watch out for: if you use -P to explicitly activate a profile, all activeByDefault profiles get deactivated. So if you have a dev profile with activeByDefault true and you run mvn package -Pprod, only the prod profile is active. The dev one shuts off. That surprises freshers who expect both to run. In production environments, we typically use environment variable activation rather than -P flags because it's clearer in audit logs and less prone to human error.

interview/java/build-profiles.codeExample:
```xml
<profiles>
    <profile>
        <id>dev</id>
        <activation>
            <activeByDefault>true</activeByDefault>  <!-- automatic for local builds -->
        </activation>
        <properties>
            <environment>development</environment>
        </properties>
    </profile>
    
    <profile>
        <id>prod</id>
        <activation>
            <property>
                <name>env.BUILD_ENV</name>  <!-- activated when BUILD_ENV env var exists -->
                <value>production</value>
            </property>
        </activation>
        <properties>
            <environment>production</environment>
        </properties>
    </profile>
    
    <profile>
        <id>integration-tests</id>
        <activation>
            <jdk>[17,)</jdk>  <!-- only on JDK 17+ -->
            <file>
                <exists>src/test/resources/integration-test.properties</exists>
            </file>
        </activation>
        <build>
            <plugins>
                <plugin>
                    <artifactId>maven-failsafe-plugin</artifactId>
                    <executions>
                        <execution>
                            <goals><goal>integration-test</goal></goals>
                        </execution>
                    </executions>
                </plugin>
            </plugins>
        </build>

</profiles>
```

mistakes: Using compile scope for everything including JUnit, which bloats the final JAR and breaks separation of concerns
interview/java/dependency-management.direct: Dependency scope in Maven controls when a dependency is available on the classpath. The main scopes are compile (default, available everywhere), test (only during testing), runtime (execution only, not compilation), and provided (compile-time only, supplied by the runtime container).
interview/java/dependency-management.spoken: Dependency scope in Maven controls when a library is available on the classpath—it's how Maven decides what goes into your final JAR and what's available at different build stages. There are four main scopes you'll use as a Java developer. The compile scope is the default. If you don't specify a scope, that's what you get. It means the dependency is available everywhere—during compilation, during testing, and in your final artifact. You'd use this for Spring Framework, Jackson for JSON, or any library your code directly imports. The test scope is for testing frameworks like JUnit and Mockito. These are only on the classpath when you're compiling or running tests. They never get packaged into your production JAR, which is important because you don't want multi-megabyte testing libraries shipped to production. The runtime scope is for libraries you need when the app runs but not during compilation. The classic example is a database driver like MySQL Connector. Your code imports java.sql.Connection and other JDBC interfaces, but it never directly imports com.mysql.cj classes—those get loaded at runtime via reflection. So you mark the driver as runtime scope. Finally, the provided scope is for libraries the container already supplies. If you're deploying a WAR to Tomcat, Tomcat already has servlet-api, so you mark it as provided. Maven includes it during compilation so your code compiles, but excludes it from the WAR so you don't have two versions causing conflicts. One common mistake freshers make is using compile scope for everything, which bloats your JAR with test and runtime-only libraries. Always think about when you actually need each dependency.

mistakes: Only knowing the default lifecycle and thinking 'clean' is just a phase, not a separate lifecycle
interview/java/maven-lifecycle.direct: Maven has three built-in lifecycles: default (handles project build and deployment), clean (removes build output), and site (generates project documentation). Each lifecycle is independent and consists of a sequence of phases.
interview/java/maven-lifecycle.spoken: Maven has three built-in lifecycles that are completely independent of each other. The default lifecycle is the main one you use for building projects — it includes all the phases like compile, test, package, install, and deploy. The clean lifecycle is simpler, it just has two phases that remove all the build output from your target directory. And the site lifecycle generates project documentation and reports. The key thing to understand is that these lifecycles don't automatically trigger each other. When you run a command like mvn clean package, you're actually telling Maven to run two separate lifecycles in sequence. First it runs the clean lifecycle to wipe out old artifacts, then it runs the default lifecycle up to the package phase. This is different from phases within a lifecycle, where running a later phase automatically runs all the earlier ones. For example, if you just run mvn package without clean, Maven won't delete your target directory first — it'll just run the default lifecycle phases leading up to package. In real development work, you'll use the default lifecycle constantly for building and testing. You'll combine it with clean when you want to be absolutely sure you have a fresh build, like when you're switching Git branches or investigating weird build issues. The site lifecycle is less common, mostly used when you need to generate documentation for stakeholders or create project reports.

mistakes: Describing Maven only as 'it manages dependencies' without mentioning the full build lifecycle or the convention principle that makes it different from Ant
interview/java/maven-overview.direct: Maven is a build automation and dependency management tool for Java projects that uses 'convention over configuration' — it defines standard directory layouts and build lifecycle phases so you follow conventions instead of writing custom build scripts. You get clean, compile, test, and package commands that just work without explicit configuration.
interview/java/maven-overview.spoken: Maven is a build automation tool for Java that manages dependencies and executes the full build lifecycle from compiling code to packaging deployable artifacts. The key idea is convention over configuration — Maven gives you standard directory layouts and build phases so you don't write custom scripts. For example, your Java source always goes in src slash main slash java and tests in src slash test slash java. When you run mvn package, Maven automatically compiles your code, runs tests, and creates a JAR file without you configuring those steps explicitly. This is different from older tools like Ant where you'd write hundreds of lines of XML to define every compilation step. In a Spring Boot project, you just declare spring-boot-starter-web in your pom dot XML, and Maven downloads not just that library but also all its transitive dependencies like Tomcat and Jackson. The convention approach means every Maven project looks the same, which is huge for team productivity. One common mistake freshers make is treating Maven as just a dependency downloader — it's actually orchestrating your entire build process. If you need lots of custom build logic or non-Java languages, you might choose Gradle instead, but for standard Java backend work, Maven's conventions eliminate a ton of boilerplate.

mistakes: Installing Gradle globally and using 'gradle build' instead of './gradlew build' — risks version mismatches
interview/java/maven-vs-gradle.direct: The Gradle Wrapper is a script (gradlew / gradlew.bat) checked into the project that downloads and runs the exact Gradle version specified for the project — ensuring everyone and every CI server uses the same Gradle version without needing Gradle installed globally.
interview/java/maven-vs-gradle.spoken: The Gradle Wrapper is a script you check into your project that lets anyone build your code without installing Gradle globally. It's the gradlew file on Unix or gradlew.bat on Windows. When you run ./gradlew build, the script first checks if the right Gradle version is already downloaded. If not, it downloads it automatically, then runs your build. The version is specified in a properties file, so everyone on the team and every CI server uses the exact same Gradle version. This solves the version mismatch problem. If I have Gradle 7 installed and you have Gradle 8, we'd get different build results. With the wrapper, we both use whatever version the project says to use, say Gradle 8.5. You commit the wrapper files to Git — the gradlew scripts and the gradle wrapper directory. One common mistake freshers make is installing Gradle globally and typing gradle build instead of ./gradlew build. That defeats the whole purpose because you're using your globally installed version, not the project's version. Maven eventually copied this idea and created the Maven Wrapper, which works the same way.

mistakes: Thinking packaging, name, or dependencies are required elements when they're actually optional with sensible defaults
interview/java/pom-xml.direct: pom.xml (Project Object Model) is Maven's project configuration file that defines how your project is built and what dependencies it needs. The four required elements are modelVersion (always 4.0.0), groupId (organization identifier), artifactId (project name), and version (release number).
interview/java/pom-xml.spoken: The pom.xml file is Maven's project configuration file — it's the first thing Maven looks for in your project root. POM stands for Project Object Model, which means Maven treats your project as an object with properties and behaviors rather than just a pile of source files. There are four required elements you must have. First is modelVersion, which should always be 4.0.0 — this hasn't changed since Maven 2.0 and tells Maven which POM schema version you're using. Second is groupId, which is your organization identifier in reverse domain format like com.techcorp. Third is artifactId, which is your project name — this becomes part of your JAR filename. Fourth is version, which is your release number like 1.0.0 or 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT for development versions. Everything else is optional but commonly added. For example, packaging defaults to jar if you don't specify it. One thing that surprises people is the effective POM concept — Maven doesn't just use your pom.xml directly. It merges your file with any parent POM you've inherited from, plus Maven's built-in super POM that provides defaults. You can see the final merged result by running mvn help:effective-pom. That's why you sometimes see behavior you didn't explicitly configure — it's coming from parent POMs.

mistakes: Confusing development workflow (mvn spring-boot:run) with production deployment (java -jar) or not knowing that spring-boot:run doesn't create a JAR
interview/java/running-spring-boot-with-.direct: You run 'mvn spring-boot:run' from the project root directory, which uses the spring-boot-maven-plugin to compile your code and start the embedded Tomcat server directly without creating a JAR file. This is the standard development workflow that lets you iterate quickly on code changes.
interview/java/running-spring-boot-with-.spoken: To run a Spring Boot app with Maven, you use the command mvn spring-boot:run from your project root. This is the standard development workflow. The spring-boot-maven-plugin compiles your code, gathers all dependencies, and starts the embedded Tomcat server in one go. You don't get a JAR file with this approach — it runs directly from the compiled classes in your target directory. It's like cooking and serving directly from the kitchen instead of packing everything into a takeout container first. This makes iteration really fast during development. You change your code, stop the app with Ctrl-C, run mvn spring-boot:run again, and you're back up. One common mistake freshers make is running this command from the wrong directory. You need to be where your pom.xml file is located, not inside src or target. Another pitfall is expecting this to create a JAR — it doesn't. If you need a JAR for deployment, you'd use mvn package instead. The spring-boot:run goal is purely for development convenience. It's also worth knowing that this command works great with DevTools. When you have DevTools as a dependency, you get automatic restarts when you recompile, which makes the development cycle even smoother. But again, this is a development-time tool. For production, you'd build a JAR and run it with java -jar.

mistakes: Only thinking of build tools as 'download dependencies' tools — they do much more including compilation, testing, and packaging orchestration
interview/java/what-is-a-build-tool.direct: A build tool automates compiling source code, running tests, managing dependencies, and packaging the application — eliminating the need to manually run javac and track JAR files. It ensures reproducible builds across all environments.
interview/java/what-is-a-build-tool.spoken: A build tool automates the entire process of turning source code into a runnable application. It compiles your Java files, runs your tests, manages external libraries, and packages everything into a JAR or WAR. Without it, you'd manually run javac for every file, download dozens of dependencies by hand, and track version compatibility yourself. That's error-prone and doesn't scale. In a real project, say a Spring Boot microservice, Maven or Gradle downloads Spring dependencies from Maven Central, compiles your code in the right order, runs JUnit tests, and creates an executable JAR. It also ensures reproducibility — the same pom.xml on my machine, your machine, and the Jenkins server produces identical builds. That's critical in teams. The key insight is that build tools don't just download libraries. They orchestrate the entire build lifecycle from validation to deployment. One common mistake freshers make is thinking Maven only manages dependencies. It actually handles compilation, testing, packaging, and more. That's why every professional Java project uses one from day one.

mistakes: Mixing matcher and exact value arguments like when(mock.method(any(), 'literal')) which throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException
interview/java/argument-matchers.direct: Argument matchers in Mockito let you stub and verify method calls with flexible patterns instead of exact values. any() matches any argument, eq(value) matches a specific value, and type-specific matchers like anyString() or anyInt() match by type. When using matchers, all arguments in that method call must be matchers—if you need to mix a matcher with a literal, wrap the literal with eq().
interview/java/argument-matchers.spoken: Argument matchers let you stub and verify Mockito method calls without hardcoding exact values. Instead of saying this mock must receive the number 42, you say it can receive any Long. The most common matchers are any for any non-null argument, anyString or anyInt for type-specific matching, and eq for exact values. Here's the critical rule freshers miss: if you use one matcher in a method call, every argument in that call must be a matcher. So if you write when method call with any and then a plain string literal, Mockito throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException. You have to wrap that literal with eq. Why? Mockito records matchers on an internal stack as you call them, and it expects the count to match the method's parameter count—mixing breaks that. In real tests, you'd use matchers when the exact value isn't predictable, like a generated timestamp or a UUID. For example, verifying that an audit logger was called with any timestamp but a specific event name: verify auditLog dot record with anyLong and eq of ORDER_CREATED. One common mistake is overusing any in verify—it makes your test pass even when wrong data is sent, hiding bugs. Use specific matchers or custom logic with argThat when the argument actually matters for correctness. The balance is: matchers give you flexibility, but don't sacrifice precision when the value is important to what you're testing.

mistakes: Assuming @InjectMocks will throw a clear error if injection fails — it does not, it silently continues with null fields
interview/java/inject-mocks.direct: @InjectMocks tries three injection strategies in order: constructor injection (matching by type), setter injection, then field injection. If none succeed, it creates the object with no injection — no error is thrown, leading to null fields that cause NPE at runtime.
interview/java/inject-mocks.spoken: When you use at-InjectMocks, Mockito follows a three-step process to wire your mocks into the test subject. First, it tries constructor injection — it looks for the largest constructor that it can satisfy with the available at-Mock fields, matching by type. If that doesn't work, it tries setter injection, looking for methods like setDependencyName. If that also fails, it falls back to field injection using reflection to directly assign mocks to matching fields. Here's the tricky part: if all three phases fail, Mockito doesn't throw an error. It just creates the object and leaves unmatched fields as null. You won't discover the problem until your test runs and throws a NullPointerException. That's why constructor injection in production code is so important — it forces compile-time validation of dependencies and aligns perfectly with Mockito's first injection phase. In my tests, I use at-ExtendWith with MockitoExtension to make sure the annotations are processed. For complex setups where I need different mock configurations per test, I skip at-InjectMocks entirely and manually construct the service in at-BeforeEach, passing mocks explicitly. That way, the wiring is visible and any mismatch fails immediately at compile time.

mistakes: Forgetting @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) which enables the annotation processing, or not understanding that injection silently fails if no matching strategy works
interview/java/mock-vs-stub-vs-spy.direct: @InjectMocks creates an instance of the class under test and automatically injects @Mock and @Spy dependencies into it. It tries constructor injection first, then setter injection, then field injection. This eliminates manual instantiation like new OrderService(mockRepo, mockEmail) in every test method.
interview/java/mock-vs-stub-vs-spy.spoken: At-InjectMocks is a Mockito annotation that creates an instance of your class under test and automatically injects all the at-Mock and at-Spy dependencies into it. So instead of writing new OrderService with all the mocks in parentheses in every test method, you just annotate the field with at-InjectMocks and Mockito does it for you. Here's how it works. Mockito tries three injection strategies in order. First, it looks for a constructor that matches your mock types and calls it—that's constructor injection and it's the preferred way. If there's no matching constructor, it tries calling setter methods like setRepository. If that fails, it uses reflection to directly assign values to private fields. That's field injection. The gotcha is if all three strategies fail, Mockito doesn't throw an error. It still creates the object but leaves dependencies as null. Then your test crashes with NullPointerException when it tries to use them. The mistake freshers make is forgetting to put at-ExtendWith MockitoExtension dot class on the test class. Without that, Mockito's annotation processing never runs. Your at-Mock fields stay null and at-InjectMocks doesn't create anything. You'll see NullPointerException on the first line of your test and wonder why. So always pair those two annotations together. Another tip—write your service classes with constructor injection for dependencies. That's Spring's best practice anyway, and it makes at-InjectMocks work cleanly because constructor injection is Mockito's first choice.

mistakes: Forgetting @ExtendWith and getting NullPointerException when mocks are not initialized.
interview/java/mockito-setup.direct: Add @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) to the test class, use @Mock to declare mock dependencies, and @InjectMocks for the class under test. MockitoExtension initializes all annotated mocks before each test method runs automatically.
interview/java/mockito-setup.spoken: To set up a Mockito test in JUnit 5, you start by adding the @ExtendWith annotation with MockitoExtension.class at the top of your test class. This tells JUnit to let Mockito handle the mock lifecycle. Inside the class, you use @Mock to create fake versions of your dependencies—like repositories or external services. Then you use @InjectMocks on the class you're actually testing, and Mockito automatically injects those mocks into it. For example, if I'm testing an OrderService that needs a PaymentGateway and an InventoryRepository, I'd mark both of those as @Mock and the OrderService as @InjectMocks. When the test runs, MockitoExtension initializes all the mocks before my test method starts, so everything's wired up and ready to go. One thing freshers often miss—if you forget the @ExtendWith annotation, your mocks will be null and you'll get a NullPointerException the moment you try to use them. The extension is what actually creates the mock objects; without it, the annotations are just decorations that do nothing. That's the core setup—those three annotations in the right places, and you've got a working Mockito test.

mistakes: Adding @SpringBootTest to every service test, which loads the entire Spring context and makes the test suite 50-100x slower
interview/java/testing-spring-services.direct: Use @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) to run the test with Mockito, @Mock to create a mock repository, and @InjectMocks to inject that mock into your service. This is a true unit test—no Spring context loads, runs in milliseconds. Only use @SpringBootTest when you need the full application context for integration testing.
interview/java/testing-spring-services.spoken: To write a unit test for a Spring service using Mockito, you start by annotating the test class with at-ExtendWith MockitoExtension dot class. That's the JUnit 5 way to activate Mockito. Then you create mocks for the service's dependencies using at-Mock. For example, if your OrderService depends on an OrderRepository, you'd write at-Mock private OrderRepository orderRepository. Next, you annotate the service itself with at-InjectMocks, which tells Mockito to create a real OrderService instance and inject the mock repository into it. Inside your test method, you use when and thenReturn to define the mock's behavior. Say when orderRepository dot save is called with any Order, return a saved Order with an ID. Then you call your service method and use JUnit assertions to verify the result. The key thing here is this runs without Spring—no application context, no database connection, nothing. It's pure Java object testing. That's why it's so fast. You can run hundreds of these tests in a couple seconds. One mistake I see freshers make is adding at-SpringBootTest to these tests. That loads the entire Spring application, which takes several seconds per test. For unit testing service logic, you don't need Spring at all. Save at-SpringBootTest for end-to-end integration tests where you're testing the whole application flow.
