mistakes: Using verify() to check return values instead of assertions on the actual result — verify checks that a method was called, not what it returned
interview/java/verify.direct: verify(mock).method(args) asserts that method(args) was called exactly once on the mock. If not called, or called with different args, the test fails. This is behavior verification — checking that your code interacted with dependencies correctly.
interview/java/verify.spoken: I'd say verify is how you check that your code called a method on a mock with the right arguments. It's behavior verification — you're asserting that an interaction happened, not checking what it returned. So if I've got a service that calls orderRepository dot save, I write verify orderRepository dot save order to make sure that call actually occurred. This matters a lot for void methods or methods with side effects, like saving to a database or sending an email. There's no return value to assert on, so verify is how you confirm the action took place. By default, verify checks the method was called exactly once. If it wasn't called at all, or was called with different arguments, the test fails. One thing freshers mess up is trying to use verify to check return values. That's not what it does. You stub the return value with when then-return, then you assert on the result your code produces. Verify just checks the call happened. I also wouldn't verify every single mock interaction — only the ones that are critical to the behavior being tested. Over-verifying makes tests brittle because they break whenever implementation details change, even if the behavior is still correct.

mistakes: Thinking mocking is a shortcut to avoid writing real implementations, missing that it's about decoupling test scope from external systems.
interview/java/what-is-mocking.direct: Mocking replaces a real dependency with a controlled fake that you configure to return specific values. It isolates the class under test from its dependencies—database, external APIs, file system—so you test only the unit's logic, not its dependencies.
interview/java/what-is-mocking.spoken: Mocking is replacing a real dependency with a fake one that you control. You'd say: It's about isolation. When I test a service, I don't want the test to fail because the database is down or an external API is slow. I mock those dependencies so the test only exercises the service's logic. For example, if I'm testing an order service that fetches data from a repository, I'd mock the repository to return a specific order. Then I test that the service calculates the total price correctly. The mock gives me control—I can make it return success, failure, empty data, whatever scenario I need. Without mocking, every test would need a running database, test data setup, and network access. That's slow and brittle. The key thing is mocking draws a boundary. I'm testing the order service, not the repository or the database driver. If the repository has its own bugs, that's a different test. This keeps tests fast and focused. One pitfall freshers hit is mocking everything, even simple value objects like a product DTO. You only mock things with side effects—external systems, I-O operations, things outside your control. If it's a plain data class, just create a real instance.

mistakes: Configuring the stub after calling the method under test, which means the mock returns null instead of the stubbed value
interview/java/when-thenreturn.direct: Use when(mock.method(args)).thenReturn(value) to configure a mock to return a specific value when that method is called with those arguments. This is the fundamental stubbing pattern in Mockito. Set up the stub in the Arrange phase before executing the code under test.
interview/java/when-thenreturn.spoken: I'd use when followed by the mock method call, then thenReturn with the value I want to stub. For example, if I'm testing an OrderService that depends on an OrderRepository, I'd write when orderRepository dot findById one-L dot thenReturn Optional dot of order. This tells Mockito that whenever findById is called with the argument one-L during this test, return that specific order object wrapped in an Optional. The key is doing this in the Arrange phase before I call the service method I'm actually testing. If I stub it after the service method runs, it's too late and the mock will have already returned null. One thing that confuses freshers is argument matching. If I stub findById with one-L but my service calls it with two-L, the stub won't match and I'll get a null return. For flexible matching, Mockito provides argument matchers like any or anyLong, so I can write when orderRepository dot findById anyLong then return some default order. You can also chain multiple return values. If I write thenReturn order-one comma order-two, the first call returns order-one and the second call returns order-two. That's useful for testing loops or retry logic. To stand out, I'd mention that when-thenReturn is for methods that return values. For void methods, you need a different syntax called doNothing or doThrow. And if the return value needs to depend on the input arguments, you'd use thenAnswer instead of thenReturn because thenReturn is always static.

mistakes: Treating backtracking as 'just recursion', or forgetting to undo the choice after exploring
interview/java/backtracking-intro.direct: **Backtracking** is recursion that **builds a candidate step by step and undoes (backtracks) a choice when it can't lead to a valid solution**. The extra ingredients over plain recursion are **choose -> explore -> un-choose** and **pruning** (abandoning dead branches early). It explores the **decision tree** of all possibilities, making it ideal for permutations, subsets, N-Queens, and constraint problems.
interview/java/backtracking-intro.spoken: All backtracking is recursion, but not all recursion is backtracking, and the difference is what makes this question interesting. Plain recursion typically breaks a problem into subproblems, solves them, and combines the results, like computing factorial or Fibonacci. Backtracking is a specific style of recursion where I build up a candidate solution one choice at a time, and the key idea is that the moment a partial candidate can't possibly lead to a valid complete solution, I abandon it and undo my last choice. The defining pattern is choose, explore, un-choose. I make a choice, I recurse to explore where that choice leads, and then critically I undo the choice, restoring the state so I can try the next option from the same point. That undo step, restoring state after exploring, is the single thing that most distinguishes backtracking from plain recursion, and it's also the thing freshers most often forget, which corrupts the results for the sibling branches. The other distinguishing feature is pruning: before I even explore a branch, I check whether it can lead anywhere valid, and if not, I skip it entirely. Pruning is what keeps backtracking from blindly exploring an exponential search space. Conceptually, I'm walking a decision tree of all possible candidates, going deep, and retreating whenever I hit a dead end. This is the pattern behind permutations, subsets, combinations, N-Queens, Sudoku solvers, and word search. One last tip: when I record a solution, I store a copy of it, not the mutable working list, otherwise later undo operations will mutate what I already saved.

mistakes: Checking 3 and 5 before the combined 15 case, so 15 prints 'Fizz' instead of 'FizzBuzz'
interview/java/common-fresher-programs.direct: **FizzBuzz**: print 1..n, but print **Fizz** for multiples of 3, **Buzz** for multiples of 5, and **FizzBuzz** for multiples of both (i.e. 15). The trap is **order**: check **15 (both) first**, then 3, then 5. Even cleaner is to **build a string** by appending 'Fizz' if divisible by 3 and 'Buzz' if by 5, printing the number only if the string is empty.
interview/java/common-fresher-programs.spoken: FizzBuzz is a classic warm-up. I print the numbers from one to n, but for multiples of three I print Fizz, for multiples of five I print Buzz, and for multiples of both, which is multiples of fifteen, I print FizzBuzz. The thing it's really testing is whether I handle that both-multiples case correctly, because there's a subtle ordering trap. If I write the if-else with the modulo-three check first, then fifteen satisfies it and prints Fizz, and it never reaches the FizzBuzz case. So in the if-else style, I check the combined case first, either modulo fifteen equals zero or divisible by both three and five, then check three, then five, then fall back to printing the number. The approach I actually prefer, and would mention to stand out, is to build up a string. I start with an empty string, append Fizz if the number is divisible by three, append Buzz if it's divisible by five, and then at the end, if the string is still empty I print the number, otherwise I print the string. This naturally handles fifteen, because both appends fire and I get FizzBuzz, and there's no ordering to get wrong. It's also more extensible: if someone adds a new rule, like print Bazz for multiples of seven, I just add one more append line instead of rewriting a tangle of nested conditionals. It's O of n, and while it's simple, doing it cleanly signals I write tidy conditional logic.
interview/java/common-fresher-programs.deep:
Rotate right by k using the **reversal trick** in O(n) time, **O(1)** space: first **`k %= n`** (k can exceed n), then **reverse the whole array**, **reverse the first k**, and **reverse the rest**.

The three reversals leave the array rotated right by k.

The naive 'shift one position k times' is O(n*k); an extra-array copy is O(n) time but O(n) space.

A common mistake is checking 3 and 5 before the combined 15 case, so 15 prints 'Fizz' instead of 'FizzBuzz'

mistakes: Calling any recursion 'DP', or applying DP without overlapping subproblems (then it's just divide-and-conquer)
interview/java/dynamic-programming-intro.direct: **Dynamic programming (DP)** solves problems by breaking them into **overlapping subproblems** and **storing each subproblem's answer** so it's computed only once. Use it when the problem has **optimal substructure** (the optimum is built from sub-optima) **and overlapping subproblems** (the same subproblem recurs). It turns exponential recursion into **polynomial** time, via **memoization** (top-down) or **tabulation** (bottom-up).
interview/java/dynamic-programming-intro.spoken: Dynamic programming is an optimization technique for problems that break into subproblems, but with two specific properties. The first is overlapping subproblems, meaning a naive recursive solution would solve the same smaller problem over and over. The textbook example is Fibonacci, where computing fib of n recursively recomputes fib of three, fib of two, and so on, an exponential number of times. The second property is optimal substructure, meaning the optimal solution to the whole problem is built from optimal solutions to its subproblems. When both properties hold, the core DP idea is to compute each distinct subproblem only once and store its answer, so I never recompute it. That single change collapses exponential recursion into polynomial time. For Fibonacci, the naive version is O of two to the n, but once I store results it becomes O of n. There are two ways to implement DP. Memoization is top-down: I keep the natural recursion but add a cache, and before computing a subproblem I check whether it's already in the cache. Tabulation is bottom-up: I fill a table starting from the base cases and build up to the answer, often letting me drop space down to constant. A point I'd make to show understanding is that not every recursion is DP. If the subproblems don't actually overlap, like in merge sort, then there's nothing to cache and it's just divide-and-conquer. So when I approach a DP problem, I first define the state, what dp of i means, then the transition between states, then the base cases.
interview/java/dynamic-programming-intro.deep:
**0/1 knapsack**: pick items (each used **at most once**) to maximize value within a weight **capacity**.

`dp[i][w]` = max value using the first `i` items with capacity `w`.

For each item, choose the better of **skip** (`dp[i-1][w]`) or **take** (`dp[i-1][w - wt] + val`, if it fits). **O(n*W)** time; reducible to **O(W)** space by iterating weight **backwards**.

A common mistake is calling any recursion 'DP', or applying DP without overlapping subproblems (then it's just divide-and-conquer)

mistakes: Using nested loops to count (O(n^2)) when one map pass works, or a HashMap where a 26/256 int array is faster
interview/java/frequency-counting.direct: The **frequency counting pattern** uses a **hash map** (or a fixed-size array for known alphabets) to tally **how many times each element appears** in a single pass. It turns many 'count / compare / find duplicate / most common' problems from **O(n^2)** nested scanning into **O(n)** time with **O(k)** space, where k is the number of distinct elements. Reach for it whenever you need counts, duplicates, anagrams, or 'majority/top' answers.
interview/java/frequency-counting.spoken: The frequency counting pattern is one of the most reusable tools in interviews. The idea is simple: I make a single pass over the input and tally how many times each element appears, usually in a hash map keyed by the element with the count as the value. Once I have those counts, a whole family of questions becomes easy: detecting duplicates, checking if two strings are anagrams, finding the first non-repeating character, finding the top K most frequent elements, the majority element, or whether a string can be rearranged into a palindrome. The reason this pattern matters is complexity. A brute force approach to many of these problems compares every pair of elements, which is O of n squared. Counting frequencies first is O of n time and O of k space, where k is the number of distinct elements. So I trade a little memory for a big speedup. One refinement I'd mention: when the set of possible elements is small and known, like lowercase English letters or ASCII characters, I don't even need a hash map. I can use a fixed-size integer array, int of twenty-six for lowercase letters, and index it with the character minus the letter a. That's faster and lighter than a hash map because it avoids hashing and boxing. In Java, a clean way to increment counts in a map is the merge method, calling merge with the key, one, and Integer sum, which either inserts one or adds one to the existing count. So whenever a problem mentions counts, duplicates, most common, or anagrams, frequency counting is the first thing I reach for.
interview/java/frequency-counting.deep:
The **frequency counting pattern** uses a **hash map** (or a fixed-size array for known alphabets) to tally **how many times each element appears** in a single pass.

It turns many 'count / compare / find duplicate / most common' problems from **O(n^2)** nested scanning into **O(n)** time with **O(k)** space, where k is the number of distinct elements.

Reach for it whenever you need counts, duplicates, anagrams, or 'majority/top' answers.

mistakes: Coding immediately without clarifying constraints or stating the brute force and its complexity first
interview/java/interview-approach-framew.direct: Use a repeatable framework: **(1) Clarify** inputs, outputs, constraints, and edge cases; **(2) Examples** - work a small case by hand; **(3) Brute force** out loud with its complexity; **(4) Optimize** by spotting a pattern (hashing, two pointers, etc.); **(5) Code** cleanly while narrating; **(6) Test** with normal, edge, and boundary cases; **(7) Analyze** final time/space. Talk through every step - communication is scored as much as the code.
interview/java/interview-approach-framew.spoken: I follow a consistent framework so I stay structured under pressure and so the interviewer can follow my thinking. First, I clarify the problem. I restate it in my own words and ask about input types and ranges, the expected output format, and edge cases like empty inputs, nulls, duplicates, or negative numbers. Second, I work through a small concrete example by hand to make sure I actually understand what's being asked. Third, I state a brute force solution out loud along with its time and space complexity, because a working brute force is far better than a broken attempt at the optimal solution, and it gives me a baseline. Fourth, I look for a way to optimize by recognizing a pattern, things like using a hash map for lookups, two pointers, a sliding window, or sorting first. Fifth, I write the code cleanly with good variable names while narrating what I'm doing and why. Sixth, I test by tracing through normal cases, edge cases, and boundaries by hand, fixing anything I catch. And seventh, I state the final time and space complexity. The thread running through all of this is communication. Interviews score how I think and collaborate, not only whether I reach the answer, so I keep talking through my reasoning at every step rather than going silent and coding in my head.

mistakes: Writing the recursive case first and forgetting the base case, causing a StackOverflowError
interview/java/recursion-basics.direct: **Recursion** is when a method calls itself to solve a **smaller version of the same problem**. Every recursive solution needs two parts: a **base case** (the stopping condition) and a **recursive case** (which shrinks the problem toward the base case). Missing either causes infinite recursion and a `StackOverflowError`.
interview/java/recursion-basics.spoken: Recursion is when a method calls itself to solve a problem by breaking it into smaller identical pieces. There are two essential parts you can't skip. First is the base case — that's your stopping condition. Without it, the function recurses forever and you get a StackOverflowError. Second is the recursive case, which is where you call the function again but with a smaller input that moves you closer to the base case. Let me give you factorial as an example. The base case is when n equals one or zero, you just return one. The recursive case is returning n times factorial of n minus one. So if you call factorial of five, it computes five times factorial of four, which computes four times factorial of three, and so on down to factorial of one. That's five stack frames deep. Once it hits the base case, the stack unwinds and each call returns its result back up. The key thing to understand is the call stack. Every recursive call creates a new stack frame with its own copy of the variables. Those frames pile up until the base case, then pop off as results return. That's why deep recursion can cause stack overflow in Java — the JVM has a limited stack size. A common mistake freshers make is writing the recursive case first and forgetting the base case entirely. Always write your base case first, test it, then write the recursive case.

mistakes: Recomputing the entire window sum or property from scratch at each position instead of maintaining a running state
interview/java/sliding-window.direct: The **sliding window** technique maintains a contiguous subarray or substring that slides over the data. Instead of recomputing from scratch at each position, you **add the element entering and remove the element leaving**. This turns many **O(n^2)** brute-force solutions into **O(n)** for problems on contiguous subarrays or substrings.
interview/java/sliding-window.spoken: The sliding window technique is a way to efficiently process contiguous subarrays or substrings. Instead of recalculating everything for each position, you maintain a running state and update it incrementally. You add the new element coming into the window and remove the element leaving the window. This turns a nested loop solution that's O of n squared into a single pass that's O of n. There are two main types. Fixed-size windows are used when the problem gives you an exact size k, like find the maximum sum of any three consecutive elements. You compute the first window once, then slide by adding the next element and subtracting the first element of the previous window. Variable-size windows are for problems with conditions, like longest substring with at most K distinct characters. You use two pointers. The right pointer expands to add elements. When the condition breaks, the left pointer contracts to restore validity. You track the maximum or minimum window size you see. The key mistake freshers make is using nested loops to recompute each window from scratch. That's what you're trying to avoid. The whole point is incremental update. You'd use this pattern whenever you see the words contiguous, consecutive, subarray, or substring combined with optimization keywords like maximum, minimum, longest, or shortest. It shows up constantly in coding interviews because it's a clean way to demonstrate you understand how to optimize brute force solutions.

mistakes: Not realizing two-end pointers usually require sorted input, or confusing the two-end variant with the fast/slow variant
interview/java/two-pointers.direct: The **two-pointer technique** uses two indices moving through data — typically one at each end or both from the same start — based on conditions. It reduces many **O(n^2)** brute-force problems to **O(n)** by replacing nested loops, on sorted or otherwise structured data.
interview/java/two-pointers.spoken: The two-pointer technique uses two indices that move through an array or string based on problem conditions. It's called two-pointer because you literally maintain two integer variables, like left and right, and move them independently. The core idea is to eliminate nested loops by making smart decisions about which direction to move each pointer. There are two main variants. The two-end variant starts pointers at opposite ends and moves them inward. This is perfect for sorted array problems like finding a pair that sums to a target. If the current sum is too small, you move left rightward to get bigger values. If it's too large, you move right leftward. Each move eliminates an entire range of pairs, not just one, so you scan the whole space in O of n time instead of O of n squared. The same-direction variant has both pointers starting at the beginning but moving at different speeds or conditions. Think of a slow pointer tracking where valid elements should go, and a fast pointer scanning ahead to find them. This is how you remove duplicates from a sorted array in place. The mistake freshers make is trying two pointers on unsorted data when the algorithm needs sorted input, or forgetting to skip duplicates in problems like three-sum. To stand out, name specific problems for each variant and explain the invariant each maintains, like slow tracks the last unique position. That shows you've actually implemented these patterns, not just read about them.

mistakes: Saying Spring Boot replaces Spring — it doesn't. It uses Spring under the hood and just reduces configuration pain.
interview/java/spring-boot.direct: Spring Framework is a comprehensive Java framework for building enterprise applications — but it requires extensive XML or Java configuration for every feature. Spring Boot is an opinionated layer on top of Spring that eliminates boilerplate: it auto-configures components, embeds a web server (Tomcat), and lets you start coding business logic immediately with minimal setup. Think of Spring as a fully customizable toolkit, and Spring Boot as a pre-assembled workstation.
interview/java/spring-boot.spoken:
Imagine you want to build a house. The Spring Framework gives you every possible tool, material, and blueprint — but you have to assemble everything yourself. You choose the foundation, wire the electricity, plumb the pipes, one piece at a time. You have ultimate control, but setup takes days before you can even hang a picture.

Spring Boot hands you a move-in-ready house. The plumbing works, the electricity is on, and you have a key. You can immediately start decorating — which is what matters (your business logic). If you don't like the default light fixtures, you can still swap them out.

Technically, Spring Boot does three major things:

**1. Auto-Configuration** — When you add `spring-boot-starter-web` to your dependencies, Spring Boot sees Tomcat and Spring MVC on the classpath and automatically configures an embedded web server, a JSON serializer (Jackson), and a request dispatcher. You didn't write a single line of configuration.

**2. Starter Dependencies** — Instead of manually adding 15 individual libraries for web development (servlet API, Tomcat, Jackson, validation, etc.), you add one dependency: `spring-boot-starter-web`. It pulls everything you need in compatible versions.

**3. Embedded Server** — Traditional Spring apps produce a WAR file you deploy to an external Tomcat. Spring Boot apps produce a JAR with Tomcat embedded inside. You run `java -jar app.jar` and your server starts. This is crucial for containerized deployments (Docker, Kubernetes).
interview/java/spring-boot.deep:
## What Spring Boot Automates and How

Spring Boot's magic is not magic — it's a set of well-defined conventions that eliminate repetitive configuration. Understanding the mechanism makes you faster at debugging when auto-configuration does something unexpected.

### Auto-Configuration: Reading the Classpath

When your application starts, Spring Boot scans every JAR on your classpath for `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`. Each listed class is a `@Configuration` that conditionally creates beans.

The key annotation is `@ConditionalOnClass` — it says "only activate this configuration if a specific class exists on the classpath." For example:

```java
// From Spring Boot internals (simplified)
@Configuration
@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)         // only if JDBC is on classpath
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "spring.datasource.url")  // only if URL is configured
public class DataSourceAutoConfiguration {
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean                 // only if user hasn't defined their own
    public DataSource dataSource(DataSourceProperties props) {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create()
            .url(props.getUrl())
            .username(props.getUsername())
            .build();
    }
}
```

The `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` is critical: if you define your own `DataSource` bean, auto-configuration backs off. You always have the final say. This is the "opinionated but not dictatorial" philosophy.

### Starter Dependencies: Curated Library Sets

A starter is a Maven POM (or Gradle module) that pulls in a group of compatible libraries. `spring-boot-starter-web` brings:
- Spring MVC (web framework)
- Embedded Tomcat (web server)
- Jackson (JSON serialization)
- Hibernate Validator (request validation)
- SLF4J + Logback (logging)

Without starters, you'd manually add each library and hope the versions are compatible. Starters guarantee version compatibility through Spring Boot's dependency management BOM (Bill of Materials).

```xml
<!-- ONE dependency replaces 10+ individual library declarations -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <!-- version managed by parent POM — no version tag needed -->
</dependency>
```

### Embedded Server: JAR vs WAR Deployment

Traditional Java web applications produce a **WAR** file that you deploy to an external Tomcat server. This means installing, configuring, and maintaining Tomcat separately — and deploying means copying a WAR into Tomcat's `webapps/` folder.

Spring Boot embeds Tomcat (or Jetty, or Undertow) inside your JAR. The result: `java -jar myapp.jar` starts your entire application. No external server installation, no WAR deployment, no Tomcat configuration files.

```bash
# Traditional (WAR)
# 1. Install Tomcat
# 2. Configure server.xml, context.xml
# 3. Build WAR: mvn package
# 4. Copy target/myapp.war to /opt/tomcat/webapps/
# 5. Start Tomcat: /opt/tomcat/bin/startup.sh

# Spring Boot (JAR)
mvn package                      # builds executable JAR with embedded Tomcat
java -jar target/myapp-1.0.jar   # done — server starts inside the JAR
```

This is essential for **containerized deployments** (Docker, Kubernetes). A Docker image just needs a JRE and your JAR — no Tomcat layer to maintain:

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
COPY target/myapp-1.0.jar /app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"]
```

### application.properties vs application.yml

Spring Boot reads configuration from `application.properties` (or `application.yml`) in `src/main/resources/`. Every auto-configured bean reads its settings from here:

```properties
# Server
server.port=8080
server.servlet.context-path=/api

# Database
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb
spring.datasource.username=admin
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}  # environment variable

# JPA
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate
spring.jpa.show-sql=false
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true

# Profiles — environment-specific config
# application-dev.properties  (activate: --spring.profiles.active=dev)
# application-prod.properties (activate: --spring.profiles.active=prod)
```

**Profiles** let you maintain separate configs per environment. `application-dev.properties` might use H2 in-memory database while `application-prod.properties` uses PostgreSQL. Activate with `--spring.profiles.active=prod` at startup.

### Spring Boot Actuator: Production Monitoring

Adding `spring-boot-starter-actuator` exposes HTTP endpoints for health checks, metrics, and environment info:

```
GET /actuator/health    → {"status": "UP"}
GET /actuator/metrics   → JVM memory, thread counts, HTTP request stats
GET /actuator/env       → all configuration properties (sanitized)
GET /actuator/info      → build version, git commit, custom metadata
```

Kubernetes uses `/actuator/health` for liveness and readiness probes. Prometheus scrapes `/actuator/prometheus` for metrics. These endpoints are what make Spring Boot applications production-ready out of the box.

mistakes: Thinking you need XML configuration or manual file loading — freshers often don't realize Spring Boot does this automatically.
interview/java/application-properties.direct: application.properties (or application.yml) is Spring Boot's central configuration file, located in src/main/resources. It configures the application: server port, database URL, logging levels, feature flags, and any custom properties you define. Spring Boot reads it automatically at startup — no extra configuration needed.
interview/java/application-properties.spoken: application.properties is the main configuration file in Spring Boot. It's where you put all your settings — things like database connection details, server port, logging levels, and custom properties your application needs. You just create this file in the resources folder, and Spring Boot automatically reads it when the app starts. No extra code needed. This is different from older Java frameworks where you'd have to write file-loading code or deal with XML configuration. The format is really simple: just key equals value, one per line. For example, you'd write server.port equals 8081 to change the port, or spring.datasource.url equals your database URL. You can inject these values into your code using the at-Value annotation. It's super convenient because you can change configurations without touching your Java code — just edit the properties file. One thing to watch out for: don't commit real passwords or API keys in this file to Git. In production, those should come from environment variables instead. Spring Boot has a whole hierarchy of where it looks for properties, and environment variables actually override what's in the file. That's how you keep secrets safe while still using properties for everything else.

mistakes: Freshers say 'Spring Boot does everything automatically' without understanding the classpath scanning and conditional logic that drives which beans get created.
interview/java/auto-configuration.direct: Auto-configuration is Spring Boot's mechanism that automatically creates and configures beans based on what's on the classpath and what properties are set. If spring-data-jpa is on the classpath and a datasource URL is in properties, Boot auto-configures a JPA EntityManagerFactory, transaction manager, and repositories — without you writing any of that configuration.
interview/java/auto-configuration.spoken: Auto-configuration is Spring Boot's conditional bean creation system. It looks at your classpath and properties, then creates the beans you need automatically. Here's how it works: when you add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa to your project, Spring Boot sees the JPA classes on the classpath and checks if you've provided a database URL in your properties file. If both conditions are met, it auto-configures an EntityManagerFactory, a transaction manager, and enables repository scanning — everything you need for database access. The key word is conditional. Every auto-configuration class uses annotations like at-ConditionalOnClass or at-ConditionalOnProperty to check whether it should activate. If you add the H2 database driver, Boot sees it and configures an embedded database. If you define your own DataSource bean, Boot's at-ConditionalOnMissingBean check detects it and skips the auto-configured version. That's how Spring Boot gives you smart defaults but lets you override anything. One thing freshers miss: this isn't magic or guessing. It's a deterministic decision tree. You can see exactly what got auto-configured by running your app with the debug flag or hitting the actuator conditions endpoint. That report shows which auto-configs activated and which didn't, along with the reasons. Understanding this separation between conditions and bean creation is what separates someone who uses Spring Boot from someone who understands it.

Whether the candidate understands that auto-configuration is a conditional bean creation mechanism, not just 'magic' that happens automatically.

mistakes: Explaining component scanning as just 'finding classes' without mentioning bean registration or the ApplicationContext.
interview/java/component-scan.direct: Component scanning is Spring Boot's automatic bean discovery mechanism. At startup, Spring scans specified packages for classes annotated with @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, and registers them as beans in the ApplicationContext. This eliminates manual bean configuration XML and enables dependency injection across your application.
interview/java/component-scan.spoken: Component scanning is how Spring Boot automatically discovers and registers your application's beans without writing XML config. When the application starts, Spring examines all classes in the package containing your main class, plus sub-packages, looking for annotations like at-Component, at-Service, at-Repository, or at-Controller. Think of it like Spring going through your codebase with a checklist, finding marked classes and registering them in the ApplicationContext so they can be injected elsewhere. For example, if you've got a BookService class annotated with at-Service in the com.example.bookstore.service package, and your main class with at-SpringBootApplication is in com.example.bookstore, Spring will find that service automatically. You can then inject BookService into a controller using constructor injection, and it just works because both classes were discovered during the scan. One thing freshers often miss — the at-SpringBootApplication annotation already includes at-ComponentScan, so you don't need to add it explicitly. The most common pitfall is putting classes outside the main package tree, like having your main class in com.example.app but utility classes in com.example.shared. Spring won't find those utilities because they're not under the scan root. To fix that, you'd need to explicitly configure at-ComponentScan with additional base packages. The key takeaway is component scanning eliminates boilerplate configuration by using conventions — put your classes in the right packages with the right annotations, and Spring handles the rest.

mistakes: Thinking you need to install Tomcat separately or confusing embedded servers with the microservices architecture pattern itself.
interview/java/embedded-server.direct: An embedded server is a web server like Tomcat, Jetty, or Undertow that's packaged directly inside your Spring Boot application JAR. Instead of deploying a WAR to an external Tomcat installation, you run java -jar myapp.jar and both your code and the server start together as one self-contained executable.
interview/java/embedded-server.spoken: An embedded server is a web server like Tomcat that's packaged directly inside your Spring Boot JAR file. When you run java -jar myapp.jar, the server starts automatically in the same process as your application code. In traditional Java web development, you'd install Tomcat separately, then deploy your WAR file to it. With Spring Boot, Tomcat is just another dependency in your pom.xml. This approach solves several real problems. First, it eliminates environment differences—your dev machine, staging server, and production all run the exact same Tomcat version because it's bundled with your code. Second, it makes Docker images much simpler. Instead of a base Tomcat image plus your application layer, you just need a JRE and your executable JAR. Third, there's zero server configuration to do. Spring Boot auto-configures Tomcat with sensible defaults like port 8080 and 200 worker threads, so your REST endpoints work immediately. The most common mistake freshers make is thinking they still need to download and install Tomcat from Apache. You don't—it's already in your dependencies when you include spring-boot-starter-web. Another pitfall is confusing the deployment model with architecture. Embedded servers are how you run your app, not what makes it a microservice. Even a monolith can use embedded Tomcat. The key insight is that this model treats the server as a library, not infrastructure, which is why it fits cloud deployments so well.

mistakes: Saying it 'just makes controllers' without mentioning automatic response-body serialization, or using plain @Controller for a REST API and getting view-resolution 404s.
interview/java/rest-controller-basics.direct: **@RestController** is a meta-annotation combining **@Controller** and **@ResponseBody**. It marks a class as a web controller and automatically serializes each method's return value to JSON (via **Jackson**) in the HTTP response body — so you don't add `@ResponseBody` to every method. It's the standard annotation for REST APIs that return data rather than HTML views.
interview/java/rest-controller-basics.spoken:
The RestController annotation is a Spring Boot annotation that makes building REST APIs much simpler. It combines two annotations: Controller, which marks the class as a web controller, and ResponseBody, which tells Spring to write the return value directly into the HTTP response body. The big benefit is that every method in the class automatically sends JSON back to the client without you manually converting objects or adding ResponseBody everywhere.

For example, if I have a method that returns an Order object, Spring Boot uses Jackson, the default JSON library, to serialize it to JSON, matching the field names in your Java class to JSON properties. This is perfect for REST APIs because you are returning data, not HTML views.

It helps to know where the controller sits in the request flow. A request from the client first hits the dispatcher servlet, which is the front controller. The dispatcher servlet routes it to the right RestController method. The controller usually calls a service for the business logic, the service calls a repository for data access, and the repository talks to the database. On the way back, the controller's return value is converted to JSON and sent to the client.

One thing freshers get wrong is using plain Controller when they mean to build a REST API. With plain Controller, Spring tries to find an HTML template and you get 404 errors. Another point: RestController only affects responses. To read incoming JSON in a POST or PUT, you still need the RequestBody annotation. So for an API consumed by a frontend or mobile app, RestController is exactly what you want.
interview/java/rest-controller-basics.deep:
**@RestController** is a meta-annotation combining **@Controller** and **@ResponseBody**.

It marks a class as a web controller and automatically serializes each method's return value to JSON (via **Jackson**) in the HTTP response body — so you don't add `@ResponseBody` to every method.

It's the standard annotation for REST APIs that return data rather than HTML views.

Saying it 'just makes controllers' without mentioning automatic response-body serialization, or using plain @Controller for a REST API and getting view-resolution 404s.

mistakes: Thinking starters are mere shortcuts, and adding individual libraries (e.g. jackson-databind) alongside a starter, creating duplicates and version drift.
interview/java/spring-starter-dependenci.direct: A **Spring Boot starter** is a curated, pre-tested set of dependencies bundled into a single Maven/Gradle artifact. Instead of hand-adding `spring-webmvc`, `jackson-databind`, and `tomcat-embed` and matching their versions, you add **spring-boot-starter-web** and get all of them with **compatible versions** managed by the `spring-boot-dependencies` **BOM**.
interview/java/spring-starter-dependenci.spoken:
A Spring Boot starter is a dependency that bundles multiple libraries together so you do not have to add them one by one. It solves the problem of dependency management and version conflicts. For example, if I want to build a REST API, I add spring-boot-starter-web to my pom. That single dependency automatically brings in Spring MVC for handling HTTP requests, Jackson for converting Java objects to JSON, and an embedded Tomcat to run the application.

The key benefit is that all these libraries are pre-tested together with compatible versions. I do not have to worry about whether one version of Jackson works with a particular version of Spring MVC, because Spring Boot has already figured that out. The version numbers come from the spring-boot-dependencies bill of materials in the parent POM, so I never specify versions for individual libraries.

One mistake freshers make is adding a starter and then manually adding the same libraries again, like adding spring-webmvc after already having starter-web. That creates duplicates and can cause version conflicts. The starter already includes everything you need. Another example is spring-boot-starter-data-jpa, which gives me Hibernate, Spring Data JPA repositories, and transaction management in one go. It is a huge time saver and it prevents the dependency hell that older Spring projects used to have. The naming convention is also worth knowing: official starters are spring dash boot dash starter dash something, while third-party starters put the name first and end with spring-boot-starter.

mistakes: Saying Spring Boot is 'newer and better' or treating them as alternatives, instead of explaining that Boot depends on and configures Spring Framework.
interview/java/spring-vs-spring-boot.direct: **Spring Framework** is the core: the **IoC/DI container** plus modules like Spring MVC, Spring Data, and Spring Security — it provides the actual functionality. **Spring Boot** is built *on top of* Spring Framework and adds **auto-configuration**, **starter dependencies**, and an **embedded server**. Boot removes the manual configuration work; the features themselves still come from Spring Framework.
interview/java/spring-vs-spring-boot.spoken:
I would start by saying Spring Framework is the foundation and Spring Boot is the productivity layer on top of it. Spring Framework gives us dependency injection through the IoC container, the Spring MVC web framework, Spring Data for databases, and features like the Transactional annotation for transaction management. That has been around since 2003 and it is the core you write your business logic against.

Spring Boot came out in 2014 to solve the configuration problem. Before Boot, setting up a Spring MVC REST API meant manually configuring the dispatcher servlet in web dot xml, registering a Jackson message converter as a bean, setting up component scanning, and deploying a WAR file to an external Tomcat. Boot auto-configures all of that. When I add spring-boot-starter-web to my pom, Boot detects it and automatically sets up Spring MVC, Jackson for JSON, and an embedded Tomcat. I can write a RestController, return a plain object, and it just works, because Boot wired the JSON conversion behind the scenes.

The key thing to make clear is that Boot does not replace Spring. When I use the Service annotation or the Autowired annotation, those come from Spring Framework. Boot just removes the boilerplate so I can focus on writing my actual order service and repository classes. The embedded server is another big benefit, because I can package everything as a single JAR and run java dash jar, which makes Docker and cloud deployments far simpler than managing a separate Tomcat. So they are not alternatives. Learning Spring Boot means you are using Spring Framework too, every single time.

Whether the candidate understands Spring Boot is a layer on top of Spring Framework, not a separate or competing framework, and can map specific Boot features to the framework features they auto-configure.

mistakes: Saying Spring Boot 'replaces' Spring or is a different framework, instead of recognizing it sits on top of the same Spring core and still uses @Autowired, @Transactional, the IoC container, etc.
interview/java/what-is-spring-boot.direct: **Spring Boot** is an opinionated framework built on top of the **Spring Framework** that removes most of Spring's manual configuration. It was created in 2014 to fix the problem that plain Spring needed hundreds of lines of XML or Java config just to start an app. It works through **auto-configuration**, **starter dependencies**, and an **embedded server**, following a **convention-over-configuration** philosophy where sensible defaults run out of the box and you override only what differs.
interview/java/what-is-spring-boot.spoken:
Spring Boot is a framework built on top of the regular Spring Framework that removes almost all of the configuration overhead. Before Spring Boot, even a simple Spring application needed hundreds of lines of XML or Java config just to set up basic things — component scanning, a dispatcher servlet, a data source, a transaction manager. Spring Boot was created back in 2014 to fix exactly that pain.

The important thing to get right in an interview is that Spring Boot is not a different framework competing with Spring. It is Spring, with the tedious setup already done for you. Underneath, you are still using the same IoC container and the same annotations like Autowired and Transactional.

It works through three main ideas. First, auto-configuration: Spring Boot looks at the libraries on your classpath and automatically wires sensible default beans. If it sees JPA, it configures a data source and an entity manager. Second, starter dependencies: instead of pulling in ten libraries and matching their versions yourself, you add one coordinate like spring-boot-starter-web and you get Spring MVC, Jackson, and embedded Tomcat as a tested, version-aligned set. Third, an embedded server: Tomcat ships inside your JAR, so instead of deploying a WAR to an external Tomcat you just run java dash jar app dot jar.

The whole philosophy is convention over configuration. Reasonable defaults work out of the box, and you only write configuration for the parts that differ from the norm. A common fresher mistake is manually creating beans that Boot would have configured for you. Let auto-configuration do its job, and override only when the defaults don't fit. That balance of sensible defaults plus easy overrides is why Spring Boot became the standard way to build Spring apps.

interview/java/spring-core.spoken:
**AOP** stands for Aspect-Oriented Programming, and in Spring it's how you handle **cross-cutting concerns** — things like logging, security, and transactions that affect many parts of your application but don't belong in any single class.

The idea is simple: instead of copying logging code into every service method, you write it once in an **aspect** and declare where it should apply using a **pointcut expression**. Spring then wraps your beans in **proxies** that intercept method calls and run the aspect logic automatically. When you use `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, or `@Secured`, you're actually using AOP under the hood — Spring creates a proxy that adds the behavior around your method.

The key thing to know is that Spring AOP is **proxy-based**, which means it only works on method calls that go through the proxy. If a method calls another method in the same class (self-invocation), the proxy is bypassed and the advice won't run. That's probably the most common gotcha with Spring AOP.
interview/java/spring-core.question: What is AOP in Spring?
interview/java/spring-core.title: Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP) - Cross-Cutting Concerns

mistakes: Believing @Autowired matches by field name rather than by type first, or not realizing it works on constructors, setters, and fields — and that field injection breaks plain unit tests.
interview/java/autowired.direct: **@Autowired** tells Spring to **automatically inject a dependency** by finding a matching bean in the application context. Spring resolves the dependency **by type first**, then by name if several candidates match. If no bean is found and the dependency is required, Spring throws **NoSuchBeanDefinitionException** at startup instead of failing later at runtime.
interview/java/autowired.spoken: At-Autowired tells Spring to automatically inject a dependency into your class. Instead of creating objects yourself with the new keyword, you let Spring's container provide them. Spring looks in its application context for a bean that matches the type you need. If it finds one, it injects it. If not, the app won't start and you'll see NoSuchBeanDefinitionException. You can put at-Autowired on constructors, setters, or fields. Constructor injection is the preferred approach because it makes your dependencies explicit in the method signature and lets you declare fields as final. That means your objects are immutable once created. It also works in plain unit tests without needing the Spring container. Field injection is quicker to write but it hides dependencies from callers and makes testing harder. You'd need reflection or the full Spring context just to inject a mock. Spring resolves dependencies by type first. If you have several beans of the same type, Spring then checks the parameter or field name to pick the right one. If it's still ambiguous, you get an error at startup. One pitfall freshers hit is mixing manual object creation with at-Autowired. If you write new OrderService somewhere, Spring never touches that instance, so it won't inject anything. Always let Spring create beans by marking classes with at-Service or at-Component.

mistakes: Thinking bean definition and bean instance are the same thing, when definition is the recipe and instance is the cooked meal
interview/java/bean-definition.direct: A bean definition is the metadata blueprint Spring uses to create and manage a bean. It contains the class type, scope (singleton or prototype), constructor arguments, property values, and lifecycle callbacks. Spring stores these definitions in the BeanFactory and instantiates objects from them when needed.
interview/java/bean-definition.spoken: A bean definition is the metadata blueprint Spring uses to create a bean. It's not the bean itself—it's the recipe containing the class name, scope like singleton or prototype, constructor arguments, and lifecycle methods. When Spring starts, it scans your code for annotations like at-Service or at-Component and builds BeanDefinition objects. These live in the BeanFactory. Later, when you ask for a bean, Spring reads the definition and instantiates the actual object. Think of it like a cooking recipe versus the finished meal. The recipe describes ingredients and steps, but you can't eat it. You cook the meal from the recipe. Why does this matter? Because Spring analyzes all definitions upfront before creating any beans. That's how it detects circular dependencies and figures out the creation order. If you manually call new OrderService, there's no definition, so Spring can't inject dependencies or apply at-Transactional. One mistake freshers make is thinking the definition and instance are the same. They're not. The definition is created at startup; the instance is created when needed. For singleton scope, that's also at startup, but for prototype scope, a new instance is created every time you ask for the bean. Understanding this split helps you debug NoSuchBeanDefinitionException errors and know when Spring is managing your object versus when you're on your own.

interview/java/bean-definition.question: What is a bean definition in Spring?
interview/java/bean-definition.title: Spring Bean Definition Explained

mistakes: Only mentioning singleton and prototype, forgetting the three web scopes (request, session, application)
interview/java/bean-scopes.direct: **Bean scope** defines how many instances of a bean Spring creates and how long each lives. The two core scopes are **singleton** (the default — one instance per ApplicationContext) and **prototype** (a new instance every time it's requested), plus three web scopes: **request**, **session**, and **application**. Crucially, singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM.
interview/java/bean-scopes.spoken: Bean scope controls how many instances Spring creates and how long they live. There are five scopes. Singleton is the default — Spring makes one instance per ApplicationContext and reuses it everywhere. It's what you use for services and repositories because they're stateless. Prototype scope creates a new instance every time you inject it or call getBean. You'd use this for something with mutable state, like a report generator that builds data step by step. Then there are three web scopes. Request scope gives you one instance per HTTP request — created when the request starts and destroyed when it finishes. Session scope is one instance per user session, perfect for a shopping cart that lives across multiple requests. Application scope is one instance per ServletContext, shared by everyone — that's rare, maybe for app-wide config. One tricky thing is you can't just inject a request or session scoped bean into a singleton. You need proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS so Spring injects a proxy that delegates to the current request or session instance. If you don't, the app won't start. The key insight is that singleton means one per ApplicationContext, not per JVM, and singleton beans must be stateless because they're shared across threads. If you store user-specific data in a singleton, one user can see another user's data. That's when you reach for prototype or session scope instead.

mistakes: Claiming they're identical and interchangeable, missing that @Repository adds exception translation that the others don't
interview/java/component-annotations.direct: All four are **stereotype annotations** that register a class as a Spring bean, and @Service, @Repository, and @Controller are all specializations of **@Component**. @Component is the catch-all stereotype; the other three add **semantic intent** — @Service for business logic, @Repository for persistence, @Controller for web. The one functional difference is that **@Repository** adds automatic persistence exception translation.
interview/java/component-annotations.spoken: I'd say they're all ways to register beans with Spring, but they're not interchangeable. At the base level, at-Component is the catch-all stereotype that tells Spring to manage a class as a bean. The other three are specializations of it. When you use at-Service, you're marking a class that contains business logic—things like OrderService or PaymentProcessor. It's semantic: it tells other developers this is where the business rules live. At-Repository is for data access classes like UserRepository. What makes it special is it doesn't just register the bean—it also enables exception translation. That means if your database throws a SQLException or Hibernate throws some vendor-specific error, Spring automatically wraps it in a DataAccessException. This lets you swap databases or ORMs without rewriting error handling. At-Controller is for the web layer in traditional MVC apps. Methods return view names like user-dashboard, and Spring resolves those to Thymeleaf or JSP templates. The big mistake freshers make is using at-Component everywhere because it works. Technically yes, but you lose the architecture clarity and features like exception translation. In a real Spring Boot app, you'd use at-Service for business logic, at-Repository for database access, and at-RestController—not at-Controller—for REST APIs.

mistakes: Confusing DI with IoC and treating them as the same thing — IoC is the broad principle, DI is the specific technique Spring uses to apply it.
interview/java/dependency-injection.direct: **Dependency Injection (DI)** is a design pattern where Spring supplies an object with its dependencies instead of the object creating them itself. Instead of writing `new UserRepository()` inside a service, the class declares what it needs and the **Spring IoC container** injects a ready-to-use instance through the constructor. This separation of object creation from usage is what makes Spring applications **loosely coupled** and easy to test.
interview/java/dependency-injection.spoken: Dependency Injection is a design pattern where Spring gives an object its dependencies instead of the object creating them. So if my OrderService needs an OrderRepository, I don't write new OrderRepository inside the service. I just declare the repository in the constructor, and Spring injects a ready-to-use instance. This is how Spring implements Inversion of Control, which means the framework controls object creation, not my code. The biggest advantage is loose coupling. My OrderService depends on an interface, not a concrete class, so I can swap the database implementation for an in-memory one without touching the service. It also makes testing much easier. In a unit test I can inject a mock repository and check the order logic with no real database connection. One mistake freshers make is using field injection with the Autowired annotation on a private field because it looks simpler. Constructor injection is better because the dependencies are explicit in the signature and you can mark the fields final. When an interviewer asks this, they want to know that you understand why DI exists, not just what it is, so I always mention testability and loose coupling with a concrete example like swapping a repository implementation.

What is the difference between IoC and DI?
Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?
Show a concrete payoff: a constructor-injected repository can be replaced with a mock in a unit test, so the test needs no real database.
Whether you understand that DI is how Spring implements Inversion of Control, and why handing dependencies to the container makes code testable and loosely coupled.

interview/java/dependency-injection.title: Dependency Injection in Spring Explained

mistakes: Freshers only know field injection because @Autowired on a field is the shortest to type, and can't explain the testability cost.
interview/java/di-types.direct: The three DI types are **constructor injection** (dependencies via the constructor — the recommended default), **setter injection** (via setter methods — for optional dependencies), and **field injection** (@Autowired directly on a field — convenient but discouraged in production). Constructor injection wins because it allows final fields and makes the class testable without Spring.
interview/java/di-types.spoken: Spring supports three types of dependency injection. The first is constructor injection, where you pass dependencies through the class constructor. That's the recommended approach because it lets you make fields final and guarantees every required dependency is provided up front. The second is setter injection, where you use a setter method to inject a dependency after the object is created. That works well for optional dependencies that aren't critical to the class. The third is field injection, where you put the at-Autowired annotation directly on a field. It's the shortest to write, but it's discouraged in production because you can't make the field final and it's harder to unit test. Here's a concrete example. In an OrderService you'd use constructor injection for the PaymentGateway, because you can't process an order without it. You'd use setter injection for a NotificationService, because sending a confirmation is nice to have but not essential. Field injection might show up in older code, but modern teams avoid it. The mistake freshers make is using field injection everywhere because it looks clean, and that creates real problems when you try to test the class without starting the whole Spring container. In an interview, always say constructor injection is the industry default, then explain that it gives you immutability and easy testing.

probes.text: Why is constructor injection recommended over field injection?
When would you use setter injection?
What is the benefit of final fields in constructor injection?
State clearly that constructor injection is recommended, then back it with final fields, plain-Java testing, and fail-fast startup.
Whether you know all three DI styles and can justify why constructor injection is the production default, not just recite them.

mistakes: Confusing IoC with DI or thinking they're the same thing — IoC is the principle, DI is one implementation
interview/java/ioc-container.direct: Inversion of Control (IoC) means the framework controls object creation and lifecycle, not your code. Instead of writing new UserService(), you declare a @Service class and Spring creates, wires, and manages its lifecycle. Control over object creation is 'inverted' from your code to the framework.
interview/java/ioc-container.spoken: Inversion of Control means Spring controls object creation, not your code. In traditional Java, you'd write new OrderService, then new PaymentProcessor, manually wiring everything. With IoC, you just mark OrderService with the at-Service annotation and Spring creates it for you. The control over when and how objects are created is inverted from your code to the framework. It's like the Hollywood Principle: don't call us, we'll call you. You declare what you need, Spring figures out the how. Here's why it matters in real projects. When OrderService needs PaymentProcessor, you don't hardcode new PaymentProcessor in the constructor. Spring injects it, so you can swap implementations without touching OrderService. That's loose coupling. During testing, you pass a mock PaymentProcessor and test OrderService in isolation. In production, Spring injects the real one. The container also manages lifecycle. It calls your at-PostConstruct method after wiring dependencies, perfect for opening database connections. Then it invokes at-PreDestroy before shutdown to clean up. One mistake freshers make: using new inside Spring beans. If you create dependencies manually, Spring can't manage them or apply transaction logic. Always let the container instantiate collaborators. Another pitfall: confusing IoC with Dependency Injection. IoC is the big idea — framework controls flow. DI is one way to implement IoC, where dependencies are injected. Event listeners and callbacks are also IoC, but they're not DI. So when an interviewer asks about IoC, talk about control inversion, then explain DI as the mechanism Spring uses to achieve it.

mistakes: Knowing web annotations but not configuration or lifecycle annotations, or treating all stereotypes as identical
interview/java/spring-annotations-overvi.direct: Key Spring annotations: **configuration** (@Configuration, @Bean, @ComponentScan), **stereotypes** (@Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller), **injection** (@Autowired, @Qualifier, @Value), **web** (@RestController, @GetMapping), and **lifecycle** (@PostConstruct, @PreDestroy). These cover bean definition, dependency injection, web layer mapping, and lifecycle hooks that every Spring developer uses daily.
interview/java/spring-annotations-overvi.spoken: The most important Spring annotations fall into five categories. First, you've got configuration annotations like at-Configuration and at-Bean. These let you define beans explicitly when you need control, like wiring up a third-party library class. Second, there are stereotype annotations: at-Component is the general one, but you should use at-Service for business logic, at-Repository for data access, and at-Controller for web handlers. Spring auto-detects these when it scans your packages. Third, injection annotations like at-Autowired and at-Value. At-Autowired wires dependencies, and constructor injection is preferred over field injection because it makes your class immutable and easier to test. At-Value injects configuration from properties files. Fourth, web annotations like at-RestController and at-GetMapping. These map HTTP requests to your methods. And fifth, lifecycle annotations like at-PostConstruct and at-PreDestroy for initialization and cleanup. A common mistake freshers make is using at-Component everywhere instead of the specific stereotypes, which loses semantic meaning and framework benefits. Another is using field injection with at-Autowired instead of constructor injection. To stand out, group the annotations by purpose like I just did and give a concrete example for each category. That shows you understand the framework architecture, not just individual annotations.

mistakes: Writing a CustomerRepositoryImpl class by hand (causing a bean conflict), confusing CrudRepository with JpaRepository, or assuming findAll returns a List
interview/java/crud-repository.direct: **`CrudRepository<T, ID>`** is Spring Data's base interface providing the core CRUD methods: `save()`, `findById()`, `findAll()`, `count()`, `delete()`, and `existsById()`. You only declare the interface with your entity type `T` and primary-key type `ID` — Spring **generates the implementation at runtime** (a dynamic proxy backed by `SimpleJpaRepository`), so there is no DAO boilerplate. Note the return types: `findById()` returns `Optional<T>` and `findAll()` returns `Iterable<T>`, not `List<T>`.
interview/java/crud-repository.spoken: CrudRepository is Spring Data's core interface that gives you the basic database operations without writing any code. I just create an interface that extends CrudRepository and specify the entity type and the id type, and Spring does the rest. It provides save for inserting or updating, findById to fetch by primary key, findAll to read everything, delete to remove records, and helpers like count and existsById. The interesting part is what happens at startup. Spring scans my interfaces, sees they extend CrudRepository, and generates a concrete implementation in memory using a proxy. That proxy is backed by a class called SimpleJpaRepository, which holds the real Hibernate logic, and it gets registered as a bean so I can inject it anywhere. I never write a repository implementation myself. For example, if I have a Customer entity with a Long id, I write interface CustomerRepository extends CrudRepository of Customer and Long, and immediately I can call save and findById. Two details worth knowing: findById returns an Optional so I'm forced to handle the missing case safely, and findAll returns an Iterable rather than a List. If I need pagination, sorting, or batch operations, I'd upgrade to JpaRepository, which extends CrudRepository and adds more methods and a List return type.

mistakes: Writing @Query JPQL for simple conditions derived methods already handle, or omitting @Transactional on deleteBy
interview/java/derived-query-methods.direct: **Derived query methods** let Spring Data JPA generate the query from the **method name**. Declaring `findByLastName(String name)` produces `WHERE last_name = ?` — no SQL, no `@Query`. Spring **parses the name at startup** into a query, so a typo or unknown field fails the application boot (fast feedback), not at runtime.
interview/java/derived-query-methods.spoken: Derived query methods are a Spring Data JPA feature where I just write a method signature in my repository interface and Spring generates the query by reading the method name. For example, if I write findByLastName with a String parameter, Spring builds a select with a where clause on the last name field. I don't write any SQL or annotations. This works because Spring parses the method name at application startup. It breaks the name into parts — findBy means it's a select, LastName maps to the last name field on my entity, and the parameter becomes a where condition. I can combine conditions with And or Or, like findByEmailAndStatus. There are operator keywords too, like findByAgeGreaterThan, and result shapers like OrderBy, Top, and IgnoreCase. The mistake freshers make is writing a custom Query annotation for simple lookups that a derived method handles perfectly. Another gotcha is delete methods: if I write deleteByStatus I have to add Transactional, or it throws at runtime. Something interviewers like to hear is that if my method name doesn't follow the grammar or references a field that doesn't exist, the application fails at startup with a clear error, which is much better than discovering it in production. So derived methods keep repositories clean and readable, and when the names get long with many conditions, that's the signal to switch to a Query annotation with JPQL.

interview/java/derived-query-methods.codeExample:
```java
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {

    List<User> findByLastName(String lastName);                 // WHERE last_name = ?

    Optional<User> findByEmailAndStatus(String email, String status); // AND

    List<User> findByAgeGreaterThanOrderByCreatedAtDesc(int age);     // > ? ORDER BY ... DESC

    List<User> findByCreatedAtBetween(LocalDateTime start, LocalDateTime end); // BETWEEN

    long countByDepartment(String department);                 // COUNT(*)

    boolean existsByEmail(String email);                        // EXISTS

    @Transactional
    void deleteByStatus(String status);                        // DELETE — needs a transaction
}
```

mistakes: Omitting the no-arg constructor or marking the class final, breaking instantiation and lazy-loading proxies
interview/java/entity-annotations.direct: **`@Entity`** marks a class as a JPA-managed entity mapped to a table. At startup, Hibernate scans `@Entity` classes and builds the mapping. The class needs three things: a **`@Id`** field, a **no-arg constructor** (JPA instantiates via reflection on load), and it **must not be `final`** (JPA subclasses it for lazy-loading proxies).
interview/java/entity-annotations.spoken: The Entity annotation is the fundamental one that tells JPA a Java class represents a database table. When I mark a class with Entity, I'm saying this object should be persisted and JPA should manage its lifecycle. At startup, Hibernate scans for these annotations and builds the mapping between the class and the table. There are three requirements freshers often miss. First, I need an Id field for the primary key, because that's how JPA uniquely identifies a row. Second, I must have a no-arg constructor, because JPA uses reflection to create the object before it fills in the fields from the database. Third, the class can't be final, because JPA creates proxy subclasses at runtime for lazy loading and change tracking, and you can't subclass a final class. A real example: in an e-commerce app I create a Product class with name, price, and createdAt, put Entity on the class and Id on the id field, and now calling save generates the insert, and loading populates my object. The classic mistake is adding a constructor with parameters but forgetting the empty one — it compiles but crashes at runtime when JPA tries to instantiate the entity. I usually make the no-arg constructor protected so it satisfies JPA but isn't part of my public API. And in Spring Boot 3.2 the imports come from the jakarta persistence package, not the old javax one.

What is @Table and when do you need it?
Why should @Entity classes not be final?
Connect each requirement to a mechanism: no-arg constructor → reflective instantiation, non-final → runtime proxy subclassing
Whether you know the three entity contract requirements and why JPA needs them (reflection + proxies)

mistakes: Not knowing which side owns the relationship, or forgetting that bidirectional relationships need mappedBy on the inverse side
interview/java/entity-relationships.direct: The four JPA relationship types are **@OneToOne**, **@OneToMany** (one parent, many children), **@ManyToOne** (many children, one parent), and **@ManyToMany** (join table). Each can be **unidirectional or bidirectional**, and exactly one side must be the **owning side** that controls the foreign key.
interview/java/entity-relationships.spoken:
JPA gives us four relationship types. The OneToOne annotation maps one entity to exactly one other, like a User to a UserProfile. The OneToMany and ManyToOne annotations are two sides of the same coin — a Department has many Employees, and each Employee belongs to one Department. The ManyToMany annotation maps many-to-many relationships like Students and Courses, where one student can take many courses and one course can have many students.

The key idea to get right is the owning side. In every relationship, one side owns the foreign key. For a OneToMany and ManyToOne pair, the ManyToOne side is always the owner because it's the side that physically holds the foreign key column. You put the JoinColumn annotation on the owning side to name that column. On the inverse side, you use the mappedBy attribute to point back to the field on the owning side. If you forget mappedBy, Hibernate thinks you have two separate relationships and creates duplicate columns or an extra join table, which breaks your schema.

A common mistake is putting the OneToMany annotation on both sides without mappedBy. Another is using cascade type ALL without realising that deleting a parent then deletes all its children. In real projects you'd reach for ManyToOne for things like orders and order items, OneToOne for splitting a large entity, and ManyToMany for things like users and roles. And if you need extra data on a many-to-many link, like an enrollment date, you don't use ManyToMany — you create a junction entity with two ManyToOne fields instead.

mistakes: Using 'JPA' and 'Hibernate' interchangeably without realising JPA is only the interface contract and Hibernate is the engine behind it
interview/java/hibernate-basics.direct: **Hibernate** is an **ORM framework** and the most popular **JPA implementation**. **JPA is the specification** (interfaces and annotations); Hibernate provides the concrete code that fulfils it. Spring Boot's `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` ships **Hibernate as the default provider**.
interview/java/hibernate-basics.spoken:
JPA is the specification and Hibernate is the implementation. Think of JPA as the blueprint — it defines the interfaces and annotations, like the Entity annotation and the EntityManager interface, that describe how persistence should work. Hibernate is the actual builder that follows that blueprint and does the work.

When you add the spring-boot-starter-data-jpa dependency to a Spring Boot project, you get both: the JPA interfaces you code against, plus Hibernate running behind the scenes. This separation is powerful because you're writing to a standard. If you ever needed to, you could swap Hibernate for another JPA provider like EclipseLink without changing your code. In practice Hibernate is so dominant that most projects just use it.

The key thing is knowing which layer you're touching. When you annotate a class with the Entity annotation, that's JPA. Hibernate reads it and generates the actual SQL. A common fresher mistake is importing org dot hibernate classes directly in service code when they should stick to the jakarta persistence imports to keep things standard. In an interview, showing you understand this specification-versus-implementation distinction proves you know the architecture, not just the syntax.

mistakes: Confusing JPA (the spec) with Hibernate (the implementation), or not understanding the EntityManager and persistence context lifecycle.
interview/java/jpa-basics.direct: JPA (Java Persistence API) is a specification (jakarta.persistence) that maps Java objects to relational database tables, letting developers save and query entities using object-oriented APIs instead of hand-written SQL and JDBC boilerplate. It exists because relational databases and object-oriented languages have an impedance mismatch -- objects have identity, inheritance, and associations, while tables have rows, foreign keys, and joins -- and bridging that gap manually in every application is repetitive and error-prone. Hibernate is the most popular JPA implementation, and Spring Data JPA builds on top of JPA to eliminate even the persistence-layer boilerplate by generating repository implementations from interface method names.
interview/java/jpa-basics.spoken: JPA is the Java Persistence API, a specification for object-relational mapping. It maps Java classes annotated with @Entity to database tables, and it lets you interact with the database through an EntityManager instead of writing raw SQL and JDBC code. The reason it exists is the impedance mismatch between objects and tables: objects have inheritance and associations, while tables have rows and foreign keys, and bridging that gap manually in every application is repetitive and error-prone. Hibernate is the most popular implementation of the JPA spec, and Spring Data JPA builds on top by generating repository implementations from interface method names, so you can write findByPriceLessThan and Spring derives the SQL at runtime. The key concept to understand is the persistence context -- it is a first-level cache that tracks entity state changes and synchronizes them with the database on commit. The biggest pitfall I watch for is the N+1 problem, where a lazy relationship triggers a separate query per entity, which I solve with join-fetch or entity graphs.

interview/java/jpa-basics.question: What is JPA and why does it exist? It provides a standard Java specification for object-relational mapping so that developers can persist Java objects to relational databases without writing JDBC boilerplate.
