mistakes: Extending CrudRepository 'because it's simpler', then converting Iterable to List in every service method and missing flush()/batch operations when they're needed
interview/java/jpa-repository.direct: **JpaRepository** is the top of Spring Data's repository hierarchy — it extends **CrudRepository** and **PagingAndSortingRepository** and adds JPA-specific methods (`flush()`, `saveAndFlush()`, `deleteAllInBatch()`). It also returns **`List<T>`** instead of `Iterable<T>`, so service code is cleaner and needs no conversion. Extend `JpaRepository` by default; drop to `CrudRepository` only for a deliberately minimal API surface.
interview/java/jpa-repository.spoken: JpaRepository is the most complete interface Spring Data gives you for JPA entities. It extends both CrudRepository and PagingAndSortingRepository, so you get basic create, read, update, delete plus pagination and sorting out of the box. The main reason I extend JpaRepository instead of CrudRepository is the return type. JpaRepository returns a List, while CrudRepository returns an Iterable. A List is directly usable in my service and controller layers, so I don't have to write conversion code every time I call findAll. JpaRepository also adds JPA-specific methods. The flush method forces Hibernate to write pending changes to the database immediately, which is handy when I need a generated id for the next step. saveAndFlush combines a save and an immediate flush. And deleteAllInBatch issues a single delete statement instead of loading each entity and deleting it one by one, which is much faster for bulk cleanup. A mistake I see freshers make is extending CrudRepository because it sounds simpler, and then they end up with Iterable everywhere and constant conversion. The thing to understand is that JpaRepository is a strict superset. It has everything CrudRepository has plus more, so in a normal Spring Boot app on PostgreSQL there's no downside to making it the default.

How do you implement pagination with JpaRepository?
What is getReferenceById() and when would you use it?

interview/java/jpa-repository.question: What is JpaRepository and why do you extend it instead of CrudRepository?
interview/java/jpa-repository.title: JpaRepository vs CrudRepository — Why Use JpaRepository

mistakes: Switching everything to EAGER after one LazyInitializationException — a panic fix that loads too much data on every query and hides the real issue
interview/java/lazy-vs-eager-loading.direct: **Lazy loading** delays fetching related entities until you actually access them; **eager loading** fetches them immediately alongside the parent. In JPA, **@OneToMany** and **@ManyToMany** default to **LAZY**, while **@ManyToOne** and **@OneToOne** default to **EAGER**. Choose lazy by default and fetch eagerly only in the queries that need it.
interview/java/lazy-vs-eager-loading.spoken:
Lazy loading means JPA waits to fetch related entities until you actually access them in your code. Eager loading fetches them immediately, in the same query as the parent. So if I load an Order with lazy items, Hibernate doesn't load the order items until I call get items in my code. With eager, it does a JOIN right away and loads everything together.

The defaults matter. The OneToMany and ManyToMany associations are lazy by default, because collections can be huge. The ManyToOne and OneToOne associations are eager by default, because it's usually just one extra row.

Here's the trade-off. Lazy saves memory and query time when you don't need the data, but it can cause the N plus one problem if you access lazy collections in a loop — one query for the list, then one query per item. Eager avoids that but wastes resources when you don't use the data.

A common mistake freshers make is switching everything to eager when they hit a LazyInitializationException. That's the wrong fix. The right approach is to keep lazy as the default and use JOIN FETCH or EntityGraph in the specific queries where you know you need the related data. That gives you fine-grained control: lazy by default, eager only where it makes sense.

interview/java/spring-mvc-rest.spoken:
In Spring, the cleanest way to handle exceptions in REST APIs is using **`@RestControllerAdvice`** combined with **`@ExceptionHandler`** methods. You create a single global handler class that catches exceptions thrown by any controller.

Each `@ExceptionHandler` method targets a specific exception type. For example, you'd have one method that catches `ResourceNotFoundException` and returns a **404** with a structured JSON error body, another that catches `MethodArgumentNotValidException` for **400** validation errors, and a catch-all for `Exception.class` that returns a **500**.

The key benefit is **consistency** — every error response has the same shape: `timestamp`, `status`, `error`, `message`, and `path`. Your API consumers can write one error-parsing logic on their end. Without this, you'd have scattered try-catch blocks in every controller returning errors in different formats.

I always make sure the fallback handler logs the full stack trace on the server but only returns a generic message to the client — you never want to leak internal details in production.
interview/java/spring-mvc-rest.question: How do you handle exceptions in REST APIs?
interview/java/spring-mvc-rest.title: REST Exception Handling - Global Error Responses

mistakes: Using @SpringBootTest for every test including simple service unit tests, making the test suite run 10-50x slower
interview/java/spring-boot-test-annotati.direct: **@SpringBootTest** loads the **full Spring application context** for integration testing — every bean, all auto-configuration, and every layer wired together just like production. Reach for it when you need to verify layers actually work end-to-end, **not** for isolated unit tests where mocks run 10–50x faster.
interview/java/spring-boot-test-annotati.spoken: I'd say the SpringBootTest annotation is the one you use for integration testing in Spring Boot. It loads the full application context, meaning all your beans, auto-configuration, and wiring happen just like when you run the app normally. You'd use this when you need to test that multiple layers work together — like verifying a controller endpoint calls a service, the service calls a repository, and data actually gets saved to the database. The key thing to understand is that it's expensive. Starting the full context takes several seconds per test class, so you don't want to use it for simple unit tests where you're just testing business logic. For those, you'd use plain JUnit with Mockito and the Mock annotation. One thing freshers often miss is the webEnvironment option. By default it uses MOCK mode, which gives you a mock servlet environment. If you need a real HTTP server running — say you're using TestRestTemplate — you set webEnvironment to RANDOM_PORT. I'd also mention that Spring caches contexts between test classes to save time, so if you add test-specific properties or use the DirtiesContext annotation everywhere, you kill that optimisation and your suite becomes really slow.

mistakes: Using @SpringBootTest for service tests and calling them unit tests, or thinking unit tests always require Spring context.
interview/java/unit-vs-integration-test.direct: A **unit test** checks a single class in isolation using **mocks** and never starts Spring. An **integration test** boots part or all of the Spring context and verifies real **wiring** between components. Unit tests run in milliseconds with Mockito; integration tests use **@SpringBootTest** or slice annotations like **@WebMvcTest**.
interview/java/unit-vs-integration-test.spoken: A unit test checks a single class in isolation using mocks. It doesn't start the Spring container. You'd use Mockito to mock dependencies like repositories or external services, then test just the business logic. For example, testing a service method that calculates order totals—you'd mock the repository and verify the calculation logic. An integration test is different. It starts the Spring context, either fully with the SpringBootTest annotation or partially with slice annotations like WebMvcTest. It tests how real beans wire together. So you'd write an integration test to verify that a controller actually calls the service, and the service actually saves to the database. The key difference is speed. Unit tests run in milliseconds because there's no context startup. Integration tests take three to five seconds just to boot Spring before running any assertions. In a real project, you'd want maybe eighty percent unit tests and twenty percent integration tests. That's the testing pyramid—lots of fast tests at the base, fewer slow tests higher up. The mistake freshers make is putting the SpringBootTest annotation on every test. That turns everything into an integration test, and your test suite becomes painfully slow.

mistakes: Using @SpringBootTest for every test, loading the entire application context and making tests slow
interview/java/webmvctest.direct: @WebMvcTest is a Spring Boot test slice annotation that loads only the web layer components—controllers, filters, @ControllerAdvice, and MockMvc infrastructure—without starting the full application context, services, or repositories.
interview/java/webmvctest.spoken: At-WebMvcTest is a test slice annotation that loads only the web layer components you need to test controllers. It's like unit testing for your REST endpoints. When you use it, Spring Boot starts only the controller classes, MockMvc, and web infrastructure—it doesn't load services, repositories, or the database. This makes your tests really fast, usually finishing in under two seconds. Here's the key part freshers miss: because services aren't loaded, you have to provide them as at-MockBean in your test class. So if your controller has an at-Autowired OrderService, you declare at-MockBean OrderService in the test, then use Mockito's when method to stub what it returns. I'd use at-WebMvcTest whenever I'm testing just the controller logic—like verifying that a GET endpoint returns the right JSON structure, or that a POST with invalid data returns 400 Bad Request. The mistake I see freshers make is using at-SpringBootTest for everything, which loads the entire application context and makes tests slow. at-WebMvcTest is way faster because it focuses on just the web layer, and if the test fails, you immediately know it's a controller problem, not something deeper in the service or database layer.

mistakes: Selecting a non-aggregated column alongside an aggregate without GROUP BY.
interview/java/aggregate-functions.direct: **Aggregate functions** collapse many rows into a single summary value. The five core ones are **COUNT** (number of rows), **SUM** (total), **AVG** (mean), **MIN**, and **MAX**. With `GROUP BY` they produce one value per group; without it, one value for the whole table.
interview/java/aggregate-functions.spoken: Aggregate functions take many rows and reduce them to a single summary value. The five you use all the time are COUNT, which tells you how many rows, SUM, which adds up a numeric column, AVG for the average, and MIN and MAX for the smallest and largest values. On their own they summarize the whole table, so SUM of total gives you total revenue across every order. Combined with GROUP BY, they give you one value per group, like revenue per region. A detail that interviewers like to probe is NULL handling. Every aggregate except COUNT star ignores NULLs. So if I run AVG of bonus and half the employees have a NULL bonus, the average is computed only over the people who actually have a bonus, which changes the denominator and can surprise you. COUNT star counts every row including the ones with NULLs, while COUNT of a specific column skips the NULLs in that column. One rule that trips up freshers: if you select a normal column alongside an aggregate, that column has to appear in the GROUP BY, otherwise the query is ambiguous and most databases reject it. And remember you can't filter on an aggregate in WHERE; conditions on a COUNT or SUM go in HAVING.

How do aggregate functions handle NULL values?
Why must non-aggregated columns appear in GROUP BY?
Note that all aggregates except COUNT(*) ignore NULLs.

interview/java/aggregate-functions.codeExample:
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*)   AS total_orders,
       SUM(total)  AS revenue,
       AVG(total)  AS avg_order,
       MIN(total)  AS smallest,
       MAX(total)  AS largest
FROM orders;
```

Sample output:

| total_orders | revenue | avg_order | smallest | largest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 6000 | 1200 | 200 | 2500 |

*One row, five summary values for the whole table.*

mistakes: Relying only on application validation and skipping DB constraints.
interview/java/constraints.direct: **Constraints** are rules the database enforces on column data to guarantee **integrity**. The main ones are **PRIMARY KEY** (unique + not null identity), **FOREIGN KEY** (references another table), **UNIQUE**, **NOT NULL**, **CHECK** (custom condition), and **DEFAULT**. They reject bad data at the database level, no matter which app writes it.
interview/java/constraints.spoken: Constraints are rules you attach to your tables that the database enforces automatically, rejecting any insert or update that breaks them. Their whole purpose is data integrity: they keep the data valid no matter which application, script, or person is writing to the table. The main constraints are primary key, which uniquely identifies each row and is both unique and not null; foreign key, which links a column to another table's primary key and enforces referential integrity so you don't get orphan rows; unique, which prevents duplicate values; not null, which forces a column to always have a value; check, which enforces a custom condition like salary greater than zero; and default, which supplies a fallback value when none is given. The reason I always define constraints at the database level, rather than relying only on application validation, is that they're the last line of defense. Application code can have bugs, and often more than one service writes to the same database, so a constraint guarantees that even if the app logic fails, genuinely invalid data simply can't get in. The only caution is not to over-constrain, where an overly strict check ends up blocking legitimate edge cases.
interview/java/constraints.deep:
**Constraints** are rules the database enforces on column data to guarantee **integrity**.

The main ones are **PRIMARY KEY** (unique + not null identity), **FOREIGN KEY** (references another table), **UNIQUE**, **NOT NULL**, **CHECK** (custom condition), and **DEFAULT**.

They reject bad data at the database level, no matter which app writes it.

Relying only on application validation and skipping DB constraints.

probes.text: What is a FOREIGN KEY constraint and what does CASCADE mean?

Whether you know the main constraint types and that they enforce integrity at the DB level.

interview/java/constraints.codeExample:
```sql
CREATE TABLE employees (
  id        INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,      -- unique identity
  email     VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL UNIQUE,         -- required + no duplicates
  dept_id   INT REFERENCES departments(id),       -- foreign key
  salary    DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (salary > 0),     -- custom rule
  status    VARCHAR(10) DEFAULT 'ACTIVE'          -- fallback value
);

-- this fails the CHECK constraint:
INSERT INTO employees (email, salary) VALUES ('a@x.com', -100); -- rejected
```

*The database rejects the negative salary regardless of what the app sent.*

interview/java/constraints.title: SQL Constraints — Enforcing Data Integrity

mistakes: Lumping all SQL together and assuming everything can be rolled back.
interview/java/ddl-dml-dql.direct: SQL commands are grouped by purpose: **DDL** (Data Definition Language) defines structure — `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`; **DML** (Data Manipulation Language) changes data — `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`; **DQL** (Data Query Language) reads data — `SELECT`. DDL auto-commits; DML is transactional.
interview/java/ddl-dml-dql.spoken: SQL commands are grouped into families based on what they do, and knowing the categories helps you reason about behaviour. DDL, data definition language, is about structure: CREATE to make a table, ALTER to change it, DROP to remove it, and TRUNCATE to empty it. DML, data manipulation language, is about the data inside tables: INSERT to add rows, UPDATE to change them, and DELETE to remove them. DQL, data query language, is about reading data, and that's essentially just SELECT, the R in CRUD. The behavioural difference that interviewers love is around transactions. DDL statements auto-commit, meaning their effect is permanent immediately and they typically commit any pending work, so you can't roll a CREATE or DROP back in most databases. DML, on the other hand, is transactional: you can wrap inserts, updates, and deletes in a transaction and either commit them or roll them back. There are two more families worth naming to show depth: DCL, data control language, which is GRANT and REVOKE for permissions, and TCL, transaction control language, which is COMMIT and ROLLBACK. So the quick mental map is DDL for structure, DML for data changes, DQL for reads, plus DCL and TCL for security and transactions.
interview/java/ddl-dml-dql.deep:
SQL commands are grouped by purpose: **DDL** (Data Definition Language) defines structure — `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`; **DML** (Data Manipulation Language) changes data — `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`; **DQL** (Data Query Language) reads data — `SELECT`.

DDL auto-commits; DML is transactional.

mistakes: Selecting a non-aggregated column that isn't in GROUP BY.
interview/java/group-by-having.direct: **GROUP BY** collapses rows that share the same value(s) into groups, so aggregates (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`) produce **one result per group**. Every column in the SELECT must be either inside an aggregate or listed in `GROUP BY`.
interview/java/group-by-having.spoken: GROUP BY takes rows that share the same value in one or more columns and collapses them into groups, so that an aggregate function produces one result per group instead of one for the whole table. So GROUP BY department with COUNT star gives me the headcount for each department, one row per department, and I can add AVG of salary to get the average pay per department in the same query. The rule that trips up almost every beginner is the SELECT column rule: every column you put in the SELECT list must either be wrapped in an aggregate function or appear in the GROUP BY clause. The reason is that each output row represents a whole group, so if you select a column like employee name that isn't grouped or aggregated, the database has no way to know which name to show for that group, and it rejects the query. It also helps to know where GROUP BY sits in execution: it runs after WHERE, so you filter individual rows first, and before HAVING and SELECT, so HAVING can then filter the groups. One more practical note: GROUP BY does not sort the output, so if you want the departments in a particular order you have to add an explicit ORDER BY.

interview/java/group-by-having.codeExample:
```sql
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount, AVG(salary) AS avg_pay
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;
```

Sample output:

| department | headcount | avg_pay |
|---|---|---|
| Tech | 12 | 95000 |
| Sales | 7 | 60000 |
| Finance | 4 | 88000 |

*One summary row per department.*

mistakes: Indexing everything, assuming indexes are free.
interview/java/indexes-basics.direct: A **database index** is a sorted data structure (usually a **B-tree**) that lets the database find rows by a column's value without scanning the whole table — like a book's index. It makes reads (`WHERE`, `JOIN`, `ORDER BY`) much faster but **slows writes** and uses extra storage.
interview/java/indexes-basics.spoken: A database index is a separate, sorted data structure, usually a B-tree, that the database keeps alongside your table to find rows quickly by a column's value. The analogy everyone uses is the index at the back of a book: instead of reading every page to find a topic, you look it up in the index and jump straight to the right page. Without an index, finding a row by a column means a full table scan, reading every single row, which is order n. With an index, the database walks the B-tree in roughly order log n, so on a million-row table that's about twenty steps instead of a million reads. Indexes make reads much faster, which helps WHERE lookups, JOIN matching, and ORDER BY sorting. But the key thing to say in an interview is that indexes are not free. Every time you insert, update, or delete a row, the database also has to update every index on that table, so indexes slow down writes. They also take up extra storage. So the skill isn't adding indexes everywhere; it's adding them on the columns you actually filter or join on, and avoiding them on columns with very few distinct values, like a boolean, where they don't help much. You also lose the index if you wrap the column in a function in your WHERE clause.
interview/java/indexes-basics.deep:
**EXPLAIN** (or `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`) shows the database's **query execution plan** — how it will run a query.

You read it to see whether a query uses an **index** (look for `index`/`ref`/`range`) or does a **full table scan** (`ALL` in MySQL, `Seq Scan` in Postgres), then add or fix indexes accordingly.

A **database index** is a sorted data structure (usually a **B-tree**) that lets the database find rows by a column's value without scanning the whole table — like a book's index. It makes reads (`WHERE`, `JOIN`, `ORDER BY`) much faster but **slows writes** and uses extra storage.

Indexing everything, assuming indexes are free.

mistakes: Adding a WHERE filter on the right table after a LEFT JOIN, silently turning it into an INNER JOIN.
interview/java/joins.direct: **INNER JOIN** returns only rows that match in both tables. **LEFT JOIN** returns all rows from the left table plus matches from the right (NULLs where none match). **RIGHT JOIN** is the mirror — all rows from the right table plus left matches.
interview/java/joins.spoken: A join combines rows from two tables based on a matching condition, and the three you use most are inner, left, and right. An inner join returns only the rows that have a match in both tables, so if a customer has no orders, that customer simply doesn't appear. A left join, sometimes called left outer join, returns every row from the left table plus the matching rows from the right, and where there's no match it fills the right-side columns with NULL. So with customers left-joined to orders, even a customer with zero orders shows up, just with a NULL total. A right join is the exact mirror: all rows from the right table plus matches from the left. The trap that catches a lot of freshers is mixing a left join with a WHERE filter on the right table. If I do a left join and then write WHERE order total greater than zero, those NULL rows fail the condition and get dropped, which silently turns my left join back into an inner join. The fix is to move that condition into the ON clause instead of WHERE, so the unmatched left rows are preserved. So the mental model is: inner keeps intersections, left and right keep one whole side, and where you put a filter, ON versus WHERE, decides whether the outer rows survive.

What is a FULL OUTER JOIN?

mistakes: Defaulting to SELECT * everywhere, and assuming clauses run in the order they are typed.
interview/java/select-queries.direct: **SELECT** retrieves rows from one or more tables. The written form is `SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition GROUP BY ... HAVING ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT n`, but SQL's **logical execution order** is FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. Prefer naming explicit columns over `SELECT *` in real code.
interview/java/select-queries.spoken: The SELECT statement is the core read command in SQL. You name the columns you want, the table after FROM, a WHERE clause to filter rows, ORDER BY to sort, and LIMIT to cap how many rows come back. So to get the names and cities of adult customers, oldest first, top three, I'd write SELECT name, city, age FROM customers WHERE age greater than or equal to eighteen ORDER BY age descending LIMIT three. The thing that tripped me up early is that SQL doesn't run clauses in the order you type them. The logical execution order is FROM first to pick the table, then WHERE to filter, then GROUP BY and HAVING, then SELECT to compute the output columns, then ORDER BY, and finally LIMIT. That explains a classic confusion: you can use a column alias from SELECT inside ORDER BY because ORDER BY runs after SELECT, but you cannot use that alias in WHERE because WHERE runs first. Two habits I keep: name the exact columns instead of SELECT star so I'm not shipping data nobody asked for, and always pair LIMIT with ORDER BY, otherwise the database is free to return rows in any order and pagination becomes inconsistent.

probes.text: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
How do you implement pagination in SQL?
Why should you avoid SELECT * in production?
Explain why a SELECT alias works in ORDER BY but not in WHERE — because SELECT runs after WHERE.
Whether you know SELECT clause order and that logical execution order differs from written order.

interview/java/select-queries.codeExample:
```sql
-- customers table
SELECT name, city, age
FROM customers
WHERE age >= 18
ORDER BY age DESC
LIMIT 3;
```

Sample output:

| name | city | age |
|---|---|---|
| Anita | Pune | 41 |
| Ravi | Mumbai | 33 |
| Neha | Delhi | 27 |

*Only the named columns come back, filtered to adults, sorted oldest first, capped at three rows.*

mistakes: Writing a subquery that returns multiple rows where a single value is expected, which throws a runtime error.
interview/java/subqueries.direct: A **subquery** is a query nested inside another query, wrapped in parentheses. It can appear in the **WHERE** clause (to filter against its result), the **FROM** clause (as a derived table), or the **SELECT** list (as a scalar value). The inner query runs to feed a value or a set to the outer query.
interview/java/subqueries.spoken: A subquery is simply a query nested inside another query. The inner query runs first to produce something, and the outer query uses that result. There are three main places a subquery shows up. The most common is in the WHERE clause, where you filter against its result; for example, select customers whose id is IN the set of customer ids from the orders table, which finds everyone who placed an order. The second place is the FROM clause, where the subquery acts as a derived table, a temporary result set you can query further; one rule there is that a derived table must be given an alias. The third place is the SELECT list, where a scalar subquery returns exactly one row and one column, like showing each order's total next to the overall average total. The key skill is matching the subquery's shape to where it's used. If you compare with equals, the subquery must return a single scalar value; if it returns multiple rows you need IN instead. For membership tests against possible nulls, I prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN. And I keep an eye on correlated subqueries, which re-run for every outer row and can be slow, because a join often does the same job faster.

probes.text: What is the difference between a correlated and non-correlated subquery?
When is a JOIN better than a subquery?
Why must a derived table have an alias?
Match the subquery shape to the context: scalar for `=`, a column for `IN`, a table for `FROM`.
Whether you know the three places a subquery can appear and what shape each one must return.

interview/java/subqueries.codeExample:
```sql
-- WHERE: customers who placed at least one order
SELECT name
FROM customers
WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);

-- SELECT (scalar): each order next to the overall average
SELECT id, total, (SELECT AVG(total) FROM orders) AS avg_total
FROM orders;

-- FROM (derived table): top spender per region
SELECT region, MAX(spent) AS top
FROM (SELECT region, customer_id, SUM(total) AS spent
      FROM orders
      GROUP BY region, customer_id) AS per_cust
GROUP BY region;
```

Sample output (second query):

| id | total | avg_total |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1200 | 900 |
| 2 | 600 | 900 |
| 3 | 900 | 900 |
interview/java/subqueries.question: What is a subquery in SQL and where can you use it?
interview/java/subqueries.title: Subqueries in SQL — Definition and Usage

mistakes: Putting aggregate conditions in WHERE, or expecting NULL rows to pass a normal comparison.
interview/java/where-clause.direct: The **WHERE** clause filters rows *before* grouping and selection, keeping only rows where the condition is **true** (not false, not unknown). It runs right after FROM/JOIN, supports `=, <>, <, >, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, IS NULL`, and combines conditions with `AND`/`OR`.
interview/java/where-clause.spoken: The WHERE clause filters which rows make it into your result. It runs early in execution, right after FROM and any joins, and well before GROUP BY and SELECT, so it works on individual rows, not on groups. A row only survives if its condition is true; if the condition is false, or unknown because of a NULL comparison, the row is dropped. You build conditions with the usual operators: equals, not equals, less than, greater than, plus handy ones like BETWEEN for ranges, IN for a set of values, LIKE for pattern matching, and IS NULL for missing data. You combine them with AND and OR, and it's worth remembering AND binds tighter than OR, so use parentheses when mixing them. Two traps I keep in mind. First, you can't put aggregate conditions like COUNT greater than five in WHERE, because grouping hasn't happened yet; that belongs in HAVING. Second, for performance, avoid wrapping the column in a function, like YEAR of a date column, because that prevents the database from using an index. Instead I write a range condition on the raw column, which stays index-friendly.

probes.text: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
Why does a function on a column prevent index usage?
How does three-valued logic affect WHERE?
Note WHERE filters rows while HAVING filters groups, and that sargable predicates use indexes.
Whether you know WHERE filters individual rows before GROUP BY and uses three-valued logic.

interview/java/where-clause.codeExample:
```sql
SELECT name, city, age
FROM customers
WHERE age BETWEEN 18 AND 30
  AND city IN ('Pune', 'Delhi')
  AND phone IS NOT NULL;
```

Sample output:

| name | city | age |
|---|---|---|
| Neha | Delhi | 27 |
| Karan | Pune | 22 |

mistakes: Jumping straight into writing code without understanding the problem
interview/java/approaching-coding-proble.direct: The first step is to fully understand the problem before writing any code. Read carefully, identify inputs and outputs, ask clarifying questions, and work through examples including edge cases before touching the keyboard.
interview/java/approaching-coding-proble.spoken: The very first thing I do when given a coding problem is make sure I actually understand what's being asked. I don't start coding right away because that usually leads to solving the wrong problem. Instead, I read the problem statement twice. The first time I get the general idea, and the second time I'm looking for specific details like input size, constraints, or edge cases. Then I restate the problem back to the interviewer in my own words. Something like if I understand correctly, you want me to find the first number that appears more than once in the array. This catches any misunderstandings early. Next, I ask one or two clarifying questions even if the problem seems clear. For example, what should I return if there are no duplicates, or can the array be empty? These questions show I'm thinking about edge cases. After that, I manually trace through a small example on the whiteboard. I'll take an input like two, five, three, two, eight and walk through what happens at each step. This helps me see the pattern before I write any code. Only after I've done all of this do I actually start writing Java. It might feel slow at first, but it saves a ton of time because I don't have to rewrite code when I realize I misunderstood something. The interviewer sees that I approach problems methodically, which is exactly how you'd work on a real production feature. One mistake freshers make is thinking silence looks bad, so they rush to start typing. But interviewers actually respect when you take a minute to think. It shows you're careful and deliberate, not just randomly trying things until something works.

mistakes: Freshers assume interviewers want perfection rather than problem-solving process and honest communication about what they know and don't know.
interview/java/common-fresher-mistakes.direct: Freshers commonly jump into coding without clarifying requirements, go silent when stuck instead of thinking aloud, exaggerate their experience with frameworks, forget to test their code, and fail to ask thoughtful questions at the end showing genuine interest.
interview/java/common-fresher-mistakes.spoken: I'd say the biggest mistake freshers make is treating interviews like exams where you either know the answer or you don't. In reality, interviewers want to see how you think through problems. The first thing that trips people up is jumping straight into code without asking clarifying questions. If you're given a problem like "write a method to find duplicate orders," you should ask: do we care about performance, what's the expected data size, should I handle null inputs? That shows you understand real requirements aren't always clear. The second mistake is going silent when stuck. I've learned to think aloud even when I'm uncertain. Say something like "I'm considering two approaches here" or "I know HashMap would work but I'm thinking about the memory trade-off." It keeps the interviewer engaged in your process. Another big one is resume honesty. If you list Spring Boot as a skill, you need to explain dependency injection and basic annotations. Claiming expert level after a weekend tutorial makes you look dishonest when you can't answer follow-ups. Also, freshers often forget to test their code. Even if you don't write formal unit tests, walk through your logic with a sample input out loud. Finally, not asking questions at the end signals you just want any job, not this specific role. I always prepare questions about the team's tech stack evolution or code review practices. It shows I'm thinking about growth, not just getting hired.

probes.text: Mention a specific mistake you made in a mock interview or coding practice and what you changed — shows reflection and growth mindset.
Self-awareness and ability to learn from common pitfalls — candidates who recognize these patterns show preparation maturity.

mistakes: Writing code silently for minutes or giving vague narrations like 'just looping through the list' without explaining the why
interview/java/explaining-your-thought-p.direct: Narrate at three levels: what you are doing (the action), why you chose that approach (the reasoning), and what trade-offs you see (the alternatives). Use structured phrases like 'My first instinct is X because...', 'The trade-off here is...', and 'I considered Y but rejected it because...' to signal organized thinking.
interview/java/explaining-your-thought-p.spoken: You'd say: 'When I'm coding in an interview, I narrate at three levels. First, I explain what action I'm taking, like I'm using a HashMap to store frequencies. Second, I explain why I chose that approach, for example, because HashMap gives O(1) lookups and the problem needs fast repeated access. Third, I mention what I considered but rejected, like I thought about using a TreeMap for sorted keys, but the problem doesn't require sorting so I'd just add complexity. I use phrases like my first instinct is to use two pointers because the array is sorted, or the trade-off here is speed versus memory, I'm optimizing for speed. If I hit a bug, I treat it like a verbal investigation. I say something like I expected the loop to stop at the second-to-last element, but it's going to the last element, so I have an off-by-one error in my boundary condition. I avoid silent coding because the interviewer can't see inside my head. Even if my solution isn't perfect, strong narration shows I think systematically. One mistake freshers make is over-explaining syntax, like now I'm declaring an integer variable, instead of explaining the algorithm. Another mistake is backtracking silently when something breaks. If I delete code, I say out loud, I realized my null check is in the wrong place because the list could be empty before I access the first element. That shows composure and debugging skill. Finally, I check in with the interviewer after outlining my approach. I ask does this plan make sense before I start coding. That way if I'm heading in the wrong direction, we course-correct early instead of wasting ten minutes on the wrong solution. The goal is to make my internal reasoning audible and organized, so the interviewer sees I can communicate complex logic clearly, which is critical when you're working on a team and need to explain your code in pull request reviews or design discussions.'

probes.text: Can you narrate your thought process for solving the two-sum problem?
How do you explain an approach you are not fully confident about?

Use explicit transition phrases that signal you are moving between phases: 'Let me first understand the constraints', 'Now I'll plan the approach', 'I'll code this in two passes', 'Finally I'll trace through an edge case'

mistakes: Freshers often panic and either freeze completely or attempt to bluff their way through with generic buzzwords
interview/java/handling-unknown-question.direct: Be honest that you're not sure, then demonstrate reasoning: connect to related concepts you do know, think through the logic, and arrive at a reasonable answer. Don't bluff — experienced interviewers detect it immediately and it damages trust.
interview/java/handling-unknown-question.spoken: When I don't know the answer to a technical question, I'm honest about it right away. I'll say something like, I haven't worked with that directly, but let me think through it based on what I do know. Then I connect it to related concepts. For example, if asked about Redis and I've only used HashMap for caching, I'd explain that caching generally involves key-value lookups with fast access times, and reason that Redis probably extends those principles to distributed systems. I verbalize my thinking process out loud so the interviewer can follow my reasoning. Even if I don't reach the perfect answer, it shows I can work through unfamiliar problems logically. The key mistake I've seen other freshers make is bluffing with buzzwords. They'll claim to know something, then stumble when asked follow-up questions. Interviewers detect this immediately, and it kills trust. It's way better to admit you're learning and demonstrate curiosity. I might finish by saying, This is new to me, but I'm genuinely interested — what resources would you recommend to learn more? That shows I'm coachable and eager to fill gaps in my knowledge, which is what junior developers do every day.

probes.text: Verbalize your thought process out loud as you reason through the problem, showing structured thinking even when you don't know the answer
Your honesty, intellectual humility, and ability to reason through unfamiliar problems under pressure

mistakes: Spending weeks reading books and watching tutorials without ever practicing under pressure, then freezing or rambling during the actual interview because you never rehearsed the format.
interview/java/mock-interview-approach.direct: Prepare through structured mock interviews that simulate real conditions: use platforms like Pramp or Interviewing.io for live practice with strangers, solve LeetCode problems under timed conditions (30-45 minutes per problem), rehearse your project explanations out loud to a friend or recording device, and get concrete feedback on both technical accuracy and communication clarity from peers or mentors after each session.
interview/java/mock-interview-approach.spoken: I prepare for technical interviews through structured mock practice that simulates real conditions. Here's my routine: every week, I do two 45-minute mock interviews—one coding session on Pramp where I solve a LeetCode medium problem while explaining my approach out loud to a stranger, and one behavioral mock with a friend where I practice my STAR stories and get feedback on clarity. I treat these sessions seriously: I set a timer, use a shared Google Doc instead of my IDE so I don't rely on autocomplete, and I avoid Googling anything during the problem. After each mock, I spend 15 minutes reviewing what went wrong. For example, after my first few mocks, I realized I was jumping straight into coding without asking clarifying questions, so now I force myself to spend the first three minutes discussing edge cases and constraints with the interviewer. I also maintain a spreadsheet tracking which problem types I struggle with—I noticed I was slow on HashMap problems, so I drilled 10 more of those before my next mock. The key mistake I see freshers make is only solving problems alone and never practicing the interview format itself. You might know how to solve Two Sum, but if you've never explained your approach out loud while someone watches and asks questions, you'll freeze in the real interview. Mock interviews taught me that interviews test communication and composure under pressure just as much as coding ability.

probes.text: Share a specific weekly routine with metrics, like 'I do two 45-minute mock interviews every Saturday morning—one coding, one behavioral—and track my completion rate and feedback scores in a spreadsheet to measure improvement.'
Whether you understand that interview success requires deliberate practice of the interview format itself, not just passive study of concepts—it's a performance skill you build through repetition.

mistakes: Freshers often wait passively for results or send generic thank-you emails that add no value, missing the chance to reinforce their interest.
interview/java/post-interview-follow-up.direct: Write down the questions you were asked while memory is fresh, note what went well and what you'd answer differently, send a thank-you email within 24 hours, and continue job searching while waiting.
interview/java/post-interview-follow-up.spoken: Right after an interview, I'd do three things immediately. First, I'd document everything while it's fresh — the questions they asked, how I answered, and what I'd explain differently next time. This helps me improve for future interviews. Second, I'd send a thank-you email within 24 hours. But not a generic one. I'd reference something specific we discussed, like if we talked about their microservices architecture or a particular challenge the team is facing. That shows I was paying attention and I'm genuinely interested. Third, I'd keep applying to other jobs. It's tempting to wait after a good interview, but that's a mistake. The job search is a numbers game, especially for freshers. Even strong candidates get rejected most of the time. If I don't hear back in a week, I'd send one polite follow-up, but that's it. Multiple follow-ups look desperate. The key is treating every interview as a learning opportunity, not just a pass-fail test. If I get rejected, I've still gained interview practice and identified what to study next. If I get an offer, I've got momentum and possibly other offers to compare. Either way, I'm moving forward, not sitting around waiting for one company to decide my fate. That's the professional approach — staying proactive, documenting lessons, and maintaining momentum throughout the job search process.

probes.text: Mention specific technical discussions from the interview in your thank-you email and reference how your skills align with the team's challenges.
Evaluating whether you understand professional follow-through and can maintain momentum during the job search process.

mistakes: Overthinking by trying to discuss microservices, event-driven architectures, or distributed consensus when the interviewer just wants to hear about REST APIs and databases.
interview/java/system-design-intro-quest.direct: Freshers face simplified system design questions focusing on basic 3-tier architectures, REST API design, simple database schemas, and fundamental concepts like caching and load balancing. You won't be asked to design Netflix or Uber, but you should understand how a typical Spring Boot application serves requests and stores data.
interview/java/system-design-intro-quest.spoken: So, as a fresher, I'd expect system design questions to focus on building a simple backend application, not designing something like Instagram. The interviewer wants to see if I understand the basics of how a Java web app works from start to finish. I'd talk about creating a Spring Boot application with three layers: controllers that handle HTTP requests, services that contain the business logic, and repositories that interact with the database. For example, if they ask me to design a simple task management system, I'd explain that I'd create REST endpoints like GET slash-tasks to list all tasks and POST slash-tasks to create new ones. I'd design a database table called tasks with columns like id, user-id, title, description, and created-at. I'd also mention using Spring Security with JWT tokens so that users can only see their own tasks, not everyone's. One mistake I'd avoid is jumping into complex stuff like microservices or Kafka when a simple monolithic Spring Boot app is what's actually needed. I'd keep my answer practical and focused on technologies I've actually worked with in my projects or coursework. At the end, if there's time, I might mention one scaling idea like adding Redis for caching or using a load balancer if traffic grows, just to show I'm thinking ahead. But I wouldn't overdo it because freshers work on simple systems first, and that's totally fine.

probes.text: Mention real-world constraints like 'for a fresher project, I'd keep it simple with a monolithic Spring Boot app first, then consider breaking it down later based on actual bottlenecks.'

mistakes: Writing everything as one dense block with no spacing, making it unreadable
interview/java/whiteboard-coding-tips.direct: Use consistent indentation with spacing, write in a left-to-right top-to-bottom flow, use meaningful variable names even if short, and leave blank lines between logical sections. Plan your space before writing — start from the top-left.
interview/java/whiteboard-coding-tips.spoken: I'd say clean whiteboard code comes down to treating the board like a document that someone else needs to read quickly. First, I always start from the top-left corner and write the method signature before anything else — that gives me a clear starting point. Then I use consistent indentation, usually four spaces per level, so nesting is obvious. I leave blank lines between different sections, like between input validation and the main logic, because that makes the structure jump out visually. Variable names matter too — even on a whiteboard I'd write customerList instead of just lst, because the interviewer shouldn't have to guess what a variable holds. Before I start writing code, I'll actually pause and say something like, I'm going to need about 20 lines here, let me plan my space. That prevents the awkward situation where you run out of room halfway through. One thing I've learned is to write comments sparingly but strategically — just a quick note like guard clause for nulls or recursive case here helps the interviewer follow along. If I make a mistake, I don't panic — I just cross it out cleanly and rewrite the corrected line nearby. The goal is making my thought process transparent, because in a whiteboard interview, the code is really a conversation tool more than a final artifact.

interview/java/testing.spoken:
Integration testing is about verifying that **multiple components work together correctly**. While unit tests isolate a single class by mocking everything around it, integration tests wire real collaborators together—controller to service to repository to database—and exercise the actual path a request takes.

The reason we need them is that many bugs live in the **seams between components**. A unit test for your `OrderService` might pass perfectly with a mocked repository, but the real repository could have a broken JPQL query or a missing column mapping. Only an integration test would catch that.

In Spring Boot, you typically use `@SpringBootTest` to boot the full context or **slice annotations** like `@WebMvcTest` and `@DataJpaTest` to test specific layers. The test pyramid model recommends about 70 % unit tests, 20 % integration tests, and 10 % end-to-end tests.

The key trade-off is **speed versus confidence**. Integration tests take seconds instead of milliseconds, but they prove the feature actually works end-to-end. The sweet spot is targeting them at areas where unit tests are blind: database interactions, HTTP serialization, transaction boundaries, and bean wiring.

mistakes: Reciting definitions without explaining why each pillar matters. Confusing abstraction (hiding complexity) with abstract classes (a Java mechanism). Thinking encapsulation just means private fields with getters and setters
interview/java/01-java-fundamentals.direct: **Encapsulation** — private fields + behavior methods (`withdraw()` not `setBalance()`). **Inheritance** — IS-A via `extends`; no multiple via classes (diamond problem); IS-A test first. **Polymorphism** — overloading = compile-time (compiler picks), overriding = runtime (JVM picks by actual object type). **Abstraction** — interface = 100%, abstract class = partial; it's a design principle, not the `abstract` keyword. All four in one line: `List<String> list = new ArrayList<>()`.
interview/java/01-java-fundamentals.spoken:
OOP organizes code around objects — each object combines its data and behavior in one place. In Java, a class is the blueprint and an object is an instance of it. The four principles that define how you design those objects are Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Abstraction.

**Encapsulation**
- Keep fields `private` and expose them only through public methods
- The class should own its own logic — `account.withdraw(100)` is encapsulation; `account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - 100)` is not, because you've moved the logic outside the class
- This also protects you from change — if `balance` moves from `double` to `BigDecimal`, no caller breaks because they never accessed the field directly

**Inheritance**
- A child class acquires the properties and methods of a parent using `extends` — `Dog extends Animal`
- Before using it, ask: is this an IS-A relationship? A dog *is* an animal — that works. A car *has* an engine — that's composition, not inheritance
- Java supports single, multilevel, and hierarchical inheritance. Multiple inheritance through classes isn't allowed because of the diamond problem — use interfaces for that

**Polymorphism**
- One interface, many implementations — the same method call behaves differently depending on the object
- Compile-time: method overloading — same name, different parameters, the compiler picks the right version
- Runtime: method overriding — `Shape s = new Circle(); s.area()` calls Circle's version because the JVM looks at the actual object type, not the reference type

**Abstraction**
- Hide the how, expose the what — like an ATM: you use it without knowing how the banking system works behind it
- An `interface` is 100% abstraction — just the contract, no implementation
- An `abstract class` is partial — it can have some concrete methods along with the abstract ones
- Use an interface when defining a capability like `Flyable`; use an abstract class when there's shared implementation to inherit

The four work as a system, not a checklist. `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>()` uses all of them — `List` is the abstraction, `ArrayList`'s fields are encapsulated, any List can substitute via polymorphism, and `ArrayList` satisfies the contract through inheritance.

mistakes: Assuming HashMap is always the best choice, or not knowing that TreeMap uses a Red-Black tree internally
interview/java/02-collections-data-struc.direct: HashMap offers O(1) average operations with no ordering. TreeMap provides O(log n) operations with natural/custom sorted order. LinkedHashMap gives O(1) average with insertion or access order maintained — ideal for LRU caches.
interview/java/02-collections-data-struc.spoken:
HashMap, TreeMap, and LinkedHashMap are Java's three most commonly compared `Map` implementations — each making different trade-offs between access speed and ordering guarantees.

**HashMap:**
- O(1) average for put/get — bucket array with hash-based indexing, no ordering guarantee
- The right default for key-value lookup when iteration order doesn't matter

**TreeMap:**
- Sorted keys via Red-Black tree — O(log n) for all operations
- Real value: NavigableMap operations like `subMap()`, `headMap()`, `tailMap()`, `floorKey()`, `ceilingKey()`
- Null keys not allowed — comparing null throws NPE; HashMap puts null at bucket 0

**LinkedHashMap:**
- HashMap plus a doubly-linked list — preserves insertion order by default
- Set `accessOrder=true` in constructor to switch to access-order mode — every `get()` moves the entry to the tail
- Override `removeEldestEntry()` to evict when size exceeds a limit — instant LRU cache in a few lines

I recommend HashMap as the default, TreeMap when you need sorted iteration or range queries, and LinkedHashMap when insertion order or LRU eviction matters.

mistakes: Conflating RUNNABLE with 'currently executing on a CPU' — RUNNABLE includes both 'ready to run' and 'actually running' because Java does not distinguish between the two at the API level
interview/java/04-concurrency-multithrea.direct: A Java thread has 6 states defined in Thread.State: NEW (created, not started), RUNNABLE (executing or ready to execute), BLOCKED (waiting for a monitor lock), WAITING (waiting indefinitely for another thread), TIMED_WAITING (waiting with a timeout), and TERMINATED (finished execution).
interview/java/04-concurrency-multithrea.spoken:
Java defines six thread states in `Thread.State` — and the most important thing to know is that RUNNABLE does not mean currently executing.

**States:**
- NEW: before `start()` is called
- RUNNABLE: eligible for CPU time — may or may not be actively running; there is no separate RUNNING state in the Java enum
- BLOCKED: waiting for a `synchronized` monitor held by another thread
- WAITING: called `wait()`, `join()`, or `park()` without a timeout — deliberately parked until signaled
- TIMED_WAITING: same but with a timeout — `sleep()`, `wait(millis)`
- TERMINATED: `run()` completed; cannot be restarted — calling `start()` again throws `IllegalThreadStateException`

**Debugging significance:**
- BLOCKED threads all pointing to the same monitor → lock contention; the lock-holder is shown in the dump
- Repeated identical RUNNABLE stacks → CPU-burning loop or spin
- WAITING threads → typically correct producer-consumer pattern

I recommend focusing on the BLOCKED vs WAITING distinction when reading thread dumps — it tells you whether you have a locking problem or a design-level wait.
interview/java/04-concurrency-multithrea.deep:
ThreadLocal gives each thread its own independent copy of a variable, eliminating the need for synchronisation when each thread needs isolated state.

Common uses include per-thread database connections, request-scoped context (like user identity in a web request), and SimpleDateFormat instances.

The primary pitfall is memory leaks in thread pools: if the ThreadLocal is not explicitly removed, the value outlives the logical request and accumulates across reuses of the same thread.

Conflating RUNNABLE with 'currently executing on a CPU' — RUNNABLE includes both 'ready to run' and 'actually running' because Java does not distinguish between the two at the API level

mistakes: Thinking String literals go on the stack — they go in the String Pool on the heap (Java 7+)
interview/java/05-jvm-internals-performa.direct: The JVM has per-thread areas (stack, PC register, native method stack) and shared areas (heap, metaspace, code cache). The heap stores objects; metaspace stores class metadata; stack stores method frames; code cache stores JIT-compiled native code.
interview/java/05-jvm-internals-performa.spoken:
The JVM divides memory into thread-private areas and shared areas — knowing which area maps to which error is the first step in any JVM diagnosis.

**Thread-private (no synchronization needed):**
- Stack: one per thread; holds method frames with local variables and partial results; size via `-Xss`; deep recursion → `StackOverflowError`
- PC register: current instruction pointer
- Native method stack: for JNI calls

**Shared areas:**
- Heap: all objects and arrays; garbage collected; sized via `-Xms`/`-Xmx`; exhaustion → `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`
- Metaspace: class metadata and bytecode; replaced PermGen in Java 8; uses native memory, grows dynamically; cap via `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize`
- Code cache: JIT-compiled native code; fixed size; exhaustion stops JIT compilation

**Heap structure:**
- Young generation (Eden + Survivor spaces) + Old generation for most collectors
- G1, ZGC, and Shenandoah use region-based layouts instead of contiguous fixed-size generations

I recommend understanding these areas because every JVM error maps to a specific region — knowing which area is involved tells you where to start looking.
interview/java/05-jvm-internals-performa.deep:
Traditional java.io is stream-oriented and blocking — each read/write blocks the calling thread until data is available.

Java NIO (New I/O, java.nio) is buffer-oriented and supports non-blocking mode via Selectors, letting a single thread multiplex thousands of channels.

NIO2 (Java 7) added the AsynchronousChannel API for true async completion callbacks. Choose traditional IO for simple, low-concurrency file processing; NIO for high-concurrency network servers.

Thinking String literals go on the stack — they go in the String Pool on the heap (Java 7+)

mistakes: Treating IoC and DI as synonyms — IoC is the broad principle (framework calls you, not you calling the framework), DI is one specific way to achieve it.
interview/java/06-spring-core.direct: IoC is the design principle where the framework — not your code — controls object creation and lifecycle. Dependency Injection is the mechanism Spring uses to implement IoC: dependencies are provided to a class from the outside rather than created internally. This decoupling is what makes Spring applications testable, configurable, and loosely coupled.
interview/java/06-spring-core.spoken:
Spring's whole model is built around one insight — the `new` keyword is a hard dependency. When `OrderService` does `new StripeGateway()` inside its constructor, those two classes are permanently coupled. You can't swap the gateway, test in isolation, or configure differently per environment without modifying `OrderService`. IoC and Dependency Injection are Spring's solution to that problem.

**Inversion of Control**
- IoC means the framework controls object creation and lifecycle — your class doesn't reach out and wire itself
- Spring's `ApplicationContext` is the IoC container: it reads your `@Component` and `@Bean` declarations, creates beans, resolves dependencies, and manages their lifecycle
- The shift: you declare what you need, Spring decides which implementation to provide based on what's registered

**Dependency Injection**
- DI is the specific mechanism — dependencies come in from outside the class (constructor, setter, or field) instead of being created internally with `new`
- This is what makes testing clean: `new OrderService(mockGateway)` in a unit test, `StripeGateway` in production — `OrderService` never changes
- IoC and DI are not synonyms: IoC is the principle, DI is one mechanism. Service Locator is another IoC pattern — in DI, the container pushes dependencies in; the class doesn't ask for them

**Constructor injection**
- The Spring team's recommendation for mandatory dependencies: `final` fields, explicit constructor signature, testable without the container
- Since Spring 4.3, a class with one constructor doesn't need `@Autowired` — Spring uses it automatically. Add Lombok's `@RequiredArgsConstructor` and you get zero-boilerplate injection
- The practical tell: constructor injection exposes circular dependencies at startup (`BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`). Field injection hides them and produces partially-initialized proxy beans that fail only at runtime

Field injection looks cleaner — one `@Autowired` per field — but you can't unit test without Spring, dependencies are invisible, and `final` is impossible. In modern Spring projects, constructor injection for mandatory deps and setter injection for optional ones is the standard. Field injection is a legacy pattern worth moving away from.

probes.text: Why does the Spring team recommend constructor injection over field injection?
What happens when Spring finds two beans of the same type — how does it resolve ambiguity?
How does @Qualifier work with dependency injection?
Explain why constructor injection is preferred over field injection: it makes dependencies explicit, enforces immutability, and allows unit testing without a Spring context.
Whether the candidate distinguishes the principle (IoC) from the mechanism (DI) and can articulate why this matters beyond textbook definitions.

mistakes: Saying 'Spring Boot is a different framework' or treating them as competitors rather than layers in the same stack.
interview/java/07-spring-boot.direct: Spring Boot is not a replacement for Spring Framework — it's an opinionated layer on top that eliminates boilerplate configuration. Spring provides the ecosystem (IoC, AOP, MVC, Data, Security), while Spring Boot provides auto-configuration, embedded servers, starter dependencies, and production-ready defaults so you can go from zero to running application in minutes instead of hours.
interview/java/07-spring-boot.spoken:
Spring Boot is not a different framework — it is Spring Framework with decisions already made for you. The same `ApplicationContext`, the same IoC container, the same AOP proxies. What Spring Boot adds is conventions, auto-configuration, embedded servers, and starter POMs that wire everything together automatically.

**What Spring Boot adds**
- Auto-configuration: Spring Boot reads `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` conditions at startup and registers beans only when the right dependencies are on the classpath and you have not already defined your own
- Embedded server: Tomcat, Jetty, or Netty ships inside the JAR — no deployment to an external container required
- Starter POMs: `spring-boot-starter-web` pulls in exactly the right set of dependencies at compatible versions

**What stays the same**
- The IoC container is identical — `ApplicationContext`, `BeanPostProcessor`, `@Autowired`, `@Transactional` all work exactly as in raw Spring
- Debugging an auto-configuration issue requires understanding raw Spring: which `BeanPostProcessor` runs, what condition failed, why two beans of the same type conflict

**When to use raw Spring**
- Embedding Spring into a non-boot environment (legacy app servers, custom tooling)
- Writing a Spring Boot starter or auto-configuration itself

`@SpringBootApplication` is three annotations composed: `@Configuration` (this class defines beans), `@EnableAutoConfiguration` (activate auto-config), `@ComponentScan` (scan this package). Understanding the composition means you can decompose it when you only need part of it.

mistakes: Saying 'JPA is a framework' — it's a specification with no implementation. You cannot run JPA without a provider like Hibernate, EclipseLink, or OpenJPA.
interview/java/08-data-persistence-jpa-h.direct: JPA (Jakarta Persistence API) is a specification — a set of interfaces and annotations that define how Java objects map to database tables. Hibernate is an implementation of that specification. JPA defines what to do (EntityManager, @Entity, JPQL), Hibernate adds how to do it plus extras like Session, HQL, second-level caching, and Envers for audit trails.
interview/java/08-data-persistence-jpa-h.spoken:
JPA and Hibernate are not synonyms, even though they are used together so often that the distinction blurs. Getting this right in an interview shows architectural understanding rather than just framework familiarity.

**JPA — the specification**
- Defined in `javax.persistence.*` (JPA 2.x) or `jakarta.persistence.*` (JPA 3.x / Jakarta EE)
- Annotations like `@Entity`, `@Table`, `@OneToMany`, `@ManyToOne`, `@Id`, `@GeneratedValue` are all JPA standard
- `EntityManager`, `EntityManagerFactory`, `TypedQuery`, `JPQL` — all JPA APIs
- Any compliant implementation can run code written against JPA APIs

**Hibernate — the implementation**
- The dominant JPA implementation, used by default in Spring Boot
- `Session` (Hibernate-specific) extends `EntityManager`; `SessionFactory` extends `EntityManagerFactory`
- Hibernate-specific features: `@BatchSize`, `@Fetch`, `@NaturalId`, `@Type` — use only when JPA has no equivalent

**Spring Data JPA**
- Sits above JPA — `JpaRepository` calls `EntityManager`; Hibernate is just the JPA provider underneath
- Adds derived query methods, `@Query` JPQL, `Specification`, and pagination on top of the standard JPA APIs

Whether the candidate understands the spec-vs-implementation relationship rather than treating JPA and Hibernate as interchangeable terms.

mistakes: Conflating the two concepts, or not knowing that Authorization can only work after Authentication populates the SecurityContext.
interview/java/09-spring-security.direct: Authentication answers 'Who are you?' — it verifies identity by checking credentials and produces an Authentication object stored in the SecurityContext. Authorization answers 'What are you allowed to do?' — it checks the authenticated principal's authorities against the required permissions for a resource. Spring Security enforces these as two distinct, sequential steps.
interview/java/09-spring-security.spoken:
Authentication and authorization are two distinct steps in security. Conflating them is the most common conceptual error in security interviews.

**Authentication — identity verification**
- 'Who are you?' — the user presents credentials (username/password, JWT, certificate)
- Spring's `AuthenticationManager` verifies the credentials
- On success, an `Authentication` object is stored in the `SecurityContextHolder` — containing the principal and their `GrantedAuthority` list
- Failure → `AuthenticationException` → `401 Unauthorized`

**Authorization — permission check**
- 'What are you allowed to do?' — evaluated after authentication succeeds
- Spring checks the `GrantedAuthority` list against the required role/permission for the requested resource
- Failure → `AccessDeniedException` → `403 Forbidden`

**The Spring Security flow**
- Request enters the filter chain
- Authentication filter (e.g., `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter`) extracts credentials and calls `AuthenticationManager`
- `DaoAuthenticationProvider` loads `UserDetails` via `UserDetailsService`, verifies password with `PasswordEncoder`
- On success, stores `Authentication` in `SecurityContextHolder`
- `AuthorizationFilter` checks `SecurityContextHolder` against the required authorities for the URL

`@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` on service methods adds a second authorization layer — even if someone bypasses the HTTP-level check, the method-level check still enforces the permission.

mistakes: Confusing Tasklet with Chunk — candidates often think Tasklet is just a simpler Step, not realizing they are mutually exclusive execution strategies within a Step
interview/java/10-spring-batch.direct: A Job is the top-level container representing an entire batch process, composed of one or more Steps executed in sequence or conditionally. Each Step can follow either a chunk-oriented model (read-process-write in fixed-size chunks) or a Tasklet model (a single custom unit of work). Together, they give you fine-grained control over large-volume data processing with built-in restart and retry support.
interview/java/10-spring-batch.spoken:
Spring Batch structures batch processing around a clear hierarchy: Job → Step → Chunk or Tasklet. Every level has a well-defined responsibility and is persisted to the `JobRepository`.

**The hierarchy**
- `Job`: the overall batch process — 'import monthly invoices'; composed of one or more Steps in sequence or conditionally
- `Step`: one phase of the job — 'read from CSV', 'validate records', 'write to database'; each step has its own execution status and can be restarted independently
- `Chunk`: the read-process-write model for a step; reads N items, processes each, writes the batch — all inside one transaction
- `Tasklet`: a single operation for a step — not a read-process-write loop; `execute()` returns `RepeatStatus.FINISHED` or `RepeatStatus.CONTINUABLE`

**`JobRepository` — the persistence layer**
- Stores `JobInstance` (logical job run), `JobExecution` (physical attempt), `StepExecution` (per-step state)
- Enables: restart from the last successful checkpoint; skip counting; retry tracking; execution history
- Spring Boot auto-configures `JobRepository` using the application's `DataSource`

**Chunk transaction model**
- Chunk size 100: reads 100 records, processes each, writes all 100 in one transaction
- A write failure rolls back only that chunk — already committed chunks are not re-processed on restart
- Larger chunks = fewer transactions = better throughput; smaller chunks = finer-grained checkpointing

mistakes: Candidates often memorize definitions without being able to identify violations in a real schema or explain when to deliberately denormalize.
interview/java/10-database-design.direct: Normalization is the process of organizing a relational database to reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity. The normal forms are progressive rules: 1NF eliminates repeating groups, 2NF removes partial dependencies, 3NF removes transitive dependencies, and BCNF is a stricter version of 3NF that handles edge cases with candidate keys.
interview/java/10-database-design.spoken:
Most interviews on normalization test whether you can identify violations in a real table, not whether you can recite definitions. The forms build on each other — a table in 3NF is automatically in 2NF and 1NF — and each one eliminates a different class of data anomaly.

**1NF — one atomic value per cell**
- Every column must hold a single indivisible value — so a `tags` column storing `"java,spring,sql"` violates 1NF because it packs multiple values into one cell, which means you can't filter or index individual tags without string parsing
- No repeating column groups either — `item1`, `item2`, `item3` on an order row violates 1NF because adding a fourth item requires a schema change rather than a new row

**2NF — no partial dependency on a composite key**
- 2NF applies only when the primary key is composite — every non-key column must depend on the whole key, not just part of it
- `order_items(order_id, item_id, item_name)` violates 2NF because `item_name` depends only on `item_id`, not the full composite key — which means every order line duplicates the item name, and a rename requires updating hundreds of rows instead of one
- Fix: move `item_name` to a separate `items(item_id, item_name)` table

**3NF — no column-to-column dependency**
- Non-key columns must depend directly on the primary key, not on each other — so `employees(emp_id, dept_id, dept_name)` violates 3NF because `dept_name` depends on `dept_id`, not `emp_id`
- That transitive dependency means renaming a department updates every employee row in that department instead of one row in a `departments` table

**BCNF — every determinant must be a candidate key**
- BCNF tightens 3NF for tables with overlapping candidate keys — it handles the edge cases that 3NF misses, relevant for scheduling or assignment tables with complex key constraints

In production, OLTP schemas target 3NF. For reporting and caching, teams deliberately denormalize — duplicating `customer_name` on order rows to skip a join on every report query. The key is making that trade-off intentionally with a documented sync strategy, not by accident.
interview/java/10-database-design.deep:
A database index is an auxiliary data structure — separate from the table — that maps column values to row locations for fast lookups.

B-Tree indexes store values in a balanced tree supporting equality and range queries in O(log n).

Hash indexes map values through a hash function for O(1) equality lookups but cannot handle ranges. Composite indexes cover multiple columns with a strict left-prefix rule. Covering indexes include all columns a query needs, enabling index-only scans that skip the heap entirely.

Candidates often memorize definitions without being able to identify violations in a real schema or explain when to deliberately denormalize.

interview/java/10-mysql.direct: InnoDB is the default MySQL engine offering ACID transactions, foreign keys, row-level locking, and crash recovery. MyISAM is an older engine with faster read performance for non-transactional workloads but lacks transactions, foreign key support, and uses table-level locking. For most modern Java/Spring Boot applications, InnoDB is the correct choice.
interview/java/10-mysql.spoken:
InnoDB and MyISAM are the two MySQL storage engines that come up most in interviews — InnoDB has been the default since MySQL 5.5 and the right choice for virtually every modern application.

**InnoDB — the default for good reason**
- InnoDB supports full ACID transactions, which means a multi-statement operation like debit account A and credit account B either both succeed or both roll back on crash — something MyISAM simply cannot do
- Row-level locking means concurrent writers block each other only when they touch the same row; MyISAM uses table-level locking, which means a single UPDATE blocks every other write on the table
- InnoDB enforces foreign key constraints at the database level, which means referential integrity is guaranteed even if the application has a bug; MyISAM ignores foreign key declarations entirely

**MyISAM — where it still exists**
- MyISAM was the historical default before MySQL 5.5 and is still present in legacy codebases; its main advantage was slightly faster reads on simple SELECT-heavy workloads with no concurrent writes
- Full-text search in older MySQL versions required MyISAM — but InnoDB has supported full-text indexes since MySQL 5.6, removing the last real reason to use MyISAM in new development
- If you encounter a MyISAM table in an existing system, the migration path to InnoDB is `ALTER TABLE t ENGINE=InnoDB` — it rebuilds the table with full InnoDB capabilities

For any new table in a Spring Boot application: InnoDB. The transaction and row-locking guarantees are non-negotiable for any data that matters, and full-text search, spatial queries, and all other specialized capabilities are available in InnoDB today.

mistakes: Using RANK vs ROW_NUMBER incorrectly — RANK leaves gaps for ties, ROW_NUMBER never does
interview/java/10-postgresql.direct: Window functions perform calculations across related rows without grouping them away. RANK/DENSE_RANK compute position within a partition. ROW_NUMBER assigns unique sequential numbers. LAG/LEAD access previous/next row values without a self-join.
interview/java/10-postgresql.spoken:
Window functions perform calculations across related rows without collapsing them — unlike GROUP BY which gives you one row per group, window functions annotate every row with a computed value while keeping all rows visible.

**ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK — the tie question**
- `ROW_NUMBER()` assigns unique sequential integers regardless of ties — so two employees with the same salary get 1 and 2 arbitrarily
- `RANK()` assigns the same number to ties but skips after them (1, 1, 3) — so the next-highest salary is rank 3, not rank 2
- `DENSE_RANK()` assigns the same number to ties and doesn't skip (1, 1, 2) — which means the next-highest salary is always one step above the tied group; use this when gaps in ranking would be confusing to users

**PARTITION BY and ORDER BY — the two control levers**
- `PARTITION BY` divides rows into groups for the window function to operate within — `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC)` ranks each employee within their department, not globally
- Without PARTITION BY, the function operates across the entire result set; combining both gives you group-scoped rankings without GROUP BY

**Deduplication with ROW_NUMBER**
- The most common production use: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at DESC)` assigns rank 1 to each user's latest record — wrap it in a CTE or subquery and filter `WHERE rn = 1` to keep only the latest row per user without a correlated subquery or self-join

**LAG and LEAD for row-to-row comparisons**
- `LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month)` returns the previous row's value — `amount - LAG(amount)` computes month-over-month change in one pass, eliminating a self-join on date columns
- `SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)` computes a running total without any subquery

Window functions execute after WHERE and GROUP BY but before ORDER BY — filter on window function results by wrapping the query in a CTE or subquery.
interview/java/10-postgresql.deep:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and shows actual vs estimated rows, execution time, and the chosen plan nodes.

Look for Seq Scan on large tables (needs index), high cost nodes, and large row estimate mismatches (stale statistics).

Use indexes, rewrite subqueries, or update statistics to fix.

A common mistake is using RANK vs ROW_NUMBER incorrectly — RANK leaves gaps for ties, ROW_NUMBER never does
