mistakes: Setting Cache-Control: no-cache everywhere (disables caching); returning wrong Vary headers (poisons CDN); generating weak ETags on dynamic data (no real savings)
java-backend-intermediate/rest-api/http-.direct: HTTP caching has two main mechanisms: **freshness** (Cache-Control directives like `max-age`, `public`, `private`, `no-cache`, `no-store`, `immutable`) tell caches how long a response stays fresh without revalidation; **validation** (ETag, Last-Modified + If-None-Match/If-Modified-Since) lets a cache check with origin cheaply — 304 Not Modified if unchanged, saving bandwidth. Use together: set `Cache-Control: max-age=300, public` for fresh reuse; set ETag so stale caches revalidate cheaply. In Spring Boot: use `ResponseEntity.ok().cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(5, TimeUnit.MINUTES)).eTag(etag).body(...)` or `ShallowEtagHeaderFilter` for auto-ETags; combine with CDN (CloudFront, Cloudflare) and compression (Brotli > gzip) for real production wins.
java-backend-intermediate/rest-api/http-.spoken:
HTTP caching reduces origin load, tail latency, and bandwidth by reusing responses. The HTTP/1.1 RFC defines two complementary mechanisms.

**Freshness — how long can I reuse without asking the server?**
- Set by Cache-Control max-age in seconds
- While fresh, cache serves without contacting origin
- Expires header is the older alternative

**Validation — this is stale, is it still good?**
- Set by ETag (opaque content hash) or Last-Modified timestamp
- Cache sends conditional request with If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since
- Origin returns 304 Not Modified if unchanged (no body, cheap) or 200 with new body if changed

**Combined they give the right behavior**
- max-age=60 plus ETag: fresh for 1 minute, then cheap revalidation
- Matches real-world data patterns

**Cache-Control directives that matter**
- public: any cache may store (CDN, proxy, browser)
- private: only browser; never CDN
- max-age=N: fresh for N seconds
- s-maxage=N: overrides max-age in shared caches (CDN)
- no-cache: may cache but must revalidate before serving
- no-store: don't cache at all (secrets, PII)
- must-revalidate: don't serve stale even if origin unreachable
- immutable: content never changes (versioned assets)
- stale-while-revalidate=N: serve stale for N seconds while revalidating in background
- stale-if-error=N: serve stale for N seconds if origin 5xx

**The three layers of cache**
- Browser cache: per user
- CDN: CloudFront, Cloudflare, Fastly; shared at edge
- Origin reverse proxy: nginx, Varnish
- All see the same headers; good design uses all three

**Common mistakes**

*no-cache is not 'no caching'*
- no-cache means 'store but revalidate before serving'
- no-store means 'don't cache at all'
- Huge difference; use no-store for PII and secrets

*public on user-specific data*
- CDN will serve one user's data to another
- Always private + Vary: Authorization for user-specific

*Vary header pitfalls*
- Vary: * effectively disables caching
- Vary: User-Agent splits cache into hundreds of variants
- Be precise: Accept-Encoding cheap; Authorization needed for per-user

*ETag generation cost*
- Content hash on every request means no CPU savings
- Better: version plus updated_at (O(1) generation)
- ShallowEtagHeaderFilter is easy but computes hash from full body

**Stale-while-revalidate is a game changer**
- Fresh 30 seconds; during next 5 minutes serve stale immediately, revalidate in background
- User never waits for revalidation
- p99 latency drops dramatically
- Supported by modern browsers and CDNs

**Stale-if-error for resilience**
- If origin returns 5xx during revalidation, serve stale for additional N seconds
- Buys headroom during incidents
- Combined with SWR, survives minor blips transparently

**Spring Boot patterns**

*Static assets with versioned URLs*
- main.abc123.js with max-age=1 year, immutable, public
- Change content means change URL; no invalidation needed

*API responses with ETag*
- ResponseEntity.ok().cacheControl(...).eTag(etag).body(p)
- WebRequest.checkNotModified(etag) compares If-None-Match and returns 304

*User-specific data*
- CacheControl.maxAge(60, SECONDS).cachePrivate()
- Vary: Authorization
- Browser caches per user; CDN doesn't cache

*Stale-while-revalidate*
- CacheControl.maxAge(30s).staleWhileRevalidate(5min).staleIfError(30min)
- Huge p99 wins for low-volume dynamic data

**Compression**
- gzip universal; 70% reduction on JSON
- Brotli 20 to 30% better than gzip; all modern browsers support
- Don't compress under 1KB; overhead exceeds savings
- Don't compress images or video; already compressed
- Vary: Accept-Encoding to cache per compression type

**CDN integration**
- Default cache key is URL plus Vary headers
- Invalidation by URL pattern; slow and expensive
- Prefer versioned URLs over manual invalidation
- Target CDN hit rate above 80% for public content

**Cache key design**
- Vary: Accept-Encoding is cheap and valuable
- Vary: Authorization for per-user cached content
- Avoid Vary: User-Agent unless you handle dozens of variants
- Query string handling configurable in CloudFront/Cloudflare

**The production pattern**
- Static assets: max-age=1 year, immutable, versioned URLs
- Rarely-changing API: max-age=5 min, public, ETag, stale-while-revalidate
- User-specific data: max-age=1 min, private, Vary: Authorization
- Auth tokens and PII: no-store
- Tune per endpoint; measure hit rates; adjust

**Observability**
- CDN hit rate (target > 80% for public content)
- Origin request rate (inverse of effectiveness)
- 304 response rate (shows validation working)
- Response size with and without compression

**The strategic answer**
- Cache-Control for freshness; ETag or Last-Modified for validation
- CDN with well-tuned headers is the cheapest scaling win
- stale-while-revalidate plus stale-if-error for resilience
- Versioned URLs for immutable assets
- Measure hit rates; tune; repeat
- Well-cached API serves 99% of traffic from edge without touching your Spring Boot servers

mistakes: Using the deprecated springfox library (Swagger 2) instead of springdoc (OpenAPI 3)
java-backend-intermediate/rest-api/opena.direct: Use springdoc-**OpenAPI**-starter-webmvc-ui to auto-generate OpenAPI 3 spec from your code. Enrich with @Operation, @ApiResponse, and @Schema annotations. Expose the UI at /**Swagger**-ui.html.
java-backend-intermediate/rest-api/opena.spoken:
Springdoc generates OpenAPI 3.x documentation from your Spring MVC controllers automatically — no XML, no separate doc server. The generated spec is the contract that clients, tests, and SDK generators consume.

**Setup**
- Add `springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui` dependency
- Swagger UI is available at `/swagger-ui.html`; the raw OpenAPI JSON/YAML at `/v3/api-docs`
- Springdoc introspects `@RequestMapping`, `@RequestBody`, `@PathVariable`, return types — zero additional annotations needed for basic documentation

**Enriching the documentation**
- `@Operation(summary = "Create order", description = "...")` — describes the endpoint
- `@ApiResponse(responseCode = "201", description = "Order created")` — documents response codes
- `@Schema(description = "ISO 4217 currency code", example = "USD")` — documents DTO fields with examples

**Securing Swagger UI**
- Configure `@SecurityScheme(type = SecuritySchemeType.HTTP, scheme = "bearer")` on a configuration class
- Annotate secured endpoints with `@SecurityRequirement(name = "bearerAuth")`
- Developers click 'Authorize', enter a JWT, and test protected endpoints directly from the UI

Export the spec at `/v3/api-docs.yaml` and use `openapi-generator-cli` to produce type-safe client libraries — one source of truth for the API contract shared between backend and frontend teams.

mistakes: Putting validation logic inside the service layer with manual if-checks instead of using constraint annotations that work across controllers, services, and JPA entities.
java-backend-intermediate/rest-api/reque.direct: **@Valid** (or **@Validated**) on a controller parameter triggers Bean Validation on the request body or **query** object. For complex rules not covered by standard annotations, you implement ConstraintValidator with your own @Constraint annotation, keeping validation logic reusable, declarative, and testable independently of Spring.
java-backend-intermediate/rest-api/reque.spoken:
Bean Validation in Spring MVC validates request data before it reaches your service layer, keeping business logic clean and producing consistent `400` responses for invalid input.

**How it wires together**
- Add `@NotBlank`, `@NotNull`, `@Size`, `@Pattern` etc. on DTO fields
- Add `@Valid` to the `@RequestBody` parameter in the controller method
- Spring calls the validator before invoking the controller method; on failure it throws `MethodArgumentNotValidException`
- Handle in `@ControllerAdvice`: `ex.getBindingResult().getAllErrors()` gives every constraint violation

**Custom constraints**
- Create `@UniqueEmail` annotation + `UniqueEmailValidator implements ConstraintValidator<UniqueEmail, String>`
- `isValid(String value, ConstraintValidatorContext ctx)` — inject a repository and check uniqueness; Spring manages the validator as a bean
- Cross-field validation: annotate the DTO class itself with a class-level constraint that receives the entire object

**`@Valid` vs `@Validated`**
- `@Valid` is the standard Java annotation — use for method parameters in controllers
- `@Validated` is Spring's annotation — enables validation groups (validate different subsets of constraints for create vs update operations)

Cascade validation: a DTO with a nested object field must annotate that field with `@Valid` to propagate validation into the nested object — omitting it silently skips validation of nested constraints.

mistakes: Using RestTemplate for new code; no timeouts; no connection pool tuning; no circuit breaker; blocking in WebFlux
java-backend-intermediate/rest-api/rest-.direct: In 2026, pick by model and async needs: **Spring 6 HTTP Interface** (`@HttpExchange`) is the modern default — declarative, works with `RestClient` (sync) or `WebClient` (reactive), minimal boilerplate, built-in. **WebClient** is the reactive/non-blocking client — use for high-concurrency or WebFlux apps. **`RestClient`** (Spring 6.1+) is the modern synchronous replacement for RestTemplate — fluent, built on top of same HTTP infra. **RestTemplate** is in maintenance mode — still supported, no new features, migrate away for new code. **OpenFeign** is still popular via Spring Cloud OpenFeign — declarative like HTTP Interface but external dep; use if you're already on Spring Cloud. **Default pick for new Spring 6+ code: `@HttpExchange` backed by `RestClient` for sync or `WebClient` for reactive.** Wrap with Resilience4j for circuit breaking, timeouts, retries; tune connection pool; propagate trace headers.
java-backend-intermediate/rest-api/rest-.spoken:
In 2026, pick by model and async needs.

**Spring 6 HTTP Interface (@HttpExchange) is the modern default**
- Declarative interface-based
- Works with RestClient (sync) or WebClient (reactive)
- Minimal boilerplate; built-in to Spring 6+
- Reduces need for Feign in Spring-native apps

**RestClient (Spring 6.1+)**
- Modern synchronous replacement for RestTemplate
- Fluent API
- Built on same HTTP infra
- Recommended synchronous choice for new code

**WebClient**
- Reactive, non-blocking
- Used in WebFlux apps; whenever non-blocking I/O needed in Spring MVC
- Streaming, SSE, async responses
- With Project Loom virtual threads, the pure concurrency advantage softens; still right for streaming or fully reactive pipelines

**RestTemplate**
- Legacy synchronous; in maintenance mode
- No new features since Spring 5
- For new code, use RestClient or @HttpExchange

**OpenFeign (Spring Cloud OpenFeign)**
- Declarative HTTP client from Netflix OSS
- Similar to @HttpExchange conceptually but richer ecosystem (Resilience4j integration, logging, custom encoders)
- Still widely used in Spring Cloud stacks
- Case weakens in Spring 6+ with native @HttpExchange

**JDK HttpClient, Apache HttpClient 5, OkHttp**
- Low-level libraries Spring can sit on top of
- Use for specific features (HTTP/2 tuning, HTTP/3, connection pooling)

**Default pick for Spring 6+ new code**
- @HttpExchange backed by RestClient for sync
- Or WebClient for reactive
- Wrap with Resilience4j for circuit breaking, timeouts, retries
- Tune connection pool
- Propagate trace headers

**Usage examples**

*@HttpExchange*
- Define interface with @GetExchange, @PostExchange annotations
- Configure with RestClient builder
- Build via HttpServiceProxyFactory + RestClientAdapter
- Cleaner than Feign for simple cases; no external dep

*RestClient*
- Fluent: builder.baseUrl().defaultHeader()
- client.post().uri().body().retrieve().onStatus().body()
- Imperative modern sync

*WebClient*
- Reactive; Mono/Flux
- client.get().uri().retrieve().onStatus().bodyToMono().timeout()
- Use in WebFlux; can .block() in MVC (but if everywhere blocking, don't need WebClient)

*OpenFeign*
- @FeignClient(name, url); Spring Cloud discovers via Eureka/Consul
- Integrates with LoadBalancer, Resilience4j, Sleuth

**Production concerns**

*Timeouts non-negotiable*
- Connect timeout: 1 to 2s internal, 5s external
- Read timeout: 2 to 10s internal, 10 to 30s external
- Total/request timeout: overall ceiling
- Default clients often have huge or no timeouts; requests hang forever

*Connection pool tuning*
- Default pool sizes rarely fit production
- Tune: max connections per route, total max, idle timeout, evict policy
- Monitor pool saturation
- Example: Apache HttpClient 5 with PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager

*Resilience4j for circuit breaker, retry, bulkhead, timeout*
- @CircuitBreaker, @Retry, @Bulkhead, @TimeLimiter annotations
- Config in application.yml: slidingWindowSize, failureRateThreshold, waitDurationInOpenState, maxAttempts, timeoutDuration
- Fallback method for graceful degradation

*Observability*
- Metrics: Micrometer auto-instruments; http.client.requests with URI, method, status, outcome
- Tracing: Spring + OpenTelemetry / Micrometer Tracing auto-propagates traceparent
- Logging: careful not to log bodies (PII/secrets); log correlation id, URL, status, duration

*Auth propagation*
- Propagate JWT / auth context for on-behalf-of-user
- Service-to-service: OAuth2 client credentials or mTLS
- ExchangeFilterFunction (WebClient), RestClient interceptors, or RequestInterceptor (Feign) to inject tokens

*MDC / tracing headers propagation*
- When switching threads, MDC can be lost
- Spring Cloud Sleuth / Micrometer Tracing handle propagation
- Verify trace IDs appear in downstream logs

*Error handling patterns*
- Don't let RestClientException bubble unfiltered; map to domain exceptions
- 4xx client error: don't retry
- 5xx server error: retry idempotent
- 429 rate limited: back off
- 503 unavailable: retry
- Idempotency keys on non-idempotent POSTs when retrying

**Trade-offs**

*RestClient vs WebClient*
- Sync RestClient: simpler debugging, stack traces, Transactional boundaries
- Reactive WebClient: non-blocking, streaming, high concurrency, backpressure
- With Project Loom, sync Tomcat + RestClient handles high concurrency efficiently
- Still pick WebClient for streaming, fully reactive pipelines, or WebFlux apps

*@HttpExchange vs Feign*
- @HttpExchange native to Spring 6; no extra dep
- Feign has deeper ecosystem (Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, decoders)
- New code on Spring 6+: @HttpExchange usually wins
- Existing Spring Cloud projects: Feign entrenched

*When NOT to use declarative*
- Complex dynamic URL; computed headers per request
- Per-call ExchangeFilterFunction or interceptor
- Streaming with per-chunk logic
- Use imperative RestClient or WebClient directly

*HTTP/2 adoption*
- WebClient (Reactor Netty), RestClient (JDK HttpClient), Apache HttpClient 5 all support
- Multiplexing reduces connection overhead

*HTTP/3 (QUIC) emerging*
- Experimental; production niche

*gRPC as alternative*
- Internal microservice calls often better in gRPC: HTTP/2, Protobuf, strong types
- REST still default for public APIs

*Circuit breaker antipattern*
- Fallback that masks errors silently
- Fallback should return cached/default, queue for later, or clearly indicate failure
- Don't paper over bad dependencies; fix them

*Retry antipattern*
- Retrying non-idempotent POSTs without idempotency keys
- Retrying on client errors
- Exponential backoff + jitter; cap attempts (3 typical)

*Timeout antipattern*
- 30s default; thread pool exhaustion
- Aggressive internal timeouts
- Timeout budget accounts for retries

*Testing*
- MockWebServer (okhttp): full HTTP mock
- WireMock: classic Java HTTP mock
- MockRestServiceServer (Spring): mock client side
- Prefer real HTTP mocks over mocking RestTemplate

*Security*
- TLS for all external; validate certificates
- mTLS for service-to-service (Istio or manual)
- Secrets in Vault/Secrets Manager
- Never log tokens

**The strategic answer**
- Spring 6+ new code: @HttpExchange + RestClient (or WebClient) default
- RestTemplate only for legacy maintenance
- OpenFeign where Spring Cloud stack entrenched
- Timeouts, connection pool, Resilience4j are essential
- Observability with Micrometer and distributed tracing
- Test with MockWebServer/WireMock; not by mocking client directly
- Consider gRPC for internal service-to-service calls

mistakes: Equating 'REST' with 'uses HTTP and JSON' — missing statelessness and HATEOAS
java-backend-intermediate/rest-api/rest-.direct: **REST** has 6 architectural constraints: client-server, stateless, cacheable, uniform interface, layered system, and optional code-on-demand. Most 'REST APIs' are actually HTTP APIs — true REST requires **HATEOAS** which few implement.
java-backend-intermediate/rest-api/rest-.spoken:
REST is not a protocol or a library — it is an architectural style defined by six constraints. The term is widely misused: most APIs described as 'REST APIs' are actually HTTP APIs that partially follow REST principles.

**The constraints that matter in interviews**
- **Stateless** — every request contains all information needed to process it; the server holds no session state; this constraint is what enables horizontal scaling without sticky sessions
- **Uniform interface** — resources identified by URI, manipulation through representations, self-descriptive messages, and HATEOAS; the uniform interface is what defines REST, not just using HTTP
- **Layered system** — client cannot tell if it is talking directly to the server or through a proxy, load balancer, or CDN; enables transparent infrastructure changes

**Richardson Maturity Model**
- Level 0: single URI, all operations via POST (SOAP-style)
- Level 1: separate resources (`/orders`, `/customers`)
- Level 2: HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) + correct status codes — this is what most 'REST APIs' actually implement
- Level 3: HATEOAS — responses contain links to related actions; clients discover capabilities rather than hardcoding URIs

Resource-based URIs represent things, not actions: `/orders/123/cancel` is action-based; `/orders/123` with `PATCH {"status": "cancelled"}` is resource-based and the correct pattern.

mistakes: Interviewers want to see that you know the full loop from schema to compilable Java code.
java-backend-intermediate/rest-api/scena.direct: You write a `.proto` file declaring your messages and service contracts, then use the protoc compiler (typically via the **protobuf**-maven-plugin or Gradle's protobuf plugin) to auto-generate Java source files. The generated stubs include POJOs for messages and abstract base classes for services that you implement on the server side and use as type-safe clients.
java-backend-intermediate/rest-api/scena.spoken:
Protocol Buffers are gRPC's schema and serialization format — the wire format that makes gRPC payloads 5–10× smaller than JSON. The workflow has three parts: writing the schema, generating code, and implementing the service.

**The `.proto` schema:**
- Define message types (data shapes) and a service contract (RPC methods) in a `.proto` file under `src/main/proto`
- The key insight is that field numbers — not field names — identify data on the wire; you can rename fields freely without breaking backward compatibility because the binary encoding uses numbers, not names
- Never reuse deleted field numbers — mark them with `reserved` to prevent accidental reuse that would silently misinterpret old binary data from clients still on the previous schema

**Code generation:**
- Configure the `protobuf-maven-plugin` with the `protoc-gen-grpc-java` extension so `mvn compile` automatically runs `protoc` and drops generated stubs into `target/generated-sources`
- No separate protoc installation needed — the plugin downloads the right binary for the current OS, keeping CI reproducible across developer machines

**Service implementation:**
- Extend the generated `ImplBase` class, override your RPC methods, and drive responses through `StreamObserver` — call `onNext` to send data and `onCompleted` to close the stream

**Version alignment — the most dangerous footgun:**
- The `protoc` compiler version, `protobuf-java` runtime, and `grpc-java` stubs all need to be compatible with each other; a mismatch between the protoc version that generated stubs and the runtime library causes subtle serialization bugs that are hard to trace
- Pin all three versions in the parent POM as a single discipline to prevent hours of debugging that nobody expects from a code generator

I recommend `java_multiple_files = true` in your `.proto` files so each message generates a separate Java file — without it, all messages nest inside one outer class, making imports verbose and IDE navigation painful in large schemas.

mistakes: Candidates often jump straight to the controller and skip DispatcherServlet, HandlerMapping, and HandlerInterceptors, missing three of the most important extension points.
java-backend-intermediate/rest-api/sprin.direct: Spring MVC uses a single front controller, **DispatcherServlet**, which delegates to a chain of specialized components: HandlerMapping finds the controller method, HandlerAdapter invokes it, ViewResolver (or message converters for **REST**) renders the response, and exception resolvers handle errors along the way.
java-backend-intermediate/rest-api/sprin.spoken:
Every HTTP request to a Spring MVC application passes through a fixed pipeline. Knowing each stage is what allows you to place cross-cutting logic in the right layer.

**The pipeline**
- The request hits the servlet container (Tomcat), which forwards it to `DispatcherServlet` — the front controller registered for `/*` or `/`
- `HandlerMapping` resolves which controller method handles this URL + HTTP method combination
- `HandlerInterceptor.preHandle()` runs — authentication checks, logging, rate limiting at the MVC layer
- `HandlerAdapter` invokes the controller method — resolving `@RequestParam`, `@PathVariable`, `@RequestBody` from the request
- `HttpMessageConverter` reads the request body (JSON → Java object) and writes the response body (Java object → JSON)
- `HandlerInterceptor.postHandle()` runs after the handler but before the view is rendered
- The response is written; `HandlerInterceptor.afterCompletion()` runs regardless of success or exception

**Where exceptions go**
- Exceptions thrown by the handler method are caught by `HandlerExceptionResolver`
- `@ExceptionHandler` methods in a `@ControllerAdvice` are picked up by `ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver`

The distinction between `Filter` and `HandlerInterceptor`: a Filter executes before `DispatcherServlet` sees the request — it has no knowledge of which controller will handle it. An interceptor executes inside `DispatcherServlet`, after the handler is resolved.

mistakes: Saying 'just add v1 to everything' without explaining why and the deprecation strategy
java-backend-intermediate/rest-api/versi.direct: URI versioning (/v1/users) is the most pragmatic — visible, cacheable, easy to test. Header versioning (X-API-Version: 2) keeps URLs clean but breaks caching. Media type versioning is **REST**-pure but complex to implement and test.
java-backend-intermediate/rest-api/versi.spoken:
API versioning is how you evolve your API without breaking existing clients. The choice of strategy affects discoverability, REST compliance, and operational complexity.

**Three strategies**
- **URI versioning** (`/api/v1/orders`, `/api/v2/orders`): most common, discoverable, easy to route in API gateways and load balancers; Stripe's model
- **Header versioning** (`API-Version: 2` or custom header): keeps URIs stable; requires custom routing logic; harder to test without tooling
- **Accept/Content-Type versioning** (`Accept: application/vnd.company.v2+json`): fully REST-compliant; version is a content negotiation concern; GitHub uses this; complex to implement and consume

**Deprecation — the part most teams get wrong**
- Announce the sunset date in the `Sunset: Sat, 01 Jan 2027 00:00:00 GMT` response header on every response from the deprecated version
- Monitor traffic — never remove a version while clients are still calling it; check logs or API gateway metrics
- Provide a concrete migration guide: what changed, what the new endpoint looks like, how to migrate field by field

**In Spring MVC**
- Path prefix versioning is the cleanest: `@RequestMapping("/v1")` on a separate controller class per version
- Copy-paste versioned controllers is an anti-pattern — prefer a shared service layer and version only the request/response DTOs that changed

mistakes: Applying skip to write-phase exceptions without considering that a failed write rolls back the entire chunk — Spring Batch then re-reads items one at a time to isolate the bad row, which surprises many candidates
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/b.direct: Spring Batch provides built-in **retry** and **skip** policies on chunk steps. **Retry** re-attempts processing or writing for a configured exception type up to a limit before failing — appropriate for **transient failures** (deadlock, network blip). **Skip** silently discards items that cause specified exceptions up to a tolerance count — appropriate for **bad records** (parse error, validation). Together with `SkipListener` and `RetryListener` they let you build fault-tolerant pipelines that survive dirty data and infrastructure flaps without aborting the entire batch run.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/b.spoken:
Spring Batch's fault tolerance has two complementary policies — skip and retry — and a third concept around when rollback applies.

**Skip — discard and continue:**
- For predictable bad records (parse, validation)
- `faultTolerant().skip(Exception.class).skipLimit(N)`
- SkipListener fires for every skipped item — write to a dead-letter destination

**Retry — try again:**
- For transient failures (deadlock, 503)
- `faultTolerant().retry(Exception.class).retryLimit(N).backOffPolicy(...)`
- ExponentialBackOffPolicy prevents retry storms
- RetryListener emits metrics and observability signals

**The single-item recovery cycle:**
- When a chunk write fails, Spring Batch rolls back the chunk
- Then re-reads each item one at a time to isolate the bad row
- Good items succeed individually; bad item is skipped (if configured) or fails the step
- Processors must be idempotent — they may run twice for the same input

**`noRollback` and `processorTransactional(false)`:**
- `noRollback(ValidationException.class)` — declares an exception expected and benign
- `processorTransactional(false)` — processor outputs not rolled back
- Together they refine the rollback contract

**The hard problem — non-transactional side effects:**
- Emails, API calls, Kafka publishes are NOT undone by rollback
- Move them to a separate step that runs after success
- Or use the outbox pattern — write a row inside the chunk transaction, dispatch from a separate step

**Anti-patterns to call out:**
- `skipLimit(Integer.MAX_VALUE)` — silent data corruption
- `skip(Exception.class)` — masks real bugs
- Retry without backoff — compounds the failure
- Retry on non-idempotent processors — duplicate side effects

In an interview I'd emphasize the single-item recovery cycle and the idempotency requirement — those are what separate practitioners from rote knowledge.

mistakes: Confusing Tasklet with Chunk — candidates often think Tasklet is just a simpler Step, not realizing they are mutually exclusive execution strategies within a Step
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/b.direct: A **Job** is the top-level container representing an entire batch process, composed of one or more **Steps** executed in sequence or conditionally. Each Step follows either a **chunk-oriented model** (read-process-write in fixed-size chunks inside one transaction) or a **Tasklet model** (a single custom unit of work). The **JobRepository** persists every JobInstance, JobExecution, and StepExecution to a relational database, which is what enables restartability, audit trails, and skip/retry tracking — features that distinguish Spring Batch from a hand-rolled batch loop.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/b.spoken:
Spring Batch structures batch processing around a clear hierarchy: Job, Step, and either Chunk or Tasklet at the step level. Every layer is persisted to the JobRepository, which is what makes restart and audit possible.

**The hierarchy**
- **Job** — the overall batch process, like 'import monthly invoices'; composed of one or more Steps in sequence or conditionally
- **Step** — one phase of the job; each Step has its own execution status and can be restarted independently
- **Chunk** — the read-process-write model for a step; reads N items, processes each, writes the batch — all inside one transaction
- **Tasklet** — a single operation for a step; not a read-process-write loop; `execute()` returns `RepeatStatus.FINISHED`

**JobRepository — the persistence layer**
- Stores `JobInstance` (logical job run identified by Job name + JobParameters)
- Stores `JobExecution` (one physical attempt at the JobInstance)
- Stores `StepExecution` (per-step state plus serialized ExecutionContext for restart)
- Spring Boot auto-configures it from the application's `DataSource`

**Chunk transaction model**
- Chunk size 100 means: read 100 records, process each, write all 100 in one transaction
- A write failure rolls back only that chunk — already committed chunks are not re-processed on restart
- Larger chunks: fewer transactions, better throughput; smaller chunks: finer-grained checkpointing

**Tasklet vs Chunk**
- Chunk model is for streaming work — rows in a table, lines in a file
- Tasklet is for one-shot work — truncating a table, sending a notification, calling a stored procedure
- They are mutually exclusive within a single Step

In an interview, I'd emphasize the JobRepository — most candidates skip it, but it's what makes Spring Batch suitable for production rather than a hand-rolled loop.

mistakes: Confusing skip (bad record) with retry (transient failure); over-small chunk sizes; using chunk for non-streaming work
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/c.direct: Spring Batch **chunk-oriented processing** reads items one at a time (`ItemReader`), transforms them (`ItemProcessor`), then writes them in a **batch of N** (`ItemWriter`) inside a single transaction. The cycle is: read → process → accumulate until chunk-size → write + commit. If any step fails, the **whole chunk rolls back**; `skip` and `retry` policies let you tolerate bad records or transient failures without killing the job. Typical chunk sizes are 50-1000 for JDBC; tune based on row size and DB round-trip cost. Use **tasklets** for one-shot operations (file cleanup, stored-proc calls) where there's no natural stream of items.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/c.spoken:
Spring Batch chunk-oriented processing reads items one at a time via `ItemReader`, transforms them with `ItemProcessor`, then writes them in a batch of N via `ItemWriter` inside a single transaction. If any step fails, the whole chunk rolls back; skip and retry policies let you tolerate bad records or transient failures without killing the job.

**The chunk lifecycle:**
- Begin transaction
- Read up to `chunk_size` items, processing each as it arrives
- Pass the buffered list to `ItemWriter.write(items)` in one call
- Commit transaction

**Skip vs retry:**
- **Skip** — for bad records that should be logged and ignored
- **Retry** — for transient failures like DB deadlocks or network blips
- Both require `.faultTolerant()`

**The single-item recovery cycle is the subtle part:**
- When a write fails, Spring Batch rolls back the chunk and re-reads each item individually
- The good items are written one at a time; the bad item is skipped or fails the step
- This is why processors must be idempotent — they may run twice for the same input

**Tuning advice:**
- Chunk size 100-500 for JDBC; measure to find the sweet spot
- `JdbcBatchItemWriter` usually matters more than chunk size for throughput
- For JPA writers, set `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50` and `hibernate.order_inserts=true`

**Tasklet vs chunk:**
- Chunk for streaming work (process every row in X)
- Tasklet for one-shot work (delete old files, call a stored procedure)

In an interview, I'd emphasize the single-item recovery mechanism and the idempotency requirement — those are what catch candidates.

mistakes: Thinking Spring Integration can replace Spring Batch for bulk data processing — it lacks chunk transactions, job restart, skip/retry policies, and the execution metadata model
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/c.direct: **Spring Batch** is designed for **scheduled, finite, high-volume** data processing — bounded datasets with start/end semantics, restart capability, and transactional chunk processing. **Spring Integration** is designed for **event-driven, continuous, message-based** integration workflows that connect heterogeneous systems via channels, transformers, and adapters. They are complementary, not competing — Spring Integration can trigger and orchestrate Spring Batch jobs (file arrival → launch job), and Spring Batch can use Spring Integration channels as item sources or sinks for remote partitioning.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/c.spoken:
Spring Batch and Spring Integration solve fundamentally different problems but are frequently combined.

**Spring Batch — structured bulk processing:**
- Designed for: processing millions of records from a file or database on a schedule
- Key features: `JobRepository` for state persistence, restart from failure, skip/retry policies, partitioned parallel processing, chunk-level transaction management
- Use when: defined start, defined end, need to track how many records were processed, skipped, committed

**Spring Integration — event-driven message routing:**
- Designed for: connecting systems and routing messages in real time
- Key features: message channels, adapters (file system, JMS, AMQP, SFTP, email), transformers, routers, filters
- No concept of job state, checkpointing, or restart — continuous pipeline

**The canonical hybrid pattern:**
- Spring Integration watches an S3 bucket or SFTP folder for new files
- When a file arrives, Integration launches a Spring Batch job with the file path as a `JobParameter`
- Spring Batch reads, processes, and writes the file's records with full fault tolerance
- Integration handles the event-driven trigger; Batch handles the heavy data processing

**Decision rule:**
- Bounded dataset, needs restart/skip/retry — Spring Batch
- Continuous event stream, system integration, message routing — Spring Integration
- Both, with Batch triggered by Integration events — standard enterprise pattern

**Common pitfalls:**
- Using Integration for bulk processing because it 'feels lighter' — works at small scale, breaks when you need restart
- Using Batch for real-time events because the team already knows it — chunk commits add latency
- Not using `RunIdIncrementer` when launching Batch from Integration — restart semantics get confusing

In an interview I'd emphasize that the question is rarely 'which one' — it's usually 'how do they fit together'.

mistakes: Returning null from `ItemProcessor` to skip an item is correct, but many candidates try to throw an exception instead, which triggers retry/skip logic unintentionally
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/i.direct: In chunk-oriented processing, **`ItemReader`** reads one item at a time until the chunk size is reached, **`ItemProcessor`** optionally transforms or filters each item (returning `null` to skip), and **`ItemWriter`** receives the entire chunk as a list to persist in **one transaction**. This separation makes each piece independently testable and swappable. The contract details — `read()` returns `null` at end-of-data, `process()` returns `null` to filter, `write()` receives `Chunk<T>` (Spring Batch 5) so a single bulk INSERT replaces N round-trips — are what make chunk steps fast and restart-safe.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/i.spoken:
The chunk-oriented step has three roles, each with a precise contract.

**`ItemReader` — read one item at a time**
- Spring Batch calls `read()` repeatedly until it returns `null`
- `null` is the normal end-of-data signal; throwing is for errors
- Built-in readers: `FlatFileItemReader`, `JdbcCursorItemReader`, `JdbcPagingItemReader`, `JpaPagingItemReader`, `KafkaItemReader`

**`ItemProcessor` — transform or filter one item**
- Receives one item; returns the transformed item or `null` to skip
- `null` silently removes the item from the chunk — never reaches the writer
- Stateless by design; compose with `CompositeItemProcessor`

**`ItemWriter` — write the entire chunk**
- Receives `Chunk<T>` (Spring Batch 5) — all processed items
- Bulk INSERT/UPDATE in one DB call; never loop and write one at a time
- Built-in writers: `JdbcBatchItemWriter`, `JpaItemWriter`, `FlatFileItemWriter`, `KafkaItemWriter`

**Fault tolerance subtlety:**
- Skip on write failure triggers a chunk rollback and single-item replay to isolate the bad row
- Every item in the failed chunk reprocesses — processors must be idempotent
- Non-transactional side effects (emails, API calls) are NOT rolled back; use a final tasklet or outbox pattern

**Thread safety:**
- `FlatFileItemReader` and `JdbcCursorItemReader` maintain cursor state — wrap in `SynchronizedItemStreamReader` for multi-threaded steps
- Paging readers are safer for concurrency since each page is independent

In an interview I'd emphasize the null-return semantics and the single-item retry behaviour — those are what catch candidates.

mistakes: Adding a timestamp or run-id parameter every time to force a new `JobInstance` — valid, but candidates should know it also defeats automatic restart for that run
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/j.direct: **Job parameters** uniquely identify a `JobInstance` — the same Job name plus the same parameters always map to the same instance, preventing duplicate runs. When a job fails, its `JobExecution` is marked `FAILED` in the JobRepository, and re-launching with the same parameters triggers a **restart** that skips already-committed steps and resumes from the last failed or incomplete step. The reader's position (saved in `ExecutionContext` as `read_count`) is the checkpoint — `FlatFileItemReader` seeks forward by line count, paging readers skip by offset, and partitioned jobs restart only the failed partitions.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/j.spoken:
Spring Batch's restart capability is one of its most powerful features — a job that fails at record 50,000 can resume from record 50,001 rather than starting over. This requires understanding how parameters, instances, and executions relate.

**The identity model:**
- `JobInstance` = Job name + `JobParameters`; represents a logical run
- `JobExecution` = one physical attempt of a `JobInstance`; a failed JobInstance gets a new JobExecution on restart
- `StepExecution` = one attempt of one step; stores `read_count`, `write_count`, `commit_count`, plus the `ExecutionContext` for restart state

**Starting vs restarting:**
- First run: `jobLauncher.run(job, params)` creates a new JobInstance and JobExecution
- Restart: same parameters find the existing FAILED JobInstance and create a new JobExecution; completed steps are skipped
- A COMPLETED JobInstance cannot be re-launched by default — use `allowStartIfComplete(true)` per step if needed

**Late binding with `@StepScope`:**
- `@StepScope @Bean FlatFileItemReader reader(@Value("#{jobParameters['inputFile']}") String file)`
- The file value is not available at context load time; `@StepScope` defers bean creation until the step starts
- Essential for parameterized readers and writers

**Parameter design:**
- Business parameters are identity (`processingDate`, `region`)
- Technical parameters are additive (`run.id` from `RunIdIncrementer`)
- Conflating them — like UUID on every launch — defeats restart entirely

In an interview, I'd emphasize the JobInstance vs JobExecution distinction and the late binding via `@StepScope` — both are common gotchas that signal production experience.

mistakes: Using `@Scheduled` in a multi-replica deployment; not enabling Quartz clustering
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/j.direct: Spring's **`@Scheduled`** is fine for a single instance, but in **multi-node deployments** every pod fires the same job — you need a scheduler with **distributed locking**. **Quartz** supports this via a **JDBC-backed JobStore with `org.quartz.jobStore.isClustered=true`** — DB row locks ensure only one node picks up each trigger. The integration pattern: configure Quartz tables (`qrtz_*`), create a `JobDetail` + `Trigger` that calls `JobLauncher.run(batchJob, params)`, enable clustering. Alternatives are **ShedLock** (lightweight DB lock atop `@Scheduled`) and **Kubernetes CronJob** (orchestration outside the app). For mature production Spring Batch, Quartz clustered mode plus `JobLauncher` is the standard combo.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/j.spoken:
Spring's `@Scheduled` works for single-instance deployments, but in a cluster every replica fires the trigger — you need a scheduler with distributed locking.

**Quartz clustered mode is the standard answer:**
- JDBC-backed JobStore with `org.quartz.jobStore.isClustered=true`
- All nodes share the same Quartz schema
- One node grabs the trigger row lock and runs the job
- Bridge to Spring Batch via `QuartzJobBean` calling `JobLauncher.run(job, params)`
- Always include a unique parameter (timestamp or `RunIdIncrementer`) so each fire creates a new `JobInstance`

**ShedLock is the lightweight alternative:**
- `@Scheduled` plus `@SchedulerLock(name, lockAtMostFor, lockAtLeastFor)`
- Backed by a `LockProvider` (JDBC, Redis, ZooKeeper)
- Only one node holds the named lock at a time
- Use when you want simplicity over Quartz's rich features

**Kubernetes CronJob is the operational alternative:**
- K8s schedules a fresh Pod at each tick
- Pod runs the Boot app, runs the batch job, exits
- No scheduler inside the application
- Use when you're K8s-native and want operational separation

**Production practices:**
- Apply Quartz DDL via Flyway, not `initialize-schema`
- Set explicit misfire policies — `fire-and-proceed` for daily reports, `do-nothing` for high-frequency syncs
- Size the Quartz thread pool to peak job concurrency
- Set `requestRecovery(true)` on JobDetails so node crashes don't orphan work
- Make Batch jobs idempotent — recovery may re-run them
- Emit Micrometer metrics for misfires, durations, in-flight jobs

**Anti-patterns to call out:**
- `@Scheduled` in a multi-replica deployment
- Same `JobParameters` every run (`JobInstanceAlreadyCompleteException`)
- `initialize-schema: always` in production
- Long-running jobs starving the Quartz thread pool

In an interview I'd emphasize that the choice is operational, not technical — Quartz, ShedLock, and K8s CronJob all work; pick by team expertise and infrastructure context.

mistakes: Using multi-threaded step with non-thread-safe reader; partitioning when a simpler strategy would work
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/p.direct: Spring Batch has four parallelism strategies. **Multi-threaded step** runs one step on multiple threads sharing the reader/writer (reader must be thread-safe; restart weakens). **Parallel steps** run independent steps concurrently via a `split` in the job flow. **Async processor/writer** wraps each item in a `Future` on a thread pool — best when the **processor is I/O-bound**. **Partitioning** splits input into ranges; a master step launches N worker steps locally or on remote JVMs via messaging — scales best and preserves restartability per slice. Choose based on where the bottleneck is: CPU (partitioning / multi-threaded), per-item I/O (async), independent workloads (parallel steps).
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/p.spoken:
Spring Batch has four parallelism strategies, and the right one depends on where the bottleneck is.

**Multi-threaded step:**
- One step, multiple threads share reader/writer
- Reader must be thread-safe — wrap in `SynchronizedItemStreamReader`
- Restart semantics weaken — `ExecutionContext` position imprecise
- Use for I/O-bound steps where restart-order isn't critical

**Parallel steps via split:**
- Independent steps run concurrently using a `TaskExecutor`
- Each step has its own reader/writer — no thread-safety issues
- Each has independent restart state
- Use for genuinely independent workloads (loading reference tables in parallel)

**Async processor/writer:**
- `AsyncItemProcessor` wraps the processor in a `Future` on a thread pool
- `AsyncItemWriter` unwraps the futures and writes actual results
- Reader stays single-threaded — no thread-safety issues
- Use when the processor is I/O-bound (HTTP calls, external lookups)

**Partitioning:**
- Master step splits input via `Partitioner` into N slices
- Each slice runs as an independent worker step with its own reader/writer
- Local partitioning — workers in one JVM via `TaskExecutor`
- Remote partitioning — workers on separate JVMs via Kafka, AMQP, JMS messaging
- Worker step must be `@StepScope` to receive partition context via `@Value("#{stepExecutionContext['x']}")`
- Best scalability + restart semantics — failed partitions restart independently

**Decision framework:**
- Bottleneck in processor (per-item I/O) → async processor/writer
- Multiple independent workloads → parallel steps
- Huge dataset that splits naturally → partitioning
- Simple single-machine, restart not critical → multi-threaded
- None fit or small dataset → stay single-threaded; tune chunk size and writer choice first

**Pitfalls to call out:**
- Multi-threaded + non-thread-safe reader — corruption
- Partitioning + non-idempotent writer — duplicates on restart
- Oversized/undersized grid — framework overhead or idle workers
- Skewed partitioner — one worker does 90% of work; prefer hash for uniformity
- Writer contention on a single DB index — all partitions serialize on the same lock

In an interview I'd emphasize that you measure first, then pick the strategy. Multi-threaded step is rarely the right answer in 2026 — async or partitioning almost always beat it on both performance and correctness.

mistakes: Jumping to 'add more threads' without identifying the real bottleneck
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/s.direct: **Frame it as a triage** — treat slowdown and failure as potentially separate problems. Gather data first: **`StepExecution` history** (start/end, read/write/skip counts, exceptions), **DB-side metrics** (query plans, lock waits, replication lag), **host metrics** (CPU, GC), and **data-volume trends**. Compare a recent slow run against an older fast run to identify what changed. Typical culprits in order of likelihood: **data growth**, **index regression**, **lock contention**, **chunk size or JDBC batching misconfigured**, **retry storms**, and **resource contention**. Fix in tiers: optimize query and add index → increase chunk size and JDBC batching → introduce partitioning → move to off-peak window. Always document the diagnosis so it isn't rediscovered next quarter.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/s.spoken:
I'd treat slowdown and failure as potentially separate problems and triage in three phases.

**Phase 1 — gather data (15 minutes):**
- StepExecution history from BATCH_* tables — duration, read/write counts, skip and rollback counts per step
- Actuator metrics — `spring.batch.chunk.write` and `spring.batch.item.process` p50/p99
- DB-side — slow query log, `pg_stat_statements`, lock waits, replication lag
- Host — CPU, GC pauses, disk IO
- Compare a recent 6h run against an older 2h run; the step that grew most is the bottleneck

**Phase 2 — hypothesis testing:**
- Volume growth (40% of cases) — `read_count` larger than last month; throughput unchanged
- Throughput regression (25%) — same volume, slower; check query plans, missing indexes, lock contention
- Failure-driven (15%) — `rollback_count` climbing; retry storms; identify the exception and decide to skip, retry less, or fail fast
- Infrastructure regression (10%) — DB downsized, slower storage, JVM upgrade, network change

**Phase 3 — fix in tiers:**
- Quick wins first — chunk size 100→500→1000→2000, JDBC batch alignment, missing index, ANALYZE, off-peak
- Scaling — partitioning by hash key, async processor/writer for per-item I/O, read from replica, bulk loaders
- Re-architect — CDC/streaming, materialized views, analytical engines

**Patterns to call out:**
- Don't scale before diagnosing — adding partitioning when the cause is a missing index just makes 10 workers do 10× the wasted work
- Over-tuning chunk size has diminishing returns; 100→500 is 2-3×, 500→2000 is 10-30%
- Idempotency is non-negotiable for retries, skip, and partitioning
- Retry storms can silently double run time

**Documentation and prevention:**
- Build a slow-job runbook with exact SQL, actuator endpoints, log commands
- Add alerts on duration thresholds, skip rate, rollback count
- Synthetic load test in CI with scaled-down data
- Track volume growth and alert on projected SLA breach

In an interview I'd emphasize that the first question is always 'how much did the data grow?' — answers the problem in five minutes more often than candidates expect.

mistakes: Using `fixedRate` for a slow task (overlaps pile up) or forgetting distributed locking in a cluster
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/s.direct: Enable with **`@EnableScheduling`**; annotate methods with **`@Scheduled`** specifying one of: **`fixedRate`** (time between start times — overlap possible if task is slow), **`fixedDelay`** (time between end-of-last and next start — never overlaps), or **`cron`** (time-of-day expressions). The default thread pool is **single-threaded**; configure a `TaskScheduler` with adequate threads or tasks block each other. In **clustered deployments** `@Scheduled` fires on every replica — use **ShedLock**, **Quartz clustered**, or **Kubernetes CronJob** for single execution. Keep tasks **idempotent**, short, and observable.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-batch/s.spoken:
Spring's `@Scheduled` is the simplest way to run a method on a timer inside one JVM.

**Three timing modes:**
- `fixedRate` — N ms between start times; can overlap with multi-thread pool
- `fixedDelay` — N ms between end and next start; never overlaps
- `cron` — time-of-day expressions; Spring's 6-field format with leading seconds

**Two pitfalls everyone hits:**
- Default thread pool is single-threaded; multiple scheduled methods queue up
- Configure `ThreadPoolTaskScheduler` with `setPoolSize(10)`, error handler, graceful shutdown
- In multi-replica deployments every replica fires — duplicate runs without coordination

**Cluster-safe options:**
- ShedLock — `@Scheduled` plus `@SchedulerLock(name, lockAtMostFor, lockAtLeastFor)`; backed by JDBC/Redis/Mongo
- Quartz clustered — heavier; rich misfire and recovery semantics
- Kubernetes CronJob — schedules outside the app; Pod runs and exits at each tick

**Cron pitfalls to call out:**
- Spring 6-field vs Unix 5-field — leading seconds field; common migration bug
- Timezone — `zone = "UTC"` for stable infra schedules; named zones are DST-aware
- `*` in day-of-month and day-of-week is 'every day' (no AND semantics)
- Feb 29 — use `L 2 *` for last day of February, not `29 2 *`

**Operational hygiene:**
- Keep tasks short — delegate heavy work to a queue/Executor; method is a trigger, not the worker
- Always idempotent — failure mid-task, retries, lock expiry can cause double-runs
- Log start, end, duration, outcome with MDC
- Emit Micrometer metrics (`@Timed` or manual sample); alert on missed fires (no run in 2x period)
- Wrap the body in try/catch — uncaught exceptions are logged but the run is lost

**Decision framework:**
- Single replica → plain `@Scheduled`
- Multiple replicas, simple job → `@Scheduled` plus ShedLock
- Complex scheduling or dynamic schedules → Quartz clustered
- K8s-native, operational separation → Kubernetes CronJob
- Don't stack solutions — pick one scheduler

In an interview I'd emphasize that `@Scheduled` is great for in-process periodic work, but the moment you have more than one replica or need recovery semantics, graduate to ShedLock or Quartz.

mistakes: Exposing `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*` in production without authentication, leaking environment variables, heap dumps, and internal metrics
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/ac.direct: Spring Boot Actuator exposes operational HTTP and JMX endpoints — `/health`, `/info`, `/metrics`, `/env`, `/beans`, `/heapdump`, `/threaddump` — without writing custom monitoring code. By default only **`/health` and `/info` are exposed over HTTP**; everything else requires explicit opt-in via `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`. In production, layer four defenses: **expose only what monitoring needs**, **secure with Spring Security role-based access**, **isolate on a separate `management.server.port`**, and **split health into liveness/readiness groups** for Kubernetes probes. Setting `exposure.include=*` in production is the most common Actuator security incident.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/ac.spoken:
Spring Boot Actuator gives you production observability — health, metrics, environment, thread dumps — without deploying a separate monitoring agent. The defaults are safe for development; exposing it fully in production is a security incident.

**The four hardening layers**
- Exposure control: `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,prometheus` — never `*`
- Spring Security with `EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint()` — keep `/health` and `/info` public, require `ACTUATOR` role for everything else
- Separate management port: `management.server.port=9090` — moves Actuator off the public port; combine with a NetworkPolicy so only monitoring can reach it
- Health groups: split `liveness` (minimal ping) from `readiness` (DB, Redis, Kafka) so Kubernetes restarts only when the process is genuinely broken

**Why exposure matters**
- `/env` leaks every property including passwords if injected as env vars
- `/heapdump` returns the full JVM memory — secrets, session tokens, decrypted credentials
- `/beans` and `/conditions` reveal the architecture and let attackers plan further probes

**Health detail control**
- `management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized` — `UP`/`DOWN` for the load balancer, component details for authenticated callers
- Custom `HealthIndicator` beans add app-specific checks — external API reachability, queue depth — and integrate into the same response monitoring already watches

In an interview, I'd emphasize that **the strongest defence is network isolation**, not authentication. Authentication is a layer; an isolated management port behind a NetworkPolicy is a moat.

conceptLabels: Spring Boot is an opinionated layer ON Spring
mistakes: Confusing Spring Boot with Spring ('they're the same') — missing auto-configuration, starters, and the embedded server, which are the point of Boot; or believing Boot replaces Spring rather than configures it.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/au.direct: Spring Boot is an opinionated layer on top of the Spring Framework that auto-configures the application based on classpath, embeds a web server (Tomcat/Jetty), and removes XML/boilerplate via sensible defaults — so a developer can run a production-ready application with `java -jar` or a single `main` method. It exists because the raw Spring Framework, while powerful, required significant manual configuration (XML, then Java config), dependency wiring, and an external servlet container to run; that ceremony slowed development and made onboarding hard. Spring Boot's auto-configuration, starters, and embedded server collapse weeks of plumbing into minutes, while staying 100% Spring under the hood.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/au.spoken: Spring Boot is an opinionated layer on top of the Spring Framework that auto-configures the application based on the classpath, embeds a web server, and removes XML and boilerplate via sensible defaults — so you can run a production-ready app with one command. It exists because raw Spring, while powerful, required significant manual configuration and an external servlet container to deploy, which slowed development and made onboarding hard. The pieces I anchor on are auto-configuration, which inspects the classpath and creates beans you'd otherwise write — if Tomcat's present it configures an embedded server, if a DataSource is present it configures one — and you override only what differs. Starters, which are curated, tested dependency sets that prevent version conflicts. The embedded server, which runs inside the jar so the app is self-contained and runnable with java -jar. And the fact that it's still Spring underneath — every Boot behavior is Spring beans, so I can override any auto-config by defining my own bean, and actuator's /beans endpoint lists what's there. The tension I'm honest about is convention versus control: the auto-configuration can feel like magic, but every auto-config has a conditional and is overridable, so the control is always there when I need it.

mistakes: Saying 'Spring Boot is a different framework' or treating them as competitors rather than layers in the same stack
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/co.direct: Spring Boot is **not a replacement** for Spring Framework — it's an opinionated layer on top that eliminates boilerplate configuration. Spring provides the ecosystem (**IoC, AOP, MVC, Data, Security**), while Spring Boot provides **auto-configuration, embedded servers, starter dependencies**, and production-ready defaults so you can go from zero to running application in minutes instead of hours. Every Spring Boot app is still a Spring app — the same `ApplicationContext`, the same `BeanPostProcessor`s, the same proxies — Boot just stops you from writing the configuration that wires it together.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/co.spoken:
Spring Boot is not a different framework — it is Spring Framework with decisions already made for you. The same `ApplicationContext`, the same IoC container, the same AOP proxies. What Spring Boot adds is conventions, auto-configuration, embedded servers, and starter POMs that wire everything together automatically.

**What Spring Boot adds**
- Auto-configuration: reads `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` conditions at startup and registers beans only when the right dependencies are on the classpath and you have not already defined your own
- Embedded server: Tomcat, Jetty, or Netty ships inside the JAR — no deployment to an external container required
- Starter POMs: `spring-boot-starter-web` pulls in exactly the right set of dependencies at compatible versions

**What stays the same**
- The IoC container is identical — `ApplicationContext`, `BeanPostProcessor`, `@Autowired`, `@Transactional` all work exactly as in raw Spring
- Debugging an auto-configuration issue requires understanding raw Spring: which `BeanPostProcessor` runs, what condition failed, why two beans of the same type conflict

**When to use raw Spring**
- Embedding Spring into a non-Boot environment (legacy app servers, custom tooling)
- Writing a Spring Boot starter or auto-configuration itself

`@SpringBootApplication` is three annotations composed: `@Configuration` (this class defines beans), `@EnableAutoConfiguration` (activate auto-config), `@ComponentScan` (scan this package). Understanding the composition means you can decompose it when you only need part of it.

java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/co.title: Spring Framework vs Spring Boot — What's the Difference?

mistakes: Assuming `application.yml` always wins over `application.properties` — in fact they have the same precedence, and if both exist Spring Boot loads both with properties processed first, so yml values win for duplicates
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/co.direct: Spring Boot loads configuration from many sources and merges them into a unified `Environment` with a strict precedence order: **command-line args > environment variables > profile-specific files > base `application.{yml,properties}` > defaults**. `application.yml` supports hierarchical structure and multi-document files; `application.properties` is flat key=value pairs — both have the same precedence, so the file loaded last wins for duplicates. Environment variables use **relaxed binding** (`SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` maps to `spring.datasource.url`) and are essential for twelve-factor app deployments where credentials and per-environment values must be injected at runtime, never committed to source.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/co.spoken:
Spring Boot aggregates configuration from multiple sources with a strict priority order. Knowing the order is essential for understanding why a property has a particular value in a given environment.

**Priority order (highest to lowest)**
- Command-line arguments (`--server.port=9090`) — always win
- Environment variables (`SERVER_PORT=9090`) — override property files; the standard for Docker and Kubernetes
- Profile-specific files (`application-prod.properties`) — override the base file for active profiles
- `application.properties` / `application.yml` — the base defaults

**Properties vs YAML**
- `application.properties`: flat key-value, readable, no indentation sensitivity
- `application.yml`: hierarchical structure, good for deeply nested config; but YAML null vs empty string behavior is a common trap — `key:` is null, which causes `@Value("${key}")` to throw `IllegalArgumentException`
- If both files exist at the same location, properties is loaded first; yml takes precedence for any key in both

**Environment variable relaxed binding**
- `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` automatically maps to `spring.datasource.url` — dots and dashes become underscores; uppercase is standard for container environments

**Verifying configuration**
- `/actuator/env` shows every property source in priority order so you can see exactly which value was resolved
- `--debug` prints the conditions evaluation report for auto-configuration

Use property files for developer defaults, profile-specific files for environment overrides, and environment variables or secrets managers for production credentials — never hardcode credentials in any property file committed to version control.

mistakes: Thinking that switching embedded servers requires code changes — it is a single dependency swap because Spring Boot abstracts the server behind `WebServer`/`ServletWebServerFactory` interfaces
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/em.direct: Spring Boot defaults to **embedded Tomcat** but supports Jetty and Undertow by excluding `spring-boot-starter-tomcat` and adding the desired alternative — a single dependency swap, no code changes. **Tomcat is the most battle-tested**; **Undertow offers the lowest memory footprint and highest servlet throughput**; **Jetty is a solid middle ground** with strong WebSocket and SSE support. All three are configured through the `server.*` property namespace. For reactive WebFlux apps the default is **Netty** — an event-loop server that suits non-blocking I/O.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/em.spoken:
Spring Boot embeds the web server inside the JAR — Tomcat by default, with Jetty, Undertow, and Netty as alternatives. Choosing and configuring the right server affects throughput, memory usage, and the concurrency model.

**Switching servers**
- Exclude `spring-boot-starter-tomcat` from `spring-boot-starter-web` and add `spring-boot-starter-jetty` or `spring-boot-starter-undertow`
- Spring Boot auto-detects the server implementation on the classpath — no code changes required
- WebFlux applications use Netty by default; Netty is non-blocking and handles thousands of concurrent connections on a small thread pool; Tomcat uses one thread per request

**Key Tomcat settings**
- `server.tomcat.threads.max=200` (default) — the maximum number of simultaneous requests; increase for high-concurrency workloads, but each thread consumes memory
- `server.tomcat.accept-count` — the queue depth when all threads are busy; requests beyond this are rejected

**Common configuration**
- `server.port=8080`, `server.compression.enabled=true`, `server.ssl.key-store` — configured via `application.properties` without touching code
- `server.shutdown=graceful` — allows in-flight requests to complete before the JVM exits

**Programmatic customization**
- `WebServerFactoryCustomizer<TomcatServletWebServerFactory>` exposes server-specific knobs that have no property equivalent
- Guard with `@ConditionalOnClass` so the bean activates only when the matching server is on the classpath

The decision between Tomcat and Netty is architectural: blocking I/O with Tomcat suits traditional request-response Spring MVC; non-blocking event-loop Netty suits reactive WebFlux. Do not mix — using a blocking call inside a Netty event loop blocks the loop and kills throughput.

mistakes: Only mentioning `application.properties`; forgetting environment variables and command-line overrides; hardcoding the port for production rather than using `${PORT}` substitution
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/pr.direct: The standard way is `server.port=8081` in `application.properties` or `application.yml`. But Spring Boot's property binding accepts the same value from multiple sources with a strict precedence: **command-line arguments** (`--server.port=8082`) > **JVM system properties** (`-Dserver.port=8082`) > **OS environment variables** (`SERVER_PORT=8082`) > **profile-specific property files** > **`application.properties`** > **defaults**. Setting `server.port=0` tells Spring Boot to pick a random free port at startup — ideal for integration tests using `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)` with `@LocalServerPort` injection to avoid port conflicts in parallel CI runs.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/pr.spoken:
The simplest way to configure the server port is `server.port=8081` in `application.properties` or `application.yml`. But the more interesting answer is Spring Boot's externalized configuration model.

The same property can come from multiple sources with a strict precedence.
- From highest to lowest: **command-line arguments**, **JVM system properties**, **OS environment variables**, **profile-specific property files**, **`application.properties`**, and finally defaults.
- So `java -jar app.jar --server.port=8082` beats the env var, which beats the file.

Relaxed binding is a nice detail — Spring maps `SERVER_PORT` env var directly to `server.port` without any code.

Setting **`server.port=0`** is a useful trick for integration tests — Spring picks a free port at startup, and you inject it with `@LocalServerPort`. This avoids port conflicts when tests run in parallel in CI.

For production, I never hardcode the port in the packaged JAR. I use `${PORT:8080}` so the artifact respects the platform's `PORT` env var — that's how Heroku, Cloud Run, and Cloud Foundry all work.

The broader point: externalized configuration is the reason the same JAR is deployable across dev, staging, and production without rebuilding. That's the 12-Factor App principle and the real answer to why Spring Boot structures properties this way.

mistakes: `COPY`ing the fat JAR as a single layer so every code change invalidates the entire JAR layer and forces a full re-push of hundreds of megabytes
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/sc.direct: Spring Boot 2.3+ supports **layered JARs** that split the JAR into four ordered layers — `dependencies`, `spring-boot-loader`, `snapshot-dependencies`, and `application` — so Docker only rebuilds and re-pushes layers that change. Combined with Spring Boot's **Cloud Native Buildpacks** support (`./mvnw spring-boot:build-image`) or a multi-stage Dockerfile that extracts layers, this dramatically reduces image push times and build duration. Always set `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75` so the JVM respects the container's memory limit instead of seeing the host's total memory.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/sc.spoken:
A standard fat JAR Docker image means every code change invalidates the entire layer — developers wait minutes for Docker to re-download and unpack hundreds of megabytes of unchanged dependencies. Layered JARs fix this by splitting the JAR into dependency-order layers that Docker caches independently.

**The layer structure**
- Layer 1: `dependencies` — almost never changes
- Layer 2: `spring-boot-loader` — changes only on Boot upgrades
- Layer 3: `snapshot-dependencies` — changes occasionally during development
- Layer 4: `application` — changes on every build
- Docker caches the first three; only the last is rebuilt on a code change — a build that took 3 minutes drops to 10 seconds

**Multi-stage Dockerfile approach**
- Stage 1: extract the layered JAR with `java -Djarmode=layertools -jar app.jar extract`
- Stage 2: copy each layer separately with `COPY --from=builder /extracted/dependencies ./`
- Docker sees four separate `COPY` instructions and caches each independently
- Always set `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75` so the JVM respects container limits

**Buildpacks alternative**
- `./mvnw spring-boot:build-image` produces a layered, secure, OCI-compliant image with no Dockerfile
- Buildpacks apply OS patches and security hardening automatically — no manual base image updates
- `pack rebase` updates the OS layer of existing images without rebuilding the application

**Common pitfalls**
- CI cache not preserved between runs — layer benefit disappears
- Forgetting `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75` — OOM under container limits
- SNAPSHOT internal libraries thrashing the snapshot-dependencies layer

In an interview, the strong answer is: **layered JARs + Buildpacks (or layered Dockerfile) + container-aware JVM memory + preserved CI cache — that's the production-grade Spring Boot image recipe**.

mistakes: Thinking starters contain code, not knowing the autoconfigure vs starter module split, and forgetting `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` so user overrides are silently ignored
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/st.direct: A **Spring Boot Starter** is an **opinionated dependency descriptor** — an essentially empty Maven/Gradle artifact that pulls in a curated, version-aligned set of transitive dependencies plus **auto-configuration** that wires sensible defaults. Internally, starters rely on two mechanisms: **BOM-managed versions** via `spring-boot-dependencies` and **auto-configuration classes** listed in `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` (Spring Boot 2.7+). To build a custom starter, you create two modules: `*-spring-boot-autoconfigure` (contains `@AutoConfiguration` classes with `@ConditionalOn*` guards and `@ConfigurationProperties`) and `*-spring-boot-starter` (the empty 'marketing' artifact that consumers add). Conditionals ensure safe behavior when optional libs are absent and let users override defaults.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/st.spoken:
A Spring Boot Starter is an opinionated dependency descriptor — an essentially empty Maven or Gradle artifact that pulls in a curated, version-aligned set of transitive dependencies plus auto-configuration that wires sensible defaults.

**The three roles of a starter**
- Dependency grouping — `spring-boot-starter-web` brings Spring MVC, Jackson, Tomcat, validation
- Version alignment — the `spring-boot-dependencies` BOM pins all transitive versions to a tested combination
- Auto-configuration — starters pull autoconfigure JARs that activate when classes and beans are detected

**How auto-configuration fires**
- `@SpringBootApplication` triggers `@EnableAutoConfiguration`
- Spring scans `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` (Boot 2.7+)
- Each listed class becomes a candidate; activates only if `@ConditionalOn*` guards pass
- Common conditionals: `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`, `@ConditionalOnProperty`, `@ConditionalOnWebApplication`
- Ordering via `@AutoConfigureBefore`, `@AutoConfigureAfter`, `@AutoConfigureOrder`

**Building a custom starter — the two-module pattern**
- `*-spring-boot-autoconfigure`: contains `@AutoConfiguration` classes, `@ConfigurationProperties`, and the `AutoConfiguration.imports` file
- `*-spring-boot-starter`: empty POM that depends on the core library plus the autoconfigure module
- Consumer adds the starter; conditionals ensure the auto-config activates only when appropriate and steps aside when the consumer defines their own bean

**Best practices for starter authors**
- Always `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` on beans the consumer might override
- Use `@ConditionalOnClass` to guard against missing optional libraries
- `@ConditionalOnProperty(matchIfMissing = true)` for on-by-default opt-out features
- One `@AutoConfiguration` per feature area (main wiring, metrics, health, security)
- Pair `@ConfigurationProperties` with `spring-boot-configuration-processor` for IDE auto-completion
- Test with `ApplicationContextRunner` — no full Boot context needed, super fast

**Debugging a missing bean**
- Enable `logging.level.org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure=DEBUG` or hit `/actuator/conditions`
- Look at the negative matches section — usually `@ConditionalOnClass` failed, a property is missing, or a bean is already defined

**Format change to know**
- Boot ≤ 2.6: `META-INF/spring.factories` with the `EnableAutoConfiguration` key
- Boot 2.7+: `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`
- Boot 3.x: same file; `@Configuration` deprecated for auto-configs in favor of `@AutoConfiguration`

In an interview, the strong answer is: **starters are empty POMs that aggregate dependencies and trigger auto-configuration; a custom starter is two modules — autoconfigure for the code, starter for the empty aggregator — with `@ConditionalOn*` guards that always let consumers override**.

mistakes: Using `@SpringBootTest` for every test including repository-only or controller-only tests, causing very slow test suites, or accidentally breaking context caching by adding test-specific `@MockBean` in a way that creates a unique context per test class
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/te.direct: `@SpringBootTest` loads the **full application context** and is suitable for integration tests, but it is slow. **Test slice annotations** like `@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`, and `@JsonTest` load only the slice of the context relevant to the test (controllers, JPA layer, JSON serialization), making them much faster. Spring Test **caches `ApplicationContext`s** across test classes that share identical configuration — so the expensive context startup happens once per unique configuration combination. The cache key includes `@MockBean` declarations, `@ActiveProfiles`, and `@TestPropertySource` — variation in any of those creates a separate context.
java-backend-intermediate/spring-boot/te.spoken:
Spring Boot provides test slice annotations that load only the beans relevant to what you are testing. Using `@SpringBootTest` for everything works but is unnecessarily slow — a repository test that starts the web layer and message brokers wastes seconds on every CI run.

**Test slices**
- `@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)` — loads only MVC infrastructure, the specified controller, and related `@ControllerAdvice`; no database, no service layer; use `@MockBean` for dependencies
- `@DataJpaTest` — loads only JPA/Hibernate + an embedded H2 database; no web layer; tests repository logic in isolation
- `@SpringBootTest` — loads the full `ApplicationContext`; use for end-to-end integration tests only

**Context caching**
- Spring caches `ApplicationContext` instances across test classes that share the same configuration
- `@MockBean` is the most common cache-buster — each unique set of mocked beans creates a distinct context
- Extract shared mocks into a base test class or `@TestConfiguration` class to maximize cache hits across the test suite
- Enable `org.springframework.test.context.cache=DEBUG` to see cache hits and misses

**Embedded vs real database**
- `@DataJpaTest` defaults to H2; if your query uses a PostgreSQL-specific function, the test passes with H2 and fails in production
- `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)` + Testcontainers runs the real database in CI — the only reliable approach for dialect-specific queries

In an interview, the strong answer is: **slices for fast focused tests, full `@SpringBootTest` for end-to-end paths, and a base class to keep mock signatures consistent so the cache actually works**.
