conceptLabels: React's core model is UI = f(state)
mistakes: Memorizing hooks (useState, useEffect) without explaining the UI = f(state) model, the virtual DOM, or why one-way data flow matters.
java-fullstack-intermediate/react-core/h.direct: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components, using a virtual DOM and unidirectional data flow to keep complex interfaces predictable. It exists because building large interactive UIs by directly manipulating the DOM (jQuery-style) becomes unmaintainable: state and view drift, events tangle, and the code resists change. React's model — describe the UI as a function of state, let it compute the diff and update the DOM — scales to large apps because the mental model is 'UI = f(state)', and the developer thinks in transformations, not DOM mutations.
java-fullstack-intermediate/react-core/h.spoken: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components, using a virtual DOM and unidirectional data flow to keep complex interfaces predictable. It exists because building large interactive UIs by directly manipulating the DOM becomes unmaintainable — state and view drift, events tangle, and the code resists change. The mental model I stress is UI equals a function of state: a component is a function of its state and props that returns the view, and React keeps the DOM in sync with that output — you think in transformations, not DOM mutations. The core runtime is the virtual DOM and reconciliation: React renders a lightweight tree, diffs it against the previous one with the Fiber algorithm, and applies the minimal change to the real DOM. Components and props are the reusable, composable units, where props are immutable inputs passed down. State and hooks let function components hold state and side effects — useState for local state, useEffect for syncing with the outside world, and the common bugs there are stale closures and missing dependency-array values, which is why the React team now teaches to derive state where possible rather than sync with effects. One-way data flow — data down via props, actions up via callbacks — makes the flow traceable at scale. And I always stress stable keys for lists, a real id not the array index, so reconciliation matches items across reorders. The honest tension is that the declarative model abstracts away the DOM, which frustrates fine-grained control, and the escape hatches like useRef and useMemo are overused — the virtual DOM is not free, which is why React Server Components and concurrent rendering exist.

mistakes: Testing implementation details (the internal state, the hook calls) instead of behavior — producing brittle tests that break on every refactor and test the wrong thing.
java-fullstack-intermediate/react-testin.direct: React testing is the practice of verifying that React components render the correct output, behave correctly under user interaction, and integrate properly with the rest of the app — using unit (Jest/RTL), integration, and end-to-end (Cypress/Playwright) tests. It exists because React's component model is highly testable (a component is a pure function of props/state), and without tests, regressions slip in as the UI grows and refactors. Testing at the right level — mostly integration tests with React Testing Library, E2E for critical flows — keeps the suite fast and meaningful, and the guiding principle is 'test behavior, not implementation'.
java-fullstack-intermediate/react-testin.spoken: React testing is the practice of verifying that React components render the correct output, behave correctly under user interaction, and integrate properly — using unit, integration, and end-to-end tests. It exists because React's component model is highly testable, since a component is a pure function of props and state, and without tests regressions slip in as the UI grows. The guiding principle I stress is 'test behavior, not implementation' — query the DOM the way a user would, by role, label, or text, and assert what's visible, not the internal state or hook call counts, because that keeps tests robust to refactors. React Testing Library embodies this: its philosophy is that the more your tests resemble the way the software is used, the more confidence they give. The testing trophy is the modern shape — mostly RTL integration tests, which are the sweet spot of fast and meaningful, a few E2E tests with Cypress or Playwright for the critical flows like login and checkout, and pure unit tests for the pure logic. The honest tensions are confidence versus speed — E2E gives the most confidence but is slow and flaky, so you reserve it for the few flows that matter most — and mocking, which is necessary for APIs and heavy dependencies but over-mocking makes tests pass while the real integration breaks, so you mock at the network boundary with MSW and sparingly. And I avoid snapshot tests for the most part because they're brittle and tend to approve any change without reading it.

conceptLabels: Chunk size is a tuning knob
mistakes: Describing chunking without the resume/protocol piece — missing why per-chunk retry and a resume protocol (tus, S3 multipart) are what make it actually reliable.
java-fullstack-intermediate/realtime-upl.direct: Resumable (chunked) upload is a technique that splits a large file into fixed-size chunks, uploads each chunk independently (with retry), and the server reassembles them — allowing an upload to resume from the last successful chunk if the network drops. It exists because a single monolithic upload of a large file (video, dataset) over a flaky mobile or satellite network will almost certainly fail, forcing the user to restart from zero — which is unacceptable for gigabyte uploads. Chunking plus per-chunk retry plus a resume protocol (like tus, or S3 multipart) makes large uploads reliable and resumable, and enables parallelism and progress reporting.
java-fullstack-intermediate/realtime-upl.spoken: Resumable, or chunked, upload is a technique that splits a large file into fixed-size chunks, uploads each independently with retry, and the server reassembles them, allowing an upload to resume from the last successful chunk if the network drops. It exists because a single monolithic upload of a large file over a flaky network will almost certainly fail and force a restart from zero, which is unacceptable for gigabyte uploads. The flow I describe is: split the file into chunks, upload each as a separate request with its own retry, and on reconnect ask the server which chunks it already has — the tus protocol does this with a HEAD request that returns the upload offset, and S3 multipart does it by listing completed parts — then upload only the missing chunks and have the server reassemble them in order. The protocols I name are tus, the open HTTP protocol for resumable uploads, and S3 multipart, the cloud object-store equivalent, and I stress using a proven protocol rather than inventing one because the server has to handle out-of-order, duplicate, and abandoned chunks, which the protocols already solve. The chunk size is a tuning knob — smaller chunks mean more retry resilience and finer progress but more request overhead, larger chunks are faster but lose more on a retry, so typically 5 to 25 megabytes. The honest tension is reliability versus complexity — chunked upload is far more reliable but adds client and server complexity, so the resolution is to lean on tus or S3 multipart.

```python
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter

# (1) SESSION: reuse the connection; set auth/headers once.

              status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504])
s.mount('https://', HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry))

# (4) PAGINATION: loop pages until empty.

    items = r.json()
    if not items: break
    all_items.extend(items); page += 1
```

python-backend-fresher/type-hints-basics.direct: Optional[X] means 'X or None' — a value that might be absent (e.g., a user not found). Union[X, Y] means 'X or Y' — a value of one of several types (e.g., an id that's int or str). Since Python 3.10, you write these with the pipe: X | None and X | Y, which are shorter and preferred. Use Optional when a value can be missing (a nullable field, a maybe-not-found result), and Union when a value can legitimately be one of several types. mypy checks that you handle None (narrow the type) and that operations are valid for all members of a union.

ruby-backend-fresher/active-record-basic.direct: The N+1 problem is when you fetch N records and then trigger one extra query per record to load an association — 1 query for the posts plus N queries for each post's comments (N+1 total), which is slow. It happens when you call an association method on each record in a loop (post.comments inside posts.each). You fix it with eager loading: Post.includes(:comments) loads all the comments in one extra query upfront (or one JOIN), so iterating no longer fires per-row queries. Spot it in the log as repeated SELECTs on the associated table.

ruby-backend-fresher/authentication-basi.direct: Token auth is authenticating with a token the client sends on each request (usually in the Authorization header: Authorization: Bearer <token>), instead of a session cookie. It's used for APIs and SPAs where the client isn't a browser with cookies — mobile apps, other services, a React front end. On login the server issues a token (random, stored hashed in the DB, or a signed JWT), the client stores it and sends it on each request, and the server verifies it to find the user. It's stateless (no session to look up) and works cross-origin, unlike cookie sessions.
ruby-backend-fresher/authentication-basi.spoken: Token authentication is authenticating with a token the client sends on each request — usually in the Authorization header as Authorization Bearer token — instead of a session cookie. It's used for APIs and SPAs where the client isn't a browser with cookies: mobile apps, other services, a React front end. On login the server issues a token, a random secret stored hashed in the database or a signed JWT, the client stores it and sends it on each request, and the server verifies it to find the user. It's stateless, with no session record to look up, and works cross-origin, unlike cookie sessions which are tied to a single domain. A common mistake is sending the token in a query param, because that gets logged, instead of the Authorization header, or storing tokens in localStorage, where XSS can steal them, or storing the token in the database in plaintext, when you should store a hash like a password.

Token auth is authenticating with a token the client sends on each request (usually in the Authorization header: Authorization: Bearer <token>), instead of a session cookie.

It's used for APIs and SPAs where the client isn't a browser with cookies — mobile apps, other services, a React front end.

On login the server issues a token (random, stored hashed in the DB, or a signed JWT), the client stores it and sends it on each request, and the server verifies it to find the user. It's stateless (no session to look up) and works cross-origin, unlike cookie sessions.

```ruby
# Issue a token on login
class Api::SessionsController < ApplicationController
  def create
    user = User.authenticate(params[:email], params[:password])
    if user
      token = SecureRandom.hex(32)                # or a signed JWT
      user.update(auth_token: Digest::SHA256.hexdigest(token))  # store hashed!
      render json: { token: token }                # send to client
    else
      render json: { error: 'invalid' }, status: :unauthorized
    end
  end
end

# Verify on each request (a before_action)
class ApiController < ApplicationController
  before_action :authenticate_token!

  def authenticate_token!
    token = request.headers['Authorization']&.sub('Bearer ', '')
    user = User.find_by(auth_token: Digest::SHA256.hexdigest(token))
    render json: { error: 'unauthorized' }, status: :unauthorized unless user
    @current_user = user
  end
end
```

ruby-backend-fresher/blocks-and-iterator.direct: A block is an unnamed chunk of code you pass to a method, written with braces {} (one-liners) or do/end (multi-line): [1,2,3].each { |n| puts n }. A method calls the block with yield — yield runs the block, and yield(value) passes a value to it. The block is what makes iterators like each and map work: the method does the looping, and yield hands each element to the block you provide. You can check block_given? before yielding, and a block turns a method into a custom iterator without writing the loop yourself.

A common mistake is forgetting block given, because yield with no block raises LocalJumpError, and confusing yield, which calls the block, with return, which exits the method.

ruby-backend-fresher/blocks-and-iterator.direct: Method chaining is calling one method after another on the same result, each returning the receiver (or a new value) so the next method applies: 'hello'.upcase.reverse gives 'OLLEH' (upcase returns a new string, reverse is called on it). It works when each method returns the object the next method needs — strings return strings, arrays return arrays, ActiveRecord relations return relations (where(...).order(...).limit(...)). The chain reads left to right as a pipeline, and it's idiomatic Ruby because most methods return a new value rather than mutating in place (use ! methods like map! to mutate).

ruby-backend-fresher/blocks-and-iterator.direct: Enumerable is a module mixed into Array and Hash (and others) that gives you a large set of iteration methods: each (iterate), map (transform to a new array), select (keep matching), reject (drop matching), reduce (fold to one value), find (first match), sort, group_by, flat_map. You include Enumerable in your own class and define each, and you get all of them for free. They're the heart of Ruby's collection-processing style — short, expressive chains that replace most loops.

You include Enumerable in your own class and define each, and you get all of them for free. They're the heart of Ruby's collection-processing style — short, expressive chains like map then select then reduce that replace most explicit loops and read like a pipeline of what you want, not how to loop. A common mistake is using each when map or select or reduce expresses the intent better and more briefly, and not knowing reduce's accumulator, the running value, where you pass the initial value.

```ruby
nums.select { |n| n.even? }               # [2, 4] (keep matching)
nums.reject { |n| n.even? }               # [1, 3, 5] (drop matching)
nums.reduce(0) { |sum, n| sum + n }       # 15 (fold to one value)
nums.find { |n| n > 3 }                   # 4 (first match)
nums.group_by { |n| n.even? }            # {true=>[2,4], false=>[1,3,5]}
nums.flat_map { |n| [n, n * 10] }         # [1,10,2,20,3,30,4,40,5,50]

# Include in your own class — define each, get the rest:
class Deck
  include Enumerable
  def initialize; @cards = (1..52).to_a; end
  def each(&b); @cards.each(&b); end   # now map/select/sort all work
end
```

ruby-backend-fresher/blocks-and-iterator.direct: The &:sym shorthand converts a symbol to a block that calls that method on each element: names.map(&:upcase) is names.map { |n| n.upcase }. The & before a symbol (or any object with to_proc) turns it into a block, and the symbol's to_proc returns a proc that sends the method to its argument. It's a concise idiom for 'call this method on each item' — common with map, select, sort_by — and reads cleanly once you know it. It's not magic: &:upcase is just shorthand for the block { |x| x.upcase }.
ruby-backend-fresher/blocks-and-iterator.spoken: The ampersand-colon shorthand converts a symbol to a block that calls that method on each element: names dot map ampersand colon upcase is the same as names dot map with n n dot upcase. It's a concise idiom for call this method on each item — common with map, select, sort_by, and flat_map — and reads cleanly once you know it. It's not magic: ampersand-colon-upcase is just shorthand for the block that calls upcase on each element. A limitation is that it only works for a single method with no arguments, so you can't pass args this way. A common mistake is not recognizing it as shorthand, because it looks cryptic until you know to_proc.

```ruby
  def self.call(user, cart)
    new(user, cart).call
  end

  def initialize(user, cart)
    @user, @cart = user, cart
  end

    order = nil

      order = Order.create!(user: @user, total: @cart.total)
      @cart.items.each { |item| order.items.create!(item.to_h) }

    end
    OrderMailer.with(order: order).receipt_email.deliver_later  # job
    order
  end
end

    order = PlaceOrder.call(current_user, current_cart)
    if order
      redirect_to order_path(order)
    else

  end
```

```ruby
# Frequency map: count characters

# O(1) lookup: two-sum (find a pair that sums to target)
def two_sum(nums, target)
  seen = {}
  nums.each do |n|
    return [seen[target - n], n] if seen.key?(target - n)
    seen[n] = n
  end
  nil
end

# Two pointers on a sorted array (pair sum)
def two_sorted(nums, target)
  lo, hi = 0, nums.length - 1
  while lo < hi
    s = nums[lo] + nums[hi]
    return [nums[lo], nums[hi]] if s == target
    s < target ? lo += 1 : hi -= 1
  end
end

# Sliding window: max sum of k consecutive
def max_sum(nums, k)
  win = nums.first(k).sum
  best = win
  (k...nums.length).each do |i|
    win += nums[i] - nums[i - k]
    best = [best, win].max
  end
  best
end
```

```ruby
def bubble(arr)
  n = arr.length
  loop do
    swapped = false
    (1...n).each do |i|
      if arr[i - 1] > arr[i]
        arr[i - 1], arr[i] = arr[i], arr[i - 1]
        swapped = true
      end
    end
    break unless swapped
  end
  arr
```

```ruby
# Opposite ends: pair sum on a SORTED array
def pair_sum(nums, target)
  lo, hi = 0, nums.length - 1
  while lo < hi
    s = nums[lo] + nums[hi]
    return [nums[lo], nums[hi]] if s == target
    s < target ? lo += 1 : hi -= 1     # too small -> lo up; too big -> hi down
  end
  nil
end

# Opposite ends: reverse in place
def reverse!(arr)
  lo, hi = 0, arr.length - 1
  while lo < hi
    arr[lo], arr[hi] = arr[hi], arr[lo]
    lo += 1; hi -= 1
  end
  arr
end

# Fast/slow: find the middle of a linked list (or a cycle)
# slow moves 1, fast moves 2; when fast hits the end, slow is at the middle
```

```ruby
# Define a custom exception (inherit from StandardError!)
class PaymentError < StandardError
  attr_reader :order_id
  def initialize(msg, order_id: nil)

def charge(order)
  raise PaymentError.new('card declined', order_id: order.id) if order.failed?
end

begin
  charge(order)
rescue PaymentError => e
  logger.error("payment failed for #{e.order_id}: #{e.message}")
  # handler acts on the REAL cause, not a generic StandardError
end

# Keep it under StandardError (NOT Exception) so default rescue catches it.
```

mistakes: Rescuing Exception (catches SystemExit/signals), or not knowing bare rescue catches StandardError (not Exception).
ruby-backend-fresher/error-handling-basi.direct: All exceptions descend from Exception. Under it: StandardError (the normal app errors you rescue — RuntimeError, ArgumentError, NoMethodError, TypeError) and other branches (SystemExit for exit, SignalException for signals, NoMemoryError). The rule: rescue StandardError or below; don't rescue Exception (it catches SystemExit and signals). A bare rescue catches StandardError (the default), which is most app errors. When you define a custom exception, inherit from StandardError (or a specific one like StandardError) so it's caught by the default rescue. Knowing the hierarchy tells you what a rescue will and won't catch.

mistakes: Unguarded retry (infinite loop) or retrying a deterministic bug (it fails the same way forever).
ruby-backend-fresher/error-handling-basi.direct: retry (inside a rescue) re-runs the begin block from the top, used to retry a transient failure (a flaky network call). You must guard it with a counter so you don't retry forever: attempt = 0; begin; attempt += 1; api.call; rescue NetworkError => e; raise if attempt >= 3; sleep(2 ** attempt); retry; end. This retries up to N times with exponential backoff (sleep 1, 2, 4...) before giving up and re-raising. retry is for transient, recoverable errors only; don't retry a bug (it'll fail the same way forever). The gem 'retryable' wraps this, but the hand-rolled version shows you understand backoff.
ruby-backend-fresher/error-handling-basi.spoken: retry, inside a rescue, re-runs the begin block from the top, used to retry a transient failure like a flaky network call. You must guard it with a counter so you don't retry forever: set attempt to zero, begin, increment attempt, call the API, rescue NetworkError, raise if attempt is at least three, sleep with exponential backoff, and retry. This retries up to N times with exponential backoff — sleep 1, then 2, then 4 — before giving up and re-raising. retry is for transient, recoverable errors only; don't retry a bug because it'll fail the same way forever and you'll loop until the process dies. The gem retryable wraps this, but the hand-rolled version shows you understand backoff. A common mistake is unguarded retry, which loops forever, and retrying a deterministic bug, which fails the same way every time.

```ruby
def call_with_retry(api, max_attempts: 3)
  attempt = 0
  begin
    attempt += 1
    api.call                       # may raise NetworkError
  rescue NetworkError => e
    raise if attempt >= max_attempts   # give up after N tries
    sleep(2 ** (attempt - 1))           # 1s, 2s, 4s (exponential backoff)
    retry                              # re-run the begin block
  end
end

# Use it for TRANSIENT failures only:
#   - network timeouts
#   - rate-limited (429) API
#   - a brief infra blip
# DON'T retry a bug (ArgumentError) — it fails the same way every time.

# The 'retryable' gem wraps this, but the hand-rolled version shows backoff.
```

ruby-backend-fresher/git-and-bundler-bas.direct: SemVer is a version scheme MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (e.g. 2.4.1): increment MAJOR for a breaking change (an API that's no longer compatible), MINOR for a new backward-compatible feature, PATCH for a backward-compatible bug fix. The promise: a user can update to a higher MINOR or PATCH safely (no breakage), but a MAJOR bump means they must check for breaking changes. Bundler's '~> 2.4' (>= 2.4, < 3.0) trusts this — it allows MINOR/PATCH updates but blocks a MAJOR. Knowing SemVer tells you when a gem update is safe (same MAJOR) and when to read the changelog (MAJOR bumped).

ruby-backend-fresher/oop-and-design-basi.direct: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) and SOLID are design principles for changeable code. In Ruby: DRY means extract a repeated method or validation to one place; SOLID shows up as small classes with one responsibility (SRP), modules for sharing behavior (over deep inheritance), and dependency injection (pass the logger in, don't hardcode it). The Ruby twist: duck typing and modules let you satisfy LSP/ISP/DIP lightly — you don't need formal interfaces; if two objects respond to the same methods, they're interchangeable. Apply the principles pragmatically: extract real duplication, keep classes focused, prefer modules over inheritance, and inject dependencies — but don't over-engineer simple code.

ruby-backend-fresher/rest-api-basics/aut.direct: For an API (no sessions/cookies), the common patterns: token auth (the client sends a header Authorization: Bearer <token>; the server looks up the user by the token), and JWT (a signed token encoding the user id + expiry; the server verifies the signature). In Rails: a token is often a column on User (user.auth_token) or a separate API key table; a before_action checks it (authenticate_user! reads the header, sets @current_user). Devise + devise-jwt add JWT to the full-stack Devise flow. For stateless APIs, JWT/token avoids server sessions; for a first-party SPA, a secure cookie + same-site may be simpler. Always use HTTPS so the token isn't sniffed, and never log tokens.

```ruby
# Client sends a header:  Authorization: Bearer <token>

# app/controllers/api_controller.rb
module Api
  class ApiController < ApplicationController
    before_action :authenticate_user!   # protect all API controllers

    private
    def authenticate_user!
      token = request.headers['Authorization'].to_s.sub('Bearer ', '')
      @current_user = User.find_by(auth_token: token)
      render json: { error: 'unauthorized' }, status: :unauthorized unless @current_user
    end

    def current_user; @current_user; end
  end
end

# An API controller inheriting it is protected:
module Api
  class PostsController < ApiController
    def index
      render json: current_user.posts   # @current_user is set
    end
  end
end
```

```ruby
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]

nums.map { |n| n * 2 }        # [2, 4, 6, 8]   (new array)
nums.select { |n| n.even? }   # [2, 4]         (keep matches)
nums.reject { |n| n.even? }  # [1, 3]         (drop matches)
nums.find { |n| n > 2 }       # 3              (first match; nil if none)
nums.reduce(0) { |s, n| s + n } # 10          (fold to one value)
nums.sort                    # [1, 2, 3, 4]
nums.sort_by { |n| -n }       # [4, 3, 2, 1]   (sort by key)
nums.each { |n| puts n }     # prints 1..4; returns original (not a new array)
nums.uniq                    # dedupe
nums.include?(3)             # true (membership)
nums.flatten                 # [[1,2],[3]] -> [1,2,3]

# map vs each: map returns a NEW array; each returns the ORIGINAL.
[1,2,3].each { |n| n * 10 }  # returns [1,2,3]  (NOT [10,20,30])
[1,2,3].map  { |n| n * 10 }  # returns [10,20,30]

# Bang versions mutate in place:
a = [1,2,3]; a.map! { |n| n*10 }; a  # [10,20,30]

# Composition (read left to right):
nums.select { |n| n.even? }.map { |n| n * 10 }  # [20, 40]
```

ruby-backend-fresher/ruby-language-basic.direct: Arrays and Hashes are Ruby's core collections. An Array is an ordered, integer-indexed list: [1, 2, 3]; a[0] == 1; a << 4 appends; a.each, a.map, a[0..1] (slice). A Hash is a key-value map: {name: 'Ada', age: 30}; h[:name] == 'Ada'; h[:city] = 'NYC' adds. ruby-backend-fresher/ruby-language-basic.direct: Conditionals: if/elsif/else/end (if x > 0 ... elsif x == 0 ... else ... end), unless (unless done ... end — opposite of if), and the modifier form (puts 'hi' if x > 0). case/when for multi-way (case x; when 1..5 then 'small'; when String then 'str'; else 'other'; end). Loops: while (while i < 10 ... i += 1; end), until (until done ... end), and the idiomatic iterators (10.times { |i| ... }, array.each { |x| ... }, 1.upto(5) { |n| ... }).   include Enumerable
```ruby
  def initialize(*items); @items = items; end
  def each(&b); @items.each(&b); end   # REQUIRED by Enumerable
end

b.select { |n| n > 1 }   # [2, 3]
b.reduce(:+)            # 6
b.sort                  # [1, 2, 3]
b.count                 # 3
b.include?(2)          # true

class Length
  include Comparable
  attr_reader :m
  def initialize(m); @m = m; end
  def <=>(other); @m <=> other.m; end   # REQUIRED by Comparable
end

a > b2                  # false
a == Length.new(2)      # true
a.between?(b2, b2)      # false
```

```ruby
class UsersController < ApplicationController

  # The whitelist (the boundary):
  def user_params

    params.require(:user).permit(:name, :email, :age)

end

# What gets through:
#   { user: { name:, email:, age:, admin: 1 } }
#   -> user_params returns { name:, email:, age: }  (admin DROPPED)

# require raises if the top key is missing:
#   params.require(:user)  ->  ActionController::ParameterMissing if no :user

# Nested attributes:

#   -> { name:, address: { city:, zip: } }

# Permit all of a sub-hash (careful!):
```

```ruby
# test/dev: :inline (run now) or :async (in-process)

# Define a job (inherits from ApplicationJob)
class MailJob < ApplicationJob

  def perform(user)                       # the work to do

  end
end

MailJob.set(wait: 5.minutes).perform_later(user)   # delayed

# Switching backends (the abstraction): change the adapter line only.
#   :sidekiq (fast, Redis, threaded) -- common in prod
#   :resque, :delayed_job           -- other backends
#   :inline (run synchronously), :async (in-process) -- test/dev
```

mistakes: Retrying non-idempotent jobs (double charges/emails) — make jobs idempotent; or retry: 0 for bad-arg errors.
ruby-backend-fresher/sidekiq-intro/job-r.direct: Sidekiq retries failed jobs automatically. By default a job retries 25 times with exponential backoff (15s, 30s, 60s, ... up to ~21 days), then moves to the dead set (morgue). You configure: `sidekiq_options retry: 5` (5 retries) or `retry: 0` (no retries) or `retry: 600`. The job's perform is wrapped in your sidekiq_retries_exhausted block for final handling. Failures are usually network/timeout blips, so retrying with backoff often self-heals. Dead jobs are viewable in the Sidekiq Web UI (/sidekiq/retries, /sidekiq/morgue) and can be retried manually. To make a job idempotent (safe to retry), ensure performing it twice has the same effect as once (check before create; use unique job ids). Don't retry non-retryable errors (a bad arg) — rescue them and re-raise with a 'skip' class, or set retry: 0 for that job.

ruby-backend-fresher/sidekiq-intro/why-b.direct: Background jobs move slow work out of the request cycle so the user gets a fast response. Sending an email (SMTP can take seconds), generating a PDF, calling a slow API, importing a CSV — if done in the controller, the user waits and the request can time out. Instead, enqueue a job (MailJob.perform_later(user), returns in ~1ms) and a worker does the slow work later. Benefits: fast responses (happy users), reliability (jobs retry on failure — a network blip doesn't lose the email), scalability (workers scale independently of web), and scheduling (send the email at 9am tomorrow). The cost: a queue store (Redis), job infrastructure, and the need for idempotency. Rule of thumb: if work takes >100ms or calls an external service, push it to a job. Sidekiq is the common backend.

ruby-backend-fresher/sql-database-basics.direct: Migrations are versioned, Ruby files that change the DB schema over time. `rails g migration CreateUsers name:string age:integer` makes a file with `create_table :users do |t| t.string :name; t.integer :age; t.timestamps end`. Run `rails db:migrate` to apply; the schema is recorded in db/schema.rb (the current state). Migrations let you evolve the schema safely (not by hand-editing the DB): they're ordered (timestamps), reversible (db:rollback), and shareable (committed to git so every dev has the same schema). Why not just run SQL? Because migrations are tracked (schema_migrations table), so they run once and in order on every environment; you can roll back; and they work across adapters (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite). Create a table, add/remove columns, add indexes (t.index / add_index for query speed), add references (t.references :user = foreign key). Never edit a migration that's been pushed — make a new one (otherwise other devs' DBs diverge).

```ruby
# Generate a migration (creates a versioned file in db/migrate/)
# rails g migration CreateUsers name:string age:integer
class CreateUsers < ActiveRecord::Migration[7.0]
  def change                       # reversible (self.up / self.down auto-derived)
    create_table :users do |t|
      t.string :name
      t.integer :age
      t.references :account          # foreign key (account_id)
      t.timestamps                   # created_at, updated_at
    end
    add_index :users, :email, unique: true   # speed up lookups
  end
end

# Apply it (runs once; recorded in schema_migrations table):
#   rails db:migrate
# Roll back the last one:
#   rails db:rollback
# Current schema is recorded in db/schema.rb (the source of truth for state).

# Common migration methods:
#   add_column    :users, :role, :string
#   remove_column :users, :age
#   rename_column :users, :name, :full_name
#   add_index     :users, :email, unique: true
#   add_reference :posts, :user, foreign_key: true
#   change_column :users, :age, :integer, default: 0

# They're reversible (db:rollback) and work across adapters (PG/MySQL/SQLite).
# Shareable: commit migrations to git; every dev runs db:migrate to catch up.

# NEVER edit a migration that's been pushed to git/merged.
#   (other devs already ran it -> their schema_migrations won't match.)
#   Make a NEW migration to change it.

# Schema loading vs migrating:
#   db:migrate   -> run migrations in order (use in prod)
#   db:schema:load -> load db/schema.rb directly (fresh DB)
# db/schema.rb is the current state; don't hand-edit it either.
```

mistakes: Looping over records and touching an association without includes (1 query per record).
ruby-backend-fresher/sql-database-basics.direct: N+1: you fetch N records, then trigger 1 query PER record for an association, instead of 1 query for all. `User.all.each { |u| u.posts.count }` runs 1 query for users, then 1 PER user for posts count = N+1 queries. With 100 users that's 101 queries instead of 2. Fix: eager-load with `includes` — `User.all.includes(:posts)` loads posts in 1-2 queries (a JOIN or a second IN query) for ALL users. Detect N+1: the bullet gem warns in dev/test, or watch the log for many identical queries in a loop. Variants: `preload` (2 queries, no join — good when you don't filter on the association), `eager_load` (a JOIN — when you WHERE on the association), `includes` (Rails picks). For counts alone, counter caches (`posts_count`) avoid the query. The cost of N+1: many small queries are far slower than one batched query, especially over the network. Rule: if you loop and touch an association, eager-load it.

Types: INNER JOIN (rows that match in both), LEFT JOIN (all left rows; NULLs where right doesn't match), RIGHT/FULL (less common).
```ruby
# SELECT * FROM users
User.all                              # relation (lazy; SQL runs when forced)

# SELECT id, name FROM users  (lean rows -> less memory)
User.select(:id, :name)
User.select('id, name, age')

# WHERE (parameterized/safe):
User.where(active: true)              # WHERE active = TRUE
User.where('age > ?', 18)             # WHERE age > 18 (bound)

# ORDER / LIMIT / OFFSET:
User.order(created_at: :desc).limit(10).offset(20)

# Chain (lazy relation): SQL runs when you force it
rel = User.where(active: true).order(:name)   # no SQL yet
rel.to_a          # -> SELECT ... (runs now)
rel.each { ... }  # -> runs
rel.count         # -> SELECT COUNT(*)

# Get values (not objects) -- fast for one column:
User.pluck(:email)          # ['a@x', 'b@y', ...]  (SELECT email)
User.pluck(:id, :name)      # [[1,'Al'], [2,'Bo'], ...]
User.distinct.pluck(:role)  # unique roles

# Lookups:
User.find(1)                # by primary key (raises if missing)
User.find_by(name: 'Al')    # first match (nil if none)
User.exists?(id: 1)         # SELECT 1 ... LIMIT 1 (boolean)

# Aggregates:
User.count                  # SELECT COUNT(*)
User.minimum(:age)
User.group(:role).count     # { 'admin' => 2, 'user' => 50 }

# DON'T load a big table into memory:
#   User.all.to_a  # loads EVERYTHING
# Stream in batches instead:
User.find_each(batch_size: 1000) { |u| do_stuff(u) }   # SELECT ... LIMIT 1000 OFFSET ...

# Summary: select (columns), where (filter, safe), order/limit, pluck (values),
#          lazy chaining, find_each for big tables.
```

```ruby
end
```

```ruby
require 'rails_helper'
```

ruby-backend-fresher/testing-basics/unit.direct: Unit tests check one piece in isolation (a method, a model's validation): `UserTest` asserts `User.new(name: '').valid?` is false — fast, no DB/HTTP, pinpoint failures. Integration tests check multiple parts working together: a request spec hits `post '/users', params: ...` and asserts the DB changed and the response is 302 — slower (full stack: routing, controller, model, DB, views) but catches wiring bugs unit tests miss. Rails layers: model tests (unit), controller/request tests (integration), system tests (full browser, JS). Pyramid: many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration, very few system (slow). Unit tests tell you WHAT broke precisely; integration tests tell you the WIRING works. Both matter: unit for fast feedback on logic, integration for confidence the pieces connect. Don't write only integration (slow, hard to localize) or only unit (misses wiring); balance them.

```ruby
# spec/requests/users_spec.rb (request spec)
RSpec.describe 'Users', type: :request do
  it 'creates a user' do
    post '/users', params: { user: { name: 'Al' } }
    expect(response).to have_http_status(:found)   # 302 redirect
    expect(User.count).to eq(1)                    # DB changed

  end
end

class UsersTest < ActionDispatch::SystemTestCase
  test 'create via form' do
    visit '/users/new'
    fill_in 'Name', with: 'Al'
    click_on 'Create'
    assert_text 'Al'
  end
end
```

mistakes: Giving vague, general answers ('I'm a great team player') with no specific past example — missing the STAR structure and the past-behavior premise.
shared/behavioral/all.direct: A behavioral interview is a structured interview that asks a candidate to describe past behavior in specific situations to predict future performance — the premise (grounded in industrial psychology) that past behavior is the best predictor of future behavior. Every company uses it because technical skills alone don't determine success: how a candidate handled conflict, failure, ambiguity, or a tight deadline in the past reveals how they'll collaborate, communicate, and lead on the team. The structured format (STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result) keeps answers specific and comparable across candidates, reducing bias.
shared/behavioral/all.spoken: A behavioral interview is a structured interview that asks you to describe past behavior in specific situations to predict future performance — the premise, grounded in industrial psychology, that past behavior is the best predictor of future behavior. Every company uses it because technical skills alone don't determine success: how you handled conflict, failure, ambiguity, or a tight deadline in the past reveals how you'll collaborate and lead on the team. The structured format is STAR — Situation, Task, Action, Result — which keeps answers specific and comparable and reduces bias. The way I answer is with a specific past instance, not a hypothetical, and I keep the Action in the first person — what I specifically did, not what the team did — and I quantify the Result where I can. I prepare specific stories across the themes that come up: conflict, failure, ambiguity, a tight deadline, leadership, and a time I disagreed with a decision. The honest tension is preparation versus authenticity — rehearsed generic answers score poorly because the interviewer hears a script, while fully unprepared answers ramble, so the resolution is to prepare the bones of five to seven stories and deliver them conversationally. And the thing I stress is that a real failure with a genuine lesson is far stronger than a fake weakness like 'I work too hard' — interviewers are trained to spot that, and it signals low self-awareness, which is the opposite of what the round tests.

mistakes: Saying the virtual DOM is always faster than direct DOM manipulation — it isn't, but it makes complex apps easier to reason about and generally good enough
shared/frontend/intermediate.direct: React's reconciliation is its algorithm for determining what changed in the UI and efficiently updating the real DOM. It maintains a virtual DOM — a lightweight JS object tree — and when state/props change, it creates a new virtual DOM tree, diffs it against the previous one using the reconciler, and only applies the minimum set of real DOM changes needed. This diffing is O(n) rather than O(n³) because React makes two assumptions: elements of different types produce different trees, and the key prop identifies stable list elements across renders.
shared/frontend/intermediate.spoken: The virtual DOM is React's scratchpad. Instead of touching the real DOM every time something changes — which is slow because the browser has to recalculate layout and paint — React builds a tree of plain JavaScript objects describing what the UI should look like. When something changes, React builds a new tree, compares it to the old one (the diff), and only updates the real DOM for what actually changed. The comparison algorithm is called reconciliation.
shared/frontend/intermediate.deep:
**The two heuristics that make reconciliation O(n):**

1. **Different element types = tear down and rebuild**: If a `<div>` becomes a `<section>`, React doesn't try to convert it — it destroys the entire subtree and creates a fresh one. This is why conditionally rendering `<ComponentA />` vs `<ComponentB />` at the same position causes full unmount/remount.

2. **Keys identify stable list elements**: When rendering lists, `key` tells React which element is which across renders. Without keys (or with index keys), React matches elements by position — moving an item causes all subsequent items to re-render. With stable, unique keys, React can track moves and only update what actually changed.

```jsx
// Bad — using index as key causes unnecessary re-renders on reorder/filter
{items.map((item, index) => <Item key={index} {...item} />)}

// Good — stable unique key
{items.map(item => <Item key={item.id} {...item} />)}
```

**React Fiber (React 16+ reconciler):**

The original reconciler (called Stack) was synchronous and couldn't be interrupted. If a large component tree was rendering, the browser would freeze until it finished.

Fiber broke the rendering work into small units (fibers) that can be paused, resumed, aborted, and reused. This enables:
- Concurrent rendering (React 18+): render without blocking the UI thread
- Suspense: pause rendering while data loads
- Transitions (startTransition): mark updates as non-urgent, let urgent updates interrupt them

**The render phases:**

Reconciliation has two phases:
1. **Render phase (pure, interruptible)**: React calls your components, computes what changed, builds the new fiber tree. No DOM mutations yet.
2. **Commit phase (synchronous, uninterruptible)**: React applies the DOM changes. Runs effects. Cannot be paused.

This is why effects that touch the DOM go in `useLayoutEffect` (runs synchronously after DOM mutations, before paint) while most side effects go in `useEffect` (runs after paint).

mistakes: Forgetting that LEFT JOIN includes rows with no match (nulls in the right side). Also, doing a JOIN without an ON clause creates a cartesian product — millions of rows accidentally.
shared/tools/beginner.direct: JOINs combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column. INNER JOIN returns only matching rows from both tables. LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matching rows from the right (nulls where no match). RIGHT JOIN is the mirror of LEFT. FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, with nulls where there's no match. In practice, you'll use INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN 95% of the time.
shared/tools/beginner.spoken:
Think of two guest lists for a party: Table A (customers) and Table B (orders). A JOIN is asking 'which guests appear on both lists, or just one?'

**INNER JOIN** — 'Show me only customers who have placed orders.'
If a customer has no orders, they don't appear. If an order has no matching customer (orphaned data), it doesn't appear. Only the overlap.

In SQL you'd select the customer name and order total from `customers` inner joined to `orders` on matching customer ids—only rows that exist in both tables show up.

**LEFT JOIN** — 'Show me ALL customers, and their orders if they have any.'
Every customer appears even if they've never ordered. For customers with no orders, the order columns show NULL. This is the most common JOIN for reports.

With a left join, the same kind of select still pairs `customers` and `orders` on id, but every customer row is kept and the order columns are null when there is no matching order.

**RIGHT JOIN** — Mirror of LEFT JOIN. All rows from the right table, matching rows from the left. Rarely used — you can always rewrite as a LEFT JOIN by swapping table positions.

**FULL OUTER JOIN** — 'Show me everything — all customers and all orders, matched where possible.'
Customers without orders get NULLs in order columns. Orders without matching customers get NULLs in customer columns. Useful for finding data mismatches.

The practical rule: **start with LEFT JOIN** when you want 'all of X and their related Y if it exists'. Use INNER JOIN when you only care about rows that have matches in both tables.

probes.text: What is the difference between WHERE and ON in a JOIN?
How would you find customers who have never placed an order?
What is a self-join and when would you use it?
Draw the Venn diagram mentally and explain it. Mention performance: JOINs on indexed columns are fast, JOINs on unindexed columns can be catastrophic for large tables.

Can you write JOINs correctly and — more importantly — choose the right type based on the business question? 'Show me all customers and their orders' vs 'Show me customers who have orders' requires different JOINs.

shared/tools/beginner.codeExample:
-- Sample tables:
-- customers: id, name, email
-- orders: id, customer_id, total, order_date

-- INNER JOIN: Customers who have ordered
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count, SUM(o.total) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.name;

-- LEFT JOIN: ALL customers, even those who never ordered
SELECT c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.name;

-- LEFT JOIN to find customers WITHOUT orders
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;  -- only rows where no match exists

-- FULL OUTER JOIN: Find mismatched data
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
FULL OUTER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.id IS NULL OR o.customer_id IS NULL;

mistakes: Saying acks=all is always the right answer — it kills throughput for use cases like log aggregation
shared/tools/intermediate.direct: Kafka producers have three ack modes: acks=0 (fire-and-forget, no confirmation), acks=1 (leader partition confirms, replicas may lag), and acks=all (all in-sync replicas confirm before returning). For financial transactions or critical data, use acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2. For high-throughput metrics pipelines where occasional loss is acceptable, acks=0 maximizes throughput.
shared/tools/intermediate.spoken:
Kafka producer acks are about the **durability vs throughput trade-off**. `acks=0` is fire and forget — maximum throughput but zero guarantee the broker even received the record. `acks=1` means the partition leader confirms the write, which covers most cases, but if the leader crashes before replicating you lose that record. `acks=all` waits for every in-sync replica to confirm — this is the only mode I'd use for anything financial.

The critical detail most people miss is that `acks=all` alone isn't enough. You need `min.insync.replicas=2` on the topic, otherwise "all" can be satisfied by just the leader. The production setup I use is `replication.factor=3`, `min.insync.replicas=2`, `acks=all`, plus `enable.idempotence=true` to prevent duplicates from retries. That gives you durable, deduplicated writes that tolerate one broker failure.

For a metrics pipeline I'd use `acks=0` — losing a few data points per million doesn't matter, and you get 2-3x the throughput.
